The English spelling 'p' often corresponds to [pf] in German.
Use your existing knowledge of language to understand meanings of unfamiliar words and to identify word families.
Use the modal verb 'sollen' to mean ‘should', 'be supposed to’ in expectations or obligations, and for probability.
Use the modal verb 'müssen' to mean ‘must’ and the modal verb 'dürfen' to mean ‘may', 'allowed’.
keywords: verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want
modal verb meaning 'should, be supposed to, ought', used to express obligation, expectation or probability

5564.name: Who is supposed to do what? Modal verbs, two-verb structures, question words
5564.outcome: I can emphasise different parts of sentences by using inversion (word order two), and understand how to form sentences that use two verbs.
points: Both sounds are pronounced in the sound-symbol correspondence [kn]. This is different from English.
The modal verb 'sollen' expresses obligation or probability and requires a 2nd verb in the infinitive at the end.
Use inversion (word order two) to emphasise a particular element. The verb is always the 2nd idea in the sentence.
Open (wh) questions use inversion (word order two). For example: 'Wann soll ich die Tickets kaufen?'.
Use a comma before 'zu' in two-verb structures that don't involve a modal verb, e.g., 'Er hofft, das Buch zu lesen.'
keywords: pronounced as in 'Knie'; both sounds are pronounced, unlike the silent 'k' in English
modal verb meaning 'should, be supposed to, ought', used to express obligation, expectation or probability
inverts the subject and verb in a sentence
word meaning 'to', used with a preceding comma to form two-verb sentences in German that do not involve a modal verb

5565.name: What you want to and will do: future tense singular (will) vs 'will' (want to)
5565.outcome: I understand how to form the future tense using 'werden', and I can use context to decipher words that have more than one meaning.
points: Regular practice of sound-symbol correspondences helps to improve fluency.
Some German words have multiple meanings. Context helps you work out which meaning is intended.
The present tense of 'werden' with an infinitive at sentence end forms the future, meaning ‘will do’ or ‘going to do’.
'Werden' is irregular. The 'ich' form of 'werden' is 'werde', 'du' form 'wirst', 'sie, er, es' form 'wird'.
The German 'will' comes from 'wollen' and means 'want'. Do not confuse this with the future tense.
keywords: tense used to refer to future time, e.g., 'I will do'

5566.name: Future plans: future tense 'werden' + infinitive vs 'planen' + 'zu' + infinitive
5566.outcome: I can form different two-verb structures to discuss future plans, and can broaden my vocabulary by spotting connections between German nouns and verbs.
points: In two-verb structures, the 2nd verb is in the infinitive, at the end of the sentence.
In two-verb structures, most verbs add 'zu' before the infinitive verb.
A comma separates the verb phrases in two-verb structures, e.g., 'Ich plane, Gemüse zu essen'.
Future tense sentences with 'werden', like modal sentences, do not require 'zu' before the infinitive.
keywords: part of the verb that appears in all forms
sentence made up of two verb phrases
word meaning 'to', used with a preceding comma to form two-verb sentences in German that do not involve a modal verb

5567.name: A house move: adjective endings with definite articles (accusative)
5567.outcome: I can describe the features and contents of a house using definite articles and nominative and accusative adjective endings.
points: The sound-symbol correspondences [eu] and [äu] have the same sound, which is different from [au].
Cognates help you understand new words more quickly, since they look or sound similar to words in your own language.
It’s important to be aware of false friends - words that are similar in two languages but have different meanings.
German adjectives take endings before a noun — you need to know the noun’s gender and case to get them right.
The accusative case is used for the direct object, after most verbs and some prepositions.
keywords: form(s) used for the object or 'receiver' of the action of the verb
a word that looks or sounds similar in two languages, but does not share the same meaning

5568.name: A new home and new neighbours: word patterns and word order
5568.outcome: I can use a growing vocabulary to talk about a new home and new neighbours, varying word order to emphasise specific ideas in my responses to questions.
points: Knowing key word patterns helps us understand words more quickly and recall them more easily.
Add 'Haupt-' to nouns to mean 'main'. The created noun has the gender of its base noun: 'die Idee' - 'die Hauptidee'.
'Wo' is the question word 'where'; it asks where something is located and is answered in the dative case.
'Wohin' is the question word 'where to'; it asks where something is going and is answered in the accusative case.
Start German sentences with any element (e.g., object, adverb) to emphasise it. The verb stays in 2nd place.
keywords: a prefix added to nouns to mean 'main'
question word asking where something is going and answered in the accusative case
inverts the subject and verb in a sentence

5569.name: A new home: dative adjective endings with definite and indefinite articles
5569.outcome: I can understand and use prepositions with dative articles and adjectives to say where specific things are located.
points: After the verb 'sein', adjectives before nouns have nominative endings, because the noun is the subject of the sentence.
After most other verbs, prenominal adjectives have accusative endings, because the noun is the object of the sentence.
German [v] usually sounds like English and German [f]; to write words correctly their spelling needs to be known.
Some prepositions always require dative endings; e.g., aus; others are only ever used with the accusative, e.g., durch.
The dative adjective ending is -en for singular and plural, definite and indefinite articles.
keywords: -en ending added to all adjectives before the noun in the dative case
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

5570.name: A new neighbourhood: accusative and dative prepositions
5570.outcome: I can use different prepositions to understand and say exactly where things are in my neighbourhood.
points: German [w] sounds like English [v]; German [v] sounds like English [f].
In German words of foreign origin, [v] usually sounds like English [v].
Some German adverbs are adjective + (er)weise, where English adverbs are adjectives + ly, e.g. normalerweise - normally.
The dative case is always used after the prepositions 'aus', 'bei', 'mit', 'nach', 'seit', 'von', and 'zu'.
After 'in, an, auf, vor, neben, hinter', dative is used when talking about location in, but accusative for movement to.
keywords: case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

5571.name: What you did when on Sylt: perfect tense, telling the time: half past the hour
5571.outcome: I can talk about what happened in the past and give the time it happened using ‘halb’ to mean half past.
points: [y] commonly sounds like [ü], e.g., 'typisch'. In English words like 'Yoga' and 'Baby', [y] is pronounced as in English.
Words ending in -ic/-ical in English often end in -isch in German, e.g., 'typisch'.
There are three different ways to say 'you' in German: 'du', 'Sie' and 'man'.
The perfect tense is made up of a part of ‘haben’ or ‘sein’ in the present tense, and a past participle.
Half past the hour is expressed as half to the next hour in German, e.g., 9:30 is ‘halb zehn’.
keywords: 2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'

5572.name: Where you went and where you were: 'in', 'an', 'auf', time with 'vor' and 'nach'
5572.outcome: I can use 'in', 'an', and 'auf' with the accusative and dative to say where I went or was on a past holiday, and I can understand the time past and to the hour.
points: ‘Nach’ means 'past' and ‘vor’ means 'to' the hour when saying the time.
In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, greetings vary by region and time of day.
The accusative is used with 'in', 'an', 'auf' when there is movement to a place, e.g., ‘ich gehe in den Zoo’.
The dative is used with 'in', 'an', 'auf' when the person is at or in a place, e.g., ‘ich bin im Zoo’.
keywords: form(s) used for the object or 'receiver' of the action of the verb
case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

5573.name: A music festival: perfect and imperfect, adjective endings
5573.outcome: I can use adjectives and different tenses to describe experiences at a music festival.
points: The gender of a noun needs to be learnt, together with its meaning, spelling and sound.
Nominative adjective endings are used when the noun is the subject, the person or thing doing the action.
Accusative adjective endings are used when the noun is the direct object, directly receiving the action.
'War', 'hatte' and 'es gab' are imperfect tense verbs used to describe what things were like.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

5575.name: A music festival: perfect and imperfect tenses, question forming
5575.outcome: I can ask and answer questions about a visit to a music event.
points: Plural nouns are formed in different ways, depending on factors such as gender and how the singular form ends.
Ordinal numbers indicate position or order in a list or sequence, e.g., first, second, third; we use them for dates.
Questions are formed by inverting subject and verb; a question word can be added to create an open question.
‘Sie’ with the correct verb form should be used when asking questions in formal situations.
keywords: a naming word for people, places or things
question starting with a wh- word that has more information in the answer than yes/no
tells you the order of something, e.g., 'first', 'second', 'third', and is used with dates

5576.name: Poetry and prose: understanding and creativity
5576.outcome: I can read and identify the main features of a ballad in German, and I can use my language knowledge to transform a short prose text into a ballad.
points: A ballad is a type of poem that tells a story in short, poetic verses.
Ballads combine three elements: narrative (epic), poetic language (lyric) and direct speech or tension (dramatic).
Prose is continuous, written language, as in stories, articles and blogs, without deliberate rhyme or rhythmic pattern.
Poetry uses rhythm, line breaks, and sometimes rhyme to shape meaning and feeling differently.
To turn prose into a ballad, focus on key moments, break sentences into short, rhythmic lines, with or without rhyme.
keywords: a poem or song that tells a story
written or spoken language in its ordinary form, without metrical structure

5577.name: Future plans: 'zu' + infinitive, 'werden' + infinitive
5577.outcome: I can use a variety of vocabulary and a range of two-verb structures to express future plans.
points: Regularly practise reading aloud to improve your fluency and knowledge of sound-symbol correspondences.
We can use the present tense with a future time phrase to refer to future plans, e.g., 'Ich spiele morgen Tennis.'
We can form the future tense in German by using the present tense of 'werden' plus an infinitive.
In two-verb structures, the second verb is in the infinitive at the end of the sentence, preceded by a comma and 'zu'.
There is no 'zu' in two-verb structures using 'werden' or modal verbs (e.g., 'wollen', 'sollen').
keywords: sound-symbol correspondence is the relationship between letters and their sounds
sentence made up of two verb phrases
word meaning 'to', used with a preceding comma to form two-verb sentences in German that do not involve a modal verb

5578.name: Dreams and future goals: 'aus', 'wenn' + word order
5578.outcome: I can use my linguistic knowledge to decipher new words, use 'aus' to say where I am from and use 'wenn' to express my dreams and goals.
points: Some sound-symbol correspondences are written differently, but sound the same as each other, e.g., [eu] and [äu].
Use your previous knowledge to decipher the meaning of new vocabulary, including compound words and large numbers.
'Aus' means 'from' when used with a country or city to describe origins. 'Von' means 'from' with starting points.
Use 'wann' to ask 'when' in a question. Use 'wenn' to say 'when' in a present tense statement.
Depending on the context, 'wenn' can also mean 'if'. It triggers word order 3: 'Ich schwimme im Meer, wenn es warm ist.'
keywords: preposition meaning 'from' when used with a country or city name to describe origin; used with the dative case
conjunction meaning 'if' or 'when' which triggers word order 3
sends the verb to the end

5579.name: What is important to you? Revisit subject and object pronouns
5579.outcome: I can identify and use subject and object pronouns in spoken and written German, in the context of talking about things which are important to me.
points: Nouns are often the subject of a sentence. Sometimes, nouns are replaced by pronouns.
Subject pronouns show the grammatical gender of the subject, e.g., ‘das Lied ist toll’ - ‘es ist toll’.
Object pronouns show the grammatical gender of the object, e.g., ‘ich sehe den Mann’ - ‘ich sehe ihn’.
Use the accusative case with direct object pronouns, e.g., ‘ich sehe ihn’.
keywords: used with prepositions to indicate movement towards someone or something
a pronoun that replaces the object in a sentence
represents the person, people or thing(s) doing the verb e.g. I, we, they

5580.name: Tips for a happy life: read and respond to a text
5580.outcome: I can distinguish between subject, direct object and indirect object pronouns, and read and respond to a longer text.
points: The sound-symbol correspondence [ie] is pronounced as in 'Liebe'.
The sound-symbol correspondence [ei] is pronounced as in 'frei'.
Pronouns replace nouns. Subject pronouns replace the noun doing the action of the verb.
After most verbs, use direct object pronouns (accusative case), e.g., 'Ich habe ihn.'
After certain verbs or prepositions, indirect object pronouns (dative case) are used, e.g., 'Ich helfe ihm'.
keywords: replaces the noun receiving the action of the verb e.g. me, you, it, them
replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, from you, with them; takes the dative case
represents the person, people or thing(s) doing the verb e.g. I, we, they

5099.name: Summer experiences: -ar verbs 1st person present and past
5099.outcome: I can say what I normally do and what I did in the summer.
points: The 1st person singular preterite of -ar verbs ends in '-é'
The 1st person singular present of -ar verbs ends in '-o'
To make a sentence negative we put the negation word 'no' before the verb.
keywords: a verb whose infinitive form ends in -ar
tells the reader the action is happening now
verb tense used to express completed actions in the past e.g. 'I did'

5100.name: Spanish class experiences: -ar verbs 1st person present and past
5100.outcome: I can make predictions about what I am going to do in Spanish class this year, and talk about what I normally do and did at school.
points: We can use the 2-verb future structure 'ir + a + infinitive' to state plans and predictions.
A syllable is a single sound or 'beat' in a word.
The 1st person singular present of -ar verbs ends in '-o'.
The 1st person singular preterite of -ar verbs ends in '-é'.
keywords: tells the reader the action is happening now
verb tense used to express completed actions in the past e.g. 'I did'
a single sound or beat in a word that contains a vowel sound

5101.name: Comparing summer experiences: -ar verbs 1st and 2nd person singular
5101.outcome: I can use the preterite tense to compare my summer experiences with someone else's.
points: The 2nd person singular preterite of -ar verbs ends in (-aste).
The 1st person singular preterite of -ar verbs ends in (-é).
There is no Spanish equivalent for the English auxiliary 'did'.
keywords: preposition meaning 'around', 'along' and 'in' when used before times of the day
word that connects ideas between clauses in a sentence meaning because
verb tense used to express completed actions in the past e.g. 'I did'

5102.name: Questions about the summer holidays: -ar verbs in 2nd person singular
5102.outcome: I can ask and answer questions about summer holidays using the present and preterite tenses.
points: When the SSC sounds [a], [e] and [o] appear together, they are pronounced separately.
The 1st person singular preterite of -ar verbs ends in -é and 2nd person singular preterite in -aste.
The 2nd person singular present of -ar verbs ends in -as.
Question words are used to ask for specific information, e.g. '¿dónde?, '¿cómo?'.
keywords: describes habitual events in the present, e.g. ‘I do’
verb tense used to express completed actions in the past e.g. 'I did'
words used to ask for specific information in a question, e.g. 'what', 'where', 'when'

5103.name: People: 'ser' and 'estar' singular persons
5103.outcome: I can talk about people's traits and states using 'ser' and 'estar'.
points: The weak vowel [u] when next to [a], [e] and [o] becomes a single syllable.
The verb 'ser' means 'to, be, being' and it is used to describe permanent traits.
The verb 'estar' means 'to, be, being' and it is used to describe temporary states/moods.
Adjectives like 'listo' and 'malo' have different meanings depending on which verb is used: 'ser' or 'estar'.
keywords: Spanish verb meaning 'to be, being' used for location and temporary states
verb meaning to be, being for general traits

5104.name: People and places: 'ser' and 'estar' singular and plural persons
5104.outcome: I can describe places and people using a variety of adjectives and the verbs ‘ser’ and ‘estar’.
points: The weak vowel [i] when next to [a], [e] and [o] become a single syllable.
The verb 'ser' means 'to, be, being' and it is used to describe permanent traits.
The verb 'estar' means 'to, be, being' and it is used to describe temporary states/moods.
In Spanish, adjectives must agree with the nouns they accompany in gender and number.
keywords: Spanish verb meaning 'to be, being' used for location and temporary states
verb meaning to be, being for general traits
vowels that are always fully pronounced and don't glide into other sounds; the strong vowels are [a], [e] and [o]

5105.name: News and media: -er verbs in 1st person plural
5105.outcome: I can use -er verbs in 1st person singular (I) and 1st person plural (we) to understand and talk about activities a journalist does.
points: If the stress is on the final syllable of a Spanish word ending in 'n' or 's', there is an accent on the last vowel.
Words ending in others consonants have final syllable stress and no accent, e.g. 'beber'.
Using the surrounding words in a sentence helps to work out the meaning of unfamiliar words.
The 1st person plural (we) ending for present tense -er verbs is -emos. The 1st person singular (I) ending is -o.
keywords: a verb which has an infinitive form ending in -er
form of pronouns and verbs used to refer to 'we'
pronouncing the last syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word

5106.name: News and media: simple present for immediate plans
5106.outcome: I can use the suffix '-idad' to broaden my vocabulary, and the simple present to translate a text into Spanish about immediate plans to respond to a breaking news story.
points: The Spanish suffix '-idad' is like '-ity' in English; use it to change adjectives into nouns, e.g. 'real' - 'realidad'.
All Spanish nouns ending '-idad' are feminine.
Spanish uses the simple present to express immediate plans; instead, English uses the present continuous (-ing).
'Qué' with an accent on the 'e' is the question word 'what'. 'Que' without an accent is a conjunction meaning 'that'.
keywords: verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'
a letter or group of letters added to the end of a word to change its meaning

5108.name: Activities: singular 'hacer' and subject pronouns
5108.outcome: I can use subject pronouns and singular forms of 'hacer' to contrast the activities I do with those you, she, or he does.
points: If the stress is on the final syllable of a word ending in 'n' or 's' or a vowel, there is an accent on the last vowel.
Words ending in other consonants have final syllable stress and no accent, e.g. 'genial'.
'Hacer' means 'to do, make'. It is irregular in its 'I' form only; 'I do, I make' is 'hago'.
'Hacer' combines with many nouns to make common verb-noun phrases, e.g. 'Hago un esfuerzo'.
Subject pronouns add emphasis or clarity in Spanish; they are often used to contrast the actions of different people.
keywords: pronouncing the last syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word
Spanish verb meaning 'to do, doing' or 'to make, making'
I do, part of the verb 'hacer' meaning to do and to make
represents the person, people or thing(s) doing the verb e.g. I, we, they
common pairing of verb and noun, e.g. 'make an effort'

5109.name: Activities: plural 'hacer' and subject pronouns
5109.outcome: I can use subject pronouns and plural forms of ‘hacer’ to contrast activities that ‘we’ or ‘they’ do.
points: Applying the two rules about final syllable stress enables correct use of accents when transcribing.
Listening to familiar language in new contexts and transcribing it deepens vocabulary knowledge.
'Hacer', irregular in its I form ‘hago’, is regular in other forms. We do, make is ‘hacemos’, they do, make is ‘hacen’.
Spanish subject pronouns add emphasis or clarity, e.g. nosotros hacemos los deberes, mientras que ellas hacen deporte.
‘We’ is nosotros for boys/men or mixed gender groups, nosotras for girls/women; ‘they’ also has two forms, ellos, ellas.
keywords: pronouncing the last syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word
Spanish verb meaning 'to do, doing' or 'to make, making'
represents the person, people or thing(s) doing the verb e.g. I, we, they

5110.name: In class and at home: modal verb 'podemos'
5110.outcome: I can use an expanding range of words to talk about everyday activities that I and others can do in class and at home.
points: Listening to words with final and penultimate syllable stress helps to develop the ability to identify the stress.
Making vocabulary links using antonyms or words with related meanings can enhance recall.
The verb 'poder' is a modal verb and means 'to be able to', 'can'.
Most present tense forms of 'poder' have a vowel change in the stem, ('puedo'); 'podemos' (we can) has no vowel change.
The verb 'poder' is always followed by an infinitive, e.g. 'Podemos participar en clase.'
keywords: a word that has the opposite meaning to another word
verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want
pronouncing the second-to-last syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word
modal verb that means to be able to/can

5111.name: In class and at home: modal verb 'debemos'
5111.outcome: I can use modal verbs 'deber' and 'poder' to understand and write about what I and others must and can do in class and at home.
points: Rules about penultimate (syllable) stress tell us if we need to write an accent on the penultimate vowel.
Applying knowledge about syllable stress helps to remember how to say words that we may have forgotten how to pronounce.
'Deber' is a modal verb meaning 'to have to, must'. It is conjugated as a regular -er verb; the 'we' form is 'debemos'.
The verb deber is always followed by an infinitive, e.g. 'Siempre debemos decir la verdad.'
keywords: modal verb that means 'to have to', 'must'
verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want
pronouncing the second-to-last syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word

5112.name: A party: -ir verbs in 1st person plural
5112.outcome: I can use 1st person plural -ir verbs to talk about how we organise a party.
points: Applying knowledge about syllable stress reminds us how to say words that we may have forgotten how to pronounce.
Reading aloud accurately supports our own and others’ vocabulary learning.
We can say we know a verb when we can compose sentences of our own with its different persons.
The verb endings for Spanish -er and -ir verbs are the same for 'I', 'you (singular)', 'she', 'he', 'it' and 'they'.
The 1st person plural ‘we’ ending for -ir verbs is -imos; for -er verbs it is -emos.
keywords: verb whose infinitive form ends in -ir
form of pronouns and verbs used to refer to 'we'
pronouncing one syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word

5113.name: A party: simple present for immediate plans
5113.outcome: I can use present tense verbs to write about preparations for a party.
points: Applying knowledge about syllable stress reminds us how to pronounce words we have not used for some time.
Recalling vocabulary with a partner is very effective, especially if we can support each other with accurate stress.
Conjugated verbs in the present tense have different stress from their infinitives.
Spanish uses the simple present for habitual actions, e.g. 'Siempre hago' - 'I always do'.
Spanish also uses the simple present for today’s immediate plans, e.g. 'Hoy hago' - 'Today I am doing'.
keywords: verb changed to match its subject and tense
verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'
pronouncing one syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word

5114.name: At school: -er and -ir verbs 1st person singular preterite
5114.outcome: I can use -er/-ir verbs to talk about what I did and do at school.
points: If the final syllable is stressed and the word ends in a vowel or 'n' or 's' there is an accent on the final vowel.
The 1st person singular of -er and -ir verbs in preterite ends in -í, e.g. 'describí'.
The 1st person singular of -er and -ir verbs in present ends in -o, e.g.' describo'.
keywords: describes habitual events in the present, e.g. ‘I do’
verb tense used to express completed actions in the past e.g. 'I did'

5115.name: At school: prenominal adjectives
5115.outcome: I can use the correct position of adjectives when talking about activities at school.
points: If the final syllable is stressed and the word ends in a vowel or 'n' or 's' there is an accent on the final vowel.
The 1st person singular of -er and -ir verbs in preterite ends in -í, e.g. 'elegí'.
The 1st person singular of -er and -ir verbs in present ends in -o, e.g.' elijo'.
Usually Spanish adjectives come after the noun, except for prenominal adjectives which come before the noun.
keywords: adjectives that go before the noun

5116.name: Free time: -er and -ir verbs 2nd person singular
5116.outcome: I can use the preterite of -er and -ir verbs to talk about free time.
points: Words with stress on the third-last syllable have an accent on the stressed vowel.
The 1st person singular of -er and -ir verbs ends in (-í) in the preterite.
The 2nd person singular of -er and -ir verbs ends in (-iste) in the preterite.
keywords: form of pronouns and verbs used to refer to 'I'
form of pronouns and verbs used to refer to 'you' singular
verb tense used to express completed actions in the past e.g. 'I did'
some words in Spanish have emphasis on the third-last syllable of a word when it is spoken

5117.name: Free time: -er and -ir verbs 2nd person singular in questions
5117.outcome: I can ask and answer questions about free-time activities.
points: Words with stress on the third-last syllable have a written accent on the stressed vowel.
The 2nd person singular of -er and -ir verbs ends in -es in the present.
The 2nd person singular of -er and -ir verbs in ends in -iste in the preterite.
In Spanish we use 'de' between two nouns to describe a particular type of something.
keywords: describes habitual events in the present, e.g. ‘I do’
verb tense used to express completed actions in the past e.g. 'I did'

5119.name: What people have: 'tener' singular persons
5119.outcome: I can use the verb ‘tener’ to talk about what I and others have.
points: The SSCs [ca], [co] and [cu] are pronounced as in 'casa', 'comer', 'escuchar'.
The verb 'tener' means 'to have, having' and we use it to talk about possessions.
The singular persons of 'tener' are 'tengo' ('I have'), 'tienes' ('you have') and 'tiene' ('she, he, it has').
The Spanish singular subject pronouns are: 'yo', 'tú', 'él', 'ella'.
We need numbers to talk about plural possessions; such sentences often contain 'tener', numbers and plural nouns.

5120.name: How people feel: idiomatic uses of 'tener' + noun
5120.outcome: I can use the verb 'tener' to describe how people feel.
points: The verb 'tener' can also be translated as 'to be + adjective' when used as an idiom, 'tener + noun'.
Its singular forms are: 'tengo', 'tienes', 'tiene' and its plural forms are: 'tenemos' and 'tienen'.
The Spanish plural subject pronouns are: 'nosotros/as', 'ellos/as'. They add clarity about who the verb refers to.

5164.name: What people do at school: regular 1st persons and 2nd person singular (present)

points: When a word has antepenultimate (third-last) syllable stress, it always has an accent on the vowel of that syllable.

5170.name: Hispanic festivals: -ar verbs 3rd person preterite
5170.outcome: I can understand and correctly pronounce -ar verbs in the preterite tense in the context of a Spanish festival.

5171.name: Past trips: 'hacer' and 'ir' singular persons preterite
5171.outcome: I can use the verbs 'ir' and 'hacer' in the preterite tense to answer questions about a past trip.
points: The preterite is used for completed past events; two key irregular verbs are 'ir' and 'hacer'.
'Fui', 'fuiste' and 'fue' mean 'I went, 'you went' and 'she, he, it went' respectively.

points: The present-tense forms of 'ir' ('to go') for 'I', 'you' and 'she, he, it' are 'voy', 'vas' and 'va'.

[j] is pronounced as in 'ejemplo' and [gu] is pronounced as in 'pregunta'.

1991.name: Two musicians: singular 'être', singular adjectives
1991.outcome: I can use the verb 'être', the structure 'ne … pas' and adjectives to describe people, including francophone singers.
points: Most final consonants + final letter 'e' are silent e.g. 'dans' and 'timide'. Pronounce the consonant preceding a SFC.
Adjectives agree with the noun they describe. Add -e to most adjectives in the feminine form and learn other patterns.
The singular pronouns in French are 'je', 'tu', and 'il/elle'. The irregular verb 'être' means to be'.
Put ne … pas around the verb to negate it. 'Ne' becomes 'n' before a vowel/silent h.

points: The plural verb endings for -er verbs are -ons, -ez (pronounced like the infinitive) and -ent (silent letters).
The French name for the English Channel is 'la Manche' because of its sleeve-like shape.
'On' and ‘nous’ both mean ‘we’; 'on' in informal conversation and 'nous' in more formal situations.
'On' can mean 'everyone' (or 'people'), 'you' or 'one'; ‘nous’ is only used for 'we' with the sense of 'you and I'.
To ask information questions with 'est-ce que', keep the same word order and still use intonation.

1995.name: Future goals - Taïs Vinolo: 'aller' + infinitive, negation
1995.outcome: I can use 'aller' with infinitives to say what I'm going to and not going to do in the future.
points: [en/an] is pronouced as in 'enfant'.

When/where adverbs normally come at the start/end of a sentence and how (often) adverbs after the first verb.

2008.name: Senegal: perfect tense, inversion questions, negation 'ne... pas', 'ne … jamais'

2010.name: My everyday: numbers 32-69, time

2011.name: My everyday: 'avoir' and 'être' for feelings and states

The partitive article changes to 'de' after a quantity and in negatives.

2014.name: The French revolution: perfect tense, questions, 'ne … pas'
2014.outcome: I can use the present and perfect tenses, including negation and questions to talk about significant events in French history.
points: [tion] is pronounced as in 'attention' [tion] words are always feminine.
Form the perfect tense by combining part of 'avoir' and a past participle.
-er verb past participles change from -er to é, verbs like prendre change to 'pris' and some participles are irregular.
'Ne...pas' wraps around part of 'avoir' in the perfect tense to make negative sentences.
Ask intonation questions in the perfect tense by raising your voice. You can also add 'est-ce que' before the subject.

2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'

2015.name: The French Revolution: present and perfect tenses, 'ne…jamais'
2015.outcome: I can use a range of adverbs in the perfect tense and talk about what already/never happened.
points: Adverbs that tell us when and where are usually positioned at the start or end of the sentence.
Adverbs that tell us how (often) are usually positioned straight after the first verb in the sentence.
The perfect tense can be translated into the simple past/present perfect in English depending on the context.
'Jamais' means never. In perfect tense sentences, ne …jamais surrounds the first verb (avoir), just like ne...pas does.

2016.name: New Year: -er verbs in the perfect tense with 'être'
2016.outcome: I can use the perfect tense with 'être' to describe New Year celebrations.
points: [è/ê] is pronounced as in 'tête'.
The letter 'e' is usually pronounced as [è/ê] before double consonants or the letters c/l at the end of a word.
Movement verbs like 'aller' and 'rester' take 'être' instead of 'avoir' in the perfect tense.
Add 'e' to the past participle of verbs that take 'être' if the subject is feminine.

2017.name: New Year in Algeria: -er verbs in the perfect tense with 'être'
2017.outcome: I can use the perfect tense with the correct part of 'avoir' or 'être' to describe New Year in Algeria.
points: [a] is pronounced as in 'animal'. The tu and il/elle forms of 'avoir' contain [a].
[è/ê] is pronounced as in 'tête'. The tu and il/elle forms of 'être' contain [è/ê].
Vowels with circumflex accents often show removal of letters from French words of Latin origin. English retains the 's'.
Most verbs take ‘avoir’ in the perfect tense, but movement verbs and 'rester' take ‘être’.

2018.name: Accidents and emergencies: -er verbs in the perfect tense with 'être'
2018.outcome: I can use the plural perfect tense with 'être', past participle agreements and adverbs to describe accidents and emergencies.
points: [s] is pronounced as in 'maison'.
A double 's' between vowels is always soft but a single 's' between vowels is always a hard 's' [s] and sounds like 'z'.
Movement verbs such as 'entrer', 'tomber' and 'monter' use 'être' in the perfect tense before the past participle.
Past participles used with être must agree in gender + number with the subject of the verb. Add 's' for plural subjects.
How (often) adverbs usually go after the first verb but longer -ment adverbs usually go at the end or even the start.

2019.name: Emergency services: -er verbs in the perfect tense with 'être'
2019.outcome: I can use the perfect tense to talk about medical situations in France.
points: 'S' at the beginning of a word is soft 's' (sont) but a single 's' between vowels is a hard 's' ('vous êtes').
All French people have a 'Carte Vitale' necessary to use French health services. Call the SAMU in a medical emergency.
The present tense has one conjugated verb; the perfect tense has two verbs, a part of avoir/être + a past participle.
Use a conjugated form of 'avoir' with most verbs but use 'être' with movement verbs, and past participles must agree.
keywords: pronouncing a usually silent final consonant because a word starting with a vowel follows
2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'

2020.name: Song: J'ai cherché
2020.outcome: I can use my understanding of the perfect tense and a range of vocabulary to listen to and understand a French song.
points: The perfect tense can be translated into the simple past and present perfect in English depending on the context.
The present tense has one conjugated verb; the perfect tense has two verbs, a part of avoir/être + a past participle.
Use a conjugated form of 'avoir' with most verbs but use 'être' with movement verbs and past participles must agree.

2021.name: Free time: verbs + 'de' or 'à' + noun
2021.outcome: I can describe what I do in my free time, including verbs with 'à/de' before nouns.
points: [au] is pronounced as in 'gauche'.
Many French verbs are followed by 'à' or 'de' and a noun; 'à' and 'de' link to the definite article before the noun.
'De' is 'du' before masculine nouns, 'de la' (feminine), 'des' (plural) or 'de l'' before a vowel.
'À' is 'au' before masculine nouns, 'à la' (feminine), 'aux' (plural) or 'à l'' before a vowel.

2022.name: Free time: relative pronoun 'qui'
2022.outcome: I can describe my free time using a range of verbs in the present tense and the relative pronoun 'qui'.
points: It is important to revisit vocabulary as it boosts our long-term retention of words.
The relative pronoun 'qui' introduces a relative clause to give more information about a noun.
Translate 'qui' as who/that for describing people and which/that when describing animals/things.
The endings for verbs like 'écrire' are 's', 's' and 't', 'vons', 'vez' and 'vent'.
Some verbs are followed by 'à' before a noun and the form changes depending on the gender/number of the noun.
keywords: pronounced like a hard 'c' followed by [i], as in the word 'equipo'

2023.name: A theft: emphatic pronouns 'moi' and 'toi' after prepositions
2023.outcome: I can use emphatic pronouns when describing a crime that has happened.
points: [oi] is pronounced as in 'voir'.
Prepositions tell us how a noun is related to another noun, often in terms of place or time.
'Moi' and 'toi' are emphatic pronouns. We use them after prepositions.
keywords: used to emphasise the subject of a sentence, in comparisons, and after 'c'est'

2024.name: A theft: verbs with 'à' and 'de' before the noun
2024.outcome: I can use a range of verbs with 'à' and 'de' to talk about crime and safety.
points: Some verbs take à or de before a noun; it's important to learn each verb together with its required preposition.
The forms of 'à' and 'de' change before masculine and plural nouns to 'au', 'aux', 'du' and 'des'.
Learn the genders of all nouns so that you know which form of 'à' or 'de' to use.
keywords: word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

2025.name: School in France - then and now: -er verbs imperfect tense
2025.outcome: I can understand and use the imperfect tense in the 1st person to describe what I do now and used to do in the context of school.
points: [s] is pronounced as in 'maison'.
Add 'la' to sixième, cinquième, quatrième + troisième to say school years. The lower the number, the older the pupils.
In English, knowledge is singular + plural. When you have lots of knowledge in French, add s for plural, connissances
Use the imperfect tense to talk about events and actions that used to happen regularly in the past.
For the 1st person imperfect, take je + the stem of present tense ‘nous’ form. Add the ending -ais. e.g. 'je regardais'.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

2026.name: Primary and secondary school: -er verbs imperfect tense, ordinal numbers
2026.outcome: I can use the first and third persons of the imperfect tense to talk about how I've changed in the context of school.
points: Ordinal numbers are used to describe the order in which things happen e.g. the fourth year, the sixth lesson.
To make French ordinal numbers, add the suffix 'ième'. Remove the -e from numbers ending -e first and add 'u' to 'cinq'.
'First' (premier/première) is an exception but 'twenty-first' follows the normal pattern 'le vingt-et-unième'.
To form the imperfect tense for 'il/elle/on', take the present tense 'nous' form, remove 'ons' and add -ait.

2027.name: Childhood: then and now: key - RE and -IR verbs in the imperfect tense
2027.outcome: I can describe things now compared to how they used to be in childhood.
points: [ou] is pronounced as in 'nous'.
[u] is pronounced as in 'tu'.
Use 'un an' to count years + 'une année' to describe events or duration within a year.
Use 'ans' with 'avoir' to describe age e.g. 'J'ai douze ans' and 'Quel âge as-tu?' to ask someone's age.
To form the imperfect tense (all verb groups), take the nous form of the present tense, remove –ons, add -ais or -ait.

2028.name: Childhood: present and imperfect tenses, 'il y a' meaning 'ago'
2028.outcome: I can compare my life now to in the past using the present and imperfect tenses.
points: The present and imperfect tenses are one word tenses with the same word order so only the verb endings tell them apart.
The imperfect tense describes an ongoing action for a period of time in the past.
'Il y a' + noun means there is/are. 'Il y a' + time means ago.
Translate 'year' as 'an' after a number. So, 'il y a deux ans' means 'two years ago'.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

2030.name: Montreal - a diverse city: imperfect tense singular
2030.outcome: I can use all singular forms of the imperfect tense to talk about cultural diversity in Montreal.
points: The pronunciation difference between [é] in the perfect tense + [ai] in the imperfect tense greatly alters meaning.
[ai] is pronounced as in vrai'; [é] is pronounced as in 'écrire'.
Languages are not fixed; new words enter the language constantly whilst other words fall out of use.
The 'tu' form of the imperfect tense is formed like the 'je' form (present tense nous form, remove -ons, add -ais).
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

2031.name: Montreal - habitual and one-off past events: imperfect and perfect
2031.outcome: I can use the imperfect and perfect tenses to talk about one-off events and events that happened regularly.
points: Adjectives ending -al in English often end in -al or more commonly -el in French. The feminine form is -elle.
Use the perfect tense for specific one-off past events and the imperfect for regularly repeated past events.
Use the present tense of avoir/être and a past participle to form the perfect tense.
Use the present tense of the 'nous' form, remove -ons and add -ais/ait for the singular imperfect tense.
The verb shows if the action used to happen all the time or was a single, completed event; time phrases give detail.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

2032.name: Spring holidays: perfect tense with 'être', pronouns 'moi', 'toi', 'qui'
2032.outcome: I can understand the perfect tense with 'être' and pronouns 'moi', 'toi' and 'qui' in the context of spring holidays.
points: Sound-symbol correspondence [-ill/ille] sounds as in 'fille'; vowel + -ill/ille also has a final sound like English 'y'.
Use the emphatic pronouns 'moi' and 'toi' after a preposition.
'Qui' (who/which/that) can be used to introduce more information about a noun.
Movement + change of state verbs take 'être', not 'avoir' in the perfect tense. Past participles agree in gender/number.
keywords: pronounced like a hard 'c' followed by [i], as in the word 'equipo'
relationship between letters and their sounds

2033.name: Celebrities: perfect and imperfect
2033.outcome: I can use the present, imperfect and perfect tenses to discover more about French-speaking celebrities.
points: Use the imperfect tense to talk about events and actions that used to happen regularly in the past.

Four groups of -re verbs are: verbs like entendre, verbs like prendre, verbs like traduire and verbs like écrire.
Three groups of -ir verbs are: verbs like choisir, verbs like partir and verbs like venir.

keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

2034.name: Reading habits: pronouns 'il(s)' and 'elle(s)' meaning 'it' and 'they', 'faire'
2034.outcome: I can use the pronouns 'il, elle' and 'ils, elles' to mean 'it' and 'they' in French in the context of reading.
points: The consonants d, s, t and x are often silent at the end of a word. We call this SFC, Silent Final Consonant.
The vowel 'e' is often silent at the end of a word. This is SFe, Silent Final ‘e’. The final consonant is pronounced.
Many verbs that end in -ate in English have in fact come from French verbs ending in -er: 'éliminer' - 'eliminate'.
Every noun has a gender in French. 'Il' and 'elle' can mean 'it', and 'ils' and 'elles' mean 'they' (people and things).
The verb 'faire' is an irregular verb meaning 'to do, make'.

2035.name: Reading habits: verbs like 'prendre' and 'lire', direct objects
2035.outcome: I can write sentences with verbs and direct objects to create a short story.

The verb 'lire' means 'to read'; it follows the same verb pattern as 'dire'.

2036.name: Helping others at school: direct object pronouns 'me' and 'te'
2036.outcome: I can use direct objects pronouns 'me' and 'te' to replace a person in simple French sentences.

Some words replace their final letter with an apostrophe before a silent [h]. This is called elision: j'habite.

The direct object what or whom can also be a pronoun; 'me' and 'te' are the direct object pronouns 'me' and 'you'.

when a vowel sound is dropped and two words combined with an apostrophe to make speech smoother e.g. j'habite

2037.name: At school and university: direct object pronouns 'me' and 'te'
2037.outcome: I can read and write letters, using direct object pronouns, about school and university life in 'la Francophonie'.
points: A direct object is a noun that receives the action of the verb. It answers either 'what?' or 'whom?'.
The direct object noun for 'what' or 'whom' can be replaced by a direct object pronoun.
'Me' and 'te' are the direct object pronouns for 'me' and 'you'.
Before a vowel, direct object pronouns have a elision. 'Me' and 'te' become m’ and t’.

Soixante-dix is 70, quatre-vingts is 80, quatre-vingt-dix is 90 and cent is one hundred.

Using the direct object pronoun 'it' to replace a masculine noun we use 'le'; to replace a feminine noun we use 'la'.

replaces the noun receiving the action of the verb e.g. me, you, it, them

2040.name: Everyday activities: verbs with 'à' before the infinitive

2041.name: Decisions for the future: verbs with 'à' and 'de' before the infinitive

2042.name: Pandemic in France: impersonal expression 'il est + adjective + de'
2042.outcome: I can use impersonal and two-verb infinitive structures to talk about a global health crisis.
points: Cognates may look very similar to English but sound quite different so attention must be paid to pronunciation.
Some verbs require à or de before an infinitive e.g. aider à, arrêter de. Some like 'continuer' can have à or de.

2043.name: Pandemic in France: impersonal expressions including weather
2043.outcome: I can use impersonal phrases to talk about life during the global pandemic.

2044.name: Concorde the history: prepositions of place and movement
2044.outcome: I can use a range of place and movement prepositions to talk about the history of the Concorde.

The Concorde was a project between France and the UK after the 2nd world war to build supersonic planes.

2045.name: Concorde the history: 'sortir', 'choisir', 'venir' verbs, -ion/-ation nouns

2046.name: Occupied France: perfect tense with verbs like 'sortir' and 'choisir'

2047.name: The French Resistance: perfect tense with verbs like 'sortir' and 'choisir'

4801.name: The French colonial empire: perfect tense with verbs like 'venir' and 'entendre'

4803.name: The French colonial empire: more practice of verbs like 'entendre' and 'venir'

2048.name: Refugees in France: reflexive pronouns 'me' and 'te'

2049.name: Life in Paris: reflexive pronouns 'me' and 'te'

2050.name: New daily routines: reflexive pronoun 'se'
2050.outcome: I can use a range of vocabulary, direct object pronouns and reflexive pronouns in the singular form to describe daily life for refugees in France.

2051.name: Helping others: reflexive pronoun 'se'
2051.outcome: I can use singular reflexive and direct object pronouns to talk about caring for people and animals.
points: Use 'un an' to indicate a specific unit of time/quantity and 'une année' for description/duration. Both mean 'a year'.
Apply the pattern of adding -(n)eé to 'jour', 'matin' and 'soir' to describe different periods of time.
Use the reflexive pronoun 'se' when somebody is doing the action of the verb to himself or herself.
If someone does the action to someone else, use the direct object pronouns 'le' and 'la' for the receiver of the action.
keywords: used to indicate doing something to yourself, words like 'myself' and yourself'

2052.name: Historical figures: 'avoir' and 'être' imperfect
2052.outcome: I can use the imperfect tense in the singular forms to describe historical figures from the past.
points: [eu] is pronounced as in 'deux' and open [eu/œu] is pronounced as in 'cœur'.
When [eu/œu] is followed by a pronounced consonant, it is an open sound.
The imperfect tense is used to talk about things that used to happen regularly in the past.
To form it, take the 'nous' form of the present tense, remove -ons, add -ais (1st/2nd persons) or -ait (3rd persons).
Use 'être' in the imperfect tense with an adjective to mean 'was'. The stem for 'être' in the imperfect tense is -ét.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

2053.name: Historical figures: imperfect tense
2053.outcome: I can use the imperfect tense in the singular forms to understand and describe historic figures.
points: The imperfect tense is used to talk about things that used to happen regularly in the past.
To form, take the nous form of the present tense, remove -ons, add -ais (1st/2nd persons) or -ait (3rd persons).
The imperfect tense of il y a is il y avait, which means ‘there used to be’ or 'there was/were'.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

2054.name: Simultaneous events: perfect and imperfect tenses together
2054.outcome: I can use the perfect and imperfect tenses together, including within 'est-ce que' structures to describe simultaneous events.
points: [r] is pronounced as in 'rue'. It is different to English 'r'.
Use the perfect tense for one-off past actions and the imperfect for things that used to happen regularly.
Use the imperfect tense to express the past continuous 'was -ing'.
Use the perfect + imperfect tenses together with a conjunction to describe what happened when you were doing something.
Use 'est-ce que' in the imperfect tense with its usual structure to ask about 2 things happening at the same time.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

2055.name: A mystery: perfect and imperfect tenses together
2055.outcome: I can use the perfect and imperfect tenses together to describe simultaneous events in the context of a mystery.
points: The singular forms of ‘voir’ in the present tense are ‘vois’ (‘je’, ‘tu’) and ‘voit’ (‘il’, ‘elle’).
The verb 'voir' is used in many expressions in French like 'voir grand', 'rien à voir avec' and 'voir la vie en rose'.
Use the imperfect tense to express the past continuous 'was -ing'.
Use the perfect + imperfect tenses together with a conjunction to describe what happened when you were doing something.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

3057.name: Paris-Kiffe kiffe demain: indefinite adjectives
3057.outcome: I can use a range of vocabulary and indefinite adjectives to understand information about a French novel and describe Paris, its setting.
points: [oi] is pronounced as in 'voir'. [oin] is pronounced as in 'besoin'. [oin] is nasal only when followed by a consonant.
Indefinite adjectives go before the noun they describe. Tout le agrees in number/gender. Chaque/plusieurs don't change.
Même/autre agree in number. Quelques is an indefinite ajective meaning some. It agrees in number, so is usually plural.
keywords: a type of adjective that describes a noun in an non-specific way; in English this includes 'few' and 'some'

5581.name: Interview with a musician: present tense weak verbs, yes/no questions
5581.outcome: I can ask and answer questions in the present tense in the context of an interview with a musician.
points: Cognates are pronounced in German with different syllable stress from their English equivalents.
For present tense weak (regular) verbs, add -e, -st, -t to the stem for singular persons.
For present tense verbs, the 'wir' (we), 'Sie' (formal you) and 'sie' (they) forms are the same as the infinitive.
German has one present tense, with two English translations, simple or continuous present - I do or I am doing.
The German inversion question 'Spielst du?' can translate as either 'Do you play' or 'Are you playing?'.
keywords: when the subject pronoun and the verb switch place to form a question
part of the verb that appears in all forms
pronouncing one syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word

5583.name: German musicians: present tense open questions, word order
5583.outcome: I can ask and answer open questions about German musicians using flexible word order, and I can complete extended activities describing a favourite person in the present tense.
points: Open questions start with a question word (e.g., 'wo', 'wie', 'warum') and use verb-subject word order.
It’s important to be very confident with question words to understand information and ask questions.
German sentences can start with any other element (other than the subject) to emphasise it and then the verb second.
Present tense verbs plus the adverb 'gern' (gladly) say what we like doing. As all adverbs, it can start a sentence.
keywords: adverb meaning ‘gladly, liked to’ with the past tense
question starting with a wh- word that has more information in the answer than yes/no
inverts the subject and verb in a sentence

5584.name: A fairy tale: present tense 2nd person plural ('ihr'), dative verbs
5584.outcome: I can read and understand a modern fairy tale in which I can use verbs in the 2nd person plural ('ihr'), both dative and accusative verbs.
points: The vowels [a], [ä], [o], and [ö] need practice and clarity as an umlaut is often added to form plural nouns.
'You (plural, informal)' is 'ihr' and the verb ending is -t, e.g., 'ihr habt'. The 'ihr' form of 'sein' is 'ihr seid'.
Most verbs take the accusative (direct object) case.
Certain verbs take the dative (indirect object), which often has the meaning of giving something to someone.
keywords: verb that is used with an indirect object pronoun

5585.name: Storytelling: pronouns 'du', 'ihr', 'Sie', object word order
5585.outcome: I can understand and correctly use the different forms of 'you' in German and use verbs with direct and indirect objects in the context of a modern fairy tale.
points: To say 'you' in German, use 'du' (singular) or 'Sie' (formal) or 'ihr' (plural informal) or 'man' (you, one or people).
In a sentence with two object nouns, the indirect object (dative) always comes first.
Identify the indirect object in a sentence by asking 'to/for whom'?' something is done and looking for dative articles.
keywords: a noun in the dative case, indirectly affected by the action of the verb

5586.name: Plan an event: present strong verbs, 'you' pronouns 'ihr', 'du', 'Sie' and 'man'
5586.outcome: I can use strong verbs, including separable verbs in the present tense with the different forms of 'you' in German in the correct context when planning a party.
points: To say 'you' in German, use 'du' (singular), 'Sie' (formal), ihr (plural) or 'man' (you, one or 'people').
In the present tense, strong German verbs change their vowel in the 'du' and 'er/sie/es/man' forms.
Strong verbs stems with 'e' change to 'i' or 'ie'. Stems with 'a' change to 'ä' or 'au' to 'äu'.
keywords: a verb which changes its vowel in the verb stem of some of its forms

5587.name: Birthdays: recounting personal experiences
5587.outcome: I can understand and write about birthday experiences in past and present tenses.
points: Numbers 20 and above are formed as unit + 'und' + ten, e.g., 21 - 'einundzwanzig'.
There are a number of rules for forming noun plurals which should be learnt and practised.
Encountering previously taught language when listening and reading in German develops our comprehension.
Awareness of register helps us choose words and structures suited to spoken or written language.
keywords: a naming word for people, places or things
level of formality or style of language used, depending on the audience, purpose, and context

5588.name: What do you see? Negation: kein + indefinite article vs nicht + definite article
5588.outcome: I can explain what I see or don't see, using 'kein' or 'nicht' appropriately to negate words or sentences.
points: 'Nicht' means 'not' and 'kein' means 'no, not a' with a noun.
'Nicht' is used when the noun is preceded by the definite article, a possessive adjective, or before a proper noun.
'Kein' is used if the noun is preceded by the indefinite article.
'Kein' goes before the noun it negates.
'Nicht' goes before the element it negates, or at the end of the phrase if it negates the whole phrase.
keywords: when the ending of an adjective matches the noun it describes in gender and number
negative article ‘no’, ‘not a, an, any’ - negates nouns preceded by the indefinite article

5589.name: What you used to do: perfect tense with 'ihr' (you, familiar pl.) and 'früher'
5589.outcome: I know how to form and use the perfect tense in German, including the 'ihr' form, to discuss past events with other people.
points: Form the perfect tense with the present tense of 'haben' or 'sein', plus a past participle at the end of the statement.
Form most past participles by adding 'ge-' and '-t' around the verb stem. '-ieren' verbs do not add 'ge-'.
Verbs with prefixes 'be-', 'ver-', 'er-' don't add 'ge-' to form past participles. Their prefixes are never stressed.
The subject pronoun 'ihr' means 'you (familiar, plural)'.
Use the adverb 'früher' to translate 'used to' from English, e.g., 'Ich habe früher getanzt, aber jetzt nicht mehr.'.
keywords: adverb meaning ‘previously, in former times, in the past'
verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb
2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'

5590.name: What did they do then? Perfect, imperfect 'war', 'hatte', 'gab', compound nouns
5590.outcome: I can form compound nouns, recognise patterns in past participles and contrast different past tenses, in the context of talking about what others have done.
points: A compound noun is made up of two or more nouns. Its gender comes from the final noun, e.g., 'die Partymusik'
Some groups of verbs form their past participles following the same vowel changes, e.g., [ei] to [ie]; [e] to [o].
The imperfect tense is a one-word past tense, mostly used in written German, apart from some key verbs, e.g., 'es gab'.
Sometimes the present tense is used to narrate past events. This is the 'historical present' and is mostly written.
The purpose of the historical present is to make events feel more immediate or heighten the drama.
keywords: two or more nouns put together to make one longer noun
tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb

5592.name: Famous lives: 'als' as 'when' with the past tense
5592.outcome: I can say calendar years in German, recognise pairs of nouns and verbs, and correctly use the conjunction 'als' to talk about past events.
points: For calendar years in German, say the hundred or thousand, but leave out the 'und', e.g., 2001 - 'zweitausend(und)eins'.
Add -er or -ung to the stem of some verbs to create related nouns, e.g., 'forschen' - 'der Forscher' - 'die Forschung'.
Add -in to some masculine people nouns to create the feminine form, e.g., 'der Entdecker', 'die Entdeckerin'.
The conjunction 'als' means 'when' for a one-off past event. It triggers word order three, sending the verb to the end.
Use 'wenn' to mean 'when' for present or future events. The question word is 'wann'.
keywords: conjunction meaning ‘when’, referring to specific past events, which triggers word order 3
sends the verb to the end

5593.name: Famous German speakers: 'bevor' and 'nachdem', word order
5593.outcome: I can recognise links between nouns and verbs, form the plural of feminine person nouns and use 'bevor' and 'nachdem' to link sentences.
points: When faced with unfamiliar words, use your previous knowledge to identify noun-verb pairs, e.g., 'die Feier' - 'feiern'.
Add -nen to all feminine person nouns ending -in to form their plurals (plural rule six).
The sound-symbol correspondence [r] is formed at the back of the throat, barely moving the lips, e.g., ‘Autorin’.
The conjunction 'bevor' means 'before' and sends the verb to the end of the clause (word order three).
The conjunction 'nachdem' means 'after' and sends the verb to the end of the clause (word order three).
keywords: conjunction meaning 'before', which triggers word order three
conjunction meaning 'after', which triggers word order three
add -nen to all feminine person nouns ending -in, e.g., 'Lehrerinnen'
after certain conjunctions, the verb is sent to the end of the sentence or clause

5594.name: Childhood experiences: nouns, past tense, conjunctions
5594.outcome: I can recognise correspondences between German and English nouns and can use a range of familiar vocabulary with the past tense, to understand Germany's past and discuss my childhood.
points: German nouns ending '-heit' often correspond to English nouns ending '-ity', '-ness', e.g., 'die Sicherheit' (security).
After WW2, Germany was split into West and East Germany. Life was very different in each country.
Use the perfect tense and shorter imperfect tense forms 'war', 'waren', 'es gab', 'hatte' to narrate past events.
The conjunctions 'als' or 'bevor' trigger word order three and can be used at the start of a sentence.
If 'als' or 'bevor' begin a clause, the following clause uses word order two, creating a verb-comma-verb pattern.
keywords: imperfect tense form meaning 'there was | there were'
1st and 3rd person plural imperfect tense form of 'sein', meaning 'were'
sends the verb to the end

5595.name: Christmas market: 'alle', 'jed-', 'dies-' and 'welch-'
5595.outcome: I can use ‘all-’ and ‘jed-’ as pronouns to be specific when talking about a Christmas market.
points: [b] is pronounced like English 'p' when it's the final letter in a word, or followed by a consonant, e.g., 'der Korb'.
[b] sounds like English b when it's followed by a vowel, e.g., 'die Körbe'.
'Alle' is a pronoun meaning 'everyone' or 'everybody' and is followed by a plural verb ending -en.
'Jeder' is a pronoun meaning 'everyone' or 'everybody' and is followed by a singular verb ending -t.
'Jed-' is the determiner ‘every’ and its endings match the gender and case of the noun that follows, e.g., 'jedes Kind'.
keywords: pronoun meaning 'everyone' or 'everybody', used with a plural verb
determiner meaning ‘each, every’ which changes according to gender and case
pronoun meaning 'everyone' or 'everybody', used with a singular verb

5596.name: What I would like: 'möcht-' in one- and two-verb structures
5596.outcome: I can express what I would like and what I would like to do using 'möcht-'.
points: Practising vocabulary in a range of ways deepens knowledge and understanding.
'Möcht-' means 'would like' and can be used with a noun to say which object you would like.
'Möcht-' can be used with a second verb in the infinitive form to express what you would like to do.
When 'möcht-' is used as part of a 2-verb structure, the second verb moves to the end of the sentence.
The determiner before the object of a sentence matches the gender and case.
keywords: where the 2nd (infinitive) verb comes at the end of 2-verb sentences
a word that introduces a noun in a clause or phrase
the conditional form of the verb 'mögen', meaning 'would like'
the noun, noun phrase or pronoun that receives the action of the main verb in the active voice

5597.name: Future plans: plural future tense 'werden' + infinitive, two-verb structures
5597.outcome: I can use plural forms of 'werden' in two-verb structures to describe future plans.
points: Practising vocabulary in a variety of ways supports recall.
'Werden' meaning 'will' can be used as part of a two-verb structure to describe future plans.
In the two-verb future tense with 'werden', the second verb is an infinitive and placed at the end of the clause.
In some two-verb structures, the second infinitive verb is preceded by 'zu', e.g., 'Ich hoffe, als Arzt zu arbeiten'.
keywords: sentence made up of two verb phrases
word meaning 'to', used with a preceding comma to form two-verb sentences in German that do not involve a modal verb

5598.name: What is important: infinitive uses, 'es ist' + adjective, 'zu' + infinitive
5598.outcome: I can recognise infinitives and use them correctly in two-verb structures when talking about what is important to me.
points: The stress on cognates is often different in German compared to English, e.g., 'consequence' - 'Konsequenz'.
Regular revisiting of vocabulary is important for developing recall.
An infinitive is a verb in its long form, giving its general meaning, e.g., 'helfen' - 'to help'.
In a two-verb structure with an infinitive, the infinitive is typically the second verb and is at the end of the clause.
Some but not all two-verb structures with an infinitive use ‘zu’ before the infinitive; modal verbs and 'werden' do not.
keywords: the basic form of the verb, with no particular subject or tense indicated
pronouncing one syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word

5599.name: What is important in life: infinitive uses, verbs capitalised as nouns
5599.outcome: I can use infinitives as nouns and know when to use 'zu' with infinitives in the context of important relationships with others.
points: Using a range of strategies, e.g., synonym spotting, can help deepen vocabulary knowledge.
Using surrounding words to help infer meaning of unfamiliar words is a key strategy in reading comprehension.
Infinitive verbs can be changed into nouns by capitalising the first letter of the infinitive.
Infinitive nouns are always neuter; English equivalents end in -ing, e.g., 'das Schwimmen' - 'swimming'.
In addition to modal verbs and 'werden', a few other verbs don’t need 'zu' before the infinitive in two-verb sentences.
keywords: work out the likely meaning of an unfamiliar word based on knowledge of the surrounding words in the text and the structure of the word itself

5601.name: What you do for and with others: prepositions 'ohne', 'für', 'mit', and 'von'
5601.outcome: I can use a range of pronouns and possessive adjectives to describe how people get on.
points: Reading longer texts is a useful way to deepen knowledge of vocabulary.
Prepositions 'ohne' and 'für' are followed by a direct object and always take the accusative case.
Prepositions 'mit' and 'von' are followed by an indirect object and always take the dative case.
Possessive adjectives change spelling according to the gender of the noun they relate to and the case.
keywords: replaces the noun receiving the action of the verb e.g. me, you, it, them
replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, from you, with them; takes the dative case
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

5602.name: What you did for and with others: perfect tense
5602.outcome: I can use the perfect tense to say what happened between people in the past.
points: Reading is a good way to strengthen word knowledge and can be done in a range of ways.
The perfect tense is formed with a present tense part of 'haben' or 'sein' and a past participle.
Many past participles are formed by adding ge- to the start of the verb stem and -t to the end.
For verbs starting with be-, er- and ver-, the past participle does not have the prefix ge-.
Strong verbs in the perfect tense form the past participle by adding -en; they often have a vowel change too.
keywords: 2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'
verb whose past participle sandwiches the stem with 'ge-' and ‘-en’ and often changes the stem vowel

5603.name: Everyday actions and routines: using singular verbs reflexively
5603.outcome: I can use verbs reflexively to talk about daily routines and personal actions.
points: Using exclamations to give conversational reactions can make our German sound more natural.
Many verbs can be used reflexively to show the action is being done to oneself, e.g., 'sich waschen' - 'to have a wash'.
The meaning of a verb may change slightly when used reflexively, e.g., 'Sie setzt sie/sich hin': She puts her/sits down.
Reflexive pronouns are 'mich' myself, 'dich' yourself and 'sich' him/her/itself. 'Mich/dich' also mean 'me/you'.
Context is important when understanding the intended meaning of pronouns like 'mich' and 'dich'.
keywords: describes an action where the subject and the object of the verb are the same
used to indicate doing something to yourself, words like 'myself' and yourself'

5604.name: Everyday routine: using verbs reflexively, 24-hour clock
5604.outcome: I can talk about routine activities and times using the 24-hour clock.
points: Regular revisiting of phonic rules supports effective transcription and reading aloud.
Practising new and known vocabulary regularly supports successful recall.
For 24-hour clock, we say 'Uhr' instead of ':' and minutes are said as numbers, e.g., 'vierzehn Uhr fünfunddreißig'.
Open questions are formed by using a question word and inverting the subject and verb, e.g., 'Wann gehen wir ins Kino?'.
keywords: question starting with a wh- word that has more information in the answer than yes/no

5605.name: Festivals and traditions: using plural verbs reflexively
5605.outcome: I can use verbs reflexively to describe people's self-directed actions in the context of traditional festivals.
points: Idioms are expressions that often don’t have a literal meaning and may not translate directly into another language.
Several German idioms include ‘Wurst’ because sausage is a culturally important German food, popular at many festivals.
Stress is part of intonation and syllable stress refers to the syllable in a word that is spoken more strongly.
Plural reflexive pronouns 'uns', 'euch' and 'sich' make verbs reflexive when subject and object are the same.
In sentences where subject and object are different, 'uns' (us) and 'euch' (you all) are object pronouns.
keywords: a phrase or expression whose meaning we don't translate word-for-word, e.g. 'it's raining cats and dogs'
used to indicate doing something to yourself, words like 'myself' and yourself'
pronouncing one syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word

5606.name: Famous festivals and traditions: plural reflexive verbs, 12-hour clock
5606.outcome: I can use new and known vocabulary to describe important international cultural traditions.
points: Practising new vocabulary in a range of ways supports effective learning.
When verbs are used reflexively, the person doing the action is also the receiver of the action.
‘Halb’ means half, ‘nach’ means past and ‘vor’ means to in 12-hour clock times.
In German, ‘half past' is expressed as half of the next hour, e.g., ‘halb acht’ is 7:30.
Learning about cultural traditions strengthens language learning, improving comprehension and cultural knowledge.
keywords: describes an action where the subject and the object of the verb are the same

5607.name: New Year's resolutions: future tense
5607.outcome: I can express future events using 'werden' plus infinitive and other verbs like 'möcht-', 'vorhaben' and 'planen'.
points: Regular practice of a range of phonic rules supports pronunciation skills.
The Leitner System is a powerful tool for learning vocabulary effectively.
Future intentions can be expressed using 'werden', modal, and other verbs like 'vorhaben' and 'planen' plus infinitive.
Verbs like 'vorhaben', 'planen' and 'es ist' plus adjective need a comma and then 'zu' before the second verb.
'Werden' and modal verbs like 'wollen', 'können', 'dürfen' and 'müssen' do not need 'zu' before the second verb.
keywords: word meaning 'to', used with a preceding comma to form two-verb sentences in German that do not involve a modal verb

5608.name: New Year's resolutions: word order with two-verb structures
5608.outcome: I can express New Year's resolutions using extended sentences, a range of conjunctions and two-verb constructions.
points: Seeing vocabulary in a range of contexts is a good way to support effective learning.
Chinese New Year is celebrated every January/February by around 120,000 people of Chinese descent who live in Germany.
Conjunctions like ‘denn’ and ‘aber’ do not cause a change in word order.
Subordinating conjunctions like ‘weil’ and ‘obwohl’ send the verb to the end of the clause (word order 3).
In two-verb structures with subordinating conjunctions, the short form verb is after the infinitive at the end.
keywords: word that connects ideas between clauses in a sentence
after certain conjunctions, the verb is sent to the end of the sentence or clause

5609.name: People and things: relative clauses to define who, which, that
5609.outcome: I can understand relative clauses that identify and add information about people and things.
points: Relative clauses add information about the noun in the main clause, without starting another sentence.
English uses relative pronouns ‘who’, ‘that’, ‘which’, while German uses the definite article that matches the noun.
In German the relative pronoun kicks the verb to the end of the relative clause; this is called word order three (WO3).
Use indefinite pronouns 'jemand' ('someone') or 'niemand' ('no one') instead of a noun when the exact person is unknown.
When using 'jemand' or 'niemand' in subject relative clauses, use the relative pronoun 'der' as for masculine nouns.
keywords: a type of subordinate clause that begins with a relative pronoun
a pronoun that introduces a relative clause e.g. qui, que
after certain conjunctions, the verb is sent to the end of the sentence or clause

5611.name: Work placement as a stagehand: relative clauses
5611.outcome: I can use relative clauses to identify different objects in the context of a work experience placement as a theatre stagehand.
points: German [d] at the beginning of a word or syllable sounds like English 'd'; [d] at the end of a syllable sounds like -t.
Word mastery includes understanding and producing words without support in new contexts.
Relative clauses add information about the noun in the main clause without starting another sentence.
English uses relative pronouns ‘who’, ‘that’, ‘which’, while German uses the definite article that matches the noun.
In German, the relative pronoun kicks the verb to the end of the relative clause; this is called word order three (WO3).
keywords: retrieve and use vocabulary without prompts in speaking or writing
a type of subordinate clause that begins with a relative pronoun
a pronoun that introduces a relative clause e.g. qui, que

5612.name: A murder mystery party: relative clauses
5612.outcome: I can create adjectives from nouns adding the suffix -los, and I can use relative clauses to give further information about suspects and clues in the context of a murder mystery party.
points: Adding the suffix -los to German nouns creates adjectives with the English equivalent -less or the meaning 'without'.
Relative clauses add information about the noun in a main clause without starting another sentence.
German subject relative clauses start with a relative pronoun, 'der', 'die', 'das', 'die' and end with a verb.
Relative clauses can be embedded in main clauses, with commas before and after the clause.
keywords: a type of subordinate clause that begins with a relative pronoun
letter string added to the end of many German nouns to create adjectives with the English meaning '-less' or 'without'

5613.name: Famous people and their languages: perfect tense with 'sein', calendar years
5613.outcome: I can form the perfect tense with 'sein' and can say calendar years in German, in the context of important people and dates.
points: Stress the 2nd syllable of words that start with an inseparable prefix. Borrowed words stress the 2nd or final syllable.
Verbs of movement or which imply a change of state form the perfect tense with 'sein', e.g., 'er ist gestorben'.
Verbs which require an object are transitive verbs. Verbs that don't require an object are intransitive verbs.
Calendar years in German are said as long numbers, e.g., 'neunzehnhundertfünf' = 1905.
Calendar years 2000+ are said 'zweitausend-', e.g., 'zweitausendeins' = 2001.
keywords: a verb which does not require an object to make sense, e.g., 'to speak', 'to live'
2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'
pronouncing one syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word
a verb requiring an object to make sense, e.g., 'to say', 'to tell'

5614.name: Language and identity: separable verbs, cardinal and ordinal numbers
5614.outcome: I can use ordinal numbers when talking about past events, and use separable verbs in the perfect tense.
points: Add -te to form ordinal numbers 1-19 and -ste for 20+. Exceptions are 'erste', 'dritte', 'siebte'.
Use 'am' with dates to say 'on the' and add -n to the ordinal number, e.g., 'am zehnten Juli'.
In word order three clauses, separable prefixes rejoin the verb.
Form past participles of separable verbs by adding the prefix before ge-, e.g., 'eingeladen', 'aufgemacht'.
Understanding separable prefixes and the base verb meanings allows you to predict most meanings of separable verbs.
keywords: preposition meaning 'on the', is a contraction of 'an' and the dative definite article 'dem'
tells you the order of something, e.g., 'first', 'second', 'third', and is used with dates
two-part verb with a prefix and a main verb, e.g. 'aussehen'
sends the verb to the end

5615.name: Childhood experiences: imperfect modal verbs 'konnte', 'musste', 'wollte'
5615.outcome: I can form the imperfect tense of ‘können’, ‘müssen’ and ‘wollen’, and I am aware of aspects of childhood in Germany.
points: Months of the year are masculine and borrowed from English, but the stressed syllables are not the same.

5174.name: Past holidays: singular -er and -ir verbs in the preterite, interrogatives
5174.outcome: I can use -er and -ir verbs in the preterite to talk and ask about past holidays.

5175.name: Where are my things? 'mi', 'tu' and adverbs of position
5175.outcome: I can use possessive adjectives and adverbs of position to ask and answer questions about where my and your things are.
