5176.name: Routine events: reflexive pronouns 'me' and 'te'
5176.outcome: I can use reflexive pronouns 'me' and 'te' to describe my daily routine and ask you questions about yours.
points: The 1st person singular (I) of regular -ar verbs like 'lavar' ends in -o, the 2nd person singular (you) ends in -as.
Some Spanish verbs like 'despertar' have a stem change -e to -ie in some forms. For example: 'despierto' (I wake up).
To say that I do something to myself in Spanish we use the reflexive pronoun 'me': 'me presento' (I introduce myself).
To say that you do something to yourself, use reflexive pronoun 'te' before the verb: 'te llamas' ('you call yourself').

5178.name: People and places in Mexico: possessive adjective 'su'
5178.outcome: I can understand the different uses of the possessive adjective 'su' in the context of learning about people and places in Mexico.
points: Mexico is famous for many things including its artists, its archaeology, its food, its customs and its unique history.
Possessive adjectives go before nouns to show belonging and ownership.
'Su' is 'his', 'hers' or 'its' before a singular noun, e.g. 'su país' - 'his, her, its country'.
'Sus' is 'his', 'hers', or 'its' before a plural noun, e.g. 'sus padres' - 'his, her, its parents'.
As 'su' and 'sus' have different meanings, you will often need context to translate them accurately.

5179.name: A Mexican tradition: reflexive pronoun 'se'
5179.outcome: I can use the reflexive pronoun 'se' before a range of verbs in the context of describing the Mexican custom 'Day of the Dead'.
points: Spanish words ending in a vowel, -n, or -s naturally have penultimate syllable stress, e.g. 'vamos' and 'mundo'.

5182.name: Looking after others: pronouns 'le' and 'les'
5182.outcome: I can use indirect object pronouns to describe how I support and care for others.

5213.outcome: I can describe ongoing events in the present and the past, using the present and imperfect continuous tenses.
points: The sound-spelling correspondences [n] and [ñ] are pronounced differently: like the [n] in 'poner' and the [ñ] in 'año'.
'Estar' means 'to be' and is used to express a state or location. 'You are' is 'estás' and 'you were' is 'estabas'.
We use 'estar' in the present + present participle to describe ongoing events. This is called the present continuous.
We use 'estar' in the imperfect + present participle to describe past ongoing events; this is the imperfect continuous.
The present participle stays the same: remove the infinitive ending and add -ando for -ar verbs and -iendo for -er/-ir.
keywords: Spanish verb meaning 'to be, being' used for location and temporary states
verb tense used to describe ongoing actions in the past, e.g. 'I was doing'
describes events happening right now: 'I am doing'

5214.name: News events: -ar verbs preterite tense for interruptions
5214.outcome: I can describe past news events using the imperfect continuous with ‘cuando’ ('when') and the preterite tense for interruptions.
points: The preposition 'de' joins two nouns to describe a type of something, e.g. ‘un billete de avión’ ('a plane ticket').
We use 'estar' in the present tense + present participle to talk about ongoing events; this is the present continuous.
'Estar' in the imperfect + present participle describes what someone was doing; this is the imperfect continuous.
Sometimes an action interrupts what someone was doing. We use 'cuando' followed by the preterite to express this.
keywords: Spanish preposition meaning 'from' and 'of', also used to express possession
verb tense used to describe ongoing actions in the past, e.g. 'I was doing'
describes events happening right now: 'I am doing'
verb tense used to express completed actions in the past e.g. 'I did'

5215.name: Past experiences of work: -ar verbs imperfect tense 1st person singular
5215.outcome: I can describe what was happening and what happened at work using the preterite and imperfect.
points: The two different [r] sounds sometimes change the meaning of a word, e.g. 'pero' - 'but', 'perro' - 'dog'.
To talk about a completed event in the past, we use the preterite tense, e.g. 'mandé un correo ayer'.
To talk about something that used to happen repeatedly in the past, we use the imperfect tense, e.g. 'mandaba'.
In the imperfect tense, the verb 'estar' can be translated with 'was, were' or 'used to', e.g. 'estaba feliz'.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
a tense used for events completed in the past

5216.name: Past experiences of work: -ar verbs imperfect tense 2nd and 3rd person singular
5216.outcome: I can use imperfect tense verbs to talk about what I and others used to do in the past.
points: When a single 'r' appears within or at the end of a word, it is usually not rolled.
If the word begins with a single 'r', it is rolled, just like 'rr'.
To talk about something that used to happen repeatedly in the past, we use the imperfect tense.
'Dar' usually translates as 'to give' but it is also used to describe how something makes people feel.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

5217.name: Past celebrations: -er and -ir verbs imperfect tense
5217.outcome: I can use the preterite and imperfect tenses to talk about celebrations in the past.
points: Revisiting vocabulary often helps to move the words from your short-term to your long-term memory.
For something completed in the past, we use the preterite tense, e.g. 'serví '- 'I served', 'serviste' - 'you served'.
To talk about something that used to happen repeatedly in the past, we use the imperfect tense.
To mean 'I' remove the endings and add -ía. For 'you' add -ías and for 'she, he, it' add -ía.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
a tense used for events completed in the past

5218.name: Past routines: -er and -ir verbs imperfect tense
5218.outcome: I can use modal and imperfect tense verbs to describe my own and other people's past routines.
points: The -y at the end of an English word often changes to -ía or -ia in Spanish. e.g. energy - energía.
Words ending in -ía stress the final syllable and need an accent to show that, e.g. energía.
Words ending in -ia stress the penultimate syllable and need no accent, e.g. ciencia.
The verbs 'querer', 'poder' and 'deber' are modal verbs and are often followed by an infinitive.
To talk about something that used to happen repeatedly in the past, we use the imperfect tense.
keywords: pronouncing the last syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word
tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want
pronouncing the second-to-last syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word

5219.name: The past of a Spanish-speaking city: 'era', 'eras'
5219.outcome: I can use the verb ‘ser’ in both the present and imperfect tenses to understand a text about a Spanish-speaking city.
points: The verb 'ser' is used to talk about traits.
Its simple present forms are: 'soy', 'eres', 'es' and its imperfect tense forms are: 'era', 'eras', 'era'.
Most Spanish adjectives go after the noun. We use them to describe objective qualities (e.g. traits, origin, colours).
Prenominal adjectives go before the noun and are used to express subjective opinions or for emphasis.
Some adjectives can come before or after the noun, but their meaning changes
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
adjectives that go before the noun
verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'

5221.name: Extended reading (Don Quijote): 'había' and 'tenía'
5221.outcome: I can use imperfect tense verbs to understand and discuss an important work of Spanish literature, such as Don Quijote.
points: To talk about something that used to happen in the past, we use the imperfect tense.
To say ‘there used to be’, ‘there was’ or ‘there were’, use ‘había’. Sentences with ‘había’ often start with ‘en’.
To say ‘I, she, he used to have’ or ‘I, she, he had’ in the imperfect tense, use ‘tenía’.
With other -ar verbs, to talk about 'she' or 'he', add -aba to the stem of the verb. With -er and -ir verbs, add -ía.
Don Quijote de La Mancha, written by Miguel de Cervantes, is considered the first modern novel.
keywords: form of 'haber' meaning 'there was, were' or 'there used to be'
tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
form of 'tener' meaning 'I had, used to have' or 'she, he, it had, used to have'

5222.name: Extended reading (Don Quijote): imperfect continuous
5222.outcome: I can use the imperfect continuous to talk about what I and other people were doing in the past.
points: Words stressed on the penultimate syllable don’t have an accent if they end in a vowel, -n or -s.
The imperfect continuous describes what someone was doing, e.g. 'estaba(s) caminando por la montaña.'
The preterite tense is used for completed actions in the past.
We can give extra information about when something happened using the relative pronoun 'cuando'.
We use 'cuando' + preterite to show a short action interrupts a longer, ongoing action.
keywords: conjugation that is followed by subjunctive verb when the action hasn't yet occurred or is uncertain
verb tense used to describe ongoing actions in the past, e.g. 'I was doing'
verb tense used to express completed actions in the past e.g. 'I did'

5223.name: Work and jobs: 'eres' and 'sois', simple present -ar verbs
5223.outcome: I can use the you (singular) and you (plural) forms of 'ser' – 'eres' and 'sois', and of regular -ar verbs in the simple present to talk about work and jobs.
points: In Spanish, we use the verb 'ser' to talk about traits, including jobs.
To say 'you are', use 'eres', and to say 'you all are', use 'sois'.
The -ity at the end of an English word is often -idad in Spanish, e.g. 'tranquility' - 'tranquilidad'.
To refer to 'you' for one person with a present tense -ar verb, use the verb ending -as, e.g. 'buscas'.
To refer to 'you' for two or more people with a present tense -ar verb, use the verb ending -áis, e.g. 'buscáis'.
keywords: part of the verb 'ser' meaning 'you are', used for general traits
verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'

5224.name: Work and jobs: 'vas' and 'vais', with simple present for future events
5224.outcome: I can use the simple present tense to talk about someone else's scheduled future events.
points: If the stress is on the final syllable and the word ends in any consonant except ‘n’ or ‘s’, there is no accent.
If the stress is on the final syllable and the word ends in a vowel or ‘n’ or ‘s’, there is an accent.
To talk about where someone goes (present tense), use the verb ‘ir’, e.g. 'vais'.
To talk about what you are going to do (future plans), use a present tense form of the verb 'ir' + a + infinitive.
In Spanish we use the simple present to talk about scheduled plans in the future, e.g. 'organizáis una fiesta mañana'.
keywords: pronouncing the last syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word
verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'

5225.name: School life: -er and -ir verbs 2nd person singular and plural
5225.outcome: I can use the 'tú' and 'vosotros' forms of regular -er and -ir verbs to understand teachers talking to me and my classmates about school life.
points: To refer to 'you (singular)' simple present -er verbs, use the verb ending -es, and for 'you (plural)' use -éis.
The modal verbs 'querer', 'poder', 'deber' and 'soler' are often followed by an infinitive.
To refer to 'you (singular)' with simple present -ir verbs, use the verb ending -es, and for 'you (plural)' use -ís.
To say 'your' for two or more people, use 'vuestros' + masculine nouns and 'vuestras' + feminine nouns.
keywords: a verb whose infinitive form ends in -er
a verb whose infinitive form ends in -ir
verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'

5226.name: Friendships: gustar-type verbs
5226.outcome: I can use indirect object pronouns and gustar-type verbs to talk about friendships.
points: Some verbs ending in –cer or –cir have a spelling change in the 1st person singular.
IOPs indicate who is affected by the verb; 'le' for 'to, for him, her', and 'les' for 'to, for them'.
Gustar-type verbs use IOPs because they show an effect on someone or something.
These verbs end in -a for singular subjects and -an for plural - 'el libro les interesa', 'los libros les interesan'.
In Spanish an infinitive can be used as the subject in a sentence.
keywords: verb that uses indirect object pronouns and agree with the thing or activity causing the feeling
replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, from you, with them; takes the dative case

5227.name: Friendships: personal 'a'
5227.outcome: I can use the personal 'a' to describe relationships and actions involving friends.
points: 'Z' is added before the 'co' to keep the soft 'c' sound in verbs ending in '-cer' or '-cir', e.g. 'conocer' - 'conozco'.
To mean ‘you’, -er/-ir verbs end in -es. To mean ‘you all’, -er verbs end in -éis and -ir verbs end in -ís.
IOPs indicate the person or thing affected by the verb. Use 'le' to mean 'to, for him, her, it', and 'les' for 'them'.
Two structures are possible: subject + verb + indirect object or indirect object + verb + subject.
We use the personal ‘a’ before the object when it’s a person or a thing.
keywords: replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, from you, with them; takes the dative case
preposition placed before a direct object when that object is a specific person or animal we have a name for

5228.name: How are you feeling? 'Ser' and 'estar' 1st and 2nd person singular
5228.outcome: I can use the verbs 'ser' and 'estar' to describe states and traits of myself and others accurately.
points: To say 'I am' for a location or state, use ‘estoy’ ('estar'), and for a trait, use ‘soy’ ('ser').
To say 'you are' for a location or state, use ‘estás’ ('estar'), and for a trait, use ‘eres’ ('ser').
Some adjectives can only be used with estar because they only describe a state, not a trait, e.g. 'enfermo', 'triste'.
Some adjectives change meaning with 'ser' and 'estar', e.g. ‘aburrido’, ‘listo’, ‘moreno’ and ‘seguro’.
To ask a question in Spanish, you can simply raise your intonation at the end of the sentence.
keywords: Spanish verb meaning 'to be, being' used for location and temporary states
verb meaning to be, being for general traits

5229.name: Where people are from: 'ser' 1st and 2nd person singular and plural
5229.outcome: I can use the verb 'ser' to talk about where people are from.
points: The sounds [que] and [qui] are pronounced like a hard ‘k’ followed by ‘e’ or ‘i’. The 'u' is silent.
The sounds [gue] and [gui] are pronounced like a hard ‘g’ followed by ‘e’ or ‘i’. The ‘u’ is silent.
The verb 'ser' means 'to be, being' for traits. Its forms are: 'I am' - 'soy', 'we are' - 'somos' and 'they are' - son'.
The way to say 'you are' depends on how many people you are talking to.
To say ‘you are’ to one person, use ‘eres’. To say ‘you are’ to two or more people, use ‘sois’.
keywords: verb meaning to be, being for general traits

5232.name: At a theme park: demonstrative adjectives 'ese' and 'esa'
5232.outcome: I can use demonstrative adjectives to describe and compare experiences at a theme park.
points: The demonstrative adjective 'this' for a singular masculine noun is 'este'.
To say 'that' for a singular masculine noun, use 'ese', e.g. 'ese recuerdo'.
To say 'this' for a singular feminine noun, use 'esta', e.g. 'esta cola'.
To say 'that' for a singular feminine noun, use 'esa', e.g. 'esa cola'.
To say 'more … than', use 'más' + adjective + 'que'. To say 'less … than', use 'menos' + adjective + 'que'.
keywords: a type of adjective used to signal a specific person, place or thing

5233.name: At a market: demonstrative adjectives 'esos' and 'esas'
5233.outcome: I can use singular and plural demonstrative adjectives to ask and answer questions while shopping at the market.
points: In sounds like [cua], [cue] and [cui] the 'u' is not silent, but it combines with the 'c' to make a 'kw' sound.
To say ‘that’ for a singular masculine noun, use ‘ese’, e.g. 'ese libro'.
To say ‘those’ for a plural masculine noun, use ‘esos’, e.g. 'esos libros'.
To say ‘that’ for a singular feminine noun, use ‘esa’, e.g. 'esa bebida'.
To say ‘those’ for a plural feminine noun, use ‘esas’, e.g. 'esas bebidas'.
keywords: a type of adjective used to signal a specific person, place or thing

5234.name: Possessions at a crime scene: 'mío/a', 'tuyo/a' and 'suyo/a'
5234.outcome: I can use demonstrative and possessive adjectives to describe evidence and identify who it belongs to at the crime scene.
points: To say ‘that’ for a singular masculine noun, use ‘ese’, and for a singular feminine noun, use ‘esa'.
To say ‘this’ for a singular masculine noun, use ‘este’, and for a singular feminine noun, use ‘esta’.
To talk about possessions we use possessive adjectives.
After a singular masculine noun, use 'mío' - 'mine', 'tuyo' - 'yours' and 'suyo' - 'his, hers'.
After a singular feminine noun, use 'mía' - 'mine', 'tuya' - 'yours' and 'suya' - 'his, hers'.
keywords: specifies a particular noun, indicating ‘this’, ‘that’, ‘these’ or ‘those’
a word that goes before a noun to show ownership or belonging

5235.name: Rigoberta Menchú: -er and -ir verbs 1st and 2nd person singular (preterite)
5235.outcome: I can use the preterite tense to talk about past events in my life and other people’s lives.
points: Regular review of vocabulary moves it into long-term memory.
We only roll the 'r' when it's written as [rr] or when the [r] is at the beginning of a word.
The preterite tense is used to talk about events completed in the past.
To mean ‘I’, remove -er/-ir and add -í, e.g. 'leer' - 'leí', 'vivir' - 'viví'.
To mean ‘you’, remove -er/-ir and add -iste, e.g. 'leer' - 'leiste', 'vivir' - 'viviste'.
keywords: a tense used for events completed in the past

5236.name: Rigoberta Menchú: -ar verbs 1st and 2nd person singular (preterite)
5236.outcome: I can use -ar verbs in the preterite tense to ask and answer questions about other people's past experiences.
points: Word mastery includes recognising, understanding, and using a word in different contexts.
The preterite tense is used to talk about events completed in the past.
For -ar verbs, to say 'I', remove the -ar and -é. For 'you' add -aste, and for 'she, he, it' add -ó.
Spanish doesn’t have a word for 'do' or 'did' in questions. When asking questions, only the main verb is used.
keywords: a tense used for events completed in the past

5237.name: Diana Trujillo: 'fue', 'hizo' and 'tuvo'
5237.outcome: I can use the preterite tense of regular and irregular verbs to talk about other people's past actions and achievements.
points: The preterite tense is used to describe completed events in the past.
To mean 'she, he, it' remove the -er/-ir and add -ió. e.g. nació
To mean 'they' remove the -er/-ir and add -ieron. e.g. nacieron
Use the DOP 'lo' for him/it (masculine) and 'la' for her/it (feminine) – the thing or person receiving the action
Some verbs are irregular. Use fue, hizo and tuvo to say he/she went, did and had in the past.
keywords: replaces the noun receiving the action of the verb e.g. me, you, it, them
a verb that does not follow the regular rules
a tense used for events completed in the past

5238.name: Latin American women in NASA: -ar, -er, -ir verbs 3rd person plural preterite
5238.outcome: I can use present and preterite tense verbs to talk about Latin American women in NASA.
points: In Spanish, the accent can change the meaning of a verb from the present to the past, e.g. 'hablo', 'habló'.
In Spanish, verb endings change depending on when the action takes place and who the verb refers to.
To conjugate -ar verbs for 'they,' remove -ar and add -an for the present tense or -aron for the preterite tense.
For -er/-ir verbs, for 'they,' remove -er/-ir and add -en for the present tense or -ieron for the preterite tense.
keywords: a tense used for events completed in the past
verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'

5239.name: Holiday activities: -ar, -er, -ir verbs 1st person plural present and preterite
5239.outcome: I can use -ar, -er and -ir verbs in the preterite tense to describe past holiday activities.
points: For regular -er verbs, the verb ending -emos refers to 'we' in the present tense.
For regular -er verbs, the verb ending -imos refers to 'we' in the preterite tense.
For regular -ir verbs, the verb ending -imos refers to 'we' in the present and preterite tenses.
For regular -ar verbs, the verb ending -amos refers to 'we' in the present and preterite tenses.
keywords: form of pronouns and verbs used to refer to 'we'
verb tense used to express completed actions in the past e.g. 'I did'

5240.name: Holiday plans: 'ir' + a + infinitive
5240.outcome: I can use 'ir' + a + infinitive and 'para' + infinitive to describe a future trip.
points: The verb 'ir' ('to go, going') is irregular in the present tense.
‘Voy’, ‘vas’ and ‘va’ mean ‘I go’, ‘you go’ and ‘she, he, it goes’ respectively.
‘Vamos’, ‘vais’ and ‘van’ mean ‘we go’, ‘you all go’ and ‘they go’.
A present-tense form of 'ir' + a + infinitive means 'going to' + infinitive. It expresses future plans.
'Para' + infinitive means 'in order to' + infinitive. It describes a purpose.
keywords: the basic form of the verb, with no particular subject or tense indicated

2056.name: Mon temps libre: subject pronouns, -er verbs and 'aimer' + infinitive
2056.outcome: I can talk about what I do and what I like doing in my free time.
points: Most final consonants and final letter 'e' are silent, [-er/-ez/-é] all make the same sound and [on] is a nasal sound.
-er verbs take the following endings in the present tense: je-e, tu-es, il/elle/on-e, nous-ons, vous-ez, ils/elles-ent.
'on' can mean 'we' or you/people and 'vous' can be informal plural as well as formal.
'il(s)' and 'elle(s)' can be used for things (as well as people) and mean 'it' or 'they'.
Two-verb constructions with 'aimer' are used to say what we like doing.
keywords: the basic form of the verb, with no particular subject or tense indicated
represents the person, people or thing(s) doing the verb e.g. I, we, they

2057.name: Qui fait quoi?: -re verbs like 'prendre' and 'entendre'
2057.outcome: I can talk about who does what using a range of -re and -er verbs.
points: Many -re verbs in the present tense follow the pattern of entendre: remove -re and add -s, -s, -, -ons, -ez, -ent.
Some -re verbs follow the pattern of prendre: remove -dre in nous/vous/ils/elles forms and add -nent in ils/elles form.
[en/an] sounds like 'enfant'. This is a common sound in -re verbs.
[e] sounds like 'je' but is lengthened to sound like [ê/è] in ils/elles form of verbs like prendre: ils prennent.
-er verbs and -re verbs can be usefully combined to write/talk about my and others' daily activities.
keywords: an example of the most common group of -re verbs, meaning ‘to hear’
the basic form of the verb, with no particular subject or tense indicated

2058.name: Une personne intéressante: -re verbs like 'traduire' and 'écrire'
2058.outcome: I can use a range of -re and -er verbs to describe somebody's activities and interests.
points: Some -re verbs in the present tense follow the pattern of 'traduire' (-s added to stem for 'nous/vous/ils/elles' forms)
[s] is pronounced as in 'maison' when between two vowels.
The verb 'écrire' and its derivatives are conjugated differently (-v added to stem in 'nous/vous/ils/elles' forms).
Four groups of -re verbs are verbs like 'entendre', verbs like 'prendre', verbs like 'traduire' and verbs like 'écrire'.
All four groups of -re verbs can be combined with -er verbs to describe somebody's interests and achievements.
keywords: an example of the most common group of -re verbs, meaning ‘to hear’
an example of a further group of -re verbs, meaning ‘to translate’

2059.name: On part pour la France: -ir verbs like 'choisir' and 'partir', adjectives
2059.outcome: I can use -ir verbs and adjectives to describe a visit to a landmark in France.
points: Adjectives often change their spelling for feminine and plural forms. Those ending in -e do not change in the feminine.
Adjectives beau, nouveau and vieux have feminine forms: belle, nouvelle and vieille. Beau and nouveau add -x in plural.
Many -ir verbs in the present follow the pattern of choisir: remove -ir and add -is, -is, -it, -issons, -issez, -issent.
Many -ir verbs follow the pattern of 'partir': remove -(t)ir and add: -s, -s, -t, -ons, -ez, -ent.
The sounds [i] like 'midi', [s/ss] like 'saucisse' and [r] like 'rue' are common in verbs like 'choisir' and 'partir'.
keywords: French verb meaning to choose, choosing
French verb meaning to leave, leaving.

2060.name: Des endroits touristiques: -ir verbs like 'venir', position of adjectives
2060.outcome: I can use adjectives before and after nouns with -ir verbs like venir to describe and justify visiting places in France.
points: Many adjectives come after the noun in French.
Adjectives that come before the noun fit into five categories: BRAGS (Beauty, Rank, Age, Good/Bad and Size/quantity).
Some -ir verbs in the present follow the pattern of venir. The stem is vien(n) in all but the nous and vous forms.
[ien] is pronounced like 'bien'. [e] can be lengthened to sound like [ê/è] in the ils/elles forms of verbs like venir.
Pour + infinitive can be used to give reasons.
keywords: the placement of adjectives within a sentence before or after the noun
to, in order to; often used to give reasons

2061.name: Au château de Versailles: -ir verbs like 'ouvrir' (singular)
2061.outcome: I can use singular -ir verbs like 'ouvrir' alongside other -ir verb groups and adjectives to describe a tourist experience.
points: [ou] is pronounced like 'nous' and [u] is pronounced like 'tu'.
-ir verbs like ouvrir have the same present tense verb endings as regular -er verbs.
Four groups of -ir verbs are: verbs like choisir, verbs like partir, verbs like venir and verbs like ouvrir.
When using adjectives, it's important to know which ones precede and which follow the noun.
Le château de Versailles is a palace near Paris built by Louis XIV, famous for the Hall of Mirrors and beautiful gardens
keywords: French verb meaning to choose, choosing
an example of a group of -ir verbs, meaning 'to open'
French verb meaning to leave, leaving.

2062.name: Une visite scolaire: -ir verbs like 'ouvrir' (plural)
2062.outcome: I can understand discussions about cultural history by applying knowledge of verbs like 'ouvrir', a range of pronouns and new vocabulary.
points: All syllables are sounded fairly equally in French words, but there is usually a slight emphasis on the last syllable.
-ir verbs like ouvrir have the same present tense verb endings as regular -er verbs: e, es, e, ons, ez, ent.
The pronouns 'ils' and 'elles', meaning 'they', can refer to people or things.
The pronoun 'vous', meaning 'you', can refer to one person (formally) or more than one person (formally or informally).
Context and surrounding lanuage clarify the correct meaning of ils, elles and vous.
keywords: an example of a group of -ir verbs, meaning 'to open'
pronouncing one syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word
French pronoun meaning 'you' (when talking to more than one person)

2063.name: Des monuments historiques: 'il y a' and 'il n'y a pas'
2063.outcome: I can use ‘il y a’ and ‘il n'y a pas’ to describe what there is and isn't at historical sites.
points: Words ending in a consonant + -re(s) stress the vowel before the consonant and the -r is said very softly e.g. 'ouvres'.
'Il y a un/une/des' is used to say ‘there is’ or ‘there are’. The article agrees with the gender and number of the noun.
To say 'there isn't' or 'there aren't' we use il n'y a pas. After this, all articles change to de or d' before a vowel.
keywords: pronouncing one syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word

2064.name: Des monuments commémoratifs: contraction of definite article after 'à'
2064.outcome: I can apply rules about the contraction of definite articles after ‘à’ in the context of commemorating historical events.
points: Words ending in a consonant + -le(s) or consonant + -re(s) stress the vowel before the consonant, e.g., 'terrible'.
'à' + definite article combine to make au/à la/à l’ or aux, depending on the gender, quantity and spelling of the noun.
'à' can be translated as 'at', 'to', 'in' and 'on' depending on its place and use in the sentence.
Conflict and independence movements in Algeria and Senegal shaped their identities and relations with France.
keywords: pronouncing one syllable more heavily than other syllables in a word

2065.name: Un nouvel élève: yes/no questions with inversion, intonation and 'est-ce que'
2065.outcome: I can understand and form questions in the present tense using intonation, inversion and 'est-ce que' to get to know somebody new.
points: Yes/no questions can be formed by raising the intonation at the end of the sentence.
Yes/no questions can be formed by inversion, which means swapping the position of the subject and the verb.
Yes/no questions can also be formed by adding est-ce que to a statement. Est-ce que becomes est-ce qu' before a vowel.
In French there is no word for 'do/does' in yes/no questions.
keywords: rise and fall of the voice in speaking
when the subject pronoun and the verb switch place to form a question

2066.name: Une nouvelle vie en France: liaison, questions, jouer à/de, negation
2066.outcome: I can use ne…pas and ne…jamais for negation, jouer à/de to describe playing sports and instruments, and ask questions about new experiences.
points: When the next word begins with a vowel, -s and -t are pronounced, rather than being silent final consonants.

2067.name: Une nouvelle vie en France: negation
2067.outcome: I can use 'ne...rien' and 'ne...personne', along with 'ne...pas' and 'ne...jamais', to express a range of negative meanings.

To say 'nothing', use ne...rien. The short form verb goes between the two parts in both single and two-verb structures.
To say 'no one', use ne...personne. The verb goes between ne and personne in single-verb structures: je n'aide personne.
In two-verb structures with 'ne... personne', personne goes to the end, after both verbs: je ne vais dessiner personne.

2068.name: On organise des visites: reflexive pronouns, direct object pronouns
2068.outcome: I can use singular reflexive pronouns and singular direct object pronouns to express a range of actions and thoughts in the context of cultural visits.
points: Use reflexive pronouns (me, te, se...) before the verb when subject and object of the verb are the same person.

To replace a noun that is the object, use direct object pronouns le/la/l' before the verb to mean 'him', 'her' or 'it'.

2069.name: Ça ne vous intéresse pas? Direct object pronouns, negation
2069.outcome: I can use direct object pronouns and negation to convey what I and other people experience during visits and events.
points: A direct object pronoun replaces a noun that is the object of the verb. It comes before the verb.

2070.name: On va à un concert: direct object pronouns, reflexive pronouns and negation
2070.outcome: I can use direct object pronouns, reflexives, negation and new vocabulary to accurately convey descriptions and opinions.

2071.name: Ça t'intéresse? Direct and indirect pronouns me and te
2071.outcome: I can recognise and understand the role of indirect object pronouns 'me' and 'te' in the context of exploring museums.
points: Use me and te before the verb when 'me' or 'you' is the object of the verb: elle me trouve (she finds me).

Me and te are used frequently in dialogue between two people.

2072.name: Les musées français: Indirect object pronouns 'me' and 'te'
2072.outcome: I can confidently use indirect object pronouns 'me' and 'te' in dialogue about French museums
points: Use me and te when 'me' or 'you' is indirectly receiving the action of the verb: elle me donne un cadeau (gives to me).

[gn] is pronounced like 'ligne', [th] like 'thé', j like [jour] and [r] like 'rue'.

2073.name: Un musée décolonisé: Indirect object pronouns 'me' and 'te'
2073.outcome: I can use direct and indirect object pronouns to express opinions and react to others' points of view in the context of cultural heritage.
points: Use me and te when 'me' or 'you' is indirectly receiving the action of the verb: elle me donne un cadeau (gives to me).

2074.name: Une soirée chez amis: Direct object pronouns (le, la and l')
2074.outcome: I can use singular direct object pronouns to ask and answer questions in social situations.
points: To replace a noun that is the object, use direct object pronouns le/la/l' before the verb to mean 'him', 'her' or 'it'.

2075.name: Une famille française: indirect object pronouns 'lui' and 'vous'

2076.name: Une famille multiculturelle: direct and indirect object pronouns

2077.name: Qui a écrit...? Perfect tense with predictable and irregular past participles

2105.outcome: I can use the conditional with vouloir, alongside modal verbs, to express future wishes and career plans.
points: The sound [ai] sounds like 'vrai'.
Modal verbs state necessity or possibility and are commonly followed by a second verb as an infinitive.
The verb vouloir can be used in the conditional to express a wish. It can be followed by a noun or an infinitive.
The 1st, 2nd, 3rd person forms of vouloir in the conditional all sound the same: je voudrais, tu voudrais, il voudrait.
keywords: describes what could or would happen under certain conditions
verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want
part of the verb that appears in all forms

2106.name: Une orientation qui m'attire: extended writing and speaking
2106.outcome: I can understand descriptions of a range of different jobs and express my interests and wishes for a future career.
points: Modal verbs and the conditional with vouloir are helpful for describing work tasks and future career hopes and plans.
The conditional with vouloir can be used to personalise your writing and speaking.
Creating a checklist for range of language and another for accuracy can enhance the quality of extended writing.
When developing a personal response it's helpful to use reference materials to look up new vocabulary.
keywords: form of verb used to express what would happen
verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want

2107.name: On cherche un boulot: adjectives into adverbs
2107.outcome: I can apply rules to convert adjectives into adverbs to add detail when discussing jobs and finding work.
points: [en/an] sound like 'enfant', [è] sounds like 'tête' and [i] sounds like 'midi'.
Some adverbs are formed by adding -ment to the feminine form of adjectives when the English adverb equivalent is -ly.
Where the adjective ends in e in the masculine form, add -ment to form the adverb e.g. rapide - rapidement.
Some adverbs are formed by dropping -ant(e)/-ent (e) and adding -(am)ment/-(em)ment when the English equivalent is -ly.

2108.name: Comment se mettre au travail? Word patterns
2108.outcome: I can use my knowledge of word families to expand my range of language.
points: Ordinal numbers are created by (removing -e and) adding -ième to a number: deuxième, onzième.
in- or im- can be added to adjectives, adverbs or nouns to give the opposite meaning. English equivalent is un- or in-.
The letter [x] can be heard before a vowel. This is called liaison and is common in ordinal numbers.
[in] sounds like 'train' and [im] sounds like 'faim': incorrect, impossible.
keywords: number form that shows how many of something there are
tells you the order of something, e.g., 'first', 'second', 'third', and is used with dates

2109.name: Les pour et les contre d'un travail: extended writing and speaking
2109.outcome: I can discuss the advantages and disadvantages of jobs, adapting words to different parts of speech and to create opposite meaning.
points: Pre-rehearsal, focusing on range of language and accuracy of pronunciation, improves performance in speaking tasks.
Being able to apply word patterns, such as creating antonyms or adverbs from adjectives, expands our vocabulary.
Listening to texts and identifying sound-spelling links is crucial to good pronunciation of trickier sounds e.g. im/in.
keywords: a word that has the opposite meaning to another word

2110.name: Quel boulot? past tense questions; interrogative and demonstrative adjectives
2110.outcome: I can ask about workplaces using 'what' and 'which' questions in the perfect tense and respond using 'this' and 'that' with nouns.
points: To ask perfect tense questions using question words, add question word before the inverted auxiliary verb.
Use interrogative adjectives quel, quelle, quels, quelles to ask 'which?'.
Use demonstrative adjectives ce, cet, cette, ces to mean 'this/that/those' They often answer the question 'which?'.
[qu] sounds like 'question' or 'quatre'. [c/ç] sound like 'ici'.
keywords: a type of adjective used to signal a specific person, place or thing
a question word that appears before a noun; in Spanish this includes 'cuánto' (how much)

2111.name: Quelques difficultés au travail: past tense questions, indefinite adjectives
2111.outcome: I can ask and answer questions in the perfect tense to discuss experiences in the workplace, and use indefinite adjectives to describe people and things.
points: To ask a question in the perfect tense, use inversion, intonation or est-ce que.
t-liaison is common in inversion questions in the perfect tense: A-t-il gagné?
Indefinite adjectives are used to describe a noun in a non-specific sense. They go before the noun they describe.
Même(s)', 'autre(s)', and 'quelque(s)', meaning 'same', 'other' and 'some', agree in number with the noun.
'Tout le' meaning 'whole' or 'all' agrees in number and gender. 'Chaque' (each) and 'plusieurs' (several) do not change.
keywords: a type of adjective that describes a noun in an non-specific way; in English this includes 'few' and 'some'
the pronounced -t- between the subject pronoun and verb in perfect tense inversion questions

2112.name: Au boulot: extended writing and speaking
2112.outcome: I can describe work scenarios using a range of new and revisited vocabulary and I can ask and answer questions about past events.
points: [au/eau] sounds like 'gauche', [ou] sounds like 'nous', [u] sounds like 'tu', [ch] sounds like 'chercher'.
Extended reading texts can be exploited to enrich our vocabulary and use of complex structures.
Writing task instructions must be read carefully and answers planned to ensure coverage of all the main points.
keywords: a range of grammatical features that enable more detailed communication
relationship between letters and their sounds

2113.name: Travailler en France: questions in present tense, relative clauses
2113.outcome: I can ask and answer questions in the present tense relating to working in France and I can use relative clauses with 'qui'.
points: Questions are formed by subject-verb inversion, adding est-ce que or intonation. Question words can be added to start.
A relative clause provides more information about a noun or pronoun from the previous clause.
Qui means 'who?' in a question, but it also means 'who', 'which', or 'that' in the middle of a sentence.
keywords: pronounced like a hard 'c' followed by [i], as in the word 'equipo'
a type of subordinate clause that begins with a relative pronoun

2114.name: Des industries françaises: relative clauses
2114.outcome: I can understand longer texts about French industry and jobs, with extended sentences including a range of relative pronouns.
points: When the relative pronoun relates to the object of the sentence, we use 'que' instead of 'qui'.
Où and quand can also be used in relative clauses to detail where or when something happens.
[qu] sounds like 'question' or 'quatre', [en/an] sound like 'enfant' and [e] sounds like 'je'.
Dont is another relative pronoun; it means 'of which' or 'whose'.
keywords: adds information about the object in the main clause
a pronoun that introduces a relative clause e.g. qui, que

2115.name: Une industrie qui m'intéresse: extended writing and speaking
2115.outcome: I can understand longer texts about French industry and jobs and I can use a range of relative pronouns to extend my sentences.
points: Being able to ask questions in different tenses, as well as answer them, is key to successful communication.
Using qui, que, où and quand in relative clauses provides more information and adds complexity.
[qu] sounds like 'question' or 'quatre', [en/an] sound like 'enfant' and [e] sounds like 'je'.
keywords: a type of subordinate clause that begins with a relative pronoun
a pronoun that introduces a relative clause e.g. qui, que

2116.name: Le chef: voir, boire, croire and faire in present, the imperative
2116.outcome: I can use a range of irregular present tense verbs to describe people's roles at work and I can recognise the imperative.
points: The verbs voir (to see), boire (to drink), croire (to believe) and faire (to do, make) are irregular in the present.
The imperative is used to give instructions, commands or advice to one or more people.
The imperative exists in the second person singular (tu), first person plural (nous) and second person plural (vous).
[ai] sounds like 'vrai', [oi] sounds like 'voir' and [oy] sounds like envoyer.
keywords: a mood used to tell somebody to do something or give instructions or commands
a verb that does not follow the regular rules

2117.name: Collègues et amis: the imperative
2117.outcome: I can use the imperative when talking to friends and in more formal situations to give instructions or advice.
points: The imperative is used to tell somebody to do something, give commands and advice.
The imperative is the ‘tu’, ‘nous’ and ‘vous’ present tense verb; for -er verbs, it is the ‘tu’ form minus the -s.
The subject pronoun is not used e.g. Parle! Negative elements go around the imperative verb e.g. Ne parle pas!
It is important to distinguish between informal (tu) and formal (vous) situations when using the imperative.
keywords: a mood used to tell somebody to do something or give instructions or commands

2118.name: Je voudrais postuler: extended speaking, role-play
2118.outcome: I can ask and answer questions in a role-play scenario applying for a part time job, using a range of language and the formal register.
points: The imperative is used in a wide range of scenarios such as recipe instructions, job adverts and giving commands.
Using the imperative in conversation enables the speaker to give instructions and advice.
In a role-play scenario it is important to consider who you are talking to, and whether to use the 'tu' or 'vous' form.
Planning a speaking task answer carefully, pre-rehearsal, and immediate repetition of the task improve performance.
keywords: a mood used to tell somebody to do something or give instructions or commands

2119.name: Une rencontre: verbs like 'connaitre' in present tense
2119.outcome: I can recognise and use a range of verbs like connaitre in the present tense in the context of meeting new friends.
points: Connaitre is conjugated as follows in the present tense: connais, connais, connait, connaissons, connaissez, connaissent
Verbs like connaitre are disparaitre, apparaitre, paraitre, naitre.
An [o] sound can be open, as in 'porte', or closed, as in 'photo'. An [ô] is a closed sound.
keywords: tells the reader the action is happening now

2120.name: Avec mes amis: verbs like connaitre in present and perfect tense
2120.outcome: I can use a range of verbs like connaitre in the present and perfect tense to discuss friendships.
points: The past participles of most verbs like connaitre are formed with a 'u' ending e.g. connu, disparu, paru.
The past participle of 'naitre' is 'né(e)(s)'.
Past participles used with être must agree in gender and number with the subject of the verb.
[u] sounds like 'tu' and [é] sounds like 'écrire'.
keywords: verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb
2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'

2121.name: Avec mes amis: extended writing and speaking
2121.outcome: I can describe encounters and friendships past and present using a range of regular and irregular verbs.
points: Extended reading texts can be exploited to enrich our vocabulary and use of complex structures in familiar topics.
It is important to plan the use of tenses and the inclusion of regular and irregular verbs when creating a longer text.
Use of reference sources can help to create a personal response.
One present tense in French translates the simple present and the present continuous; important when describing a photo.
Careful planning, pre-rehearsal and immediate repetition help to improve performance in speaking tasks.
keywords: describes events happening right now: 'I am doing'
verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'

2122.name: Ce week-end: impersonal verbs
2122.outcome: I can use impersonal verbs to tell the time, describe weather, say what there is and what is necessary in the context of making plans.
points: An impersonal verb is a verb and subject that don't refer to a particular person or thing.
To say what time it is use impersonal verb il est + number + heure (s) + minutes.
Il est + adjective + de + infinitive can be used to express it is difficult/easy/forbidden to + a verb.
Il fait (with weather expressions), il y a (there is/are) and il faut (it is necessary) are useful impersonal verbs.
[y] and [i] sounds like 'midi' and 'physique'.
keywords: a verb that doesn't refer to a particular person or thing, and whose subject is most often 'il' (it)

2123.name: On se retrouve: impersonal verbs
2123.outcome: I can use impersonal verbs to say what is better, what is worth it and what is missing in the context of meeting up with friends.
points: t- liaison is common after impersonal verbs il est, il faut so it's important to look out for vowels following these.
il est + adjective + de + infinitive can be used to express it is difficult/easy/forbidden to + a verb.
Impersonal verbs il vaut mieux (it's better) and il vaut la peine de (it's worth) are followed by the infinitive.
Impersonal verb 'il manque' is used with a noun to express that something 'is missing'.
keywords: a verb that doesn't refer to a particular person or thing, and whose subject is most often 'il' (it)

2124.name: Projets pour le week-end: extended writing and speaking
2124.outcome: I can use a range of impersonal verbs in speaking and writing about plans for the weekend with friends.
points: Using a range of impersonal verbs to your writing and speaking adds variety and complexity.
Plan a speaking task answer carefully, pre-rehearse, and immediately repeat the task to improve performance.
When a speaking scenario involves talking to a single friend, use the 'tu' form of the verb.
keywords: a phrase or expression whose meaning we don't translate word-for-word, e.g. 'it's raining cats and dogs'
a verb that doesn't refer to a particular person or thing, and whose subject is most often 'il' (it)

2125.name: Que faisais-tu quand...? The imperfect tense with regular verbs ('be' + ing)
2125.outcome: I can describe what I and others were doing and what was happening using the imperfect tense.
points: The imperfect tense is used to describe what was happening or what you were doing when something else happened.
For imperfect of regular verbs remove -ons from 'nous' present tense and add: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.
[ai] sounds like 'vrai', [on] is a nasal sound like 'non', and [ez] sounds like 'écrire'.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
relationship between letters and their sounds

2127.name: Quand j'étais petit: the imperfect tense with regular verbs ('used to')
2127.outcome: I can describe what I and others used to do when we were younger using the imperfect tense of regular verbs.
points: The imperfect tense is used to describe what you 'used to' do when you were younger/in the past.
For imperfect of regular verbs remove -ons from 'nous' present tense and add:-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient
Most final consonants are silent, and this is important in imperfect verb endings e.g. -ais, -ait
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

2128.name: Activités avant et aujourd'hui: extended speaking, photo description
2128.outcome: I can successfully combine imperfect and present tenses to compare and contrast past and current activities in speaking, and I can accurately translate the imperfect tense into English.
points: The imperfect tense is used to describe what you 'used to' do and what 'was happening' or you 'were doing'.
When translating the imperfect tense, think carefully about which English meaning would make most sense for the context.
Combining the imperfect tense and the present tense is a useful way to contrast past and present activities.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

2129.name: Ma ville avant: imperfect of 'être', 'avoir' and 'faire'
2129.outcome: I can talk about what my town used to be like in the past using the imperfect tense of regular and irregular verbs.
points: 'avoir' and 'faire' have regular stems in the imperfect tense: 'av-' and 'fais-'.
'être' has an irregular stem in the imperfect tense: 'ét-'.
'être', 'avoir' and 'faire' have regular endings in the imperfect tense: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.
'il y avait' is the imperfect tense form of 'il y a', meaning 'there used to be'.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

2130.name: La transformation des villes: imperfect of être, avoir and faire
2130.outcome: I can describe the changes taking place in towns using the imperfect and present tenses to contrast past and present.
points: The imperfect tense is used to describe how something or someone 'used to' be and what regularly happened in the past.
'il y avait' is the imperfect tense form of 'il y a', and means 'there used to be'.
When a word ending in a normally silent consonant is followed by a mute 'h', the consonant is heard in liaison.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'

2131.name: La vie en ville: extended writing and speaking, photo description
2131.outcome: I can describe a town in detail, using the imperfect and present tenses. I can describe a photo and draw comparisons between two photos.
points: We use present tense for describing a photo, but a range of tenses, including imperfect, to extend the discussion.
Use 'plus' and 'moins' followed by adjectives and 'plus de' and 'moins de' followed by nouns for contrasts.
Immediate repetition of a speaking task, with reduced support, improves performance.
It's important to plan to incorporate a range of past, present and future tenses when writing an extended text.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
a naming word for people, places or things

2132.name: Chez moi, chez toi: prepositions and emphatic pronouns 'moi', 'toi'...
2132.outcome: I can use a range of prepositions and emphatic pronouns to contrast where I and other people live.
points: Emphatic pronouns are often used after prepositions.
Emphatic pronouns include 'moi' ('me') and 'toi' ('you'). They apply only to people, not things.
'Sans' (without), 'pour' (for), 'avant' (before) and 'chez' (at the house/place of) are followed by emphatic pronouns.
[an] sounds like 'enfant' and [oi] sounds like 'voir'.
keywords: used to emphasise the subject of a sentence, in comparisons, and after 'c'est'
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

2133.name: Ma ville, mon pays: prepositions and emphatic pronouns lui, elle, eux, elles
2133.outcome: I can describe my area in detail and describe people's roles within it using prepositions and emphatic pronouns.
points: [ui] sounds like 'huit' and [eu] sounds like 'deux'.
Emphatic pronouns can be used for emphasis of the subject, e.g. 'Moi, j'adore le chocolat!'.
Other emphatic pronouns are 'lui' ('him'), 'elle' ('her'), 'eux' ('them') and 'elles' ('them').
Emphatic pronouns are used with 'à' to express possession, e.g. 'Il est à toi, ce cahier?'.
keywords: used to emphasise the subject of a sentence, in comparisons, and after 'c'est'
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

2134.name: La vie quotidienne ici et ailleurs: extended speaking and writing
2134.outcome: I can compare daily life in different countries in speaking and writing, using prepositions and emphatic pronouns.
points: 'Moi', 'toi', 'lui', 'elle', 'eux', and 'elles' mean 'me', 'you', 'him', 'her', and 'them' as emphatic pronouns.
Emphatic pronouns can also be used after a comparative, e.g. 'il est plus sérieux que toi'.
Planning a speaking task answer carefully, pre-rehearsal and immediate repetition of the task improve performance.
keywords: form of adjective or adverb used to compare people, things or ideas
used to emphasise the subject of a sentence, in comparisons, and after 'c'est'

2135.name: Découvrir d'autres pays: prepositions and emphatic pronouns 'nous' and 'vous'
2135.outcome: I can discuss the advantages and disadvantages of living abroad, focusing on the use of prepositions and emphatic pronouns.
points: Nasal vowel sounds occur when one or more vowels precede a nasal consonant e.g. an, am, ain, on, en.
The emphatic pronouns 'nous' and 'vous' are used for 'us' and 'you' (plural/formal).
sans (without), pour (for), avant (before) and chez (at the house/place of) are all followed by emphatic pronouns.
keywords: used to emphasise the subject of a sentence, in comparisons, and after 'c'est'
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

2136.name: Découvrir de grandes villes: prepositions and emphatic pronouns nous and vous
2136.outcome: I can draw comparisons between different English- and French-speaking cities.
points: Nous and vous are the emphatic pronouns for us and you (plural/formal).
Emphatic pronouns often follow prepositions, e.g. pour nous, avant vous.
When a nasal vowel such as [an] is followed by a vowel, it is no longer a nasal sound but an oral vowel, e.g. ami.
Extended listening and reading texts can be exploited to enrich our vocabulary and use of complex structures.
keywords: used to emphasise the subject of a sentence, in comparisons, and after 'c'est'
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

4804.name: Où habiter: extended writing
4804.outcome: I can write about different places to live using a writing frame for support.
points: 'Moi', 'toi', 'lui', 'elle', 'nous', 'vous', 'eux', elles mean me, you, him, her, us, you and them as emphatic pronouns.
It is important to plan both the ideas and language needed and to think about structure when writing a longer text.
keywords: form of verb used to express what would happen
used to emphasise the subject of a sentence, in comparisons, and after 'c'est'
tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

2137.name: Au lycée: future plans with 'aller' + infinitive
2137.outcome: I can talk about what I will and won't do in terms of studies after my GCSEs using the future structure 'aller' + infinitive.
points: The present tense of 'aller' + infinitive means 'going to' + infinitive and describes future actions and events.
Negation is two elements, e.g. 'ne … pas' or 'ne... jamais', going around the main verb to express a negative meaning.
To negate future ideas, put 'ne … pas' around the conjugated part of 'aller', followed by the infinitive.
keywords: two elements e.g. ne … pas around the main verb expressing negative meaning

2138.name: Mes études: 'aller' + infinitive, future tense singular -er verbs
2138.outcome: I can use 'aller + infinitive' and the simple future of -er verbs to say what I or someone else will do in the context of studying.
points: [r] sounds like 'rue' and [a] sounds like 'animal'.
Aller + infinitive is a 2-verb structure to express what is going to happen.
The simple future in French is a 1-verb future tense meaning will + verb. It's 'simple' as it's formed with one word.
We conjugate the future tense of -er verbs for je, tu, il/elle/on by adding the endings -ai, -as, -a to the infinitive.

2139.name: Étudier à Paris: 'aller' + infinitive, future tense -er verbs
2139.outcome: I can discuss the opportunities for studying in France, using future structures to make plans and suggestions for the future.
points: 'Aller' + infinitive describes what is going to happen; it tends to be used in more informal conversation and writing.
The simple future expresses what will happen; it tends to be used in more formal contexts for predictions or promises.
Most consonants at the end of words are silent, e.g. 'tu mangeras'.
It is helpful to practise verb manipulation, e.g. 'jouer', 'je joue', 'je vais jouer', 'je jouerai'.

2140.name: Les événements culturels: 'aller' + infinitive, future tense plural -er verbs
2140.outcome: I can understand texts about key cultural events and equal rights in France and can recognise the use of future structures.
points: Use part of the verb 'aller' plus an infinitive to express going to do e.g. Elles vont visiter Paris.
Conjugate the simple future of -er verbs for nous, vous, ils/elles by adding the endings -ons, -ez, -ont to infinitive.
There are many popular cultural events in France each year, such as the 'marche des fiertés' in Paris.

2141.name: Cet été à Paris: 'aller' + infinitive, future tense -er verbs
2141.outcome: I can use the simple future of -er verbs accurately to talk about my own and others' future plans for a visit to Paris.
points: Conjugate the future tense of -er verbs by adding the endings -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont to the infinitive.
It is helpful to practise spoken recall of present, aller + infinitive, and simple future, as part of a 'verb workout'.
In French the stress or emphasis usually falls on the last syllable of a word or phrase.

2142.name: On va fêter: extended writing and speaking, picture task
2142.outcome: I can refer to future events both in formal writing and in informal speaking tasks and demonstrate my awareness of Francophone cultural events.
points: Use part of the verb 'aller' plus an infinitive to express going to do e.g. Elles vont visiter Paris.
Conjugate the simple future of -er verbs by adding the correct ending to the infinitive.
Use 'aller + infinitive' and the simple future to speak and write about planned visits to cultural events.
Use PALM when describing a photo and BORDER when planning extended pieces of writing.

2143.name: On y va: present and future tense of 'aller' and 'faire'
2143.outcome: I can use common irregular verbs in the present and future tense when making summer plans.
points: The present tense forms of 'aller' and 'faire' are highly irregular and must be learnt.
French has just one present tense. Time adverbs differentiate between habitual (I do) and ongoing (I am doing) actions.
[i] sounds like 'midi' and [e] sounds like 'je'.
The simple future stem for the verb 'aller' is 'ir-'. Regular future endings are added to this stem.
The simple future stem for the verb 'faire' is 'fer-'. Regular future endings are added to this stem.
keywords: describes events happening right now: 'I am doing'
verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'

2144.name: J'aurai bientôt faim: present and future tense of 'avoir' and 'être'
2144.outcome: I can use irregular verbs 'avoir' and 'être' alongside regular -er verbs in the future tense to discuss future travel plans and events.
points: 'Avoir' + noun is sometimes used to translate the English 'be' + adjective, e.g. 'j'ai faim', 'j'aurai faim'.
The simple future stem for the verb 'être' is 'ser-'. Regular future endings are added to this stem.
The simple future stem for the verb 'avoir' is 'aur-'. Regular endings are added to this stem.
[au] sounds like 'gauche'.
keywords: part of the verb that appears in all forms

2145.name: Un tour en France: present and future tense of aller, avoir, faire and être
2145.outcome: I can use present and future tenses to describe plans for a future trip exploring France.
points: It is useful to practise recalling present, aller + infinitive, then simple future e.g. je suis, je vais être, je serai.
It is important to include regular and common irregular simple future verbs when writing about future plans.
Wherever possible in your writing, it is good to demonstrate that you can move between different tenses.

2146.name: Recherches en ligne: negation with 'ne...pas', 'ne...jamais' and 'ne...rien'
2146.outcome: I can research French travel information online and understand negation in written texts.
points: Use 'ne... pas' for saying what doesn't happen, 'ne... jamais' for 'never' and 'ne... rien' for 'nothing'.
Wrap 'ne... pas', 'ne... jamais' or 'ne... rien' around the conjugated verb to make the sentence negative.
With 'aller' + infinitive, the negative words wrap around the conjugated form of 'aller'.
keywords: two elements e.g. ne … pas around the main verb expressing negative meaning

2147.name: Faire mes valises: negation with 'ne... plus' and 'ne... pas encore'
2147.outcome: I can use new negative structures alongside known negatives to discuss preparations for summer travel.
points: 'Aller' + infinitive is used to say 'going to do', and the simple future is used to say 'will do'.
'Ne … plus' is a negative structure which means 'no longer' or 'not anymore', e.g. 'mon grand-père ne travaille plus'.
When 'plus' is used in a negative sentence, we do not usually hear the 's'.
'Ne … pas encore' means 'not yet' and is used with the perfect tense, e.g. 'je n'ai pas encore fait du ski'.
keywords: two elements e.g. ne … pas around the main verb expressing negative meaning

2148.name: J'ai acheté: negation
2148.outcome: I can use negative structures in a range of tenses, when discussing holidays, to add complexity to my writing and speaking.
points: Negation in French is two elements e.g. ne … pas around the main verb expressing negative meaning.
With ne … pas, ne … jamais and ne … rien in the past, put auxiliary verb (avoir or être) between ne and pas/jamais/rien.
‘Un’, ‘une’, ‘du’, ‘de la’ and ‘des’ change to ‘de’ after a negative e.g. Je ne mange pas de viande.
In formal speech, liaison can often be heard after negative structures ne … pas, ne … plus, and ne … jamais.
Using a range of negative structures with a range of tenses adds complexity to your writing.
keywords: two elements e.g. ne … pas around the main verb expressing negative meaning

2149.name: Une série addictive: negation with 'ne... pas de' and 'ne... ni... ni...'
2149.outcome: I can understand and use negative structures to enhance description of a TV series.
points: Indefinite articles (un, une, des) and partitive articles (du, de la, de l', des) change to 'de' after a negative.
[i] sounds like midi.
The negative structure 'ne... ni... ni...' means 'neither... nor'.
keywords: two elements e.g. ne … pas around the main verb expressing negative meaning
refers to parts of things; often means 'some' in English

2150.name: J'ai vu un film: negation with 'ne...pas de', 'ne...ni...ni...' and 'ne...que'
2150.outcome: I can use a range of new and revised negative structures in the past tense to discuss TV and cinema.
points: 'Ne... que' means 'only'. 'Que' follows the verb and precedes the noun, e.g. 'il ne regarde que des films'.
For 'neither... nor', 'ne' precedes the verb and each 'ni' precedes one of the negated qualities/nouns.
[-aill-/-ail] sounds like 'taille', [-ill-/-ille] sounds like 'fille'.
keywords: a structure meaning 'only' which is formed like a negative
two elements e.g. ne … pas around the main verb expressing negative meaning

2151.name: Streaming ou cinéma? Negation
2151.outcome: I can discuss the pros and cons of TV streaming and cinema, using a range of tenses and negative structures.
points: Using a range of negative structures with a range of tenses adds strength and subtlety to your points.
Take care when translating negatives into English. Consider word order carefully. Ne...que is not negative in English.
It is important to plan both the ideas and language needed and to think about structure when writing a longer text.
It is important to create a checklist both for range of language and for accuracy when creating a longer text.
keywords: two elements e.g. ne … pas around the main verb expressing negative meaning

2152.name: Les célébrités et les réseaux sociaux: extending vocabulary (AQA)
2152.outcome: I can understand texts about celebrities and their online presence, and acquire topic-specific vocabulary.
points: There are many cognates in this topic which can be used to infer meaning of surrounding words and understand context.
Reading texts can be exploited to enrich our vocabulary on current issues.
Cognates may look very similar to English but sound quite different so attention must be paid to pronunciation.
keywords: words with the same meaning and same or similar spelling in English and French

6171.name: La technologie informatique: extending vocabulary
6171.outcome: I can understand texts about the uses, pros and cons of technology, and adopt topic-specific vocabulary.
points: Listening and reading texts can be exploited to enrich our topic-specific vocabulary.
Listening and reading texts can be exploited to enrich our use of complex structures.
It is important to include rich and specific vocabulary when presenting arguments for or against something.
keywords: an impersonal verb meaning 'it is necessary, must'

7439.name: Les célébrités et les réseaux sociaux: extending vocabulary (Edexcel)
7439.outcome: I can understand texts about celebrities and their online presence, and acquire topic-specific vocabulary.
points: There are many cognates in this topic which can be used to infer meaning of surrounding words and understand context.
Reading texts can be exploited to enrich our vocabulary on current issues.
Cognates may look very similar to English but sound quite different so attention must be paid to pronunciation.
keywords: words with the same meaning and same or similar spelling in English and French

5653.name: Länder, Sprachen, Nationalitäten: nationality, 'sein', present tense weak verbs
5653.outcome: I can form nationality nouns to talk about people and events.
points: Some nouns behave like adjectives and take the same endings.
'Sein' is irregular in the present tense.
Present tense weak verbs are formed like 'lernen'.
keywords: a type of noun that takes the same endings as adjectives
an example of a weak verb in the present tense, meaning ‘to learn, learning'

5654.name: Wer ist Bella? Was macht sie? Present tense verbs, yes/ no questions
5654.outcome: I can differentiate simple present and present continuous in German when asking and answering questions.
points: There is just one present tense in German.
Time adverbs help to translate German present tense accurately.
Subject and verb swap to make yes/no questions in German.
keywords: describes events happening right now: 'I am doing'
verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'

5655.name: Identität: language and gender, plurals, weak masculine nouns, 'seit'
5655.outcome: I can use adjectival nouns and seit with the present tense.
points: Adjectival nouns behave like adjectives.
Weak masculine nouns such as ‘Name’ add (e)n in every form except singular nominative.
All dative plural nouns add-n, except plurals ending in -s.
'Seit' with the present tense communicates how long unfinished actions have been happening.
keywords: a type of noun that takes the same endings as adjectives
nouns that add -n when they are used in the dative plural
a small set of masculine nouns that add -(en) in all forms apart from the nominative singular

5656.name: Die Schweiz, Deutschland, Bayern: numbers, word order- inversion
5656.outcome: I can use numbers and Word Order 2 to learn facts about Germany and Switzerland.
points: Subject and verb are inverted in Word Order 2 (WO2).
German numbers are written as one word.
Say single digits before tens in German numbers.
keywords: inverts the subject and verb in a sentence

5657.name: Kultur in Deutschland: wh- question words
5657.outcome: I can use wh- questions to ask about German culture.
points: The German [v] sounds like the English [f].
The German [w] sounds like the English [v].
Open questions use a question word before the verb followed by the subject.
keywords: question words that mostly begin 'wh-' in English, such as 'where'; in German they are 'Fragewörter'

5658.name: Das Oktoberfest in Deutschland: plurals add umlaut/e, n, no change; translation
5658.outcome: I can use plural nouns to ask how many there are.
points: Add '-e', with or without an umlaut, to make most masculine nouns and some neuter nouns plural.
Words ending '-el', '-en' or '-er' may not change in the plural.
To make most feminine nouns plural, add '-n' or '-en'.
keywords: inverts the subject and verb in a sentence
form for nouns that refers to more than one person place, thing or idea: des Canadiens

5659.name: Deutsch lernen: compound nouns, 'Lieblings-' and 'Haupt-', translation
5659.outcome: I can use compound nouns, 'Lieblings-' and 'Haupt-' to add greater detail to nouns in the context of learning German.
points: Combine two or more words to create a compound noun.
'Lieblings-' creates compound nouns to mean 'favourite'.
'Haupt-' creates compound nouns to mean 'main'.
A literal translation of a compound noun into English can aid understanding but is not always accurate.
keywords: a prefix added to nouns to mean 'main'
a prefix added to nouns to mean 'favourite'
two or more nouns put together to make one longer noun

5660.name: Englisch lernen: 'haben', present tense weak verbs, negation with nicht and kein
5660.outcome: I can use present tense weak verbs, 'nicht' and 'kein' to talk about learning a language.
points: Nominative case is for nouns with sein, heißen and werden; accusative case is for object nouns with all other verbs.
The verb 'haben' is irregular.
Present tense weak verbs are formed like 'lernen'.
'Nicht' negates before the definite article (meaning 'not the'), adjectives, possessives, proper nouns and after verbs.
For negation before nouns, 'kein' replaces the indefinite article to mean 'not a', 'no'.
keywords: form(s) used for the object or 'receiver' of the action of the verb
negative article ‘no’, ‘not a, an, any’ - negates nouns preceded by the indefinite article
the adverb 'not', which negates the definite article ‘the’
the case used for the subject of a sentence

5662.name: Eine neue Sprache lernen: plural rules 4 - 6
5662.outcome: I can use plural rules to form plural nouns.
points: Some masculine and neuter nouns add '-er' with an umlaut, where possible, to form the plural.
Nouns borrowed from other langauges usually add '-s' to form the plural.
Female person nouns add '-nen' to form the plural.
The German short [a] sounds like the 'a' in 'Blatt'. The short [ä] is as in the plural 'Blätter'.
The German short [u] sounds like the 'u' in 'Unterschied'; the long [u] is as in 'Uhr'.
keywords: add -er to some masculine or neuter nouns, with or without umlaut on a, o, u
add -s to nouns borrowed from other languages; for example, 'Interviews'.
add -nen to all female person nouns; for example, 'Lehrerinnen'.

5663.name: Wissen ist Macht! 'Wissen', 'kennen', 'können'
5663.outcome: I can use 'wissen', 'kennen' and 'können' to talk about knowledge.
points: The SSCs [-ss-] and [-ß-] sound the same.
'Wissen' means to know with facts.
'Kennen' means to know someone or be familiar with something.
'Können' means to be able to, to know how to do something.
keywords: a modal verb meaning 'to be able to'

5664.name: Sprachen: word order, strong verbs, adjectives identical to adverbs
5664.outcome: I can use accurate word order to understand texts and write sentences about learning languages.
points: Word order one conjunctions do not change word order.
Word order three conjunctions like 'weil' send the verb to the end.
Most German adjectives can be used as adverbs.
Strong verbs in the present tense change the stem vowel in the 2nd and 3rd person singular.
keywords: word that connects ideas between clauses in a sentence
a verb which changes its vowel in the verb stem of some of its forms
(WO1) subject - verb - object; the standard word order in a German sentence, e.g., 'Ich lerne Deutsch.'
(WO3) sends the verb to the end of the sentence or clause after certain conjunctions

5665.name: Christine Thürmer: nominalisation of infinitive verbs, plural rules 7-9
5665.outcome: I can nominalise infinitive verbs and use plural nouns when reading and translating information about speakers of multiple languages.
points: To make single syllable feminine nouns plural, add '–e' and an umlaut where possible.
To make nouns ending in '–nis' plural, add –se.
To make some neuter nouns plural, add '-(e)n'.
Use any German infinitive as a noun by nominalising it as a neuter noun.
To turn noun-verb phrases to nouns, create compound nouns.
keywords: the process of making a noun from a verb or adjective
add 'e' and an umlaut where possible to single syllable feminine nouns; for example, 'die Städte'
add '-se' to nouns ending in '-is'; for example, 'die Ereignisse'
add '-(e)n' to some neuter nouns; for example, 'die Augen'

5666.name: Falsche Ideen: 'es gibt' vs 'da ist/sind', jemanden, niemanden, relative clauses
5666.outcome: I can use 'es gibt', 'da ist', and relative clauses to talk about cultural information and stereotypes.
points: 'Es gibt' means ‘there is’ and ‘there are’. It is a general statement that something exists.
Use 'es ist' and 'da ist' to point out what there is in a specific place at a specific moment in time.
Relative clauses add information about the noun in a main clause without starting another sentence.
Use the indefinite pronouns 'jemand' (someone) and 'niemand' (no-one) instead of a noun.
keywords: means 'there is' and points out what is in a specific place at a specific time
means 'there is, there are' and is a general statement that something exists
a type of subordinate clause that begins with a relative pronoun

5667.name: Drei starke Frauen: subject pronouns, relative clauses, historic present
5667.outcome: I can understand relative clauses and the historic present in an extended text.
points: Relative clauses add information about the noun in a main clause, without starting another sentence.
Some relative clauses are embedded in a main clause.
Match subject pronouns 'er', 'sie', 'es', 'sie' with the gender and number of a noun to mean 'it' and 'they'.
The historic present narrates events in the past to make them feel more immediate.
keywords: narrates events in the past using the present tense
a type of subordinate clause that begins with a relative pronoun
represents the person, people or thing(s) doing the verb e.g. I, we, they

5668.name: Eine interessante Person: extended writing
5668.outcome: I can plan, select language, and check for accuracy to write an extended text in German about an interesting person.
points: Planning to write involves organising ideas & selecting key structures, e.g., 'da ist', 'es gibt', 'jemand', 'niemand'.
Using a checklist helps to ensure an appropirate range of language is used, e.g., relative clauses, historic present.
Accuracy is enchanced by careful checking.
keywords: means 'there is' and points out what is in a specific place at a specific time
means 'there is, there are' and is a general statement that something exists
a type of subordinate clause that begins with a relative pronoun

5669.name: Neu in Deutschland: irregular past participles, perfect tense with 'haben'
5669.outcome: I can use the perfect tense with 'haben' and irregular past participles in the context of the experiences of Syrians in Germany.
points: The past participles of some verbs do not follow a pattern.
[ch] can be soft as in 'ich' or hard as in 'Buch'.
Use the perfect tense for actions completed in the past and the present for curret acctions and circumstances.
The German perfect tense has two English translations.
Use simple past for past experiences and present perfect to emphaise ongoing effects of past actions.
keywords: sound-symbol correspondence pronounced hard [ch] as in ‘Buch’ and soft [ch] as in ‘ich’
past participles which do not fit the pattern of weak or strong past participles

5670.name: Neu in Deutschland: 'hatte', 'war', 'es gab', imperfect tense singular & plural
5670.outcome: I can use the perfect and imperfect tenses to understand the recent experiences of a young person arriving to live and study in Germany.
points: Use the imperfect forms 'hatte', 'war', 'gab' to talk about the past instead of the perfect tense.
Imperfect weak verbs are formed like 'lernen'.
Imperfect strong verbs take the same endings as 'liegen'.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'

5671.name: Namibia: extended reading, extended writing
5671.outcome: I can read and understand an extended text, then plan and select language to write an extended text in German about Namibia, checking my work for accuracy.
points: Planning to write involves organising ideas and selecting language.
Using a checklist helps to ensure an appropriate range of language is used.
Reading a text aloud helps practise prounciation and supports understanding.
Reading and understanding an extended text needs attention to vocabulary, structures and a focus on required details.
Accuracy in reading and writing is enchanced by careful checking.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'

5673.name: Heidi: perfect tense -ieren verbs, perfect tense with adverbs
5673.outcome: I can use -ieren verbs and adverbs in the perfect tense to talk more precisely about past events in the context of well-known German literature.
points: The past participles of '-ieren' verbs don't start with 'ge-'. They end with '-iert'.
Use adverbs like 'nie', 'schon', and 'noch nicht' with the perfect tense to provide more information.
Many '-ieren' verbs are near cognates.
keywords: verbs which end in ‘ieren’; for example, 'fotografieren', 'studieren'
adverbs or adverbial phrases which denote time; for example, 'nie', 'schon', 'noch nicht'

5674.name: Matthias Maurer: yes/no questions in the perfect and imperfect tenses
5674.outcome: I can form yes/no questions in the perfect and imperfect tenses to ask questions about famous German speakers.
points: [er] at the end of a word is unstressed and sounds like the English ‘uh’.
The [r] in female people nouns is consonantal and is rolled at the back of the throat.
Change verbs to male person nouns by adding –er to a verb stem.
To form a yes/no question in the perfect tense, swap the subject and the verb and send the past participle to the end.
