To form a yes/no question in the imperfect tense, swap the subject and the verb.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
a noun for someone who performs the action of a verb, usually ending in -er; for example, worker - ‘Arbeiter’
2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'

5675.name: Marietta Slomka: dictation, extended translation
5675.outcome: I can use my knowledge of various grammar features to translate a text about a famous German speaker.
points: The past participles of '-ieren' verbs don't start with 'ge-'. They end with '-iert'.
Use adverbs like 'nie', 'schon', and 'noch nicht' with the perfect tense to provide more information.
To form a yes/no question in the perfect tense, swap the subject and the verb.
In dictation, check for grammatical accuracy as well as correct sound-symbol correspondences.
keywords: the relationship between language sounds and how they are written
adverbs or adverbial phrases which denote time; for example, 'nie', 'schon', 'noch nicht'

5676.name: Meine Familie: possessive adjectives, extended reading
5676.outcome: I can use possessive adjectives to talk about family.
points: Possessive adjectives describe who a noun belongs to.
Possessive adjectives change endings depending on gender and case.
An unstressed ‘er’ sounds like the English ‘uh’.
A vocalic ‘r’ sounds like the English ‘a’ or ‘ah’.
The consonantal ‘r’ is rolled at the back of the throat.

5677.name: Deutsche Influencer: comparatives, adding -keit and -heit
5677.outcome: I can form comparative adjectives to draw comparisons in the context of famous German influencers.
points: Turn an adjective into a comparative adjective by adding 'er'.
Some comparative adjectives are irregular.
Add ‘-keit’ to adjectives to mean '–ty' or '-ness'.
Add ‘-heit’ to adjectives to mean '–ty' or '–ness'.
keywords: turns an adjective into a noun, meaning ‘-ty’ or ‘-ness’
suffix added to adjectives or adverbs to form a noun; often corresponding to English '-ty', '-ness'
form of adjective or adverb used to compare people, things or ideas

5678.name: Meine Familie: possessive adjectives, dictation
5678.outcome: I can use possessive adjectives to talk about families and plans.
points: [ei] is pronounced like 'mein'.
Possessive adjectives describe who a noun belongs to.
Possessive adjectives change endings depending on gender and case.
The preposition ‘laut’ is followed by the dative.
keywords: a preposition meaning 'according to' which is followed by the dative

5679.name: Freunde: 'gern' and 'lieber', dictation, comparative adverbs
5679.outcome: I can use 'gern' and 'lieber' to write about activities that I like and prefer to do.
points: When [er] is the stressed syllable, it usually sounds like two short syllables: 'e-uh'.
When the syllable is unstressed, [-er] sounds like ‘uh’, most often at the end of the word.
Use a verb with 'gern' to mean 'like'.
Use a verb with 'lieber' to mean 'prefer'.
Add –er to turn adverbs into comparatives.
keywords: adverb meaning ‘gladly, liked to’ with the past tense

5680.name: Wie sind deine Familie und Freunde? Adding un-, word order, superlatives
5680.outcome: I can use the correct word order when giving my opinion about photos.
points: Add ‘un’ to adjectives for their negative or opposite meaning.
Use word order two after 'meiner Meinung nach', and adverbs of time, manner, place.
Use the superlative to express the highest degree of something, e.g., the most.
To form the superlative, use ‘am’ before the adjective/adverb, and then add ‘-sten’.
Use word order three after 'ich denke, dass' and 'ich glaube, dass'.
keywords: a form of adjective or adverb used to express the highest degree of a quality, e.g., 'the tallest', 'the most interesting'
sends the verb to the end
inverts the subject and verb in a sentence

5681.name: Familie und Freunde: translation, comprehension, conversation
5681.outcome: I can use a variety of vocabulary and grammatical structures to understand and talk about friends and family.
points: We use possessive adjectives frequently when talking about friends and family.
The adverb ‘gern’ is used with a verb to mean ‘like’; ‘lieber’ with a verb means ‘prefer’.
Add –er to turn adverbs into comparatives.
The imperfect tense in German is used most often to narrate past events in writing, so is often used in stories.
When answering conversation questions, strong answers are full sentences including extra detail, opinions and reasons.
keywords: form of adjective or adverb used to compare people, things or ideas
adverb meaning ‘gladly, liked to’ with the past tense
tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

5682.name: Familie: direct object pronouns, singular and plural
5682.outcome: I can use direct object pronouns to talk about family, famous people and things.
points: We use direct object pronouns to replace a noun that is the object or 'receiver' of the verb.
Direct object pronouns are: mich-me, dich-you, ihn-him, it, sie-she,it, es-it, uns-us, euch-you, Sie-you and sie-them.
Consonantal [r] makes a rolling sound at the beginning of a word or syllable and after a consonant.
Vocalic [r] has a gentle ‘ah’ sound after after a long vowel sound, in prefixes -er and -ver, and at the end of words.
keywords: replaces the noun receiving the action of the verb e.g. me, you, it, them

5685.name: Vorbilder: accusative definite articles, verbs with accusative prepositions
5685.outcome: I can use verbs and prepositions with the accusative case to describe events and feelings in the context of sports role models.
points: Some prepositions are always followed by the accusative case: 'durch', 'für', 'ohne', 'gegen'.
Masculine definite article 'der' changes to 'den' in the accusative case.
Some verbs are followed by prepositions which take the accusative case.
Verbs which are followed by prepositions often use different prepositions in English.
keywords: used with prepositions to indicate movement towards someone or something
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

5684.name: Frauen im Motorsport: da-compounds, wo-compounds
5684.outcome: I can ask and answer questions using da- and wo-compounds.
points: The prefix 'da-' is added to prepositions to refer back to something already mentioned and avoid repetition of the noun.
We use da-compounds for inanimate nouns. We use direct object pronouns for people and animals.
We use wo-compounds to ask questions with verbs that take prepositions.
'Wo' and 'da' become 'wor' and 'dar' before prepositions starting with a vowel.
The consonantal [r] makes a rolling sound at the back of the throat and the vocalic [r] has a gentle ‘ah’ sound.
keywords: prefix added to prepositions to avoid repetition of the noun
prefix added to prepositions to form questions

5686.name: Traditionen: da-compounds, 'damit' as conjunction and wo-compounds
5686.outcome: I can use da-compounds, object pronouns and wo-compounds to discuss German traditions and memories.
points: To refer back to something inanimate already mentioned, add da- or dar- to the beginning of a preposition.
As a da-compound, 'damit' means ‘with it/them’. As a conjunction, 'damit' means 'so that'.
Use direct or indirect object pronouns, not da-compounds, to replace animate nouns (people or animals).
Use wo- compounds to ask questions by adding wo- or wor- before the preposition.
keywords: word that connects ideas between clauses in a sentence
prefix added to prepositions to avoid repetition of the noun
a pronoun that replaces the object in a sentence
prefix added to prepositions to form questions

5687.name: Karneval: indirect object pronouns, verbs with indirect objects, 'bei', 'beim'
5687.outcome: I can use dative verbs, indirect object pronouns, and dative prepositions to discuss people and activities in the context of festivals.
points: The indirect object pronouns are 'mir', 'dir, 'ihm', 'ihr', 'einem', 'uns', 'euch', 'Ihnen' and 'ihnen'.
Some verbs, called dative verbs, take indirect objects.
Some dative verbs are impersonal verbs.
'Bei' means 'at' or 'with'. When used with masculine or neuter nouns, 'bei dem' becomes 'beim'.
The biggest ‘Karneval’ celebrations in Germany take place in Cologne.
keywords: preposition meaning 'at (the)' or 'with (the)', followed by the dative case
case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, from you, with them; takes the dative case

5688.name: Traditionen: 'jed-', dative verbs, translation
5688.outcome: I can use 'jed-' in different cases to talk about ‘each’ and ‘every’ and identify dative verbs and prepositions in the context of traditions.
points: The long German [e] can be written 'e', 'eh' or ‘ee’.
'Jed-' has different endings in the nominative, accusative and dative cases.
Some verbs take indirect objects. They are also called ‘dative verbs’.
[eu] can be written as 'eu' like in 'neu' and 'äu' like in 'Häuser'.
keywords: case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
determiner meaning ‘each, every’ which changes according to gender and case

5689.name: Weltreligionen und ihre Feste: expanding vocabulary, describing photos
5689.outcome: I can understand texts about different religions and festivals and I can describe a photo of a celebration using the present tense.
points: The acronym PALM is useful for describing photos. It stands for People, Action, Location, Mood.
It is useful to add opinions to personalise photo descriptions.
There is only one present tense in German. This is important to remember when describing what is happening in a photo.
keywords: describes events happening right now: 'I am doing'
verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'

5690.name: Beziehungen: reflexive and non-reflexive verbs, reciprocal verbs
5690.outcome: I can differentiate between reflexive and non-reflexive uses of verbs and use reflexive and reciprocal verbs to talk about relationships.
points: Some verbs are reflexive in German but their English translation does not have a reflexive meaning.
The meaning of a verb can change depending on its reflexive or non-reflexive use.
Reflexive use means the subject (doer) and object (receiver) of the action are the same.
With plural verbs, reflexive pronouns can also mean 'each other', if the action is reciprocal.
keywords: A reciprocal is the multiplicative inverse of any non-zero number. Any non-zero number multiplied by its reciprocal is equal to 1
describes an action where the subject and the object of the verb are the same

5691.name: Junge Pflegende: accusative and dative reflexive pronouns, 'welch-'
5691.outcome: I can use accusative and dative reflexive verbs to talk about caring for myself and others.
points: Most reflexive verbs use accusative reflexive pronouns: 'mich', 'dich', 'sich', 'uns', 'euch', 'sich'.
If sentences already have an accusative object, the reflexive pronoun must be in the dative.
The dative reflexive pronouns are 'mir', 'dir', 'sich', 'uns', 'euch', 'sich'.
The ending of 'welch-' depends on the gender and case of the noun that follows. It follows the same pattern as 'dies-'.
keywords: case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
used to indicate doing something to yourself, words like 'myself' and yourself'

5692.name: Freunde: 'wen' and 'wem' - interrogative, word order with reflexive questions
5692.outcome: I can ask and answer questions about friends and relationships using 'wer', 'wen', 'wem' and reflexive verbs.
points: The interrogative pronoun 'wer' becomes 'wen' when it is a direct object in the accusative.
The interrogative pronoun 'wer' becomes 'wem' when it is an indirect object in the dative.
Use a long [e] sound with 'wer', 'wen' and 'wem'.
In questions with reflexive verbs, only subject and verb swap position. The reflexive pronoun now follows the subject.
Where a verb is usually followed by a preposition, this comes before the question word, e.g., 'Mit wem?', 'Für wen?'.
keywords: used to indicate doing something to yourself, words like 'myself' and yourself'
question word meaning 'who' or 'whom' which changes according to case

5693.name: Hitzefrei: 'müssen' vs 'sollen', 'sollen' vs 'sollte'
5693.outcome: I can use 'müssen' and 'sollen' to discuss necessities and obligations.
points: Modal verbs express necessity, possibility, expectation or obligation and are used with a 2nd verb in the infinitive.
'Müssen' means ‘to have to, must’ and expresses necessity.
'Sollen' translates as ‘should’ and conveys strong obligation or command but also expresses probability.
'Sollte' expresses a softer style of obligation and may be translated as ‘ought to’.
keywords: verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want
modal verb meaning 'should, be supposed to, ought', used to express obligation, expectation or probability
form of 'sollen' expressing obligation in a softer, more polite way

5695.name: Was darf man ab wann? 'Dürfen' vs 'können', wh- questions and modal verbs
5695.outcome: I can use 'können' and 'dürfen' to describe what people are able to do and what people are allowed to do.
points: 'Dürfen' refers to permission required from another person to do something.
'Können' refers to the ability to do something or the possibiity of doing something.
Open questions use a question word before the verb, followed by the subject.
In open questions using a modal verb, the 2nd verb in the infinitive is at the end of the sentence.
keywords: modal verb meaning 'to be allowed to', 'may'
a modal verb meaning 'to be able to'
verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want
question words that mostly begin 'wh-' in English, such as 'where'; in German they are 'Fragewörter'

5696.name: Das Pfandsystem: word order with 'wenn', inversion, plural nouns
5696.outcome: I can use 'wenn' to describe outcomes of actions.
points: Word order three conjunctions like 'wenn' send the verb to the end.
The subject and verb are inverted in word order two.
There are many ways to form the plural in German.
keywords: conjunction meaning 'if' or 'when' which triggers word order 3
inverts the subject and verb in a sentence
(WO3) sends the verb to the end of the sentence or clause after certain conjunctions

5697.name: Berufe: 'werden' + infinitive, wh-questions in future and conditional tenses
5697.outcome: I can use 'werden' with the infinitive to discuss my future plans.
points: To form the future tense, use the present tense of 'werden' to mean ‘will’ and an infinitive verb at the end.
To ask an open question in the future, use a question word followed by a form of 'werden', followed by the subject.
To ask an open question with 'möcht-', use a question word followed by a form of 'möcht-', followed by the subject.
keywords: the conditional form of the verb 'mögen', meaning 'would like'

5698.name: Wenn ich 16 bin: würd- with gern and lieber, imperfect subjunctive hätte, wäre
5698.outcome: I can use the conditional, 'hätte' and 'wäre' to say what I would like to do in future.
points: To talk about something something you would or might do, use 'würd-' to mean ‘would’ and an infinitive verb at the end.
Use 'gern' and 'lieber' with 'würde' to talk about what we would like or would prefer to do.
To say 'would have', use 'hätte'.
To say 'would be', use 'wäre'.
keywords: form of verb used to express what would happen
form of ‘haben’ meaning ‘would have’ which expresses a conditional idea
form of ‘sein’ meaning ‘would be’ which expresses a conditional idea
form of 'werden' meaning 'would', used with a 2nd infinitive to express a conditional idea

5699.name: Pläne: word order with 'sobald', 'solange' and 'wenn'
5699.outcome: I can use the word order 3 conjunctions 'sobald', 'solange' and 'wenn' to discuss conditions for future plans.
points: 'Sobald' means 'as soon as' and 'solange' means 'as long as'.
'Sobald', 'solange' and 'wenn' are all WO3 conjunctions, sending the verb to the end of the sentence.
Present, future and conditional tenses ('würd-' plus infinitive and 'möchte') can be used to talk about future plans.
Use 'wenn', 'sobald' and 'solange', plus 'würd- gern' and 'würd- lieber', to extend answers.
keywords: conjunction with word order 3 (WO3), meaning ‘as soon as’
conjunction with WO3, meaning ‘as long as’
conjunction meaning 'if' or 'when' which triggers word order 3

5700.name: Berufserfahrung: verbs with indirect objects, dative pronouns
5700.outcome: I can use dative verbs and indirect object pronouns when communicating with other people in the context of work experience.
points: The German [ch] can be soft or hard. Soft [ch] should not be confused with [sch].
Certain verbs are dative verbs and use indirect object (dative) pronouns.
The dative pronouns are 'mir', 'dir', 'ihm', 'ihn', 'uns', 'euch', 'ihnen'.
Some dative verbs are also impersonal like 'gefallen', 'gelingen' and 'genügen'.
keywords: case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, from you, with them; takes the dative case

5701.name: Berufserfahrung: 'Sie', 'Ihnen', interrogatives 'wer', 'wen', 'wem'
5701.outcome: I can use 'Sie' and 'Ihnen' to address other people politely in the context of enquiring about work experience.
points: 'Sie' is the polite way of saying 'you' and is a subject pronoun.
The direct object pronoun for 'Sie' is also 'Sie'. The indirect object pronoun is 'Ihnen'.
The interrogative pronoun 'wer' becomes 'wen' in the accusative.
The interrogative pronoun 'wer' becomes 'wem' in the dative.
keywords: a pronoun that replaces the object in a sentence
question word meaning 'who' or 'whom' which changes according to case

5702.name: Meine Pläne: adding -er to verb stems for male agent nouns, extended writing
5702.outcome: I can use grammar I have recently learned to write an extended text about my future plans.
points: German [s-] sounds like English 'z'. German [z] sounds like English 'ts'.
German cognates ending in ‘-tion’ have this ‘ts’ sound plus long vowel [o]n, as in 'Information'.
Add -er to verb stems to create male agent nouns; for example, 'Arbeiter', 'Helfer'. Add -in for the feminine form.
Develop writing with: different tenses, a range of vocabulary, and functions, e.g., opinions and reasons.
keywords: a noun for someone who performs the action of a verb, usually ending in -er; for example, worker - ‘Arbeiter’

5703.name: Junge Deutsche: neuter adjectival nouns, nominalisation, adjectival agreement
5703.outcome: I can use neuter adjectival nouns with 'etwas' and 'alles', and verbs as nouns, to extend my understanding of career options for young Germans.
points: Following 'etwas', capitalise an adjective and add '-es' to turn it to a neuter adjectival noun.
Following 'alles', capitalise an adjective and add '-e' to turn it to a neuter adjectival noun.
German verbs can be nominalised as neuter nouns, and used with or without 'das'.
Adjectives change spelling depending on case and gender.
keywords: a type of noun that takes the same endings as adjectives
indefinite pronoun meaning ‘everything’, often followed by an abstract adjectival noun
indefinite pronoun meaning ‘something’, often followed by an abstract adjectival noun
the process of making a noun from a verb or adjective

5704.name: Junge Deutsche: telling the time, uses of 'es'
5704.outcome: I can tell the time and use 'es' in different contexts, making meaning more concise when discussing life for young Germans.
points: 'Uhr' means 'o'clock'. 'Halb' means 'half to the next hour'.
'Es' can be used as a pronoun to replace a neuter noun.
'Es' can refer back or forward to a fact or idea, epxressed in a clause or sentence.
'Es' can be used with impersonal verbs.
keywords: part of the verb 'ser' that means she, he, it is
a verb that doesn't refer to a particular person or thing, and whose subject is most often 'il' (it)

5706.name: Junge Deutsche: weak plural masculine nouns, feminine person nouns
5706.outcome: I can form singular and plural masculine and feminine person nouns to discuss careers for young Germans.
points: Some masculine nouns, most of them referring to people or animals, add –(e)n to form the plural.
To change a masculine noun into a feminine noun, add '-in'; add 'nen' to make feminine nouns ending 'in' plural.
Some nouns, often of foreign origin, add 's' in the plural; this does not apply to person nouns.
The imperfect tense is commonly used to recount past events in writing. Irregular verb stems need to be learned.
keywords: a small set of masculine nouns that add '-(e)n' in all forms apart from the nominative singular

5707.name: Ich bin Ingenieurin: imperfect modals
5707.outcome: I can use modal verbs in the imperfect tense to talk about work and studying.
points: [o] and [ö] are long when followed by no consonants or only one consonant.
To form the imperfect of singular modal verbs, remove -en and add -te for ‘ich’, -test for ‘du’, -te for ‘sie/er/es’.
To form the imperfect of plural modal verbs, remove -en and add -ten for ‘wir’, -tet for ‘ihr’, -ten for ‘sie’.
In sentences with modal verbs, the second verb is in the infinitive at the end of the sentence.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want

5708.name: Lebenserfahrung: simple past with früher, gern, lieber, am liebsten, reflexive verbs
5708.outcome: I can use reflexive verbs and adverbs in the perfect and imperfect tenses in the context of studies and work.
points: In two-verb structures, the reflexive pronoun normally comes after the first verb.
In the perfect tense, it is more common to use the simple past versions of ‘haben’, ‘sein’, and ‘es gibt’.
Use ‘früher’ in the perfect and imperfect tenses to mean ‘used to’.
Use ‘gern’, ‘lieber’, ‘am liebsten’ in the perfect and imperfect tenses to talk about likes and preferences.
keywords: 2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'
verb used to indicate doing something to yourself, e.g., 'to wash yourself'
synonymous with the imperfect; German single-word past tense used mainly to narrate past events in writing; for example, 'war', 'hatte', 'gab'

5709.name: Karrieregespräche: perfect tense strong verbs, 'mochte', 'gefallen' vs 'gemocht'
5709.outcome: I can use irregular verbs in the perfect tense and ‘mochte’ in the imperfect tense in the context of career choices.
points: Some past participles are irregular.
In the imperfect tense, the stem of 'mögen' is 'moch-'. It still takes the regular imperfect tense endings.
'Mochte' is normally followed by a noun.
In the perfect tense, ‘mögen’ becomes 'gemocht' and means ‘liked’.
Use 'gefallen' in the perfect tense to mean ‘liked’. Use indirect object pronouns with 'gefallen'.
keywords: a past participle meaning ‘liked’, used with an indirect object
the past participle of the verb 'mögen'
the imperfect form of the verb 'mögen'
verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb

5710.name: Es war toll! Perfect tense with 'sein', 'haben' and questions, inversion
5710.outcome: I can use word order 2 and form questions in the perfect tense in the context of interesting past experiences.
points: To make a yes/no question in the perfect tense, swap the form of ‘sein’ or ‘haben’ with the subject.
To ask an information question in the perfect tense, use a question word followed by ‘sein’ or ‘haben’ then the subject.
In word order 2, invert the subject and verb.
keywords: question starting with a wh- word that has more information in the answer than yes/no
inverts the subject and verb in a sentence
question formed by inverting subject and verb where the answer is yes/no

5711.name: Der Hund ist frech! Negation with 'nicht' and 'sondern', determiners
5711.outcome: I can use determiners and negate using ‘nicht’ and ‘sondern’ in the context of past experiences.
points: [j] sounds like 'ja'.
Determiners 'jed-' ‘nächst-’ and ‘letzt-’ change their endings according to gender and case.
'Sondern' means 'but' or 'rather' and contradicts a preceding negative.
keywords: determiner meaning ‘each, every’ which changes according to gender and case
determiner meaning ‘last’ which changes according to gender and case
determiner meaning ‘next’ which changes according to gender and case
conjunction used after a negative, meaning ‘but’ or ‘rather’

5712.name: Die Ferien: perfect tense with adverbs
5712.outcome: I can use time adverbials in the perfect tense to add more detail to discussions about holidays.
points: Use time adverbials 'schon', '(noch) nie', 'noch', 'schon einmal' with the perfect tense to provide more information.
In a role play, the response to each prompt should contain at least one verb, but still be relatively brief.
In a role play, the response should match the tense of the prompt.
keywords: 2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'
task in which the student responds to several prompts in the format of a role-play
adverbs or adverbial phrases which denote time; for example, 'nie', 'schon', 'noch nicht'

5713.name: Schule - dieses Jahr: 'bis' preposition vs conjunction
5713.outcome: I can use ‘bis’ as a preposition and as a conjunction to talk about school this year.
points: When [th] is in the same syllable, it sounds like English ‘t’.
The preposition 'bis' indicates an end-point in time and means ‘until’, ‘up to’ or ‘by’.
Use a preposition (‘zu’, ‘an’, ‘in’) with the preposition 'bis' when the following noun has an article.
With days of the week, months and dates, use 'bis' with or without 'zu'.
Use conjunction ‘bis’ with word order three (sending the verb to the end) to mean ‘until’.
keywords: preposition meaning ‘until’, ‘up to’, ‘by’, and a conjunction meaning 'until'
word that connects ideas between clauses in a sentence
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

5714.name: Schule - letztes Jahr: nouns without plurals, past participles
5714.outcome: I can use past participles and my knowledge of school subjects to talk about school last year.
points: Some nouns such as 'Physik' do not have plurals.
Verbs that start in 'be-', 'ent-' or 'er-' have inseparable prefixes in the perfect tense.
'Gehen' can be combined with other infinitives such as 'schwimmen'.
Past participles of separable verbs are one word - prefix first then the past participle of main verb.
keywords: verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb
2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'
two-part verb with a prefix and a main verb, e.g. 'aussehen'

5715.name: Gruppenzwang: word order with separable verbs in single and 2-verb clauses
5715.outcome: I can use separable verbs in present and perfect tenses, in 2-verb structures, and with the correct word order to talk about school experiences.
points: The stress falls on the separable prefix of separable verbs.
Separable verbs are made up of two parts: a prefix and the main verb.
In the present tense, the prefix moves to the end of the clause.
In the perfect tense, the past participle is made up of the prefix and the base past participle.
In word order three clauses, the prefix and verb join up in separable verbs.
keywords: a two-part verb, with a prefix and a main verb, e.g., 'einladen'

5717.name: Therapiehunde: nouns and adjectives with prepositions
5717.outcome: I can use nouns and adjectives with prepositions to describe my interest and emotions in the context of therapy dogs in school.
points: [qu] sounds like in 'bequem'.
[w] sounds like in 'Antwort'.
The letter combination 'kw' in German sounds like [qu], but only occurs in compound nouns, e.g., 'Trinkwasser'.
Certain nouns are always followed by particular prepositions and cases.
Certain adjectives are always followed by particular prepositions and cases.
keywords: word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

5718.name: Das deutsche Schulsystem: adjective agreement
5718.outcome: I can add agreements to adjectives to provide details when talking about the German school system.
points: Adjective agreement occurs when adjectives precede nouns.
Adjective endings depend on case, gender and number.
[-d] sounds like 'Hemd'.
[-d-] sounds like 'Kleider'.
Listening needs close reading of questions, attention to detail and vocabulary knowledge for gap-fill questions.
keywords: when the ending of an adjective matches the noun it describes in gender and number

5719.name: Kleider machen Leute: definite and indefinite articles, extended speaking
5719.outcome: I can use definite and indefinite articles when their German usage is different from English to understand a German text and hold a conversation about school uniforms.
points: Some countries and some abstract nouns use the definite article.
The indefinite article is not used in German for professions or nationalities.
Use the indefinite article with professsions if there is an adjective before the noun.
When describing a photo, use the acronym PALM. It stands for People, Action, Location, Mood. Add your own opinions too.
In conversation, develop answers by adding opinions and reasons, varying the subject, and adding different time frames.
keywords: acronym for photo description (people and objects, action, location, mood)

5720.name: In der Schule: superlative adjectives and adverbs
5720.outcome: I can form and use superlative adjectives and adverbs when discussing topics in a school context.
points: Use the superlative to express the highest degree of something, e.g., 'the most'.
To form the superlative use ‘am’ before the adjective/adverb, and then add ‘-sten’.
Prenominal superlative adjectives use the definite article then add '-st' plus the appropriate ending to the adjective.
Some superlatives are irregular.
Superlatives can be used to develop writing.
keywords: an adjective that appears before the noun it describes
a form of adjective or adverb used to express the highest degree of a quality, e.g., 'the tallest', 'the most interesting'

5721.name: Nach der Schule: abstract neuter adjectival nouns, plural adjectival nouns
5721.outcome: I can form and use adjectival nouns to talk about after-school activities.
points: Adjectives can be turned into neuter nouns to express abstract concepts, e.g., ‘das Gute’ - 'the good thing'.
To form an abstract adjectival noun, use 'das', capitalise the adjective, and add '-e' in nominative and accusative.
Using abstract adjectival nouns can help to vary and extend opinions, e.g., ‘das Beste (daran) ist, dass...'.
Plural adjectival nouns end in '-en' when used after 'die'.
Plural adjectival nouns used without articles end in 'e' in nominative and accusative and 'en' in dative.
keywords: a type of noun that takes the same endings as adjectives

5722.name: Kleine Schule: time, manner, place, present tense with gern, lieber, am liebsten
5722.outcome: I can use adverbs of time, manner and place to talk about a school trip, and adverbs of preference to discuss differences between large and small schools.
points: Adverbs follow the order time, manner, place; using TMP with all tenses can work well to describe sequences of events.
Any adverb can start a sentence for emphasis. In this case, use word order 2 and order the remaining adverbs using TMP.
Use a verb with ‘gern’ to mean ‘like’, ‘lieber’ to mean ‘prefer’ and ‘am liebsten’ to mean ‘most preferably of all’.
Use the adverbs gern, lieber, am liebsten to develop and extend opinions on a range of themes.
keywords: superlative adverb meaning 'most preferably', 'most of all'
adverb meaning ‘gladly, liked to’ with the past tense
the order of adverbs in a German sentence - time before manner before place, abbreviated to TMP

5723.name: Freizeit: prepositions, da-compounds
5723.outcome: I can use prepositions with the accusative and dative to describe where people and things are and where they are going in the context of free time.
points: The prepositions hinter, neben, unter, über, vor, zwischen and in are used with the accusative when there is movement.
The prepositions hinter, neben, unter, über, vor, zwischen and in are used with the dative when there is no movement.
'Vor' can mean 'before', 'in front of' or 'ago'.
Use da-compounds for inanimate nouns already mentioned. Use direct or indirect object pronouns for animate nouns.
keywords: form(s) used for the object or 'receiver' of the action of the verb
prefix added to prepositions to avoid repetition of the noun
case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

5724.name: Ich fahre in die Schule: words for ‘in’ and ‘to’, wo-compounds
5724.outcome: I can use a range of prepositions to describe journeys to school and around the city and form questions with wo-compounds.
points: The preposition 'in' is followed by the accusative case if there is movement, and by the dative if there is no movement.
The prepositions 'zu', 'nach' and 'in' can all mean 'to'.
'In das' contracts to 'ins' and 'in dem' contracts to 'im'. 'Zu dem' contracts to 'zum' and 'zu der' contracts to 'zur'.
‘Zu Hause’ means ‘at home’ and ‘nach Hause’ is used for 'going (to) home'.
Use wo-compounds to ask questions with prepositions. Wo- becomes wor- before a vowel.
keywords: form(s) used for the object or 'receiver' of the action of the verb
case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word
prefix added to prepositions to form questions

5725.name: Mein Alltag jetzt und früher: '-chen' and '-lein', 'wenn' and 'als'
5725.outcome: I can use the perfect and present tenses, along with ‘wenn’ and ‘als’, to compare past and present routines and activities.
points: German [ch] can be soft or hard. The sound [ei] is pronounced like ‘frei’.
The suffixes -chen and -lein are added to make diminutive nouns. They often gain an umlaut and are always neuter.
'Wenn' means ‘when’, ‘whenever’ of ‘if’ and is used for repeated actions or conditions in the present or future.
'Als' means ‘when’ to refer to a specific past event or point in time.
Both 'als' and 'wenn' trigger word order 3, sending the finite verb to the end of the sentence or clause.
keywords: suffixes added to nouns to make diminutive or ‘little’ forms
conjunction meaning ‘when’, referring to specific past events, which triggers word order 3
conjunction meaning 'if' or 'when' which triggers word order 3
(WO3) sends the verb to the end of the sentence or clause after certain conjunctions

5726.name: Vor und nach der Schule: word order with 'nachdem' and 'bevor'
5726.outcome: I can use prepositions ‘vor’ and ‘nach’ and conjunctions ‘bevor’ and ‘nachdem’ in the context of routines and activities before and after school.
points: 'Vor' and 'nach' are prepositions used with nouns to express 'before' and 'after'. They take the dative case.
'Bevor' and 'nachdem' are conjunctions meaning 'before' and 'after' and link two clauses.
'Bevor' and 'nachdem' are followed by word order 3 and send the verb to the end of the clause.
In two-verb structures, the finite verb, not the past participle or infinitive verb, are sent to the end of the clause.
‘Bevor’ and ‘nachdem’ can also start a sentence, creating verb-comma-verb word order.
keywords: a group of words that contains a verb
word that connects ideas between clauses in a sentence
a naming word for people, places or things
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word
(WO3) sends the verb to the end of the sentence or clause after certain conjunctions

5728.name: Mein Alltag: telling the time, prepositions ‘um’, ‘seit’ and ‘vor’
5728.outcome: I can use a range of prepositions and times to talk about past and present events and routines with precision.
points: Use the 12 hour or the 24 hour clock to tell the time in German. Use 'um' to say ‘at’ with clock times.
'Um' can also mean ‘around’ or ‘approximately’ when used with numbers, and is normally followed by the definite article.
When referring to a place, 'um' means ‘around’ and is always followed by the accusative case.
'Seit' is used with present tense to express an unfinished action started in the past. It can mean ‘since’ or ‘for’.
'Vor' + length of time is used with past tense to say how long ago something happened. Use the dative case.
keywords: form(s) used for the object or 'receiver' of the action of the verb
case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
preposition meaning ‘since’ or ‘for’, followed by the dative case
preposition meaning ‘at’ with time, e.g., 'um drei Uhr' ('at three o’clock')
preposition meaning ‘ago’, followed by the dative case

5729.name: Wir treffen uns: reflexive verbs past and present, forming adverbs, role play
5729.outcome: I can use reflexive verbs in the past and present, form time adverbs of time from nouns and prepare role play answers in the context of meeting up with friends.
points: Reflexive pronouns relate the action of the verb back to the subject, so subject and object are the same.
If the action of the verb is reciprocal, or two-way, reflexive pronouns can also mean ‘each other’.
In the perfect tense, the reflexive pronoun usually comes after the first (auxiliary) verb.
To change a noun into an adverb to describe regular events, remove its capital letter and add '-s' to the end.
In a role play, say a short phrase in response to each prompt and include at least one verb in each phrase.
keywords: A reciprocal is the multiplicative inverse of any non-zero number. Any non-zero number multiplied by its reciprocal is equal to 1
an adverb indicating when a verb is performed
describes an action where the subject and the object of the verb are the same
task in which the student responds to several prompts in the format of a role-play

5730.name: Schreib eine E-Mail: informal imperatives, present tense verbs
5730.outcome: I can recognise and use the imperative of weak verbs to give instructions or advice in the context of technology.
points: There is just one present tense in German, used to translate the simple present and the present continuous in English.
Imperative verbs are used to give instructions or advice, or to tell someone to do something.
To form the imperative ‘du’ form of weak verbs, remove the ‘st’ ending from the normal present tense form and the 'du'.
To make the 'ihr' form of the imperative of weak verbs, just remove the 'ihr'. The verb stays the same.
Verbs with stems ending in ‘-d’ or ‘-t’ add an ‘-e’ to the 'du' form of the imperative.
keywords: subject pronoun meaning ‘you’, informal and singular
a mood used to tell somebody to do something or give instructions or commands
describes events happening right now: 'I am doing'
verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'

5731.name: Eine Nachricht: 'worum' and 'darum', genitive prepositions
5731.outcome: I can use the compounds ‘darum’ and ‘worum’ and understand prepositions with the genitive in the context of sharing messages.
points: Some verbs are followed by the preposition 'um' and the accusative case.
The prefix 'wor-' can be added to 'um' to make a question, usually meaning 'what about' or 'around what'?
The prefix 'dar-' can be added to 'um' to mean 'about it' or 'around it'.
'Darum' can also be a conjunction meaning 'therefore' or 'that's why'.
Prepositions 'trotz', 'statt', 'während' and 'wegen' are followed by the genitive. Masculine and neuter nouns gain 's'.
keywords: prefix added to prepositions to avoid repetition of the noun
case used to indicate possession and after certain prepositions
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word
prefix added to prepositions to form questions

5732.name: Technologie der Zukunft: 'du' & 'ihr' questions with reflexives, modals, future
5732.outcome: I can ask open and closed questions in the present and future tenses, with modal and reflexive verbs, using intonation effectively to read aloud and ask questions about future technology.
points: A closed question is formed by swapping the position of the verb and subject in a statement.
Add a question word in front of the verb to change a closed question into an open one.
In questions with reflexive verbs, only subject and verb swap position, and the reflexive pronoun follows the subject.
Future or modal (2-verb) questions swap the subject and 1st verb; the infinitive remains at the end.
Varied intonation and accurate pronunciation matter in speaking and reading aloud; punctuation and understanding help.
keywords: question that gets the answer 'yes' or 'no' and is created in Spanish by raising the tone of voice at the end of a statement
rise and fall of the voice in speaking
verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want
question starting with a wh- word that has more information in the answer than yes/no
describes an action where the subject and the object of the verb are the same

5733.name: Meine Mannschaft: stem changes 't' not 'st', 'e' before 't'/'st', 'el' stem
5733.outcome: I can use a range of present tense verbs, including those with small changes to the stem, to discuss sport and free-time pursuits.
points: Weak verbs follow a regular pattern of changes in the present tense.
For verbs stems ending in 'd', ‘t', 'm' or 'n', add 'e' before the ending in the 'du', 'er/sie/es' and 'ihr' forms.
For verb stems ending in 's', 'ß', 'x' or 'z', add just 't' instead of 'st' in the 'du' form.
For stems ending in -el, remove the 'e' in the first person singular of the present tense.
keywords: part of the verb that appears in all forms
a verb that follows a regular pattern of changes

5734.name: Liest du Romane? Questions and informal imperatives with strong verbs
5734.outcome: I can use present tense strong verbs to ask questions and use the informal imperative to give instructions or advice in the context of free-time activities.
points: Strong verbs in the present tense change the stem vowel in the 2nd and 3rd person singular: e - i, e - ie, or a - ä.
Use 'du' questions for informal singular ‘you’, and 'ihr' questions for informal plural ‘you’.
Strong verbs retain the present tense stem vowel change in the 'du' form of the imperative but they omit the umlaut.
To use the 'ihr' form of the imperative of weak and strong verbs, just remove the pronoun 'ihr'.
'Sein' is irregular in the 'du' form of the imperative. Use 'sei' for the 'du' form and 'seid' for the 'ihr' form.
keywords: subject pronoun meaning ‘you’, informal and singular
a mood used to tell somebody to do something or give instructions or commands
a verb which changes its vowel in the verb stem of some of its forms

5735.name: Meine Freizeit: present tense for future meaning, extended writing
5735.outcome: I can use the present tense with adverbs of time for future meaning and I can use the BORDER acronym to respond fully and accurately in writing.
points: Future plans can be expressed by using the present tense with a future adverb of time.
The adjective ‘nächst-’ takes different endings depending on the gender of the noun it is describing ('nächstes Jahr').
We translate the German present tense for future meaning into English using the present continuous.
It is important to plan carefully and to be able to write in three different time frames when writing a longer text.
Using the acronym BORDER is a good way to make sure you successfully cover every aspect of a writing task.
keywords: an adverb indicating when a verb is performed

5738.name: Abitur oder Ausbildung: ohne...zu..., entweder...oder..., weder...noch...
5738.outcome: I can use a range of infinitive 'zu' clauses and compound conjunctions to discuss post-16 options and plans.
points: When combined with a second verb in the infinitive, some verbs require the addition of ‘zu’ before the infinitive.
Infinitive constructions are separated from other clauses with a comma.
Use 'ohne … zu' + infinitive to mean 'without’, '(an)statt... zu' for 'instead of', 'um... zu' to mean 'in order to'.
Use the conjunction 'entweder … oder...' to mean 'either … or...' and 'weder … noch...' to mean 'neither … nor...'.
'Entweder... oder...' and 'weder... noch...' are useful for expressing options and possibilities.
keywords: a conjunction which consists of more than one word
the basic form of the verb, with no particular subject or tense indicated

5739.name: Zukunftsentscheidungen: nominalisation of infinitives, adding '-ung'
5739.outcome: I can create nouns from verbs and use a range of vocabulary in the context of future education and work plans.
points: Infinitive verbs can be turned into nouns and correspond to English '-ing' nouns, e.g., 'das Lesen' - 'reading'.
Infinitives as nouns are capitalised and are always neuter. They can be used with or without 'das'.
The suffix '-ung' is added to the stem of some verbs to form nouns, e.g., 'die Entscheidung'. They are always feminine.
Nouns ending in '-ung' have the equivalent and transparent meaning of the verb, e.g., 'lösen' becomes 'Lösung'.
keywords: the basic form of the verb, with no particular subject or tense indicated
a naming word for people, places or things
part of the verb that appears in all forms
a letter or group of letters added to the end of a word to change its meaning

5740.name: Was will ich lernen? Present modal verbs, describing photos, extended speaking
5740.outcome: I can use modal verbs to talk about what I want, must, and can do, describe a photo and develop my answers in conversation about future plans.
points: Modal verbs are usually used with a second verb in the infinitive at the end of the sentence or clause.
The stems of some modal verbs are irregular, with vowel changes in most singular forms.
When describing a photo, use the acronym PALM. It stands for People, Action, Location, Mood. Add your own opinions too.
It is helpful to predict follow-up questions on a theme for developing conversation after describing a photo.
In conversation, develop answers by adding opinions and reasons, varying the subject, and adding different time frames.
keywords: acronym for photo description (people and objects, action, location, mood)
verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want

5741.name: Gesundheit: position of indirect and direct objects with two nouns
5741.outcome: I can form sentences combining direct and indirect objects and new vocabulary in the context of health.
points: Grouping new vocabulary by word class and exploring word families is a useful tool for committing vocabulary to memory.
The accusative case is used for the direct object of a verb; the person or thing receiving the action of the verb.
The dative case is used for the indirect object of a verb; the person or thing to or for whom something is done.
In sentences with two object nouns, the indirect object noun always comes before the direct object noun.
When translating into English, some but not all verbs need ‘to’ or ‘for’ before the indirect object noun.
keywords: form(s) used for the object or 'receiver' of the action of the verb
case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
person, animal or thing that receives the action of the verb, e.g. 'he takes a book'
a noun in the dative case, indirectly affected by the action of the verb
category of words of similar function e.g. nouns, adjectives, verbs or adverbs

5742.name: Psychische Gesundheit: position of indirect and direct objects
5742.outcome: I can use direct and indirect object pronouns and form sentences combining them with nouns in the context of health.
points: A direct object pronoun replaces a noun that is the object of the verb and is in the accusative case.
An indirect object pronoun replaces the noun that the verb action is done ‘to’ or ‘for’ and is in the dative.
In sentences with two objects that are nouns, the indirect object noun comes before the direct object noun.
In sentences with two objects where there is one noun and one pronoun, the pronoun always comes first.
The long [i] in ‘ihr’, ‘ihm’, ‘Ihnen’ sounds like ‘wir’, and the [eu] in ‘euch’ sounds like ‘Deutschland’.
keywords: form(s) used for the object or 'receiver' of the action of the verb
case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
replaces the noun receiving the action of the verb e.g. me, you, it, them
replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, from you, with them; takes the dative case

5743.name: Neue Schüler: adding '-keit' and '-heit', adjectives as adverbs
5743.outcome: I can use adjectives as adverbs and create ‘-keit’ and ‘-heit’ nouns from adjectives in the context of helping others.
points: Add ‘-keit’ or '-heit' to adjectives to make feminine nouns.
Nouns ending in '-heit' or '-keit' are usually translated into equivalent English nouns ending in '-ty' or '-ness'.
Most German adjectives can be used as adverbs.
English adjectives and adverbs differ, so care must be taken when translating German adjectives used as adverbs.
In extended writing, it is important to reference three different time frames: past, present, and future.
keywords: a letter or group of letters added to the end of a word to change its meaning

5744.name: Gesund bleiben: abstract adjectival neuter nouns, adding '-los'
5744.outcome: I can form neuter adjectival nouns with ‘wenig’ and ‘viel’ and create adjectives from nouns in the context of health.
points: Adjectival nouns, like adjectives, change according to gender, case and the article used with them.
Following 'wenig' or 'viel', capitalise an adjective and add '-es' to turn it to a neuter adjectival noun.
Add the suffix '-los' to nouns to create adjectives meaning '-less' or 'without -'.
[v] in 'viel' is pronounced like English 'f' as in 'Vater', [w] in 'wenig' is pronounced like English 'v' as in 'Welt'.
[ig] at the end of a word is pronounced as in 'richtig' and a final [s] sounds like the English 's'.
keywords: a type of noun that takes the same endings as adjectives
a letter or group of letters added to the end of a word to change its meaning
word meaning 'little', often followed by a neuter adjectival noun

5745.name: Würdest du Veganer werden? Conditional with 'würde', 'hätte', 'wäre', 'sollte'
5745.outcome: I can use the conditional with 'würde' alongside 'hätte', 'wäre' and 'sollte' to discuss choices related to health.
points: To say what you would do, use 'würde' to mean ‘would’ and an infinitive verb at the end of the clause.
Use 'würde' plus 'gern' to talk about what you would like to do and 'würde' plus 'lieber' to say what you would prefer.
Use 'hätte' to mean ‘would have’, and 'wäre' to mean ‘would be’. No infinitive verb is needed, unlike with 'würde'.
'Sollte' is the conditional form of the modal verb ‘sollen’. It is used to convey what we ‘ought to’ or ‘should’ do.
keywords: form of verb used to express what would happen
form of ‘haben’ meaning ‘would have’ which expresses a conditional idea
form of 'sollen' expressing obligation in a softer, more polite way
form of ‘sein’ meaning ‘would be’ which expresses a conditional idea
form of ‘werden’ meaning would, used with a 2nd infinitive to express a conditional idea

5746.name: Isst du gesund? Nouns without plurals, plural rules
5746.outcome: I can use singular and plural nouns and appropriate quantifiers to talk about healthy eating.
points: There are nine rules for forming plurals in German.
Uncountable nouns do not have a plural form.
Use the quantifiers 'viel' and 'wenig' for uncountable nouns, use 'viele' and 'wenige' for countable nouns.
'Viel' and 'wenig' do not change according to gender or case, but plural 'viele' and 'wenige' do.
When reading aloud it is helpful to identify and correctly pronounce umlauts, which are common in plural nouns.
keywords: form for nouns that refers to more than one person place, thing or idea: des Canadiens
a type of determiner that indicates the quantity of a noun
noun which cannot be counted, only measured, e.g. (lots of) luck, (some) music, (1kg) rice.

5748.name: Gesund und ungesund: expanding vocabulary, reading skills, role play
5748.outcome: I can use cognates and time frames to understand texts about health issues and take part in a role play about healthy living.
points: Cognates are words that have the same meaning and look the same or very similar to English words.
Cognates are very useful in reading tasks, as they can help us to quickly identify the overall theme of a text.
We can use adverbs of time and verb tenses to distinguish between past, present and future actions and events
In a role play, you are required to say a short phrase in response to each prompt.
In a role play, it is important to include at least one verb in each phrase. You must also ask one question.
keywords: words with the same meaning and same or similar spelling in English and French
task in which the student responds to several prompts in the format of a role-play

5749.name: Was möchtest du? Present and conditional 'mögen'
5749.outcome: I can use 'mögen' and 'möcht-' to talk about what I like and would like in the context of shopping.
points: To talk about what you like in the present tense, use the irregular verb 'mögen'.
The forms of 'mögen' are: 'ich mag', 'du magst', 'er, sie, es mag', 'wir mögen', 'ihr mögt', 'Sie, sie mögen'.
The conditional form of 'mögen' is 'möcht-' and this is used to talk about what you would like or would like to do.
'Möcht-' can be used without a second verb, to express what you would like: for example, in a café or when shopping.
'Möcht-' is also commonly used with a second verb in the infinitive to express future wishes.
keywords: the conditional form of the verb 'mögen', meaning 'would like'
an irregular verb, meaning 'to like, liking'

5750.name: KaDeWe: cardinal and ordinal numbers
5750.outcome: I can use cardinal and ordinal numbers in the context of shopping and understand a text about Berlin's most famous department store.
points: Cardinal numbers are numbers used for counting or expressing quantity. Ordinal numbers tell us the order of something.
For numbers 13-99, say the 2nd digit first e.g., 'vierundzwanzig' = '24'. For 21-99, add ‘und’ between the two numbers.
For prices, place the € after the numbers and separate euros and cents with a comma. Always say 'Euro' in the singular.
For ordinal numbers, add -te for numbers 1-19 and -ste for 20+. To say 'on' a date, use 'am' and add -n to the number.
KaDeWe is short for 'Kaufhaus des Westens' and is a famous large department store in Berlin.
keywords: number form that shows how many of something there are
tells you the order of something, e.g., 'first', 'second', 'third', and is used with dates

5751.name: Einkaufen: 'welch-' and 'dies-' in nominative, accusative, dative
5751.outcome: I can use 'welch-' and 'dies-' to identify items and take part in a role-play about shopping.
points: The determiner 'welch-' means 'which'. Its ending changes according to the gender and case of the noun that follows.
The determiner 'dies-' means ‘this’. Its ending changes in the same way as 'welch-'.
'Welch-' and 'dies-' are very helpful for identifying items when shopping.
In a role-play, it is important to include at least one verb in each short phrase. You must also ask one question.
'Sowohl...als auch...' means 'both...and...', 'derselbe, dieselbe, dasselbe' mean 'the same' and 'jene(r)' means 'that'.
keywords: determiner meaning 'this' which changes according to the gender and case of the noun which follows
task in which the student responds to several prompts in the format of a role-play

5752.name: Die digitale Welt: verbs with prepositions, 'da-' and 'wo-' compounds
5752.outcome: I can use a range of prepositional verbs, 'da-' and 'wo-' compounds and new vocabulary in the context of the digital world and favourite online influencers.
points: Some verbs are followed by prepositions and the accusative case, and some are followed by prepositions and the dative.
We use different prepositions after verbs in English and German, so verb and preposition combinations must be learnt.
The prefix 'da(r)-' can be added to prepositions to refer to something already mentioned. This is called a da- compound.
Use 'wo-' compounds to ask questions with verbs that take prepositions.
'Dazu' can be used as a 'da-' compound, but can also be used to mean ‘in addition’ or ‘furthermore’.
keywords: prefix added to prepositions to avoid repetition of the noun
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word
prefix added to prepositions to form questions

5753.name: Nachhaltige Mode: relative pronouns, question words in relative clauses
5753.outcome: I can use relative pronouns and question words in relative clauses in the context of online shopping and sustainable fashion.
points: Relative clauses add information about the noun in a main clause, without starting another sentence.
German uses definite articles as the relative pronouns, preceded by a comma and followed by word order 3.
In two-verb clauses, the finite (conjugated) verb goes to the end of the sentence.
Question words, such as 'wo', 'warum' and 'wann' can also be used as pronouns in relative clauses.
Use 'was' to mean 'that' or 'which' when referring to a whole clause, rather than to a specific noun.
keywords: a type of subordinate clause that begins with a relative pronoun
a pronoun that introduces a relative clause e.g. qui, que
after certain conjunctions, the verb is sent to the end of the sentence or clause

5754.name: Kommunikation online: extended writing
5754.outcome: I can use the BORDER acronym to develop and extend my writing about technology and life online.
points: [sch] is pronounced like English 'sh', as in 'schreiben' and [sp] sounds like English 'sh' before 'p', as in 'spielen'.
At the start of a word, and in compound nouns and some verbs, [st] sounds like the English 'sht', as in ‘stark'.
The BORDER acronym is a useful tool to respond fully and accurately to bullet point writing prompts.
To develop answers, you can add information about another person, add a contrast or add another time frame.
You can extend written answers by adding a subordinate clause, a relative clause, or an infinitive construction.

5755.name: Digital Detox: perfect tense, imperfect tense, 'gerade'
5755.outcome: I can use strong verbs in the perfect and imperfect tenses, including with 'gerade', in the context of technology and digital detox.
points: Strong verbs form past participles with 'ge-' and '-en'. Some have a vowel change, such as 'ei' to 'ie' or 'ie' to 'o'.
The imperfect tense is usually used in written texts for narration. The perfect tense is much more common in speaking.
The imperfect tense forms ‘hatte’, ‘war’, and ‘es gab’ are often used in spoken as well as written German.
Use 'gerade' with the perfect tense to mean 'just (now)'.
Use 'gerade' with the imperfect tense to express that the action was taking place when something else happened.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'
verb which changes the stem vowel in the imperfect tense, e.g., ‘blieb’
verb whose past participle sandwiches the stem with 'ge-' and ‘-en’ and often changes the stem vowel

5756.name: Magst du Musik? Nominalisation of infinitives with 'beim' and 'am'
5756.outcome: I can use infinitive verbs as nouns with 'beim' and 'am' alongside a wide range of vocabulary to discuss musical preferences and understand texts about German music.
points: Infinitive verbs can be turned into nouns and correspond to English '-ing' nouns, e.g., 'das Lesen' - 'reading'.
To mean 'while' or 'in the process of' doing something, use 'beim' before a nominalised infinitive, e.g., 'beim Lesen'.
Use 'am' as an alternative to 'beim' before a nominalised verb, but only when a single activity is being done.
The use of 'beim' or 'am' plus the nominalised verb indicates the activity is, or was, ongoing or unfinished.
‘Deutschrap’ is a form of hip-hop which originates from the 1980s. ‘Rock am Ring’ is a famous music festival in Germany.
keywords: preposition meaning 'on the', is a contraction of 'an' and the dative definite article 'dem'
preposition meaning 'at (the)' or 'with (the)', followed by the dative case
the basic form of the verb, with no particular subject or tense indicated
the process of making a noun from a verb or adjective

5758.name: Meine Lieblingssänger: 'wenn' and 'als', superlatives
5758.outcome: I can use 'wenn' and 'als', along with superlatives, to discuss past, present and future musical preferences, artists and experiences.
points: 'Wenn' means ‘when’, ‘whenever’ or ‘if’, used for repeated actions or conditions in the present or future.
'Als' means ‘when’ to refer to a specific past event or point in time. 'Als' and 'wenn' both trigger word order 3.
Use the superlative to express the highest degree of something, e.g., 'the most beautiful', 'the best'.
To form superlatives, add '-st' to the adjective before a noun. Use ‘am’ and add ‘-sten’ to the adjective after a noun.
Some adjectives and adverbs have irregular comparative and superlative forms.
keywords: conjunction meaning ‘when’, referring to specific past events, which triggers word order 3
a form of adjective or adverb used to express the highest degree of a quality, e.g., 'the tallest', 'the most interesting'
conjunction meaning 'if' or 'when' which triggers word order 3
after certain conjunctions, the verb is sent to the end of the sentence or clause

5759.name: Interrailing: future tense, 2-verb structures, present tense with future meaning
5759.outcome: I can use the future tense and the present tense with future meaning to describe interrailing in Europe.
points: The future tense uses 'werden' in the present tense with a 2nd (infinitive) verb at the end of the sentence.
The present tense with a time adverbial can be used to express future meaning.
Time adverbials modify the time frame for a verb, for example 'this week', 'next month'.
2-verb structures send the 2nd (infinitive) verb to the end of the sentence in WO1 & 2, and to second-last place in WO3.
In reading, use title and picture clues, close reading, translation, and comprehension questions to aid understanding.
keywords: where the 2nd (infinitive) verb comes at the end of 2-verb sentences
adverbs or adverbial phrases which denote time; for example, 'nie', 'schon', 'noch nicht'

5760.name: Wiener Festwochen: inversion, time-manner-place
5760.outcome: I can use adverbs of time, manner, place correctly in statements and questions when learning about a visit to Vienna.
points: When two or more adverbs are in a sentence, the word order is time before manner before place (TMP).
Subject and verb invert in questions and in word order 2, where a sentence starts with a TMP adverb.
Wh- question words focus on time, manner, place, and TMP adverbs can start a sentence in reply.
Reading aloud benefits from initial silent rehearsal to focus on the sound-spelling correspondences.
Reading aloud also requires focus on cognates with different stress patterns from English.
keywords: when the subject pronoun and the verb switch place to form a question
the order of adverbs in a German sentence - time before manner before place, abbreviated to TMP

5761.name: Eine Reise durch Europa: dates
5761.outcome: I can use dates, years and numbers correctly and infer the meaning of unknown words when reading about and planning a trip across Europe.
points: We use ordinal numbers (e.g., 'first', 'second', 'third') for calendar dates.
To form ordinal numbers 1-19 add '-te', e.g., 'fünfte'; for ordinals 20 and over add '-ste', e.g., 'einundzwanzigste'.
For 'on the' with dates', use 'am' and add '-n' to the ordinal number, e.g., 'am zweiten März'.
For years, separate the digits into two pairs, for century and year, and place 'hundert' or 'tausend' between the pairs.
To infer the meaning of unknown words, examine the surrounding words, review given definitions and select the best fit.
keywords: preposition meaning 'on the', is a contraction of 'an' and the dative definite article 'dem'
tells you the order of something, e.g., 'first', 'second', 'third', and is used with dates

5762.name: Die Sächsische Schweiz: 'man' + verb, 'Lieblings-' and 'Haupt-'
5762.outcome: I can add prefixes to adapt the meaning of nouns, use ‘man’ + verb to express general ideas and can apply this new knowledge to a reading task.
points: Add the prefix 'Lieblings-' to nouns to mean 'favourite', e.g., 'die Lieblingsfarbe'.
Add the prefix 'Haupt-' to nouns to mean 'main', e.g., 'die Hauptstraße'.
The subject pronoun 'man' means 'one, you'. Its accusative form is 'einen' and its dative form is 'einem'.
Use 'man + verb' to translate English phrases that do not specify a particular subject, e.g., 'It is said that... '.
keywords: a prefix added to nouns to mean 'main'
a prefix added to nouns to mean 'favourite'
3rd person singular pronoun meaning 'one,' 'you', used to refer to people in general

5763.name: Badeschiff Berlin: possessive adjectives, modal verbs, 2-verb structures
5763.outcome: I can use the correct possessive pronoun to translate ‘its’ and apply my knowledge of present tense modal verbs and the two-verb rule in speaking and writing about a trip.
points: There are 16 Bundesländer (states) in Germany, 9 in Austria and 26 Kantone (states) in Switzerland.
Possessive adjectives are used with nouns to show ownership or belonging. They must agree with the noun which follows.
To translate 'its', use 'sein' with masculine or neuter nouns, and 'ihr' with feminine nouns.
Modal verbs express ideas of necessity or possibility. Use them with a 2nd verb in the infinitive at the sentence's end.
Apply the two-verb rule if there are two verbs in a sentence. The second verb goes to the end.
keywords: verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want
position of the 2nd verb at the end of two-verb sentences, e.g., 'Ich will jetzt Obst essen.'

5764.name: 16 Bundesländer: numbers, articles following 'in', 'zu', 'nach'
5764.outcome: I understand the format and use of cardinal and ordinal numbers in German, and can use the correct preposition to express 'to'.
points: Cardinal numbers (e.g., 'one') are used for counting or quantities. Ordinal numbers (e.g., ‘first’) show order.
Add '-te' to numbers 1-19 and '-ste' to numbers 20 and above to create ordinal numbers, e.g., 'fünfte' ('fifth').
For dates, use 'am' to say 'on the' and add '-n' to the ordinal number, e.g., 'am fünften August' (on the 5th August).
Use 'in' with the dative case to say 'in' and with the accusative case to mean 'into', e.g., 'ich gehe in die Schule'.
'Nach' means 'to' with place names and most countries. Use 'zu' plus dative for places with articles, people and events.
keywords: number form that shows how many of something there are
preposition which means 'in' with the dative case or 'into' with the accusative case
preposition meaning 'to', used with most countries, place names and places without articles
tells you the order of something, e.g., 'first', 'second', 'third', and is used with dates
word meaning 'to', used with a preceding comma to form two-verb sentences in German that do not involve a modal verb

5765.name: Eine Reise: present tense, separable verbs, possessive adjectives
5765.outcome: I can describe what I or others do on a trip using the simple present tense, including separable verbs and possessive adjectives.
points: German uses the simple present tense, formed by removing the '-en' from the infinitive and adding verb endings.
Separable verbs are made up of a prefix and a main verb. In the present, the prefix moves to the end of the clause.
In word order three (WO3) clauses, the prefix and verb join up in separable verbs.
Possessive adjectives are used with nouns to show ownership or belonging. They must agree with the noun which follows.
Use the possessive adjective 'sein' with masculine or neuter nouns to mean 'its'; use 'ihr' with feminine nouns.
keywords: tells the reader the action is happening now
two-part verb with a prefix and a main verb, e.g. 'aussehen'

5767.name: Die Wuppertaler Schwebebahn: past tense, past participles, time-manner-place
5767.outcome: I can form the perfect tense of different types of verbs and describe a past trip using adverbs of time, manner and place.
points: German uses the perfect tense to describe most past events, but English uses simple past for specific, completed events.
Form the perfect tense with a present tense of 'haben' or 'sein', plus a past participle at the end of the sentence.
Weak verbs form past participles by sandwiching the verb stem with 'ge-' and '-t'. '-ieren' verbs don't add 'ge-'.
Strong verbs form past participles with 'ge-' and '-en'. Separable prefixes go before 'ge-'.
The order of adverbs in a sentence is time ('um 6 Uhr'), manner ('mit Freunden'), place ('im Haus').
keywords: verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb
2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'
the order of adverbs in a German sentence - time before manner before place, abbreviated to TMP

5768.name: Romantische Straße: future tense, present tense with adverbs to express future
5768.outcome: I can recognise and use different linguistic structures to discuss future holiday plans.
points: Pronunciation is important for clear communication. Pay particular attention to the pronunciation of cognates.
To form the future tense, use the present tense of werden to mean 'will/going to’ and an infinitive verb at the end.
Use a future time phrase with the present tense to mean 'going to' or ‘-ing’, e.g., 'tomorrow I’m doing my homework'.
'Ich will' (from the verb 'wollen') means 'I want to', but is a false friend; 'ich werde' is 'I will'.

5769.name: Düsseldorf: past participles of strong and irregular verbs, questions
5769.outcome: I understand how to form the past participles of strong and irregular verbs, and can ask and answer questions in the perfect tense about a past trip.
points: The vowels [a], [o] and [e] can be pronounced long as in 'gezogen' or short as in 'gewonnen'.
Strong verbs form past participles by adding 'ge-' and '-en' around the verb stem, e.g. 'gelesen'. Others are irregular.
To form a closed question in the perfect tense, swap the position of 'haben' or 'sein' with the subject.
For open questions in the perfect tense, place a question word before 'haben' or 'sein'; the subject follows.
The past participles 'gefallen' and 'gemocht' both mean 'liked'. Use indirect object pronouns with 'gefallen'.
keywords: question that gets the answer 'yes' or 'no' and is created in Spanish by raising the tone of voice at the end of a statement
question starting with a wh- word that has more information in the answer than yes/no
verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb

5770.name: Graz: word order rules, possessive adjectives
5770.outcome: I can apply word order rules 1, 2 and 3, and recognise possessive adjectives in the genitive case, in the context of exploring a new place.
points: Use word order one with the conjunctions 'und', 'oder', 'aber', 'denn'.
Use word order three with the conjunctions 'weil', 'obwohl', 'dass', 'wenn', 'ob', 'da'.
Use word order two if starting a sentence with something other than the subject, e.g., an adverb.
Possessive adjectives are used before a noun to show ownership or belonging. They agree with the noun they describe.
The genitive case form of possessive adjectives means 'of...', e.g., 'meines Vaters' means 'of my father'.
keywords: case used to indicate possession and also used after certain prepositions
