4810.name: Le 14 juillet: indirect object pronouns me, te, lui, vous, nous, and leur
4810.outcome: I can understand and use singular and plural indirect object pronouns in texts describing the events of Bastille Day in France and its significance in French history.
points: Closed [eu] sounds like 'deux' or, when open or spelled [œu], sounds like 'coeur'.
An indirect object pronoun replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to.
The plural indirect object pronouns are: nous, vous, and leur.
Unlike direct object pronouns, indirect object pronouns don't change according to the gender of the nouns they replace.
keywords: replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, from you, with them; takes the dative case

4811.name: Une fête culturelle/religieuse: extended writing, speaking, photo description
4811.outcome: I can describe a cultural or religious festival in a French-speaking country using topic-specific vocabulary, and direct and indirect object pronouns.
points: An indirect object pronoun replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to.
Direct and indirect object pronouns avoid repetition of nouns and add sophistication.
Object pronouns can be used in your speaking, e.g. when describing a photo, or in your writing.
It is interesting and useful to know about some popular customs and celebrations in different Francophone countries.
keywords: replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, from you, with them; takes the dative case

4812.name: La diversité religieuse dans les pays francophones: extending vocabulary
4812.outcome: I can understand texts about religious diversity and can describe some Francophone customs and traditions.
points: Listening and reading texts can be exploited to enrich our topic-specific vocabulary.
France and other Francophone countries are religiously diverse.
Cognates may look very similar to English but sound quite different so attention must be paid to pronunciation.
Time adverbials and verb forms can be used to distinguish between past, present and future actions and events.
keywords: words with the same meaning and same or similar spelling in English and French

4813.name: À table! Partitive and indefinite articles, preverbal use of 'y' and 'en'
4813.outcome: I can use indefinite and partitive articles accurately to describe food and drink quantities and I can recognise when 'y' and 'en' are used to shorten sentences.
points: Use un/une (indefinite article) to describe whole things, and du/de la/de l' (partitive article) for parts of things.
Uncountable nouns, such as water or money, do not have a plural form. They are used with the partitive article.
'Y' can replace 'à' + [a place] to mean 'there', e.g. 'elle y va demain'.
'En' can replace 'de' + noun and can mean '(of) it/them', e.g. 'j'aime la confiture, j'en mange tous les jours'.
[en] is pronounced as in ‘enfant’.

4814.name: Des plats typiques: use of 'y' and 'en'
4814.outcome: I can recognise a range of typical French foods and dishes and can use 'y' and 'en' with correct word order.
points: [y] sounds like 'y' in 'physique'
Y can replace the object of a verb followed by à e.g. elle y a pensé.
We do not use 'y' for people. We use pronouns in this case e.g. Je pense à lui.
Il y en a means 'there is/are some'. It can also be used in the past tense: il y en avait and the future: il y en aura.

4815.name: Aller au restaurant: dictation, role-play
4815.outcome: I can ask and answer questions in a role-play scenario at a restaurant, using new food vocabulary and accurately incorporating partitive articles, indefinite articles, y and en.
points: French cuisine is celebrated for its wide array of dishes and foods, many of which are famous around the world.
'y' and 'en' are often used in speech to replace a group of other words.
Y means 'there' or '(to, about, in) it'. En means '(of) it/them'. When used together, 'y' comes before 'en'.
In formal role-plays, it is important to be able to understand formal speech, including 'vous' verbs and 'votre'.
keywords: task in which the student responds to several prompts in the format of a role-play
French pronoun meaning 'you' (when talking to more than one person)

2153.name: Allons-y! The imperative
2153.outcome: I can use the imperative to make suggestions and offer advice for a visit to a Francophone city.
points: The imperative only exists in second person singular (tu), second person plural (vous), and first person plural (nous).
The 'tu' form of the imperative is the same as the present tense 'je' form; er verbs end with -e, other verbs with -s.
When giving directions or instructions to a friend, use the informal imperative ‘tu’ form.
[oi] sounds like 'trois' and [oy] sounds like 'envoyer'.
‘Être’ is irregular in the imperative. The 'tu' form is 'sois' and the 'vous' form is 'soyez'.
keywords: a mood used to tell somebody to do something or give instructions or commands

4816.name: Montréal, une ville francophone: the imperative
4816.outcome: I can use regular and irregular imperative forms to give directions, instructions and make suggestions when exploring a Francophone city.
points: Montreal is the largest city in the province of Quebec in Canada. It is a bilingual city.
When giving directions or instructions to a stranger, use the formal imperative 'vous' form.
[oi] sounds like 'trois' and [oy] sounds like 'envoyer'
‘Être’ is irregular in the imperative. The 'tu' form is 'sois' and the 'vous' form is 'soyez'.
keywords: a mood used to tell somebody to do something or give instructions or commands

4817.name: Une visite en ville: role-play
4817.outcome: I can ask and answer questions in a role-play scenario in a Francophone city, incorporating the imperative.
points: Using the imperative in conversation enables the speaker to give instructions and advice, or to make suggestions.
In a role-play it's important to work out whether you will be addressed as ‘vous’ (formal) or ‘tu’ (informal).
You need to use the correct 'please': 's'il vous plait' in a formal setting, and 's'il te plait' for a friend.
keywords: a mood used to tell somebody to do something or give instructions or commands
task in which the student responds to several prompts in the format of a role-play

4818.name: La diversité culturelle: regular present tense
4818.outcome: I can use the present tense of -er, -ir and the four groups of -re verbs in the context of cultural events in France.
points: The three infinitive endings in French are -er, -ir and -re.
Regular verbs follow a common and consistent pattern when conjugated.
The four groups of -re verbs are: verbs like 'entendre', like 'prendre', like 'traduire' and verbs like 'écrire'.
'Connaitre' is conjugated in the present tense as: connais, connais, connait, connaissons, connaissez, connaissent.
keywords: a verb that follows a consistent and predictable pattern when conjugated

4820.name: Au Maroc: regular present tense verbs, present participle with 'en'
4820.outcome: I can use present participles of -er, -re, and -ir verbs, expressing two actions happening at the same time, in the context of Morocco's diverse culture.
points: Diversity in Morocco's language, culture, and food is a result of blending Berber, Arab, French and Spanish influences.
Four groups of -ir verbs are: verbs like 'choisir', verbs like 'partir', verbs like 'venir' and verbs like 'ouvrir'.
For present participles, remove -ons from the present tense 'nous' form and add -ant: 'écrire '- écrivons' - 'écrivant'.
'En' + present participle can be used when two actions happen together, e.g. 'il prépare le dîner en chantant'.
keywords: a verb form used to show how something happens, something that is happening at the same time, or to give a reason for something

4821.name: Au Maroc: read and respond to texts
4821.outcome: I can read and respond to extended texts about cultural groups in Morocco and I can use regular and irregular present participles.
points: Some regular present participles are: partant, venant, ouvrant, choisissant, entendant, prenant, connaissant, écrivant.
The present participle of faire is 'faisant'; 'faisant de' + noun means making something.
The irregular present participles of être and avoir are 'étant' and 'ayant'.
Extended reading texts can be exploited to enrich our thematic vocabulary and use of complex structures.
keywords: a verb form used to show how something happens, something that is happening at the same time, or to give a reason for something

4822.name: Une équipe francophone: adjective agreement, making comparisons
4822.outcome: I can understand descriptions of a Francophone sports team, recognising and applying knowledge of adjective agreements and comparisons.
points: To make adjectives feminine add -e, change -x to -se, -el to -elle, -en to -enne, -f to -ve, -er to -ère, or no change.
To form plural adjectives we add -s, unless the adjective ends in -x or -s. -al and -eau change to -aux and -eaux.
To make comparisons in French we use 'plus... que', 'moins... que' and 'aussi... que' with adjectives and adverbs.
keywords: form of adjective or adverb used to compare people, things or ideas

4823.name: Une équipe accomplie: present participle adjectives, comparatives, superlatives
4823.outcome: I can use comparatives and superlatives as well as present participles as adjectives to describe a sports team and its successes.
points: Present participles can be used as adjectives to describe a noun. e.g. 'une victoire surprenante'.
As adjectives, present participles agree in number and gender with the noun they are describing.
Some comparative adjective forms are irregular: 'bon' becomes 'meilleur' (better) and 'mauvais' becomes 'pire' (worse).
Superlatives describe something as the best, the most or the least e.g: le/la/les + plus/moins + adjective.
Some superlative forms are irregular: le/la/les + meilleur(e) (s) = the best; le/la/les + pire(s) = the worst.
keywords: form of adjective or adverb used to compare people, things or ideas
a verb form used to show how something happens, something that is happening at the same time, or to give a reason for something
a form of adjective or adverb used to express the highest degree of a quality e.g. 'the tallest', 'the most interesting'

4824.name: Une sportive qui m'intéresse: extended writing
4824.outcome: I can describe a sportsperson of interest, paying attention to adjective agreement rules, present participles, comparatives and superlatives.
points: Present participle adjectives can usefully be combined with other adjectives to give more information about nouns.
Comparative and superlative adjectives can be used to enhance opinions and descriptions.
It is important to communicate accurately but also to include varied and complex language.
When developing a personal response it is helpful to use reference materials to look up new vocabulary.
keywords: form of adjective or adverb used to compare people, things or ideas
a verb form used to show how something happens, something that is happening at the same time, or to give a reason for something
a form of adjective or adverb used to express the highest degree of a quality, e.g., 'the tallest', 'the most interesting'

4825.name: Une démocratie: creating nouns by adding -ion or -ation to the verb stem
4825.outcome: I can recognise new nouns by relating them to known verbs and can begin to use both to understand political contexts.
points: Adverbs can sometimes be created from adjectives, and nouns and adjectives can sometimes be created from verb stems.
[i] is pronounced as in 'midi', [on] is pronounced as in 'non!' and [tion] is pronounced as in 'attention!'.
Nouns can sometimes be created by adding -ion or -ation to the verb stem, e.g. 'manifester' - 'manifestation'.
keywords: part of the verb that appears in all forms

4826.name: Pourquoi voter? Creating nouns by adding -teur or -ateur to the verb stem
4826.outcome: I can use my knowledge of word families to expand my range of language when discussing people and their actions.
points: [eu] is pronounced closed as in 'deux' and [eu/œu] is pronounced open as in 'cœur', and [r] is pronounced as in 'rue'.
An agent noun is a noun describing a person or object doing the action of a verb.
Agent nouns can be created by adding -eur or -ateur to the verb stem, e.g. 'consommer' - 'consommateur'.
keywords: a noun describing a person or object doing the action of a verb

4827.name: Le conseil de la vie scolaire: extended speaking
4827.outcome: I can contribute to a democratic process in a school context using a range of topic-specific vocabulary to support my ideas.
points: We can work out the meaning of new words if we recognise part of the word from a related word.
Being able to apply word patterns, such as creating nouns from verb stems, significantly expands our vocabulary
Extend answers by justifying opinions and using a variety of adjectives, adverbs, pronouns and intensifiers.
keywords: a noun describing a person or object doing the action of a verb
part of the verb that appears in all forms

4828.name: Qu'en penses-tu? Possessive adjectives, direct & indirect object pronouns
4828.outcome: I can understand and give opinions on artwork and I can recognise a range of different pronouns and possessives.
points: Use possessive adjectives with nouns to say who things belong to.
When there is an '-s' or '-n' at the end of a possessive, and a vowel follows, liaison occurs.
Direct object pronouns are: 'me', 'te', 'le', 'la', 'l'', 'nous', 'vous', 'les'. They go before the verb.
Indirect object pronouns are: 'me', 'te', 'lui', 'nous', 'vous', 'leur'. They go before the verb.
keywords: replaces the noun receiving the action of the verb e.g. me, you, it, them
replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, from you, with them; takes the dative case

4829.name: Un portrait francophone: possessive adjectives, emphatic pronouns
4829.outcome: I can describe a famous piece of art, including a range of possessive adjectives and emphatic pronouns.
points: Possessive adjectives agree in number and sometimes gender with the thing that is owned.
Possessive pronouns can replace a possessive adjective + noun. Start with a definite article e.g. le mien, la mienne.
Moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles are used to mean me, you, him, her, us, you and them as emphatic pronouns.
An open [o] is pronounced as in 'porte' and a closed [o/ô] is pronounced as in 'photo'.
keywords: used to emphasise the subject of a sentence, in comparisons, and after 'c'est'
replaces a possessive adjective and a noun

4831.name: Un portrait coloré: extended speaking
4831.outcome: I can describe a picture in detail, incorporating a range of language and opinions, with reasons.
points: Including a range of direct object, indirect object and emphatic pronouns and possessive adjectives adds complexity.
When describing a picture mention: people, action, location, mood and season.
It is important to listen carefully for question type and tense in conversation questions.
keywords: replaces the noun receiving the action of the verb e.g. me, you, it, them
used to emphasise the subject of a sentence, in comparisons, and after 'c'est'
replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, from you, with them; takes the dative case

4832.name: Futurs divers: future -er verbs (singular), conditional 'vouloir' (singular)
4832.outcome: I can understand descriptions of personal future plans using verbs in the simple future and in the conditional with 'vouloir'.
points: The 1-verb future is the equivalent of 'will' + verb. It is formulated with one word.
Form the 1-verb future of -er verbs for je, tu, il/elle/on by adding the endings -ai, -as, -a to the infinitive.
The verb vouloir can be used in the conditional to express a wish. It can be followed by a noun or an infinitive.
The 1st, 2nd, 3rd person forms of vouloir in the conditional all sound the same: je voudrais, tu voudrais, il voudrait.
keywords: a form of verb used to express what will happen
form of verb used to express what would happen

4833.name: Tu aimerais? Future and conditional with -er verbs (singular)
4833.outcome: I can understand, ask and answer questions about my own and others' future family plans in the future and conditional.
points: The conditional is a verb form that expresses the idea 'would'; it is often followed by a 2nd verb in the infinitive.
The conditional of -er verbs is formed by adding the imperfect tense endings to the infinitive stem, e.g. j'aimerais.
The infinitive stem in the conditional and 1-verb future means that the sound [r], as in 'rue', is in all their forms.
[a] as in ‘animal’ and [ai] as in 'vrai' are in the endings; 'je' future ending 'ai' is exceptionally pronounced [é].
Use the conditional of 'vouloir' or 'aimer' + infinitive to say what you would 'like' to do.
keywords: form of verb used to express what would happen

4834.name: La famille de mes rêves: extended writing
4834.outcome: I can use BORDER to describe my ideal future family life using a range of future and conditional verbs.
points: The future and the conditional can be usefully combined to express plans and hopes for the future.
For the longer written task, it's important to write about both bullet points and develop ideas as much as possible.
The BORDER acronym is a useful tool to respond fully and accurately to bullet point writing prompts.
keywords: form of verb used to express what would happen

4835.name: Où se loger? Future and conditional with -er verbs (plural)
4835.outcome: I can recognise the future tense and the conditional of -er verbs in a range of texts about places to live.
points: [i] is pronounced as in 'midi', [on] as in 'non', and [ez] as in 'nez'.
Conjugate the future tense of -er verbs by adding the endings -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont to the infinitive.
The conditional has the same stem as the future tense (the infinitive).
The conditional endings are: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. These are the same as the imperfect.
keywords: form of verb used to express what would happen

4836.name: Village, ville ou ile? 'Si' + imperfect with conditional -er verbs (plural)
4836.outcome: I can compare different places to live and use 'si' with the imperfect and conditional to express where I and others would ideally like to live.
points: The conditional can be used to say what someone would do or what would happen.
The conditional endings are: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. These are the same as the imperfect.
The conditional is used in sentences with 'si' (if) and the imperfect to say what we would do if things were different.
keywords: form of verb used to express what would happen
a structure used to express a condition, translated as 'if' + past tense

4837.name: Avec des si...: future and conditional with -er verbs (plural)
4837.outcome: I can use the present, future and conditional to compare where I currently live and would ideally like to live in the future.
points: Time markers and conjunctions, combined with different verb tenses, help a reader to follow a text more easily.
Include a range of verbs in future and conditional when describing future plans and wishes.
The conditional can be used to compare real and ideal situations.
keywords: form of verb used to express what would happen

4838.name: On ira en vacances: future with 'aller', 'avoir', 'être' and 'faire'
4838.outcome: I can use the irregular verbs aller, avoir, être and faire in the 1-verb future tense to discuss future travel plans.
points: The 1-verb future tense expresses what will happen.
The 1-verb future stem for 'être' is 'ser-' and for 'avoir' is 'aur-' Regular future endings are added to these stems.
The 1-verb future stem for faire is 'fer-' and for 'aller' is 'ir-' Regular future endings are added to these stems.
keywords: a form of verb used to express what will happen

4839.name: À l'étranger: future and conditional with aller, avoir, être and faire
4839.outcome: I can use the future and conditional of irregular verbs aller, avoir, être and faire to discuss how, where, when and with whom I would travel.
points: The conditional has the same stem as the future tense for irregular verbs avoir, faire, aller and être.
For the conditional of these verbs we add the imperfect endings to the irregular stems 'aur-', 'ser-', 'ir-' and 'fer-'.
J'aurais (I would have), j'irais (I would go), je serais (I would be) and je ferais (I would be) are key conditionals.
Use the preposition 'en' when you want to say what type of vehicle you will use to travel.
keywords: form of verb used to express what would happen

4840.name: Ce serait parfait: photo description, extended writing
4840.outcome: I know when to use different tenses in a photo description task and I can describe an ideal holiday using the conditional of regular -er and irregular verbs.
points: Use the present to describe what you see on a photo, but use the future and conditional to develop the conversation.
Use time markers and other similarly useful structures to help organise longer responses using different tenses.
Include regular and common irregular future and conditional verbs when writing about future plans.
keywords: acronym for photo description (people and objects, action, location, mood)
form of verb used to express what would happen

4842.name: Une journée dans la vie d'un groupe francophone: reflexive pronouns
4842.outcome: I can recognise the use of and apply reflexive pronouns to express daily routine actions.
points: Use reflexive pronouns (me, te, se...) before the verb when subject and object of the verb are the same person.
[e] is pronounced as in 'je' and [ou] is pronounced as in 'nous'.
The singular reflexive pronouns are: 'me', 'te', 'se'. They are shortened to m', t' and s' before a silent letter/vowel.
The plural reflexive pronouns are: 'nous', 'vous', 'se'. 'Se' is shortened to s' before a vowel.
keywords: used to indicate doing something to yourself, words like 'myself' and yourself'

4843.name: Ils s'entendent bien: reflexive pronouns
4843.outcome: I can understand texts about daily routine using reflexive verbs and also texts discussing relationships and interactions with reciprocal verbs.
points: The verb spellings of regular reflexive verbs are the same as regular -er, -ir and -re verbs in the present tense.
Some verbs have a secondary meaning that uses a reflexive pronoun.
Some verbs use reflexive pronouns in French when their English translation doesn't include a reflexive idea.
Sometimes the reflexive pronoun indicates the action is exchanged between two or more subjects acting upon one another.
keywords: A reciprocal is the multiplicative inverse of any non-zero number. Any non-zero number multiplied by its reciprocal is equal to 1
describes an action where the subject and the object of the verb are the same

4844.name: Ils m'inspirent: extended writing
4844.outcome: I can describe the daily life of a famous Francophone group or individual, incorporating a range of reflexive verbs and pronouns.
points: Reflexive pronouns enable us to express an action done to oneself or two or more subjects acting upon one another.
Infinitives of reflexive verbs are always preceded by se or s’. Choose the correct pronoun when conjugating the verb.
The negative component 'ne' goes before the reflexive pronoun. 'Pas' goes after the verb.
Extend answers by giving and justifying opinions and using a variety of adjectives, adverbs, pronouns and intensifiers.
keywords: used to indicate doing something to yourself, words like 'myself' and yourself'

4845.name: Qui a fait le ménage? Perfect tense, relative clauses, negation
4845.outcome: I can understand conversation about everyday household tasks using the perfect tense, relative pronouns and negatives.
points: The perfect tense is formed by combining part of 'avoir' or 'être' (the auxiliary verb) and a past participle.
'Qui' means ‘who?’ in a question, but it is the relative pronoun ‘who’, ‘which’, ‘or ‘that’ in the middle of a sentence.
When the relative pronoun relates to the object of the sentence, we use 'que' (who/whom, that or which), not 'qui'.
In most negative phrases in the perfect tense, the negative structure goes around the part of 'avoir' or 'être'.
keywords: a pronoun that introduces a relative clause e.g. qui, que

4846.name: Je sortais la poubelle quand...:perfect, imperfect, relative clauses, negation
4846.outcome: I can talk about past events using the imperfect tense and the perfect tense, relative clauses and negation.
points: The imperfect tense is used to describe what 'was happening' or what you 'were doing' when something else happened.
Form the imperfect by removing -ons from 'nous' present tense and adding:-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient
Où and quand can be used in relative clauses to detail where or when something was happening.
For 'neither...nor', ne precedes the verb and each ni precedes one of the negated qualities/nouns.
Ne... que means 'only'. 'Que' follows the verb and precedes the noun that is limited.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
a pronoun that introduces a relative clause e.g. qui, que

4847.name: La vie quotidienne: perfect and imperfect tenses, relative clauses and negation
4847.outcome: I can discuss everyday life in the past, combining imperfect and perfect tenses, negation and relative clauses.
points: Using the perfect tense and imperfect tense together enables us to express ongoing and isolated events in the past.
Using qui, que, où and quand in relative clauses provides more information and adds complexity.
Using a range of negative structures adds subtlety and complexity to descriptions and opinions.
Combining different tenses allows students to give a more developed answers to conversation questions.
keywords: a pronoun that introduces a relative clause e.g. qui, que

4848.name: On peut acheter: present tense modal verbs
4848.outcome: I can use modals in the present tense to describe what we can, want and must do on a shopping trip.
points: To talk about what you can, know, have to, or want to do, use modal verbs: 'pouvoir', 'savoir', 'devoir', 'vouloir'.
Modal verbs are usually followed by an infinitive.
[-ill-/-ille] is pronounced as in 'fille', [-aill-/-ail] is pronounced as in 'taille'.
keywords: verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want

4849.name: On a fait les courses: irregular past participles, perfect tense modal verbs
4849.outcome: I can describe a food shopping trip in France, using a range of past participles, including modal verbs.
points: Three common irregular verbs and their past participles are: avoir (eu), faire (fait), boire (bu).
[u] is pronounced as in 'tu'. Many past participles end in 'u' and rhyme with each other.
The past participles of the four modal verbs are: dû, pu, voulu, and su.
Modal verbs in the perfect tense use 'avoir' as the auxiliary verb.
keywords: verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb

4850.name: J'ai dû attendre: irregular past participles, modal verbs present and past
4850.outcome: I can combine regular, irregular and modal verbs in the perfect and present tenses to describe positive and negative aspects of a trip to town.
points: Adding modal verbs to your written and spoken work broadens communication and adds complexity.
The irregular past participles of the four modal verbs are: dû, pu, voulu and su.
It is helpful to practise moving between present and past tense modals e.g je peux- j'ai pu; je veux- j'ai voulu.
keywords: verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want

4851.name: Avant de passer un examen: prepositions with the infinitive
4851.outcome: I can understand and give advice using 'sans', 'pour' and 'avant de' plus the infinitive.
points: [j] sounds like 'jour', [th] sounds like 'thé', [gn] sounds like 'ligne' and [h] sounds like 'heure.'
'Sans' ('without') and 'pour' ('for') are prepositions which can be followed immediately by the infinitive.
'Avant' ('before') is followed by 'de' and the infinitive, and is translated as 'before doing'.
keywords: the basic form of the verb, with no particular subject or tense indicated
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

4852.name: Après avoir préparé: 'après avoir' + past participle
4852.outcome: I can understand and give advice using 'après avoir' + past participle.
points: 'Après avoir' is used with a past participle to translate the English 'after doing' something.
If the verb takes 'être' in the perfect tense, use 'après être' instead of 'après avoir'.
When the verb used takes 'être' in the perfect tense, the past participle must agree with the subject of the sentence.
Reflexive verbs place the reflexive pronoun in front of 'être'.
keywords: verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb

4853.name: On est prêt à tout: avant de, après avoir
4853.outcome: I can complete a photo description task and accurately translate complex sentences using prepositions into French and into English, in the context of taking exams.
points: Including structures such as avant de + infinitive and après avoir + past participle enhances complexity.
Cognates help us understand the context of longer texts. Be aware of 'false friends' which don't carry the same meaning.
Pay attention to 'little words' when translating into French, e.g. avant must be followed by 'de' before the infinitive.
Account for every word when translating from French, but remember there might be a different number of words in English.
keywords: word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

4854.name: Le langage cinématographique: past participles of regular verbs
4854.outcome: I can use regular verbs in the perfect tense to talk about films.
points: The past participles of -er verbs like 'parler' end in -é.
The past participles of -re verbs like 'entendre' end in -u.
