a word that has the same or similar meaning to another word

7318.name: Le Québec: relative clauses, perfect and imperfect, extended writing (Edexcel)
7318.outcome: I can use imperfect and perfect tenses and relative clauses to write about Quebec.
points: A relative clause provides more information about a noun from the previous clause without beginning a new sentence.
Relative clauses can be formed using 'qui', 'que', 'quand' and 'où'.
Using the perfect tense and imperfect tense together enables us to express ongoing and isolated events in the past.
The BORDER acronym is a useful tool to respond fully and accurately to bullet point writing prompts.
keywords: a pronoun that introduces a relative clause e.g. qui, que

7321.name: Mes études: present and future, picture task (Edexcel)
7321.outcome: I can refer to present and future situations in the context of my studies using a range of verbs followed by the infinitive.
points: To form the 2-verb future, use part of the verb 'aller' in the present tense plus the infinitive.
Conjugate the 1-verb future of -er verbs by adding the endings -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont to the infinitive.
The future stems for ‘aller’, ‘avoir’, ‘être’ and ‘faire’ are: ir-, aur-, ser- and fer-.
Some verbs require 'à' or 'de' before an infinitive, e.g. 'arriver à', 'éviter de'.
keywords: a form of verb used to express what will happen
the basic form of the verb, with no particular subject or tense indicated

7322.name: Au collège: prepositions, transcription, listening (Edexcel)
7322.outcome: I can accurately transcribe spoken French using my knowledge of sound-symbol correspondences as well as understand listening tasks on the subject of school life.
points: It is important to have a firm knowledge of French sounds (SSCs) in order to accurately transcribe spoken French.
It is important to listen out for synonyms and distractors when answering listening comprehension questions.
keywords: incorrect but plausible answer option in reading and listening tasks, designed to test your attention to detail
relationship between letters and their sounds
a word that has the same or similar meaning to another word

7323.name: À l'université: infinitive as noun, conditional verbs, conversation (Edexcel)
7323.outcome: I can ask and answer questions about future study plans using the present, future and conditional.
points: An infinitive can be used as the subject of a sentence to express an activity. It works like a noun.
We normally translate infinitives as nouns using the -ing form of the verb in English.
The conditional has the same stem as the future tense and the same endings as the imperfect, e.g. 'j'aimerais'.
The future and the conditional can be usefully combined to express plans and hopes for the future.
keywords: form of verb used to express what would happen

7324.name: En ligne: questions in three tenses, picture task (Edexcel)
7324.outcome: I can ask questions using past, present and future tenses and describe a picture showing life online.
points: Yes/no questions in all tenses are formed by inversion of subject and verb, adding 'est-ce que' or using intonation.
To ask questions using question words, add a question word before the inverted verb or before 'est-ce que'.
Being able to ask questions in different tenses, as well as answer them, is key to successful communication.
keywords: when the subject pronoun and the verb switch place to form a question

7325.name: En ligne: Reading aloud, extended reading (Edexcel)
7325.outcome: I can apply my vocabulary knowledge and reading strategies to successfully complete exam-style reading tasks.
points: Using a checklist before a read-aloud task is a powerful and effective strategy.
In a read-aloud task, think carefully about how to correctly pronounce the letters in each word and spot tricky sounds.
When reading, we can avoid distractors by not rushing to select an answer.
Distractors can appear anywhere - in the question, the answer options or the text itself.
keywords: incorrect but plausible answer option in reading and listening tasks, designed to test your attention to detail

7326.name: En ligne: Impersonal and modal verbs, conversation (Edexcel)
7326.outcome: I can use impersonal and modal verbs to support my discussion of the positives and risks of life online, and how to stay safe online.
points: 'Il est', 'il fait', 'il y a' and 'il faut' are common impersonal verbs.
Impersonal verbs 'il vaut mieux' (it's better) and 'ça vaut la peine de' (it's worth) are followed by the infinitive.
To talk about what you can, know, have to, or want to do, use modal verbs: 'pouvoir', 'savoir', 'devoir', 'vouloir'.
If modal verbs are followed by another verb, it must be in the infinitive form.
The past participles of the four modal verbs are: 'dû', 'pu', 'voulu' and 'su'. They are used with 'avoir'.
keywords: a verb that doesn't refer to a particular person or thing, and whose subject is most often 'il' (it)
verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want

7327.name: Une visite à Bruxelles: negation, adjective agreement, role-play (Edexcel)
7327.outcome: I can recognise and use a range of negative structures and adjectives in the context of exploring a new city.
points: Use ne... pas for what doesn't happen, ne... jamais for never, ne... rien for nothing and ne... personne for nobody.
Use ne... plus for no longer, ne... ni... ni for neither, nor, ne... pas encore for not yet and ne... que for only.
To make an adjective feminine we add -e, -x → -se, -el → -elle, -en → -enne, -f → -ve, -er → -ère, or no change.
To form plural adjectives we add an -s, unless the adjective ends in -x or -s. -al and -eau change to -aux and -eaux.
keywords: when the ending of an adjective matches the noun it describes in gender and number
two elements e.g. ne … pas around the main verb expressing negative meaning

7329.name: Une visite à Bruxelles: transcription, extended listening (Edexcel)
7329.outcome: I can accurately transcribe spoken French and understand listening comprehension texts relating to Brussels.
points: Use your knowledge of French sounds to carefully write down what you hear. Check spelling carefully.
After dictation, use your knowledge of grammar to check what you've written makes sense.
Before you listen, use the English title and words provided to predict which French words you might hear.
keywords: strategy that involves anticipating what the answers might be by listing relevant French words or phrases

7330.name: Une visite à Bruxelles: position of adjectives and adverbs, writing (Edexcel)
7330.outcome: I can write about travelling abroad, using adverbs as well as adjectives.
points: Adjectives that come before the noun fit into five categories: BRAGS (Beauty, Rank, Age, Good/bad and Size/quantity).
Adverbs that describe adjectives usually precede them.
Adverbs that modify the verb and adverbs of frequency usually come after the verb.
Extend answers by using a variety of subjects, adding a different time frame and using an element of contrast.

7331.name: Des francophones célèbres: word pattern rules, role-play (Edexcel)
7331.outcome: I can identify and use word pattern rules and complete a role-play relating to a famous French-speaking person.
points: Ordinal numbers are created by (removing -e and) adding -ième to a number: 'deuxième', 'onzième'.
in- or im- can be added to adjectives, adverbs or nouns to give the opposite meaning. English equivalent is un- or in-.
-ion or -ation can be added to the verb stem to form a noun where the English equivalent is -ion or -ation.
Agent nouns can be created by adding -eur or -ateur to the verb stem, e.g. 'consommer' - 'consommateur'.
keywords: tells you the order of something, e.g., 'first', 'second', 'third', and is used with dates
task in which the student responds to several prompts in the format of a role-play

7332.name: Des francophones célèbres: reading aloud, reading comprehension (Edexcel)
7332.outcome: I can understand reading comprehension texts about famous French speakers.
points: Pay attention to French sounds and pronunciation rules as you complete the read-aloud task.
In comprehension tasks, it is important to read questions carefully before answering.
Always give the correct number of details when answering a question.
keywords: incorrect but plausible answer option in reading and listening tasks, designed to test your attention to detail

7333.name: Des francophones célèbres: imperative, present participle, writing (Edexcel)
7333.outcome: I can understand the imperative and present participles and I can write in detail about famous French speakers.
points: The imperative is used to give instructions, commands or advice to one or more people.
The imperative exists in second person singular ('tu'), first person plural ('nous') and second person plural ('vous').
French present participle ends in -ant, English present participle ends in -ing.
For present participle, remove -ons from nous form present tense and replace with -ant, e.g. écrire, écrivons, écrivant.
In writing, it is important to communicate accurately but also to include varied and complex language.
keywords: a mood used to tell somebody to do something or give instructions or commands
a verb form used to show how something happens, something that is happening at the same time, or to give a reason for something

7334.name: Contrôle oral: role-play, read aloud, picture task (Edexcel)
7334.outcome: I can confidently complete all three parts of the French speaking exam: role-play, read aloud and photo description.
points: You should answer role-play prompts with a short phrase or sentence. Do not add unnecessary detail.
It is important to have a firm understanding of sound-spelling correspondences to accurately read aloud in French.
Use the PALM acronym to structure photo descriptions.
In the conversation following the photo description, you should aim to develop answers using at least 3 verb clauses.
keywords: acronym for photo description (people and objects, action, location, mood)
relationship between letters and their sounds
a piece of information that contains a subject and a verb

7335.name: Contrôle d'écoute: dictation (Edexcel)
7335.outcome: I can confidently complete exam-style dictation tasks.
points: It is important to have a firm knowledge of French SSCs in order to accurately transcribe spoken French.
keywords: relationship between letters and their sounds

7336.name: Contrôle écrit: photo description, essay and translation practice (Edexcel)
7336.outcome: I can confidently complete the photo description, 90-word essay and translation tasks from the writing paper.
points: Use the PALM acronym to structure photo descriptions.
The BORDER acronym is a useful tool to respond fully and accurately to bullet point writing prompts.
It is important to carefully check verb endings and adjectival agreement when translating from English to French.
keywords: acronym for photo description (people and objects, action, location, mood)

7337.name: Contrôle de lecture: extended reading and translation into English (Edexcel)
7337.outcome: I can confidently complete exam-style reading comprehension and translation into English tasks.
points: It is important to have a broad vocabulary to be successful at answering reading comprehension questions.
It is important to look out for synonyms and distractors when answering reading comprehension questions.
It is important to pay close attention to verb endings to accurately translate their tense and subject into English.
It is important to be aware of false friends when translating into English.
keywords: incorrect but plausible answer option in reading and listening tasks, designed to test your attention to detail
a word that has the same or similar meaning to another word

7338.name: Contrôle d'écoute: extended listening (Edexcel)
7338.outcome: I can confidently respond to exam-style listening comprehension questions.
points: It is important to have a broad vocabulary to be successful at answering listening comprehension questions.
It is important to listen out for synonyms and distractors when answering listening comprehension questions.
keywords: incorrect but plausible answer option in reading and listening tasks, designed to test your attention to detail
a word that has the same or similar meaning to another word

7340.name: Contrôle écrit: short and long essay practice (Edexcel)
7340.outcome: I can confidently complete exam-style essay tasks from the writing paper.
points: The BORDER acronym is a useful tool to respond fully and accurately to bullet point writing prompts.

5776.name: Abenteuer im Ausland: perfect tense stem changes, perfect tense questions
5776.outcome: I can form the past participles of strong verbs with stem changes, and I can ask questions in the perfect tense about a past trip or experience.
points: Strong verbs form past participles with 'ge-' and '-en' in the perfect tense.
Some verbs have a vowel change in their past participle, such as 'ei' → 'ie', 'ie' → 'o', 'i' → 'u' or 'e' → 'o'.
To form a closed question in the perfect tense, swap the position of 'haben' or 'sein' with the subject.
For open questions in the perfect tense, place a question word before 'haben' or 'sein'; the subject follows.
keywords: question that gets the answer 'yes' or 'no' and is created in Spanish by raising the tone of voice at the end of a statement
question starting with a wh- word that has more information in the answer than yes/no
verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb
verb whose past participle sandwiches the stem with 'ge-' and ‘-en’ and often changes the stem vowel

5778.name: Freiwilligenarbeit: direct and indirect object pronouns, position of objects
5778.outcome: I can understand and use direct and indirect object pronouns and nouns in the context of voluntary work and adventures abroad.
points: A direct object pronoun replaces a noun that is the object of the verb and is in the accusative case.
An indirect object pronoun replaces the noun that the verb action is done ‘to’ or ‘for’ and is in the dative case.
In sentences with two object nouns, the indirect object noun always comes before the direct object noun.
In sentences with two objects where there is one noun and one pronoun, the pronoun always comes first.
keywords: form(s) used for the object or 'receiver' of the action of the verb
case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
replaces the noun receiving the action of the verb e.g. me, you, it, them
replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, from you, with them; takes the dative case

5779.name: Mein Brückenjahr: preposition 'bei', 'beim' and 'am' with nominalised verbs
5779.outcome: I can use 'bei' as a simple preposition and 'beim' and 'am' with nominalised verbs in the context of gap years and future adventures.
points: 'Bei' means 'at' or 'with' and takes the dative. When used with masculine or neuter nouns, 'bei dem' becomes 'beim'.
To mean ‘whilst’ or ‘in the process of’ doing something, use 'beim' before a nominalised infinitive, e.g., ‘beim Lesen’.
Use 'am' as an alternative to 'beim' to mean ‘in the process of’, but only when a single activity is being done.
The use of 'beim' or 'am' plus the nominalised verb indicates the activity is, or was, ongoing or unfinished.
In conversation, develop answers by adding opinions and reasons, varying the subject, and adding different time frames.
keywords: preposition meaning 'on the', is a contraction of 'an' and the dative definite article 'dem'
preposition meaning ‘at (the house of)', ‘for’ or ‘with’, followed by the dative case
preposition meaning 'at (the)' or 'with (the)', followed by the dative case
case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
the process of making a noun from a verb or adjective

5780.name: Das Wattenmeer: present tense weak and strong verbs, reflexives
5780.outcome: I can use a range of weak, strong and reflexive verbs in the present tense to understand texts about and to describe new places.
points: Weak verbs in the present tense follow a regular pattern of changes, like 'lernen'.
Strong verbs in the present tense change their vowel in the verb stem in the 'du' and 'er, sie, es' forms.
Strong verb stem changes in the present tense are: e to i, e to ie, and a to ä.
Use reflexive pronouns with reflexive verbs. They often relate the action to the subject of the sentence.
Some verbs have a different meaning when they are used as reflexive verbs, e.g., ‘anziehen’ and ‘sich anziehen’.
keywords: describes an action where the subject and the object of the verb are the same
verb which changes its vowel in the verb stem of some of its forms
a verb that follows a regular pattern of changes

5781.name: Wie komme ich am besten...? Formal and informal imperatives
5781.outcome: I can understand and use informal and formal imperatives for giving instructions, directions and advice.
points: Imperative verbs are used to give instructions, directions, or advice.
For the ‘du’ imperative of weak and strong verbs, remove the ‘-st’ and the 'du'. Omit umlauts added as a stem change.
To use the 'ihr' form of the imperative of weak and strong verbs, just remove the pronoun 'ihr'.
To use the formal 'Sie' form of the imperative, swap the position of the verb and subject pronoun 'Sie'.
'Sein' is irregular in the 'du' and 'Sie' forms of the imperative. Use 'sei', 'seid' and 'Seien Sie'.
keywords: formal word for ‘you’ used for adults we address by surname
subject pronoun meaning ‘you’, informal and singular
a mood used to tell somebody to do something or give instructions or commands

5782.name: Ausflüge: formal and informal questions
5782.outcome: I can create formal and informal questions in response to texts and use my knowledge of questions to help form accurate answers when speaking.
points: A closed question, also known as a yes/no question, is formed by swapping the position of the verb and subject.
Use 'du' questions for informal singular ‘you’, 'ihr' questions for informal plural ‘you’, and 'Sie' for formal 'you'.
When responding to questions about yourself, change the 2nd person language to 1st person language.
When answering questions, you may need to change subject pronouns, verbs, possessive adjectives and reflexive pronouns.
keywords: language used to refer to ‘you’, singular or plural
formal word for ‘you’ used for adults we address by surname
question that gets the answer 'yes' or 'no' and is created in Spanish by raising the tone of voice at the end of a statement
subject pronoun meaning ‘you’, informal and singular

5783.name: Feste: present tense weak and strong verbs
5783.outcome: I can use weak and strong verbs in the present tense and I can describe a photo of a celebration in detail.
points: Weak verbs in the present tense follow a regular pattern of changes, like ‘lernen’.
Strong verbs in the present tense change their stem vowel in the ‘du’ and ‘er, sie, es’ forms: e→i, e→ie, and a→ä.
When describing a photo, use the acronym PALM. It stands for People, Action, Location, Mood. Add your own opinions too.
Translate the English present continuous using the German simple present when describing what is happening in a photo.
keywords: acronym for photo description (people and objects, action, location, mood)
describes events happening right now: 'I am doing'
verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'
a verb which changes its vowel in the verb stem of some of its forms
a verb that follows a regular pattern of changes

5784.name: Recyceln: formal and informal questions, 'du', 'ihr', 'Sie'
5784.outcome: I can create formal and informal questions in the context of helping the environment.
points: The consonantal [r] makes a rolling sound at the back of the throat and the vocalic [r] has a gentle ‘ah’ sound.
A closed question is formed by swapping the position of the verb and subject in a statement. This is called inversion.
An open question is formed by adding a question word before the verb at the start of a closed question.
Use 'du' questions for informal singular ‘you’, 'ihr' questions for informal plural ‘you’, and 'Sie' for formal ‘you’.
Use rising intonation, as well as correct word order, to make it clear that you are asking a question.
keywords: formal word for ‘you’ used for adults we address by surname
subject pronoun meaning ‘you’, informal and singular

5785.name: Hilf der Umwelt! Imperative 'du', 'ihr', 'Sie'
5785.outcome: I can understand and use informal and formal imperatives for giving instructions, directions, and advice in the context of helping the environment.
points: Imperative verbs are used to give instructions, directions, or advice.
For the ‘du’ imperative of weak and strong verbs, remove the ‘-st’ and the 'du'. Omit umlauts added as a stem change.
To use the 'ihr' form of the imperative of weak and strong verbs, just remove the pronoun 'ihr'.
To use the formal 'Sie' form of the imperative, swap the position of the verb and subject pronoun 'Sie'.
'Sein' is irregular in the 'du' and 'Sie' forms of the imperative. Use 'sei', 'seid' and 'Seien Sie'.
keywords: formal word for ‘you’ used for adults we address by surname
subject pronoun meaning ‘you’, informal and singular
a mood used to tell somebody to do something or give instructions or commands

5786.name: Flüsse in Deutschland: negation, 'sondern', 'entweder...oder', 'weder...noch'
5786.outcome: I can use a range of negative structures and conjunctions in the context of describing places and possibilities.
points: Use 'nicht' before definite articles to mean ‘not the’ and 'kein' instead of the indefinite article to mean 'not a, no'.
Place 'nicht' before adjectives, adverbs, possessives and proper nouns. Place 'nicht' after verbs and whole phrases.
Use 'nichts' to mean 'nothing' or 'not anything', e.g., 'ich sehe nichts.' Use 'nie' to mean 'never'.
Use 'sondern' to mean 'but' or 'rather' when contradicting a preceding negative.
Use the conjunction 'entweder … oder...' to mean 'either … or...' and 'weder … noch...' to mean 'neither … nor...'.
keywords: negative article ‘no’, ‘not a, an, any’ - negates nouns preceded by the indefinite article
the adverb 'not', which negates the definite article ‘the’
conjunction used after a negative, meaning ‘but’ or ‘rather’

5787.name: Deutsche Städte: comparative adjectives
5787.outcome: I can use comparative adjectives to draw comparisons between places and to enhance descriptions.
points: Turn an adjective into a comparative adjective by adding '-er', e.g., 'schneller'.
To say 'than' when making a comparison, use 'als', e.g., 'meine Stadt ist größer als dein Dorf'.
Some adjectives also gain an umlaut in the comparative form, e.g., 'jünger'.
Adjectives ending -el or -er remove the penultimate ‘e’, e.g., 'teurer', 'dunkler'.
Comparatives can be useful for developing opinions, reasons and ideas when writing descriptions.
keywords: form of adjective or adverb used to compare people, things or ideas

5789.name: Wie ist die Stadt? Dative articles after 'laut'
5789.outcome: I can use 'laut' with the dative case to report what I have understood from a text or to express other people's opinions.
points: The preposition ‘laut’ means 'according to' and is followed by the dative case.
The dative definite articles are: 'dem', 'der', 'dem', 'den'. 'Dies-' follows the same pattern.
The dative indefinite articles are: 'einem', 'einer', 'einem'. Possessives follow the same pattern as these articles.
The preposition 'laut' can be used to report what we have understood from texts, pictures, or from other people.
The sound-symbol correspondence [au], as in 'laut', sounds like 'Haus'.
keywords: case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
a preposition meaning 'according to' which is followed by the dative

5791.name: Deutsche Geschichte: negation, inversion
5791.outcome: I can apply my knowledge of vocabulary, negation and word order to understand and respond to a text about the Stasi.
points: Use 'nicht' before definite articles to mean ‘not the’ and 'kein' instead of the indefinite article to mean 'not a, no'.
Place 'nicht' before adjectives, adverbs, possessives and proper nouns. Place 'nicht' after verbs and whole phrases.
Use 'nichts' to mean 'nothing' or 'not anything', e.g., 'ich sehe nichts'.
Use word order two if starting a sentence with something other than the subject, e.g., an adverb.
Use your knowledge of German pronunciation and punctuation to support your intonation when reading aloud.
keywords: rise and fall of the voice in speaking
negative article ‘no’, ‘not a, an, any’ - negates nouns preceded by the indefinite article
the adverb 'not', which negates the definite article ‘the’
inverts the subject and verb in a sentence

5792.name: Deutsche Geschichte: adjective agreement, adjectival nouns
5792.outcome: I can apply my knowledge of vocabulary to identify relationships between words and support my understanding of longer texts, and can confidently use adjective endings and adjectival nouns.
points: Exploring relationships between words supports your understanding of language in different contexts.
Adjective agreement occurs when adjectives precede a noun. Do not add endings to adjectives after a noun.
Adjective endings change depending on the gender, case and number of the noun they describe.
Neuter adjectival nouns express abstract concepts and use the ending '-e' in nominative and accusative.
Plural adjectival nouns end in '-en' after 'die'. Without articles, use '-e' in nominative and accusative; '-en' dative.
keywords: a type of noun that takes the same endings as adjectives
when the ending of an adjective matches the noun it describes in gender and number

5793.name: Deutsche Geschichte: imperfect tense, perfect tense
5793.outcome: I can apply a checklist of knowledge to support my use of the perfect and imperfect tenses, and can apply this when reading and writing in German.
points: Confidence in forming the perfect tense is important for communicating past events. Revisit key verbs often.
The perfect tense is more common in spoken German than the imperfect. Both can be used when writing in the past tense.
The imperfect tense forms ‘hatte’, ‘war’, and ‘es gab’ are often used in spoken as well as written German.
Learning imperfect tense endings, and the verb stems of strong verbs, will broaden your use of language in the past.
Being familiar with a range of past tense verb forms will support your comprehension of written and spoken German.
keywords: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb
2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'

5794.name: Rechte: perfect tense, simple past, 'seit' vs 'vor'
5794.outcome: I can use the simple past and perfect tenses and 'seit' and 'vor' to understand the historical context and recent changes relating to international human rights.
points: The perfect tense uses the present tense of 'sein' or 'haben' plus a past participle, and is used in speech and writing.
The single-verb simple past or imperfect tense in German is used most often to narrate past events in writing.
'Seit', with dative and present tense, expresses an unfinished action started in the past. It can mean ‘since’ or ‘for'.
'Vor' + length of time is used with past tense to say how long ago something happened. Use the dative case.
These structures provide a framework for discussing the history and developments in international human rights.
keywords: 2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'
preposition meaning ‘since’ or ‘for’, followed by the dative case
German single-word past tense used mainly to narrate past events in writing, e.g., 'war', 'hatte', 'gab', 'fand'
preposition meaning ‘ago’, followed by the dative case

5795.name: Arbeiter und Arbeitslose: 'obwohl', 'zu' clauses um...zu, ohne...zu, statt...zu
5795.outcome: I can use 'obwohl' with word order 3 and infinitive constructions with 'zu' to understand and discuss rights and support for both workers and unemployed people in Germany.
points: The conjunction 'obwohl' triggers word order 3, which sends the verb to the end of the sentence or clause.
When combined with a second verb in the infinitive, some verbs require the addition of 'zu'.
Infinitive constructions are separated from other clauses with a comma.
Use 'um … zu' + infinitive to mean 'in order to, 'statt... zu' for 'instead of', 'ohne... zu' for 'without'.
keywords: the basic form of the verb, with no particular subject or tense indicated
after certain conjunctions, the verb is sent to the end of the sentence or clause

5796.name: Rechte: 'wer', 'wen', 'wem'
5796.outcome: I can understand and read aloud vocabulary relating to human rights and can ask questions using 'wer', 'wen' and 'wem' when discussing rights for disabled people.
points: Learning and revisiting vocabulary benefits from read-aloud pratice to cement sound-spelling correspondences
Reading aloud needs initial practice focussing on SSCs, compound and unknown words prior to whole text practice.
The interrogative pronoun 'wer' becomes 'wen' in the accusative.
The interrogative pronoun 'wer' become 'wem' in the dative.
keywords: form(s) used for the object or 'receiver' of the action of the verb
case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
the case used for the subject of a sentence
relationship between letters and their sounds
question word meaning 'who' or 'whom' which changes according to case

5797.name: Die Vennbahn: perfect tense, imperfect tense, weak past participles
5797.outcome: I can use adverbs to give and respond to detailed responses in the past tense, form past participles of a range of weak verbs, and apply this knowledge when translating into German.
points: Use 'gern', 'lieber' and 'früher' with a past tense to mean 'liked', 'rather', 'in the past, used to'.
Weak verbs form their past participles by sandwiching the verb stem with 'ge-' and '-t', e.g., 'gespielt'.
Verbs with separable prefixes add 'ge-' after the separable prefix, e.g., 'aufgemacht'.
Verbs with inseparable prefixes do not add 'ge-' to form their past participle, e.g., 'erlebt'.
Verbs ending '-ieren' do not add 'ge-' to form the past participle. They add the suffix '-iert', e.g., 'ausprobiert'.
keywords: adverb meaning ‘previously, in former times, in the past'
adverb meaning ‘gladly, liked to’ with the past tense
verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb

5798.name: Traditionen in Österreich: comparative adverbs, postnominal superlatives
5798.outcome: I can form the comparative and superlative of a range of adverbs and adjectives, and I am familiar with several Austrian cultural traditions.
points: Use the comparative to make comparisons. Add '-er' to adjectives or adverbs to form the comparative.
Use 'als' to say 'than', e.g., 'die Maus ist kleiner als die Katze'.
Use the superlative to express the highest degree of something, e.g., 'the most interesting', 'the best'.
Use 'am' and add '-sten' to the adjective/adverb if used after a verb or noun, e.g., 'ich spiele am liebsten Fußball'.
keywords: form of adjective or adverb used to compare people, things or ideas
a form of adjective or adverb used to express the highest degree of a quality, e.g., 'the tallest', 'the most interesting'

5800.name: Traditionen in der Schweiz: abstract adjectival neuter nouns
5800.outcome: I can apply my linguistic skills to cope with longer texts, and I am confident in the use of abstract adjectival nouns, in the context of Swiss traditions.
points: Use your linguistic knowledge to break down language in longer texts and aid your understanding.
Abstract adjectival nouns refer to abstract ideas, such as 'important', 'interesting'.
After 'etwas', capitalise the adjective and add '-es' to make a neuter abstract adjectival noun.
After 'alles', capitalise the adjective and add '-e' to make a neuter abstract adjectival noun.
Use dictation tasks to reinforce your understanding of sound-symbol correspondences.
keywords: noun that takes the same endings as an adjective, and refers to an abstract idea, e.g., 'etwas Interessantes'
indefinite pronoun meaning ‘everything’, often followed by an abstract adjectival noun
indefinite pronoun meaning ‘something’, often followed by an abstract adjectival noun

5801.name: Bertha von Suttner: perfect tense change of state verbs, superlative adjectives
5801.outcome: I can use change of state verbs with 'sein' in the perfect tense and form superlatives before nouns, in the context of learning about the pacifist Bertha von Suttner.
points: Form the perfect tense using 'sein' with verbs referring to a change of state, e.g., 'ist eingeschlafen'.
Form the superlative by adding '-ste' to the end of the adjective if it comes before a noun, e.g., 'billigste'.
Some superlative forms are irregular, e.g., 'beste', 'höchste', 'meiste'. Others have umlauts as in the comparative.
In 1905, Bertha von Suttner was the first woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
keywords: 2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'
a form of adjective or adverb used to express the highest degree of a quality, e.g., 'the tallest', 'the most interesting'

5802.name: Die Brüder Grimm: plural nouns, weak masculine nouns
5802.outcome: I can form the plurals of a range of German nouns and explore their use in the context of learning about 'die Brüder Grimm'.
points: Not all nouns form their plural in the same way, but there are helpful patterns we can learn.
Some nouns add an umlaut to the vowel in their plural form, e.g., 'Bäume'. Pay attention to the change in pronunciation.
Some masculine nouns referring to people and weak masculine nouns form their plural by adding '-(e)n'.
Plural nouns add '-n' in their dative plural forms, e.g., 'den Brüdern'.
Die Brüder Grimm published a world-famous collection of fairy tales in 1812, which was called 'Kinder- und Hausmärchen'.
keywords: form for nouns that refers to more than one person place, thing or idea: des Canadiens
a small set of masculine nouns that add '-(e)n' in all forms apart from the nominative singular

5803.name: Berühmte Deutsche: subject relative clauses, wh- pronouns in relative clauses
5803.outcome: I can form relative clauses using the correct relative pronouns in the context of learning about famous German people.
points: Relative clauses add information about the noun in the main clause, without starting another sentence.
A relative clause starts with a relative pronoun - the definite article ('der', 'die', 'das') that matches the noun.
Question words such as ‘wo’ can also be used as pronouns in relative clauses.
‘Was’ can be used as a relative pronoun meaning ‘that' or 'which’ when referring to a whole clause, not a specific noun.
Many famous German figures continue to be influential in today’s world.
keywords: a type of subordinate clause that begins with a relative pronoun
a pronoun that introduces a relative clause e.g. qui, que

5804.name: Gemeinsam statt einsam: prepositions vor, nach and conjunctions bevor, nachdem
5804.outcome: I can use prepositions ‘vor’ and ‘nach’ and conjunctions ‘bevor’ and ‘nachdem’ in the context of shared living arrangements in modern Germany.
points: 'Vor' and 'nach' are prepositions used with nouns to express 'before' and 'after'. They take the dative case.
'Bevor' and 'nachdem' are conjunctions meaning 'before' and 'after' and link two clauses.
'Bevor' and 'nachdem' are followed by word order 3 and send the verb to the end of the clause.
In two-verb structures, the finite verb, not the past participle or infinitive verb, is sent to the end of the clause.
When describing a photo, use the acronym PALM. It stands for People, Action, Location, Mood. Add your own opinions too.
keywords: acronym for photo description (people and objects, action, location, mood)
word that connects ideas between clauses in a sentence
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word
after certain conjunctions, the verb is sent to the end of the sentence or clause

5805.name: Du siehst nicht krank aus: word order in 2-verb structures with conjunctions
5805.outcome: I can use word order 1 and 3 with two-verb structures when talking about the challenges of daily life for people with illnesses whose symptoms are often unseen.
points: Some conjunctions trigger word order 3 and send the verb to the end of the clause.
In two-verb structures with WO3, the finite verb, not past participle or infinitive, is sent to the end of the clause.
Two-verb structures occur with modal verbs, the future tense with 'werden' and the perfect tense with 'haben' or 'sein'.
Useful WO3 conjunctions include 'weil', 'dass', 'obwohl', 'solange', 'sobald' and 'falls'.
keywords: word that connects ideas between clauses in a sentence
sentence made up of two verb phrases
subject - verb - object - the standard word order in a German sentence, e.g., 'Ich lerne Deutsch'
after certain conjunctions, the verb is sent to the end of the sentence or clause

5806.name: Das Leben mit Behinderung: stem changes in present tense weak verbs
5806.outcome: I can use a range of present tense verbs, including those with small changes to the stem, in extended writing about living with a disability.
points: Weak verbs follow a regular pattern of changes in the present tense.
For verbs stems ending in 'd', ‘t', 'm' or 'n', add 'e' before the ending in the 'du', 'er, sie, es' and 'ihr' forms.
For verb stems ending in 's', 'ß', 'x' or 'z', add just 't' instead of 'st' in the 'du' form, e.g., 'du tanzt'.
For verb stems ending in '-el', remove the 'e' in the first person singular of the present tense, e.g., 'ich lächle'.
The BORDER acronym is a useful tool to respond fully and accurately to bullet point writing prompts.
keywords: part of the verb that appears in all forms
a verb that follows a regular pattern of changes

5807.name: Armut in Deutschland: 'bis' as preposition, 'bis' and 'wenn' as conjunctions
5807.outcome: I can distinguish between 'bis' as a preposition and conjunction and use 'bis' and 'wenn' with word order 3 when learning about the issue of poverty in Germany.
points: 'Bis' as a preposition means 'until, 'up to', by'. As a conjunction sending the verb to the end it means 'until'.
'Bis' can be used on its own with adverbs and simple time phrases.
If the noun following 'bis' has an article, use an appropriate preposition - 'zu', 'an', 'in' - and the correct case.
'Wenn' means ‘when’, ‘whenever’ of ‘if’ and is used for repeated actions or conditions in the present or future.
Both 'bis' and 'wenn' trigger word order 3, sending the verb to the end of the sentence or clause.
keywords: preposition meaning ‘until’, ‘up to’, ‘by’, and a conjunction meaning 'until'
word that connects ideas between clauses in a sentence
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word
conjunction meaning 'if' or 'when' which triggers word order 3
after certain conjunctions, the verb is sent to the end of the sentence or clause

5808.name: Diskriminerung im Alltag: 'damit' da-compound vs 'damit' conjunction
5808.outcome: I can use da-compounds and the conjunction 'damit' when discussing examples of discrimination in everyday life.
points: To refer back to something inanimate already mentioned, add da- or dar- to the beginning of a preposition.
As a da-compound, 'damit' means 'with it/them'; as a word order 3 conjunction, 'damit' means 'so that'.
In reading, use title and picture clues, close reading, translation and comprehension questions to aid understanding.
keywords: word that connects ideas between clauses in a sentence
prefix added to prepositions to avoid repetition of the noun
a conjunction which sends the verb to the end (word order 3 (WO3) ) meaning 'so that' and da-compound meaning 'with it/them'

5809.name: Meine Welt - Platz für alle: extended listening and spoken production
5809.outcome: I can use a range of strategies to aid listening comprehension and can develop my answers in a conversation about supporting others.
points: When tackling listening questions, knowledge of vocabulary is the most important element of success.
Before a listening task, read the questions carefully and predict relevant voabulary.
During listening, avoid distractors by not rushing to select the answer.
On completion of the listening, check answers against the questions.
In conversation, develop answers by adding opinions and reasons, varying the subject, and adding different time frames.
keywords: incorrect but plausible answer option in reading and listening tasks, designed to test your attention to detail
strategy that involves anticipating what the answers might be by listing relevant French words or phrases

5811.name: Energiekrise in Deutschland: future vs conditional, 2-verb rule
5811.outcome: I can use the future tense and conditional, applying the 2-verb rule when discussing the energy crisis in Germany and possible solutions.
points: To form the future tense, use the present tense of werden to mean 'will, going to’ and an infinitive verb at the end.
To form the conditional, use the conditional form of 'werden' ('würd-') meaning 'would' and an infinitive at the end.
In the 2-verb rule the 2nd (infinitive) verb is at the end of the sentence; second-last place in subordinate clauses.
'Haben' and 'sein' are 'hätte' (would have) and 'wäre' (would be) in the conditional and don't need a 2nd infinitive.
keywords: form of verb used to express what would happen
form of ‘haben’ meaning ‘would have’ which expresses a conditional idea
form of ‘sein’ meaning ‘would be’ which expresses a conditional idea
form of ‘werden’ meaning would, used with a 2nd infinitive to express a conditional idea

5812.name: Biodiversität: definite and indefinite articles after prepositions, da-compounds
5812.outcome: I can use articles after prepositions and da-compounds to understand and describe where people are and what they are doing in the context of biodiversity.
points: The prepositions 'durch, für, gegen, um' are used with the accusative. 'Aus, bei, mit, nach, von, zu' use the dative.
'An, auf, in, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen' use the accusative for movement or the dative for no movement.
Knowing the prepositions and their cases ensures that the correct form of definite and indefinite articles is used.
Use da-compounds for inanimate nouns already mentioned, including with verbs taking prepositions.
Use accusative or dative pronouns for animate nouns.
keywords: prefix added to prepositions to avoid repetition of the noun
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

5813.name: Die Umwelt: word order with questions, questions with wo-compounds
5813.outcome: I can use wo-compounds and the correct word order in questions in an interview to learn more about the environment.
points: Closed questions where the answer is yes/no are formed by inverting the subject and verb.
Open questions, which seek more information than yes/no, start with a question word followed by the verb then subject.
Use wo- and wor- prefixes with prepositions to ask questions. Prepositions do not stand alone at the end of a question.
Many verbs take prepositions and require a wo-compound when asking questions.
keywords: question that gets the answer 'yes' or 'no' and is created in Spanish by raising the tone of voice at the end of a statement
question starting with a wh- word that has more information in the answer than yes/no
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word
prefix added to prepositions to form questions

5814.name: Ab wann darf man wählen? Present and past modal verbs
5814.outcome: I can use modal verbs in the present and the imperfect tense to discuss important issues and developments.
points: Modal verbs express necessity or possibility. Use them with a 2nd verb in the infinitive at the end of the sentence.
'Dürfen' refers to permission required from another person. 'Können' refers to the ability to do something.
The stems of modal verbs are irregular, with vowel changes in most singular forms. 'Sollen' is the exception.
Modal verbs are mostly used in the imperfect tense when they describe past events. Remove any umlauts in the imperfect.
[w] sounds like 'Welt', [qu] is pronounced the same as [kw] and sounds like 'bequem', and [zw] sounds like 'zwanzig'.
keywords: verb tense used to talk about something that used to happen repeatedly
verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want

5815.name: Denken Jugendliche heute global? Accusative and dative reflexive verbs
5815.outcome: I can use accusative and dative reflexive verbs, including reciprocal forms, to understand and talk about how young people engage with global issues.
points: We usually use accusative reflexive pronouns with reflexive verbs: 'mich', 'dich', 'sich', 'uns', 'euch', 'sich'.
Some verbs are used with dative reflexive pronouns. 'Mir' and 'dir' are used instead of 'mich' and 'dich'.
In two-verb structures, such as with modal verbs, the reflexive pronoun comes directly after the first verb.
In sentences with two pronouns, the object pronoun comes before the dative reflexive pronoun.
If the action of the verb is two-way, plural reflexive pronouns can mean ‘each other’. This is called reciprocal use.
keywords: A reciprocal is the multiplicative inverse of any non-zero number. Any non-zero number multiplied by its reciprocal is equal to 1
case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
used to indicate doing something to yourself, words like 'myself' and yourself'

5816.name: Das Leben in anderen Ländern: adjectives with '-los', uses of 'man'
5816.outcome: I can create adjectives from nouns and use the pronoun 'man' to express what 'is done' and 'was done' by people in general.
points: Add the suffix '-los' to nouns to create adjectives meaning '-less' or 'without -'.
Some '-los' adjectives can be translated directly, but some have other English adjectives with equivalent meanings.
The subject pronoun 'man' is used to mean 'people' or 'you' as well as 'one'.
Use 'man + verb' to translate English phrases that do not specify a particular subject, e.g., 'It is said that... '.
'Man' is used far more commonly in German than the English subject pronoun ‘one’.
keywords: 3rd person singular pronoun meaning 'one,' 'you', used to refer to people in general
a letter or group of letters added to the end of a word to change its meaning

5817.name: Medizin früher und heute: 'es gibt' vs 'es gab', imperfect
5817.outcome: I can understand the imperfect tense in the context of past medical developments and influential ideas, and I can contrast past and present using 'es gibt' and 'es gab'.
points: Weak verbs form the imperfect tense by adding these endings to the verb stem: -te, -test, -te, -ten, -tet, -ten.
Strong verbs have irregular stems in the imperfect tense, with vowel changes and endings: -, st, -, en, t, en.
The verbs ‘sein’, ‘haben’, modal verbs and 'es gab' are commonly used in spoken as well as written German.
Use 'es gibt' to mean 'there is, are' and 'es gab' to mean 'there was, were', followed by the accusative case.
Use 'es gibt' and 'es gab' to contrast present and past.
keywords: imperfect tense form meaning 'there was | there were'
means 'there is, there are' and is a general statement that something exists
tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past

5818.name: Beim Arzt: word order with 'obwohl', role-play
5818.outcome: I can use 'obwohl' with correct word order, along with a wide range of health-related vocabulary, and take part in a role-play scenario at the doctor's.
points: The conjunction 'obwohl', meaning 'although', triggers word order 3, sending the verb to the end of the clause.
If 'obwohl' starts the sentence, use verb-comma-verb word order when linking to the next clause or sentence.
'Obwohl' can be used to develop and extend ideas by linking two sentences together.
In a role-play, you are required to say a short phrase in response to each prompt.
You must include at least one verb in each role-play answer, and you have to ask at least one question.
keywords: conjunction meaning 'although' which triggers word order 3
task in which the student responds to several prompts in the format of a role-play
after certain conjunctions, the verb is sent to the end of the sentence or clause

5819.name: Gesundheit: read and respond to texts
5819.outcome: I can read and understand a variety of texts, identifying and eliminating distractors, and write an extended text about health and lifestyle.
points: Reading and understanding texts needs attention to vocabulary, structures and a focus on required details.
A distractor is a misleading detail in a text or question option which tests your understanding of the detail of a text.
We can use time phrases and verb tenses to distinguish between past, present and future actions and events.
The BORDER acronym is a useful tool to respond fully and accurately to bullet point writing prompts.
To develop answers, you can add information about another person, add a contrast or add another time frame.
keywords: incorrect but plausible answer option in reading and listening tasks, designed to test your attention to detail

5820.name: Seien Sie sicher online! Using 'Sie' in statements, questions and the imperative
5820.outcome: I can use the pronoun 'Sie' to make statements, ask questions or give instructions and advice, in the context of life online.
points: Use 'Sie' for formal 'you' in statements, questions and the imperative.
To ask a closed question swap the position of 'Sie' and the verb. For open questions, add a question word at the start.
To form the formal imperative, swap the position of 'Sie' and the verb. 'Sein' is irregular: 'Seien Sie!'.
Intonation can help to make it clear whether you are asking a question, making a statement or giving an instruction.
The imperative can be softened by adding 'bitte', 'mal', 'doch' or 'schon'. These help us to recognise instructions.
keywords: formal word for ‘you’ used for adults we address by surname
a mood used to tell somebody to do something or give instructions or commands
rise and fall of the voice in speaking

5822.name: Eine Online-Welt. Toll, oder? Prepositional verbs, da-compounds
5822.outcome: I can use a range of prepositional verbs and da-compounds with topic-specific vocabulary to describe the advantages and disadvantages of online life.
points: Some verbs are followed by prepositions and the accusative case, and some are followed by prepositions and the dative.
We use different prepositions after verbs in English and German, so verb and preposition combinations must be learnt.
The prefix 'da(r)-' can be added to prepositions to refer to something already mentioned. This is called a da-compound.
Some da-compounds have different meanings in common usage as adverbs. Some idiomatic phrases include a da-compound.
A developed response to a question has at least 3 clauses. Include a different tense, subject, or opinion and reason.
keywords: prefix added to prepositions to avoid repetition of the noun
word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word

5823.name: Was machen sie online? Revisiting vocabulary, describing pictures
5823.outcome: I can use a range of thematic and high-frequency vocabulary and I can describe photos in the context of life online.
points: A strong knowledge of vocabulary is key to all language skills. It can be helpful to categorise words by theme.
When describing a photo, use the acronym PALM. It stands for People, Action, Location, Mood.
When describing a photo in German, translate the English present continuous with the German simple present.
To make a photo description more interesting and complex, add your own impressions (opinions, thoughts and reasons).
keywords: acronym for photo description (people and objects, action, location, mood)
describes events happening right now: 'I am doing'
verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'

5824.name: Mein Schultag: nouns and plurals, present tense, picture task (AQA)
5824.outcome: I can use the correct grammatical gender of nouns in singular and plural with the present tense of weak and strong verbs to describe a teenager's normal day.
points: All nouns in German start with a capital letter and have a grammatical gender, either masculine, feminine or neuter.
Many German nouns have plural forms, but many are used either only in the singular or the plural.
There are nine rules for forming plurals in German. Plural rules should be learnt alongside the noun gender.
Weak and strong verbs have the same present tense endings; strong verbs change stem vowel for 'du' and 'er, sie, es'.
German has one present tense which conveys both the English simple present and present continuous.
keywords: nouns in Spanish are either masculine or feminine
rules applied to noun categories to support accurate use of plurals in German - rules 1 - 5 of 9 are covered here
a verb which changes its vowel in the verb stem of some of its forms
a verb that follows a regular pattern of changes

5825.name: Mein Tag: dictation, listening (AQA)
5825.outcome: I can transcribe and understand German speakers tolking in a range of contexts about the daily life of a teenager.
points: A firm knowledge of German sound-symbol correspondence is important to transcribe spoken German in a dictation.
The most important thing for successful listening is a secure knowledge of vocabulary.

incorrect but plausible answer option in reading and listening tasks, designed to test your attention to detail

5826.name: Mein Schultag: perfect tense, conversation (AQA)
5826.outcome: I can categorise vocabulary to aid mastery, use the German perfect tense accurately and take part confidently in a conversation about my school life.
points: The perfect tense in German takes a present tense form of the auxiliary verb and a past participle.
Weak verb past participles sandwich the stem with 'ge-' and '-t'. Strong verbs use 'ge- and -'en'.
Put separable prefixes before the 'ge-', but there is no 'ge-' before inseparable prefixes or '-ieren' verbs.
Reflexive pronouns follow the auxiliary in WO1 and the subject in WO2. The German perfect has 2 English translations.
Use verb clauses in a conversation response, and extend answers with a different tense, subject, opinions and reasons.

verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb
verb whose past participle sandwiches the stem with 'ge-' and ‘-en’ and often changes the stem vowel

5830.name: An der Universität: verbs, nouns, adjectives with prepositions, role-play (AQA)
5830.outcome: I can use verbs, nouns and adjectives with prepositions, including da-compounds, and I can take part in a role-play scenario.
points: Some verbs are followed by prepositions and the accusative case, and some are followed by prepositions and the dative.

5831.name: An der Universität: read aloud, reading comprehension (AQA)
5831.outcome: I can confidently read aloud and answer reading comprehension questions about higher education and future plans.
points: It is important to have a good knowledge of sound-symbol correspondences to accurately read aloud in German.
Look out for tricky sounds and cognates, and mentally rehearse before reading aloud.

relationship between letters and their sounds

5833.name: An der Universität: present vs future, 'möchte', extended writing (AQA)
5833.outcome: I can describe future events using the present and future tense and can use a range of tenses to complete exam-style writing tasks on the topic of education, study and work.
points: Future ideas can be expressed in German using the present tense with a future time phrase.
To form the future tense, use the present tense of 'werden' to mean 'will, going to' and an infinitive verb at the end.
'Möcht-', the conditional of 'mögen', is used with a 2nd verb in the infinitive to express future wishes.

The BORDER acronym is a useful tool to respond fully and accurately to bullet point writing prompts.

the conditional form of the verb 'mögen', meaning 'would like'

5834.name: Online Leben: questions, picture task (AQA)
5834.outcome: I can form open and closed questions in the present tense, learn vocabulary by theme, and take part in a picture task in the context of life online.
points: It is helpful to categorise vocabulary by theme when revisiting large numbers of words.
Form a closed question by swapping the position of the verb and subject. Add a question word for an open question.

5835.outcome: I can transcribe and understand German speakers talking in a range of contexts about technology.

5836.name: Online Leben: questions, conversation (AQA)
5836.outcome: I can categorise vocabulary to aid mastery, ask and answer questions in three tenses, and take part confidently in a conversation about life online.
points: To form a question in the perfect tense, swap the auxiliary verb 'haben' or 'sein' with the subject.

5837.name: Deutschland: negation, role-play (AQA)
5837.outcome: I can negate sentences using 'nicht', 'kein', 'nichts' and 'nie' and I can take part in a role-play scenario.
points: Use 'nicht' before definite articles to mean ‘not the’ and 'kein' instead of the indefinite article to mean 'not a, no'.

5838.name: Deutschland: read aloud, reading comprehension (AQA)
5838.outcome: I can confidently read aloud and answer reading comprehension questions about visiting Germany and its festivals.

405.correction: Use the definite article (le/la/l'/les) for specific nouns and the indefinite article (un/une) for non-specific nouns.

2911.correction: 'Faire' has multiple meanings. 'To do' and 'to make' are the most common, but it can also mean 'to go' and 'to have', and it has other meanings in different verbal phrases.

2645.correction: Many words in French have more than one meaning. 'En' means 'in' and 'by'.

10608.correction: The long form of the verb (infinitive) means -to or -ing so it needs changing for the correct subject pronoun.

3156.belief: French infinitive verbs can only be translated by the 'to - ' structure in English.
3156.statement: French infinitive verbs can only be translated by the 'to - ' structure in English.
3156.correction: The infinitive verb can be translated as 'to -' or '-ing' e.g. 'to do' or 'doing'.

4160.belief: Like in English, French has two present tenses.
4160.statement: Like in English, French has two present tenses.
4160.correction: There is no 'be -ing' in French. There is only one present tense for both the simple present and continuous present.

5734.belief: It is possible to leave 'que' out in French like it is in English.
5734.statement: It is possible to leave 'que' out in French like it is in English.
5734.correction: Even if we would not translate 'que' (that) in English, in French we always need to put it when we mean 'think that'.

10843.belief: All verbs in the 'nous' form end in -ons.
10843.statement: All verbs in the 'nous' form end in -ons.
10843.correction: Some verbs like 'manger' behave a little differently. The 'nous' form of 'manger' is 'mangeons' so that the g sound remains soft.

5753.belief: Préféré(e) is often spelt wrong, with not enough, or indeed too many accents!
5753.statement: Préféré(e) is often spelt wrong, with not enough, or indeed too many accents!
5753.correction: 'Préféré' is favourite in its masculine form. The e that is added in the feminine form does not have an accent; 'préférée'.

2703.belief: The -ent ending of the 3rd person plural of the verb is pronounced.
2703.statement: The -ent ending of the 3rd person plural of the verb is pronounced.
2703.correction: The -ent ending of the 3rd person plural of the verb is not pronounced. It is therefore difficult to tell the difference between the 'il/elle' form and the 'ils/elles' form of verbs when spoken.

9617.belief: I still need to use the subject pronoun even if I am using a name or a noun before the verb form.
9617.statement: I still need to use the subject pronoun even if I am using a name or a noun before the verb form.
9617.correction: A noun or name can replace a subject pronoun. So 'ils chantent ensemble' could be changed to 'les garçons chantent ensemble' or 'David, Robert et Jacques chantent ensemble'.

5192.belief: There is just one way of saying 'you' in French like in English.
5192.statement: There is just one way of saying 'you' in French like in English.
5192.correction: There are two ways of saying 'you' in French. We use 'tu' for 'you singular' and 'vous' for 'you plural'.

3133.belief: When forming questions, we have to translate 'do you' into French.
3133.statement: When forming questions, we have to translate 'do you' into French.
3133.correction: There is no phrase for 'do you' in French; we can use intonation instead to form questions.

5026.belief: Numbers ending in 's' and 'x' followed by nouns beginning with a vowel are pronounced the same as numbers followed by a noun beginning with a consonant.
5026.statement: Numbers ending in 's' and 'x' followed by nouns beginning with a vowel are pronounced the same as numbers followed by a noun beginning with a consonant.
5026.correction: Numbers ending in 's' and 'x' followed by nouns beginning with a vowel are pronounced with a liasion; the final consonant of the number is pronounced. 'Trois oranges' has a liaison, 'trois chiens' does not.

3731.belief: The indefinite article 'des' changes based on gender as do the indefinite articles 'un' and 'une'.
3731.statement: The indefinite article 'des' changes based on gender as do the indefinite articles 'un' and 'une'.
3731.correction: The indefinite article 'des' does not change based on gender. Un livre - des livres. Une orange - des oranges.

139.belief: Adjectives do not change spelling based on gender or number, as in English.
139.statement: Adjectives do not change spelling based on gender or number, as in English.
139.correction: Adjectives do change spelling based on gender or number, for example: 'un chien amusant', 'deux tortues amusantes'.

5184.belief: There is just one way of referring to 'they' in French, as in English.
5184.statement: There is just one way of referring to 'they' in French, as in English.
5184.correction: There is both a masculine and feminine form of the pronoun 'they'. Use 'ils' when referring to a group of boys or a group of boys and girls, and use 'elles' when referring to a group of girls.

4133.belief: There is always a liaison when an 's' is followed by a vowel.
4133.statement: There is always a liaison when an 's' is followed by a vowel.
4133.correction: The liaison between a verb and an article (nous avons un chien) is in fact optional. An optional liaison is often used in a more formal setting, for example when reading aloud a prepared speech rather than in a more formal conversation.

9049.belief: The 's' in the liaison of 'ils ont' and 'elles ont' is pronounced like an English 's'.
9049.statement: The 's' in the liaison of 'ils ont' and 'elles ont' is pronounced like an English 's'.
9049.correction: The 's' in the liaison of 'ils ont' and 'elles ont' is pronounced like an English 'z'. This is distinguishable to 'ils sont' and 'elles sont' which have the pronounciation of an English 's' (no liaison).

4166.belief: Like in English, there is just one word for 'my' in French.
4166.statement: Like in English, there is just one word for 'my' in French.
4166.correction: French has 3 words for 'my' and the gender of the possession determines which 'my' to use; 'mon' for masculine singular nouns, 'ma' for feminine singular nouns and 'mes' for plural nouns.

5090.belief: Once you 'know' some vocabulary, you should move on.
5090.statement: Once you 'know' some vocabulary, you should move on.
5090.correction: Vocabulary and grammatical concepts need consistently revisiting in order to move it in to your long term memory. Work out what learning techniques work for you but the most important thing is repetition.

4058.correction: When 'à' is followed by 'le' it becomes 'au'.

5267.correction: 'Ou' without an accent means 'or' and 'où' with an accent means 'where'.

1769.belief: When I combine 'à' with a plural noun with 'les', it becomes 'à les'.
1769.statement: When I combine 'à' with a plural noun with 'les', it becomes 'à les'.
1769.correction: When using 'à' with a plural noun to express 'to (the)' in French, it becomes 'aux'.

497.belief: 'Au' can be used before masculine singular and plural nouns to mean 'to the' and 'at the'.
497.statement: 'Au' can be used before masculine singular and plural nouns to mean 'to the' and 'at the'.
497.correction: 'Au' can only be used before masculine singular nouns to mean 'to the' and 'at the', 'aux' needs to be used before masculine/feminine plural nouns.

91.belief: Add -e to all adjectives to make them feminine.
91.statement: Add -e to all adjectives to make them feminine.
91.correction: Some adjectives follow different patterns. 'Heureux' changes to 'heureuse' and 'naturel' changes to 'naturelle'.

2644.correction: [en] and [an] sound exactly the same as in 'enfant'.

10390.belief: To translate 'to' into French we just use 'à'.
10390.statement: To translate 'to' into French we just use 'à'.
10390.correction: There are several ways to express 'to' and 'at' in French and we need to carefully learn them to speak and write accurately.

10386.correction: Sometimes we don't actually need to translate the 'de' in a French sentence into English. For example, there is no possessive apostrophe in French so to express 'Sophie's sister' we have to say 'the sister of Sophie' - 'la sœur de Sophie'.

17.belief: The 1st person singular and 3rd person singular verb forms are always spelt the same.
17.statement: The 1st person singular and 3rd person singular verb forms are always spelt the same.
17.correction: The 1st and 3rd person singular verb forms are spelt the same for regular -er verbs, but for irregular verbs like 'être' and 'avoir' they are different.

10824.belief: The verbs 'dire' and 'prendre' have the same verb endings.
10824.statement: The verbs 'dire' and 'prendre' have the same verb endings.
10824.correction: ‘Dire’ and ‘prendre’ are high frequency -re verbs that have slightly different endings from each other, and from the most common -re pattern of endings.

1725.belief: A closed question requires 'do/does' or 'am/are/is' at the start in French, like in English.
1725.statement: A closed question requires 'do/does' or 'am/are/is' at the start in French, like in English.
1725.correction: Closed questions in French do not start with 'do/does' or 'am/are/is', they simply invert the subject and the verb: tu es anglaise, es-tu anglaise?

63.belief: The accents é and è are pronounced the same in French and can be written interchangably.
63.statement: The accents é and è are pronounced the same in French and can be written interchangably.
63.correction: It is essential to write an accent accurately as the accents é and è are pronounced differently. É is pronounced as in the word 'écrire' and è is pronounced as in the word 'trés'.

4824.belief: Nationalities use capital letters as in English: I am French.
4824.statement: Nationalities use capital letters as in English: I am French.
4824.correction: In French, nationalities do not use capital letters: je suis français.

4182.belief: Like other question words in French, 'quel' does not change based on the gender of the noun.
4182.statement: Like other question words in French, 'quel' does not change based on the gender of the noun.
4182.correction: Unlike other question words in French, 'quel' does change based on the gender of the noun, it becomes 'quelle' in the feminine form.

9587.belief: The SSCs (sound-symbol correspondences) [ai] and [è/ê] make different sounds.
9587.statement: The SSCs (sound-symbol correspondences) [ai] and [è/ê] make different sounds.
9587.correction: The SSCs (sound-symbol correspondences) [ai] and [è/ê] make the same sound in French: 'paire' and 'père'.

10716.belief: Using 'ne' before the verb makes verbs negative, like 'don't' in English.
10716.statement: Using 'ne' before the verb makes verbs negative, like 'don't' in English.
10716.correction: In French, there are two parts to negation, 'ne' before the verb and 'pas' after.

10715.belief: Using 'ne'/'n' makes verbs negatives in French, like 'not' in English.
10715.statement: Using 'ne'/'n' makes verbs negatives in French, like 'not' in English.
10715.correction: French negation has two parts, 'ne' before the verb and 'pas' after, to say what there isn't.

10605.belief: Use the indefinite article after 'il n'y a pas' like you would with 'il y a'.
10605.statement: Use the indefinite article after 'il n'y a pas' like you would with 'il y a'.
10605.correction: After 'il n'y a pas' always use 'de' (or 'd'' before words starting with vowels or silent 'h'), regardless of gender or number.

4910.belief: When negating, change any articles to 'de/d''.
4910.statement: When negating, change any articles to 'de/d''.
4910.correction: Change indefinite articles to 'de/d'' when negating but keep the definite articles the same and keep the indefinite articles when using 'être'.

152.belief: All adjectives go after the noun in French, the opposite to the word order of nouns and adjectives in English.
152.statement: All adjectives go after the noun in French, the opposite to the word order of nouns and adjectives in English.
152.correction: Most adjectives do go after the noun in French, however some adjectives go before the noun, these are pre-nominal adjectives. They refer to age, beauty, goodness and size (BAGS).

4109.belief: The letter 'c' makes a soft sound in front of 'a', 'o' and 'u'.
4109.statement: The letter 'c' makes a soft sound in front of 'a', 'o' and 'u'.
4109.correction: The letter 'c' makes a hard sound in front of 'a', 'o' and 'u'. We use the cedilla 'ç' to make a soft sound in front of 'a', 'o' and 'u': français.

9586.belief: The SSCs [ou] and [u] make the same sound in French.
9586.statement: The SSCs [ou] and [u] make the same sound in French.
9586.correction: The SSCs [ou] and [u] are similar but make different sounds in French. [ou] is pronounced as in 'nous' and [u] is pronounced as in 'tu'.

10403.belief: When translating from French to English or vice versa, you simply translate word-for-word.
10403.statement: When translating from French to English or vice versa, you simply translate word-for-word.
10403.correction: Word order is often different in French and English. In many cases, we can't translate word-for-word and you may need to paraphrase.

3160.belief: In French [qu] is pronounced the same as in English, in words like 'queen' and 'quiet'.
3160.statement: In French [qu] is pronounced the same as in English, in words like 'queen' and 'quiet'.
3160.correction: In French [qu] has the same sound as the hard 'c', this requires a lot of practice!

8678.belief: We put the 'ne... pas' together after the main verb to form a negative sentence.
8678.statement: We put the 'ne... pas' together after the main verb to form a negative sentence.
8678.correction: The 'ne... pas' is in two separate parts and must be placed either side of the main (1st) verb in the sentence.

11064.belief: The word German is always 'allemand' with a lower case 'a' in French.
11064.statement: The word German is always 'allemand' with a lower case 'a' in French.
11064.correction: With a capital letter, Allemand is a noun meaning a person from Germany. With a lower case letter it is an adjective describing someone or something that comes from Germany and also a noun meaning the German language.

2097.belief: To create inversion questions in French, you just swap the verb and subject around.
2097.statement: To create inversion questions in French, you just swap the verb and subject around.
2097.correction: As well as swapping verb and subject, a hyphen is needed betwen the verb and the subject pronoun when forming inversion questions, e.g. 'Vont-elles créer des vêtements?' - 'Are they going to create clothes?'.

4856.belief: You need to conjugate the verb following a modal verb.
4856.statement: You need to conjugate the verb following a modal verb.
4856.correction: The second verb following a modal verb must be in the infinitive form.

5174.belief: There is one verb for 'can' in French like in English.
5174.statement: There is one verb for 'can' in French like in English.
5174.correction: The verb for 'can' changes depending on whether you need specific skills/knowledge to be able to do it. If not, use 'pouvoir', if it does, use 'savoir'.

4848.belief: 'Ne... pas' goes around both verbs in a two-verb sentence.
4848.statement: 'Ne... pas' goes around both verbs in a two-verb sentence.
4848.correction: 'Ne... pas' surrounds the first verb in a two-verb sentence. If a sentence contains a modal verb and an infinitive, it will surround the conjugated modal verb.

4288.belief: You can look up any word in the dictionary, including verb forms.
4288.statement: You can look up any word in the dictionary, including verb forms.
4288.correction: The only form of the verb you find in the dictionary is the infinitive so you may still need to change it for the right person and tense.

3371.belief: Grammatical gender is the same as biological gender. If a word is feminine we think of it as a girl if it is masculine we think of it as a boy.
3371.statement: Grammatical gender is the same as biological gender. If a word is feminine we think of it as a girl if it is masculine we think of it as a boy.
3371.correction: Grammatical gender is not the same as biological gender. Spelling clues help to identify Spanish grammatical gender: nouns ending in -o are usually masculine, nouns ending in -a are usually feminine.

5880.belief: Only proper nouns have a capital letter.
5880.statement: Only proper nouns have a capital letter.
5880.correction: In German, all nouns, regardless of where they are in a sentence, have a capital letter.

3276.correction: Verbs have different forms (endings) depending on the subject. Long form ends in -en and short form ends in -t.

4081.belief: Learning the gender of nouns is not important.
4081.statement: Learning the gender of nouns is not important.
4081.correction: It is important to learn the gender of nouns so that you can use them accurately in sentences.

2607.correction: [ei] is pronounced as in the key word 'frei' and like the English 'eye'.

11002.correction: 'Wie?' has two meanings: 1. 'How?' (e.g., 'Wie geht's?' - How's it going? / How are you?_; 2. 'What?' (e.g., 'Wie ist [der Gast]?' - What is [the guest] like?). Encourage pupils to learn both meanings and specific examples.

4950.correction: You can use 'nicht' or 'kein(e)' to negate a sentence. 'Nicht' is used with adjectives whereas 'kein, keine' is used with nouns.

3902.belief: 'J' is pronounced the same in both English and German.
3902.statement: 'J' is pronounced the same in both English and German.
3902.correction: In German, 'j' is pronounced like 'yot' and sounds like the English 'y'. The German letter 'y' is called 'oopsilon'. It sounds like the German 'j' at the start of borrowed words, e.g., 'Yoga', but like a short ü 'oo' in others, e.g. 'das System'.

10980.correction: 'Wer?' means 'Who?'. A good way to remember its meaning is to think of a ‘hoover’: 'Who Wer?'.

10981.belief: 'Wer' means 'where' in English because it sounds the same.
10981.statement: 'Wer' means 'where' in English because it sounds the same.
10981.correction: 'Wer' means 'who' in English. Words that sound identical but have different meanings are called false friends and we should be aware of them.

3732.belief: The indefinite article 'ein' always refers to a masculine noun.
3732.statement: The indefinite article 'ein' always refers to a masculine noun.
3732.correction: 'Ein' could refer to a masculine or a neuter noun. Learn noun genders and look for other clues about a noun's gender. Only masculine nouns use 'einen' after forms of 'haben' and most other verbs, except 'sein'.

4808.belief: Names (e.g., Alex) and pronouns (e.g., 'er') are not interchangeable and need different verb endings.
4808.statement: Names (e.g., Alex) and pronouns (e.g., 'er') are not interchangeable and need different verb endings.
4808.correction: Names and pronouns are interchangeable and use the same verb endings.

3253.belief: German [ie] is pronounced as in English 'die'.
3253.statement: German [ie] is pronounced as in English 'die'.
3253.correction: German [ie] is pronounced as in the German 'Liebe'.

9093.belief: To say 'not a' in German, say 'nicht ein'.
9093.statement: To say 'not a' in German, say 'nicht ein'.
9093.correction: Use 'kein' to say what you do not have.

5776.belief: The present continuous, e.g., ‘He is doing’ is translated as ‘Er ist machen’.
5776.statement: The present continuous, e.g., ‘He is doing’ is translated as ‘Er ist machen’.
5776.correction: There is only one present tense in German. ‘Er macht’ = ‘He does / He is doing’.

1741.belief: In cognates, e.g., ‘Musik’, [i] makes the same sound as in English ‘music’.
1741.statement: In cognates, e.g., ‘Musik’, [i] makes the same sound as in English ‘music’.
1741.correction: The [i] sound is short (like English) when followed by 2 consonants, e.g., ‘Film’. Otherwise, it’s a long vowel.

9078.belief: The same verb endings can be added to all verb stems.
9078.statement: The same verb endings can be added to all verb stems.
9078.correction: Weak verbs (also known as regular verbs) follow a set pattern of changes to verb endings. Strong verbs (also known as irregular verbs) do not follow this pattern.

907.belief: [ch] is pronounced as in the English 'cheese'.
907.statement: [ch] is pronounced as in the English 'cheese'.
907.correction: [ch] is soft in German after [i] or [e]. It is hard after [a] [o] or [u]. This is because [a] [o] and [u] are pronounced with a more open mouth whilst [i] and [e] have a more closed mouth.

1726.belief: Closed questions in German require a translation of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’, as in English.
1726.statement: Closed questions in German require a translation of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’, as in English.
1726.correction: Swap the position of the verb and the subject to create a closed question in German. Do not use translations of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’.

11076.belief: Word order is the same in German and English.
11076.statement: Word order is the same in German and English.
11076.correction: German sentences containing adverbs have a different word order to English.

10477.belief: There are two present tenses in German, as in English.
10477.statement: There are two present tenses in German, as in English.
10477.correction: There is only one present tense in German. 'Ich lerne' means 'I learn' and 'I am learning'.

4994.belief: All nouns change in their plural form.
4994.statement: All nouns change in their plural form.
4994.correction: Different nouns have different rules for forming plurals. It is important to learn these and acknowledge that there will always be exceptions to any rule.

2958.belief: Feminine noun plurals are the same as masculine and neuter noun plurals.
2958.statement: Feminine noun plurals are the same as masculine and neuter noun plurals.
