2958.correction: Most feminine nouns add either an -e or an -en to the end of the noun in its plural form. Feminine nouns ending in -el or -er also add an -n unlike in the masculine and neuter form where nouns ending in these letters don't tend to change.

2728.correction: Whilst 'er' and 'sie' do mean 'he' and 'she', they are also the masculine and neuter words for 'it'.

9278.belief: 'Sie' always refer to feminine 'it' when used as a subject pronoun.
9278.statement: 'Sie' always refer to feminine 'it' when used as a subject pronoun.
9278.correction: 'Sie' means 'it' in the feminine form and 'they' in the plural form. 'Sie' is used for all plural forms.

9074.belief: The same plural rules apply to nouns of all three genders (masculine, feminine, neuter).
9074.statement: The same plural rules apply to nouns of all three genders (masculine, feminine, neuter).
9074.correction: There are different rules for different nouns. It often depends on whether the noun is masculine, feminine or neuter. It is important to learn the plural noun form when learning a new noun.

5614.belief: All plurals are formed in the same way.
5614.statement: All plurals are formed in the same way.
5614.correction: Nouns have different rules for plurals depending on their gender and spelling.

2741.belief: 'Es' is the only German word for 'it'.
2741.statement: 'Es' is the only German word for 'it'.
2741.correction: Object pronouns such as 'es' tell us the grammatical gender of the object of the sentence. German has three words for the object pronoun 'it' - masculine 'ihn', feminine 'sie' and neuter 'es'.

9277.correction: As a subject pronoun, 'sie' can mean 'she' or 'they'. As an object pronoun, 'sie' means 'her' or 'it'.

857.correction: [ß] is a symbol representing 'ss' and is called 'Eszett' or 'scharfes s'.

9051.belief: [s] is pronounced the same as the English 's'.
9051.statement: [s] is pronounced the same as the English 's'.
9051.correction: [s] is pronounced like the English 'z' when it comes before a vowel. Elsewhere, both [s] and [ß] are pronounced like the English 's'.

10388.belief: You translate the English present continuous with a form of 'sein', e.g., 'Ich bin machen...'.
10388.statement: You translate the English present continuous with a form of 'sein', e.g., 'Ich bin machen...'.
10388.correction: There is only one present tense in German. 'Ich mache' means 'I do' and 'I am doing'.

3105.belief: Form closed questions in German by adding 'do you...' or 'are you...', as in English.
3105.statement: Form closed questions in German by adding 'do you...' or 'are you...', as in English.
3105.correction: Swap only the position of the subject and verb in a German statement to form a closed question.

10772.correction: [v] is pronounced like an English 'f'. [w] sounds like an English 'v'.

10606.belief: You have to use an indefinite article when using 'sein' and a profession noun.
10606.statement: You have to use an indefinite article when using 'sein' and a profession noun.
10606.correction: Do not use an indefinite article when using 'sein' and a profession noun, e.g., 'Ich bin Sänger'.

3776.belief: The infinitive comes directly after the form of 'können', as in English: 'I can play guitar'.
3776.statement: The infinitive comes directly after the form of 'können', as in English: 'I can play guitar'.
3776.correction: The infinitive comes at the end of the sentence in German when used with a modal verb such as 'können', as in 'Ich kann Gitarre spielen'.

10666.belief: Always use the word 'nicht' to negate a statement.
10666.statement: Always use the word 'nicht' to negate a statement.
10666.correction: Use the correct form of 'kein' to translate 'not a/any' with nouns. Use 'nicht' with verbs and adjectives.

9033.belief: There are no rules to help you learn which verbs are strong and have a vowel change in their stem.
9033.statement: There are no rules to help you learn which verbs are strong and have a vowel change in their stem.
9033.correction: Only verbs with an 'a' or 'e' in their stem can be strong.

1884.belief: Compound nouns take the gender of their first noun.
1884.statement: Compound nouns take the gender of their first noun.
1884.correction: Compound nouns take the gender of their final noun.

10899.belief: There is no vowel change in the 2nd person singular 'du' present tense forms of strong verbs.
10899.statement: There is no vowel change in the 2nd person singular 'du' present tense forms of strong verbs.
10899.correction: The vowel in the stem of strong verbs with an 'a' or 'e' in their stem will change in the 2nd person singular 'du' present tense form.

660.belief: A bilingual dictionary lists words from A-Z in one long list.
660.statement: A bilingual dictionary lists words from A-Z in one long list.
660.correction: A bilingual dictionary is split into two sections. These is German to English, and English to German. Each section lists words from A-Z. To find the English meaning of a German word, look for it in the German to English section, and vice versa.

10527.belief: Umlauts do not make a difference to the pronunciation of a letter.
10527.statement: Umlauts do not make a difference to the pronunciation of a letter.
10527.correction: German vowels (with or without umlauts) can be short or long. Vowels are short when followed by more than one consonant. Vowels are long when there is a double vowel, followed by 'h', or a single consonant.

11072.belief: In word order 2, all the words in a sentence change position from word order 1.
11072.statement: In word order 2, all the words in a sentence change position from word order 1.
11072.correction: The verb remains in the same position in word order 2 as in word order 1. If emphasis is on the adverb, the adverb and subject swap position.

9455.belief: The sounds ‘t’ and [th] make the same sound in English as they do in German.
9455.statement: The sounds ‘t’ and [th] make the same sound in English as they do in German.
9455.correction: The sounds ‘t’ and [th] sound the same in German. Even though many words with these spellings come from English, German pronounces 't' and [th] in the same way.

4999.belief: Nouns in German have capital letters in the same situations as English nouns.
4999.statement: Nouns in German have capital letters in the same situations as English nouns.
4999.correction: German nouns are always capitalised, no matter where or how they are used in a sentence.

11077.belief: Word order tells you if a sentence is a question or a statement.
11077.statement: Word order tells you if a sentence is a question or a statement.
11077.correction: Use clues such as intonation and vocabulary meanings to help you decide if a sentence is a question or a statement, as the word order in questions is similar to word order 2.

3370.belief: The grammatical gender of feminine nouns changes to masculine in the dative case.
3370.statement: The grammatical gender of feminine nouns changes to masculine in the dative case.
3370.correction: Feminine nouns are always feminine, no matter what case their article may change to.

506.correction: 'Auf' sometimes means ‘at’ or ‘to’, especially with events or open spaces.

5727.belief: Possessive adjectives match the gender of the person who possesses the noun.
5727.statement: Possessive adjectives match the gender of the person who possesses the noun.
5727.correction: Possessive adjectives match the gender of the noun they describe, not the person who possesses it!

2452.belief: Don't change the possessive pronoun used in a question when you give your answer.
2452.statement: Don't change the possessive pronoun used in a question when you give your answer.
2452.correction: If a question is addressed to you (i.e., uses a form of 'dein', as in 'Was ist dein Lieblingssport?'), respond with the correct form of 'mein' in the answer.

5612.belief: All plural nouns are formed the same way in German.
5612.statement: All plural nouns are formed the same way in German.
5612.correction: Nouns can form their plural in different ways in German. There are rules to help you learn this.

3268.belief: All German-speakers speak the same way. There aren't different accents, unlike in the United Kingdom.
3268.statement: All German-speakers speak the same way. There aren't different accents, unlike in the United Kingdom.
3268.correction: There are both different accents and different dialects in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. This means there are different ways of saying sounds, and different vocabulary. ‘Standard German’ is the version of German taught in schools.

10866.correction: Use 'viel' with uncountable nouns (i.e., you cannot put a number in front of it) and use 'viele' with countable nouns (i.e., you can put a number in front of it).

3426.correction: 'Haben' is an irregular verb because it does not follow a regular pattern of changes in the same way a weak verb does, even if the 'ich', 'wir' and 'sie' (they) forms look like weak verbs.

233.belief: 'I am doing' is translated as 'Ich bin machen'.
233.statement: 'I am doing' is translated as 'Ich bin machen'.
233.correction: There is no present continuous ('-ing' form) tense in German, and therefore no use of the verb 'sein'. Use a time adverb to express what you are doing right now in German, e.g., 'Ich mache jetzt...'.

3777.belief: The infinitive follows the conjugated verb, as in the English 'I can play'.
3777.statement: The infinitive follows the conjugated verb, as in the English 'I can play'.
3777.correction: In German, the infinitive is placed at the end of a sentence when used with a modal verb, as in 'Ich kann spielen.'.

10612.belief: Always use 'können' to translate 'can' into German.
10612.statement: Always use 'können' to translate 'can' into German.
10612.correction: 'Can' is often used with two different meanings in English - ability or permission. Use 'können' to express ability (e.g., 'Kannst du schwimmen?') and 'dürfen' to express permission (e.g., 'Darfst du schwimmen?').

10590.belief: You can use conversational language (an informal register) whenever you want to.
10590.statement: You can use conversational language (an informal register) whenever you want to.
10590.correction: A situation affects the register we use when speaking (i.e., the words we use). You use an informal register with friends, but a formal register with a teacher. Using formal register in formal situations is important in German-speaking communities.

9652.belief: Strong verbs have a vowel change in all parts of the verb.
9652.statement: Strong verbs have a vowel change in all parts of the verb.
9652.correction: Strong verbs have a vowel change in the 2nd and 3rd person singular forms of the verb only (e.g., 'ich werfe', 'du wirfst', 'sie wirft').

9554.belief: The spellings 'ss' and 'ß' make different sounds.
9554.statement: The spellings 'ss' and 'ß' make different sounds.
9554.correction: The spellings 'ss' and 'ß' make the same sound, but write 'ss' after a short vowel, 'ß' after a long vowel.

10645.belief: Use the simple present to translate future plans from German into English, e.g., 'Nächstes Jahr spiele ich Tennis.' - 'Next year I play tennis.'.
10645.statement: Use the simple present to translate future plans from German into English, e.g., 'Nächstes Jahr spiele ich Tennis.' - 'Next year I play tennis.'.
10645.correction: Use the present continuous in English when translating future plans (that are expressed in the present tense) from German, e.g., 'Nächstes Jahr spiele ich Tennis.' - 'Next year I am going to play tennis.'.

11207.correction: 'Zu' can also mean 'too', 'closed', 'off' and 'shut'! Context is important when translating into English.

3258.belief: German numbers are said in the same way as English numbers, i.e., tens then units.
3258.statement: German numbers are said in the same way as English numbers, i.e., tens then units.
3258.correction: The unit is said before the ten in German, e.g., 'neunundvierzig' = '9 and 40' = 49. It is helpful to write from right to left when taking down numbers so that you produce them in the correct order.

4267.belief: As long as we know the meaning of a noun, we don't need to worry about its grammatical gender.
4267.statement: As long as we know the meaning of a noun, we don't need to worry about its grammatical gender.
4267.correction: Knowing the grammatical gender of a noun is very important, because the gender affects the form of other parts of a sentence, such as the article or preposition. This in turn affects the clarity and comprehensibility of the message.

100.belief: Add '-s' to form the plural of all nouns in German.
100.statement: Add '-s' to form the plural of all nouns in German.
100.correction: There is a set of rules that help you know how to form plural nouns in German. Not all nouns form their plural in the same way, so the rules need to be learned.

5867.belief: [a] is pronounced the same in Spanish and English.
5867.statement: [a] is pronounced the same in Spanish and English.
5867.correction: Whilst the [a] sound varies in English, in different words and in different places, it is only pronounced as in 'alto' in Spanish.

4852.belief: It is necessary to use pronouns with Spanish verbs.
4852.statement: It is necessary to use pronouns with Spanish verbs.
4852.correction: In most cases, it is not necessary to use pronouns with Spanish verbs. The verb itself communicates the action and the subject.

8757.correction: 'Raro' is a false friend and means 'strange'.

2684.belief: As in English, the spelling of Spanish adjectives remains the same regardless of the noun they are describing.
2684.statement: As in English, the spelling of Spanish adjectives remains the same regardless of the noun they are describing.
2684.correction: The spelling of Spanish adjectives changes from -o to -a when desciring a person or animal that is female.

2679.belief: As in English, there is one way to say 'I am' in Spanish.
2679.statement: As in English, there is one way to say 'I am' in Spanish.
2679.correction: There are two ways to say 'I am' in Spanish. These are 'estoy' (for location, mood and temporary state) and 'soy' (for general traits).

10462.belief: To turn a statement into a question in Spanish you need to alter the order of the words as in English.
10462.statement: To turn a statement into a question in Spanish you need to alter the order of the words as in English.
10462.correction: It is not necessary to alter word order when forming questions in Spanish. To turn a statement into a question, you can raise your voice at the end.

4232.belief: [ll] is pronounced the same in Spanish and English.
4232.statement: [ll] is pronounced the same in Spanish and English.
4232.correction: [ll] is pronounced differently in Spanish and English. It is important to recognise and pronounce sound-spelling links correctly to understand and be understood by other Spanish speakers.

9101.belief: To say 'I have', 'you have', 'she, he, it has' you need the words for 'I', 'you' and 'she, he, it'.
9101.statement: To say 'I have', 'you have', 'she, he, it has' you need the words for 'I', 'you' and 'she, he, it'.
9101.correction: The verbs 'tengo', 'tienes' and 'tiene' mean 'I have', 'you have' and 'she, he, it has'. You do not need to use separate pronouns 'I', 'you', 'she, he, it'.

5207.belief: There is just one word for 'some' in Spanish.
5207.statement: There is just one word for 'some' in Spanish.
5207.correction: There are two words for 'some' in Spanish, just as there are two words for 'a/an'. 'Unos' is 'some' for plural masculine nouns. 'Unas' is 'some' for plural feminine nouns.

9490.belief: Spanish needs a word for 'do' in questions, e.g. 'Do you have?' and 'What do you have?'.
9490.statement: Spanish needs a word for 'do' in questions, e.g. 'Do you have?' and 'What do you have?'.
9490.correction: Spanish questions are easy to form. Yes/no questions have the same words as statements; to make a question you raise the pitch of your voice. Information questions just add a question word, e.g. 'Qué...?' in front of the verb.

4853.belief: It is necessary to use pronouns before verbs in Spanish to know who is performing an action.
4853.statement: It is necessary to use pronouns before verbs in Spanish to know who is performing an action.
4853.correction: It is not usually necessary to use pronouns before verbs in Spanish. You can tell who is performing an action by looking at the verb ending.

10827.correction: Unlike nouns, verbs in Spanish are not masculine or feminine. 3rd person singular verbs ending in -a can refer to he or she.

5871.belief: Pronouns are necessary to understand who the subject of a verb is in Spanish.
5871.statement: Pronouns are necessary to understand who the subject of a verb is in Spanish.
5871.correction: Pronouns are not necessary to understand who the subject of a verb is in Spanish. Verb endings tell us who the subject is.

4111.belief: The letter 'c' in Spanish is always pronounced in the same way.
4111.statement: The letter 'c' in Spanish is always pronounced in the same way.
4111.correction: The pronunciation of the letter 'c' changes depending on the following vowel. [ci] and [ce] have soft 'c' sounds and [ca], [co], [cu] have hard 'c' sounds.

9446.belief: The sound [z] is pronounced the same in every Spanish-speaking country.
9446.statement: The sound [z] is pronounced the same in every Spanish-speaking country.
9446.correction: The sound [z] is pronounced differently in parts of Spain and in other parts of the world.

635.belief: It is best to focus first on the unfamiliar words in a longer text.
635.statement: It is best to focus first on the unfamiliar words in a longer text.
635.correction: This should be done in last place, when context has been read.

4377.belief: To make a noun plural in Spanish, just add -s.
4377.statement: To make a noun plural in Spanish, just add -s.
4377.correction: Spanish nouns ending in a consonant add -es for plural.

2960.belief: The feminine plural always refers to girls/women only and the masculine plural, to boys/men only.
2960.statement: The feminine plural always refers to girls/women only and the masculine plural, to boys/men only.
2960.correction: The masculine plural is used to refer to groups of women and men too.

3462.belief: 'Hay' is pronounced as the English 'hi' and means there is. There is another word for 'there are'.
3462.statement: 'Hay' is pronounced as the English 'hi' and means there is. There is another word for 'there are'.
3462.correction: The 'h' is not pronounced in 'hay' and it means both 'there is' and 'there are'.

5111.belief: Once a word is learnt, it stays in the memory forever.
5111.statement: Once a word is learnt, it stays in the memory forever.
5111.correction: Words need revisiting from time to time in order to not disappear from the memory.

2743.correction: 'Es' means 'she, he, it is' and 'son' means 'they are'.

156.belief: Adjectives do not have plurals forms, like English.
156.statement: Adjectives do not have plurals forms, like English.
156.correction: In Spanish, adjectives match the nouns they describe. If the noun is singular, the adjective will be singular as well, and the same for plural nouns.

2218.belief: The definite article 'the' translates as 'el' in Spanish and it can be used with singular nouns, both masculine and feminine.
2218.statement: The definite article 'the' translates as 'el' in Spanish and it can be used with singular nouns, both masculine and feminine.
2218.correction: There are two words for 'the' with singular nouns. The masculine singular definite article 'el' and the feminine singular definite article is 'la'.

9451.belief: The sounds [ge] and [gi] are pronounced just like in English.
9451.statement: The sounds [ge] and [gi] are pronounced just like in English.
9451.correction: Both sounds are pronounced like an 'h' followed by 'e' for [ge] and followed by 'i' for [gi]

5206.belief: There is only one word for plural 'the' in Spanish and that is 'los'.
5206.statement: There is only one word for plural 'the' in Spanish and that is 'los'.
5206.correction: In Spanish, the plural 'the' has two forms: 'los' for plural masculine nouns, and 'las' for plural feminine nouns.

9469.belief: In Spanish, adjectives always end in -o.
9469.statement: In Spanish, adjectives always end in -o.
9469.correction: In Spanish, adjectives must agree with the noun they describe in gender and number. If the noun is feminine, the adjective will end in -a, but if it is masculine, it will end in -o. If the adjective already ends in -e, it will stay the same.

10912.belief: 'I want', 'you want' and 'she, he, it wants' have the same stem as the infinitive, 'querer', so you just need to change the verb endings.
10912.statement: 'I want', 'you want' and 'she, he, it wants' have the same stem as the infinitive, 'querer', so you just need to change the verb endings.
10912.correction: 'Quiero', 'quieres' and 'quiere' are spelt slightly different to the infinitive 'querer'. They have an extra 'i'.

5868.belief: [ñ] is pronounced the same way as [n].
5868.statement: [ñ] is pronounced the same way as [n].
5868.correction: [ñ] is pronounced differently to [n]. It is pronounced as in the word 'español' and [n] as in the word 'mano'.

9447.belief: The sounds for [b] and [v] are different, as in English.
9447.statement: The sounds for [b] and [v] are different, as in English.
9447.correction: This is one of the rare cases in Spanish where one sound can have two spellings.

5001.belief: All nouns in Spanish are always used with an article, a word for 'a', 'some' or 'the'.
5001.statement: All nouns in Spanish are always used with an article, a word for 'a', 'some' or 'the'.
5001.correction: Some nouns are uncountable and have no plural. Use these without an article, as in English. For example, 'quiere dinero' means 'she, he wants money'.

3663.belief: It is impossible for a non-native to pronounce the [rr] sound.
3663.statement: It is impossible for a non-native to pronounce the [rr] sound.
3663.correction: The [r] and [rr] sounds need practice to produce them confidently. Even for native speakers, it is the last sound that children learn to produce.

133.belief: The adjective needs to agree with the verb.
133.statement: The adjective needs to agree with the verb.
133.correction: This is only the case with attribute verbs like 'ser' or 'estar' because the adjective is still referring to an implicit noun (person, thing).

3424.belief: The 'h' is sometimes pronounced in Spanish.
3424.statement: The 'h' is sometimes pronounced in Spanish.
3424.correction: The 'h' is never pronounced in Spanish, regardless of its position in the word (hola, zanahoria).

9470.belief: Spanish adjectives always follow the noun.
9470.statement: Spanish adjectives always follow the noun.
9470.correction: This is the general case, but it is not a rule. There are many cases where the adjective precedes the noun, like for certain collocations ('una gran amistad') or when more flair is sought.

3430.correction: In Spanish, 'hacer' is used for 'to do' and 'to make', there is no specific verb for either.

2131.belief: Cuál is used as in English, followed by a noun.
2131.statement: Cuál is used as in English, followed by a noun.
2131.correction: In Spanish, cuál is never followed by a noun.

3204.belief: [g] and [j] always have the same sound in Spanish, like [b] and [v] do.
3204.statement: [g] and [j] always have the same sound in Spanish, like [b] and [v] do.
3204.correction: [g] sounds different when followed by a, o, u, when it sounds just like g + a, o, u in English.

2132.belief: 'Cuánto' is used to ask about one thing and 'cuántos' for several things.
2132.statement: 'Cuánto' is used to ask about one thing and 'cuántos' for several things.
2132.correction: 'Cuánto' is used for uncountable nouns, not for one thing.

1970.belief: When we conjugate the verb we just add the ending to the infinitive.
1970.statement: When we conjugate the verb we just add the ending to the infinitive.
1970.correction: In Spanish when we conjugate a verb, first, we remove the -ar ending and then add the correct ending depending on who is doing the action of the verb.

9516.belief: All Spanish verb forms for -ar verbs end in -ar.
9516.statement: All Spanish verb forms for -ar verbs end in -ar.
9516.correction: Spanish -ar verbs end in o-, -as, -a, -amos depending on who they refer to. -o for 'I', -as for 'you', -a for 'she, he, it' and -amos for 'we'

9606.belief: The stem of the 'I, you, she/he/it' form of the verb 'poder' is spelt exactly the same as the infinitive.
9606.statement: The stem of the 'I, you, she/he/it' form of the verb 'poder' is spelt exactly the same as the infinitive.
9606.correction: The infinitive is 'poder' but when we conjugate the verb, the spelling changes for the 'I, you, she/he/it' form. 'Puedo' means 'I can', 'puedes' means 'you can' and 'puede' means 'she/he/it can.'

9197.belief: A sentence such as 'puedo participo' is correct and it means 'I can participate'. Both verbs are in the 'I' form.
9197.statement: A sentence such as 'puedo participo' is correct and it means 'I can participate'. Both verbs are in the 'I' form.
9197.correction: The sentence 'Puedo participo' is not correct because the verb 'poder' is always followed by an infinitive. To say 'I can participate' we must say 'Puedo participar.'

10488.belief: When there are two verbs together, we must conjugate both.
10488.statement: When there are two verbs together, we must conjugate both.
10488.correction: When we have two verbs together, we must conjugate the first one and use the infinitive for the second verb, i.e., 'Debo ayudar con las tareas en mi casa.'

11086.correction: In Spanish there is a difference between them: 'sí' with an accent means 'yes', and 'si' without an accent means 'if'.

11060.correction: In Spanish, the word 'coche' means 'car'. 'Coach' is 'autobús'.

9475.belief: In Spanish, after adverbs of position we always use 'del'.
9475.statement: In Spanish, after adverbs of position we always use 'del'.
9475.correction: In Spanish, after adverbs of position we use 'de', 'del' or 'de la'. 'De' when what follows is a person or place name, 'del' when what follows is a masculine noun and 'de la' when what follows is a feminine noun.

2449.belief: It doesn't matter whether we use 'ser' or 'estar' in Spanish as they both mean 'to be, being.'.
2449.statement: It doesn't matter whether we use 'ser' or 'estar' in Spanish as they both mean 'to be, being.'
2449.correction: Both verbs mean 'to be, being' but 'ser' is used to describe permanent traits and 'estar' to describe temporary states.

9098.belief: To say 'they are' it does not matter which verb 'to be' we use.
9098.statement: To say 'they are' it does not matter which verb 'to be' we use.
9098.correction: In Spanish there are two verbs 'to be'; we say 'son' (they are) to describe permanent traits, and 'están' (they are) to describe temporary states.

9515.belief: In Spanish the verb endings rarely change depending on who the verb refers to, like in English.
9515.statement: In Spanish the verb endings rarely change depending on who the verb refers to, like in English.
9515.correction: In Spanish verb endings always change depending on who the verb refers to. For -ar verbs, 'I' ends in -o, 'you' ends in -as, 'she, he, it' ends in -a, 'we' ends in -amos, and 'they' ends in -an.

3104.belief: The 'she, he, it' form of -ar verbs and the 'they' form have the same ending.
3104.statement: The 'she, he, it' form of -ar verbs and the 'they' form have the same ending.
3104.correction: The 'she, he, it' form of -ar verbs ends in -a, but the 'they' form ends in -an.

3418.belief: I can guess the meaning of the words I don't know just by looking at them.
3418.statement: I can guess the meaning of the words I don't know just by looking at them.
3418.correction: Guessing the meaning is not a reliable strategy for most words in Spanish as it may lead to misunderstanding, especially for tricky or abstract vocabulary.

5176.belief: There is only one verb to say 'I am' and 'you are' in Spanish.
5176.statement: There is only one verb to say 'I am' and 'you are' in Spanish.
5176.correction: In Spanish, there are two ways to say 'I am' and 'you are'. 'I am in general' is 'soy' and 'I am now' is 'estoy'. 'You are in general' is 'eres' and 'you are now' is 'estás'.

9517.belief: Spanish verbs follow the same pattern as English verbs. The 'I', 'you', 'we' and 'they' forms are all the same and the only change happens in the 'she, he, it' form.
9517.statement: Spanish verbs follow the same pattern as English verbs. The 'I', 'you', 'we' and 'they' forms are all the same and the only change happens in the 'she, he, it' form.
9517.correction: In Spanish, each subject has its own special ending. For -ar verbs, this is '-o' for 'I', '-as' for 'you', '-a' for 'she, he, it', '-amos' for 'we' and '-an' for 'they'.

3218.belief: [ge] and [gi] are a soft 'g' sound as in English. Spanish [j] is different so you can always hear the difference when you transcribe words with these sounds.
3218.statement: [ge] and [gi] are a soft 'g' sound as in English. Spanish [j] is different so you can always hear the difference when you transcribe words with these sounds.
3218.correction: Spanish [ge] and [gi] sounds like Spanish [j] + e and [j] + i, so you cannot hear the difference when you transcribe. However, there is often a clue from English, e.g., 'religión' in Spanish is spelled with [gi] as in English.

642.belief: The best way to learn vocabulary is to repeat the words and their meaning in your mind.
642.statement: The best way to learn vocabulary is to repeat the words and their meaning in your mind.
642.correction: A method like look, say, cover, write, check can be more effective when learning vocabulary.

10804.belief: The verb ending -o means 'I' but only if you're a boy or man.
10804.statement: The verb ending -o means 'I' but only if you're a boy or man.
10804.correction: For regular verbs, the 'I' verb form always ends in 'o'. Verb endings match the person, but don't change for gender, so 'hablo' means 'I speak' for everyone. It is adjectives that change ending -o to -a to describe a girl or woman.

2568.belief: It is easy to write Spanish from memory if I know what the words mean.
2568.statement: It is easy to write Spanish from memory if I know what the words mean.
2568.correction: Knowing what words mean when you listen to or read them doesn't mean you can write them from memory. To write from memory, you need to practise writing from memory, especially verbs, as these need to be right to communicate your message clearly.

8846.belief: Regular -er/-ir verbs in plural form always end in -en.
8846.statement: Regular -er/-ir verbs in plural form always end in -en.
8846.correction: Only the 3rd person plural form ends in -en.

9349.belief: Singular and plural verbs have the same endings.
9349.statement: Singular and plural verbs have the same endings.
9349.correction: Singular and plural verbs have different forms for first, second and third person.

9486.belief: In Spanish, like in English, there is only one 'the' and that is 'el'.
9486.statement: In Spanish, like in English, there is only one 'the' and that is 'el'.
9486.correction: In Spanish, there are four words for 'the' - 'el' that accompanies singular and masculine nouns; 'la' for singular and feminine nouns, 'los' for plural and masculine nouns, and 'las' for plural and feminine nouns.

9449.belief: The sounds [ci], [si] and [z] are pronounced the same in all the Spanish-speaking countries.
9449.statement: The sounds [ci], [si] and [z] are pronounced the same in all the Spanish-speaking countries.
9449.correction: In Latin America, parts of southern Spain and the Canary Island, [ci], [si] and [z] are pronounced the same. In the rest of Spain, [ci], [si] and [z] have different pronunciation.

4585.belief: 'Mi' and 'tu' changes according to whether the noun is feminine or masculine.
4585.statement: 'Mi' and 'tu' changes according to whether the noun is feminine or masculine.
4585.correction: In Spanish, the possessive adjectives do not change according to whether the noun is feminine or masculine. They stay the same.

5211.belief: There is only one word for 'your' in Spanish and that is 'tu'.
5211.statement: There is only one word for 'your' in Spanish and that is 'tu'.
5211.correction: In Spanish, if the possessive adjective 'your' comes before a singular or uncountable noun, we say 'tu', but if it comes before a plural noun we say 'tus'.

4996.belief: All nouns ending in 'a' are feminine.
4996.statement: All nouns ending in 'a' are feminine.
4996.correction: There are exceptions to this, like 'problema' or 'día', that's why it is important to learn the article and the noun together.

4890.belief: I need Spanish words for 'do' and 'are' to ask yes/no questions, just like in English, e.g. 'Do you go to town?', 'Are you going to the park?'.
4890.statement: I need Spanish words for 'do' and 'are' to ask yes/no questions, just like in English, e.g. 'Do you go to town?', 'Are you going to the park?'.
4890.correction: Spanish yes/no questions use the same words in the same order as Spanish statements. To make a statement into a spoken question, use raised intonation. Written questions use two question marks; the one at the start is upside down.

9103.belief: To say where someone goes, only 'a la/al' goes before the place.
9103.statement: To say where someone goes, only 'a la/al' goes before the place.
9103.correction: If the place is a city or a country, 'a' goes before the place.

9504.belief: In Spanish, we translate word-for-word from English to say 'I am going to', using 'soy' or 'estoy'.
9504.statement: In Spanish, we translate word-for-word from English to say 'I am going to', using 'soy' or 'estoy'.
9504.correction: Some structures do not allow for word-for-word translations between English and Spanish. To say 'I am going to' in Spanish, use the present tense of 'ir' + 'a' + 2nd infinitive verb.

9633.belief: There are no strategies I can use to understand words in a text; I either know them or I don't.
9633.statement: There are no strategies I can use to understand words in a text; I either know them or I don't.
9633.correction: I can use several strategies to help me understand a text: I can use the surrounding words that I do know, I can use my knowledge of patterns, e.g. for adjectives, and I can use cognates.

3968.belief: I know from the sound if a Spanish word starts with 'h'.
3968.statement: I know from the sound if a Spanish word starts with 'h'.
3968.correction: The letter 'h' is a silent letter in Spanish. We need to learn the spelling of words that start with 'h' by practising vocabulary regularly.

5762.belief: There is no preparation needed before I read Spanish aloud.
5762.statement: There is no preparation needed before I read Spanish aloud.
5762.correction: Trickier sounds can trip us up when we read aloud in Spanish. Identifying any tricky sounds, then mentally rehearsing before we read aloud can help us read more accurately and fluently.

10081.belief: We swap the verb and subject around to ask a closed, yes/no question as in English, e.g. 'Are we going to go on holiday?'.
10081.statement: We swap the verb and subject around to ask a closed, yes/no question as in English, e.g. 'Are we going to go on holiday?'
10081.correction: All closed questions in Spanish have the same word order as the equivalent statement, e.g.'Vamos a ir de vacaciones' ('We are going to go on holiday') → '¿Vamos a ir de vacaciones?' ('Are we going to go on holiday?').

10635.belief: Use the same articles after 'il y a' and 'il n'y a pas'.
10635.statement: Use the same articles after 'il y a' and 'il n'y a pas'.
10635.correction: Use the indefinite article, depending on gender and number after 'il y a' but after 'il n' y a pas', always use de regardless of gender/number and d' for any nouns starting with a vowel.

4325.belief: 'Ma' is the possessive adjective for all feminine singular nouns.
4325.statement: 'Ma' is the possessive adjective for all feminine singular nouns.
4325.correction: Use 'mon/ton' before all nouns starting with a vowel/h.

4899.belief: There is no need to use intonation when using inversion and 'est-ce que'.
4899.statement: There is no need to use intonation when using inversion and 'est-ce que'.
4899.correction: Even when we form questions with inversion or 'est-ce que', it is still important to use intonation to signal that it is a question.

3619.belief: 'Ils ont' and 'ils sont' sound the same.
3619.statement: 'Ils ont' and 'ils sont' sound the same.
3619.correction: Although these two verbs sound similar, there is a distinction between the 'z' sound created by s-liaison in 'ils ont' and the 's' sound at the beginning of 'sont' after the silent 's' on 'ils'.

92.belief: Add an -e to all person nouns to make them feminine.
92.statement: Add an -e to all person nouns to make them feminine.
92.correction: The most common way to make a person noun feminine is to add an -e to the masculine version. If nouns already end in -e, person nouns usually stay the same but the article changes. Jobs ending in 'eur' usually change to 'rice' in the feminine form.

1768.belief: Combination numbers in French are written like this: 'dix sept', 'vingt deux'.
1768.statement: Combination numbers in French are written like this: 'dix sept', 'vingt deux'.
1768.correction: French numbers which are made up of a combination of more than one number must be hyphenated, e.g. 'dix-sept' (17), 'vingt-deux' (22), and 'trente-et-un' (31).

230.belief: When I am forming information questions with 'est-ce que' I put the question word after it.
230.statement: When I am forming information questions with 'est-ce que' I put the question word after it.
230.correction: When forming information questions with 'est-ce que', the question word must come before it, e.g example: 'Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire demain?' 'What are you going to do tomorrow?'.

2867.belief: To express the date I use 'de' for 'of' so 2nd January would be 'le deux de janvier'.
2867.statement: To express the date I use 'de' for 'of' so 2nd January would be 'le deux de janvier'.
2867.correction: There is no need to translate 'of' into French to express the date. For example 2nd January would be 'le deux janvier'.

2722.belief: 'On' is equivalent to 'one' in English and is therefore is very formal and rarely used.
2722.statement: 'On' is equivalent to 'one' in English and is therefore is very formal and rarely used.
2722.correction: 'On' is very commonly used in French and can mean 'everyone', 'people', 'you' and 'one'.

5724.belief: The possessive adjective 'son, sa, ses' matches the person who owns the noun that follows. So 'his' is 'son, 'her' is 'sa' and 'their' is 'ses'.
5724.statement: The possessive adjective 'son, sa, ses' matches the person who owns the noun that follows. So 'his' is 'son, 'her' is 'sa' and 'their' is 'ses'.
5724.correction: In French, the possessive pronoun matches the noun that follows it, not the person to whom the object belongs. This is why sometimes you cannot tell whether the owner is male or female because the words for 'his' and 'her' are the same in French.

10621.belief: I use 'notre' to mean 'our' in French just with masculine nouns.
10621.statement: I use 'notre' to mean 'our' in French just with masculine nouns.
10621.correction: The possessive adjective 'notre' is used before masculine and feminine singular nouns to mean 'our' in French. We use 'nos' when the 'possessed' noun is plural.

3018.belief: It is fine to use the infinitive next to the subject pronoun.
3018.statement: It is fine to use the infinitive next to the subject pronoun.
3018.correction: The infinitive is the dictionary form of the verb but verbs change ending to match their subject (I, you, she, he etc.). Regular -er verbs always add the same set of endings.

10610.belief: If you use inversion and add a question word, you don't need to change your intonation.
10610.statement: If you use inversion and add a question word, you don't need to change your intonation.
10610.correction: Even when using inversion and/or question words, still raise your voice at the end of a sentence in French when asking a question.

2345.belief: There is no difference in French between the present and perfect tense forms 'I do' and 'I did', 'I say' and 'I said', because they sound the same.
2345.statement: There is no difference in French between the present and perfect tense forms 'I do' and 'I did', 'I say' and 'I said', because they sound the same.
2345.correction: The spellings of the past participles 'fait' and 'dit' are different to the first person (I) present tense but sound the same because of silent final consonants. Another difference is using 'j'ai' before past participles to say 'I did'.

5440.belief: The perfect tense is made up of one part like it is in English.
5440.statement: The perfect tense is made up of one part like it is in English.
5440.correction: You must have both parts of the perfect tense; the present tense of 'avoir' and a past participle. Regular past participles end in é.

5864.belief: I pronounce [r] the same in French as in English.
5864.statement: I pronounce [r] the same in French as in English.
5864.correction: The SSC [r] is very different in French. It is a raspy sound from the back of your throat like the [r] in 'rue'. It does require quite a lot of practice to master this sound.

2868.belief: I can express 'this' for all masculine nouns with 'ce'.
2868.statement: I can express 'this' for all masculine nouns with 'ce'.
2868.correction: There is another way of expressing 'this' in French for masculine nouns, which is 'cet', this is for masculine nouns beginning with a vowel or an 'h'.

1724.belief: The closed [eu] and the open [eu/œu] sounds are the same.
1724.statement: The closed [eu] and the open [eu/œu] sounds are the same.
1724.correction: There are open vowel sounds and closed vowel sounds in French. The closed [eu] sound is like the [eu] in 'peu', it is short and sharp. The open [eu/oœu] sound is a longer sound like the [œu] in 'sœur'.

3615.belief: 'Il y a' and 'il y avait' mean there is and there was in descriptions of singular things.
3615.statement: 'Il y a' and 'il y avait' mean there is and there was in descriptions of singular things.
3615.correction: 'Il y a' and 'il y avait' mean there is or there are and there was and there were. They stay the same if you are talking about one thing or more than one.

4897.belief: I need to translate the word 'did' when I form a question in French.
4897.statement: I need to translate the word 'did' when I form a question in French.
4897.correction: To form a question in French, you can either raise your voice at the end of a statement to form an intonation question, or you can add 'est-ce que' at the beginning of a sentence. There is no French equivalent for 'did' in a question.

10387.belief: I have to translate 'didn't' into French.
10387.statement: I have to translate 'didn't' into French.
10387.correction: There is no direct translation for 'didn't' in French. Using 'ne... pas' with the perfect tense expresses the equivalent of 'didn't' in French.

5032.belief: The [o] sound in French is only pronounced one way.
5032.statement: The [o] sound in French is only pronounced one way.
5032.correction: The [o] sound in French can be open, like the [o] in 'porte' and 'd'accord' or closed like the [o] in 'radio' or 'dos'.

2464.belief: I don't need to plan my written work before I start writing in French.
2464.statement: I don't need to plan my written work before I start writing in French.
2464.correction: Planning is essential for success in any written task. Using a content and language checklist helps us to plan, improve and check our drafted written work.

9437.belief: The sound 's' is always pronounced the same in French.
9437.statement: The sound 's' is always pronounced the same in French.
9437.correction: There are two 's' sounds, the hard 's' sound which sounds like a 'z', found between two vowels, including in liaisons and the soft 's' found in other words, often at the beginning, of words, between consonants and as a double 's'.

2251.correction: 'Des' is the word for 'some' but is also a form of the preposition 'de' before plural nouns.

4092.belief: 'Some' can be left out in French just like it can in English.
4092.statement: 'Some' can be left out in French just like it can in English.
4092.correction: Always use an article before food nouns in French, if it is a whole item, use the indefinite article and if it's uncountable or part of an item, use the partitive article du, de la or de l'.

2912.belief: After faire, use the definite article in French.
2912.statement: After faire, use the definite article in French.
2912.correction: Many activities such as doing homework or cooking are followed by the definite article, but sports activities with faire are followed by the partitive article e.g. 'je fais du vélo'.

10626.belief: Always use the partitive article after food and drink items, even with negative sentences.
10626.statement: Always use the partitive article after food and drink items, even with negative sentences.
10626.correction: The partitive article changes to 'de' to say what you don't eat and drink e.g. 'je ne mange pas de pizza'.

406.belief: Articles can be missed out in French like in English.
406.statement: Articles can be missed out in French like in English.
406.correction: Articles can't be omitted in French. Use the definite article with specific nouns/giving opinions and the partitive article with uncountable and non-specific nouns.

11073.belief: Word order with adverbs is the same in French and English.
11073.statement: Word order with adverbs is the same in French and English.
11073.correction: Word order with adverbs is sometimes the same and sometimes different in French and English. Think about whether the adverb is a how/how often or a where/when adverb to know where to place it in French.

141.belief: All adjectives come after the noun they describe in French.
141.statement: All adjectives come after the noun they describe in French.
141.correction: Most adjectives follow the noun they describe, but not adjectives of beauty, age, goodness and size, which come before like English adjectives.

922.belief: Only change your main verb into a past verb in French like we can do in English to form the past tense, e.g. I do → I did.
922.statement: Only change your main verb into a past verb in French like we can do in English to form the past tense, e.g. I do → I did.
922.correction: In French you need two verbs in the perfect tense for it to make sense; the correct part of 'avoir' and the past participle.

4847.belief: Ne... pas goes around the main verb (the past participle) in perfect tense sentences.
4847.statement: Ne... pas goes around the main verb (the past participle) in perfect tense sentences.
4847.correction: Just like in other double verb sentences, ne...pas goes around the first verb; in the perfect tense, that's the conjugated form of 'avoir'.

4168.belief: Like in English, 'sans' is followed by the -ing form of a verb in French.
4168.statement: Like in English, 'sans' is followed by the -ing form of a verb in French.
4168.correction: In French, 'sans' is followed by the infinitive form of a verb, e.g. 'elle part sans dire un mot' - 'she leaves without saying a word'.

40.belief: The 3rd person plural 'they' form of the verb 'sortir' is 'sorent' and of the verb 'venir' is 'vienent'.
40.statement: The 3rd person plural 'they' form of the verb 'sortir' is 'sorent' and of the verb 'venir' is 'vienent'.
40.correction: The verb 'sortir' keeps its 't' to become 'sortent' and the verb 'venir' doubles its 'n' to become 'viennent'.

5188.belief: There is only one way to say please to a person in French: 's'il vous plait'.
5188.statement: There is only one way to say please to a person in French: 's'il vous plait'.
5188.correction: There are two ways to say please in French: 'sil vous plait' for someone you don't know very well or someone in a position of responsibility like your teacher. But for friends and family you use 's'il te plait'.

5863.belief: The pronoun 'on' only means 'people in general'.
5863.statement: The pronoun 'on' only means 'people in general'.
5863.correction: The pronoun 'on' does mean 'people in general' but it is often used to mean 'we' in informal conversations, like when you are talking to friends. You will have seen this meaning before in the phrase 'on y va!' which means 'let's go!'.

11178.belief: The [y] sound is the same in French as it does in English.
11178.statement: The [y] sound is the same in French as it does in English.
11178.correction: The English [y] has two different sounds, as in 'myth', a short 'i' sound, and 'cycling' where it sounds like the word 'eye'. The French [y] sounds like the SSC [i] as in 'midi'.

9119.belief: All school systems are roughly the same.
9119.statement: All school systems are roughly the same.
9119.correction: School systems around the world can be quite different. For example in France you don't go to school on a Wednesday afternoon and you don't wear school uniform!

4898.belief: We need to use the future tense in French to describe future activities.
4898.statement: We need to use the future tense in French to describe future activities.
4898.correction: The present tense can be used with time adverbs to describe a future activity. For example, 'Mardi je vais chez Léa.' means: 'This coming Tuesday I am going to Léa's house.'. This is a future activity but the present tense has been used here.

4871.belief: All I need to know about [h] in French is that it is silent.
4871.statement: All I need to know about [h] in French is that it is silent.
4871.correction: The rules of liaison and elision apply to the French silent [h]. Before a word starting with [h], if a word ends with an SFC, the consonant is pronounced (liaison) and words like 'le' and 'que' replace their final letter with an apostrophe (elision).

102.belief: Add -s to make all nouns plural in French.
102.statement: Add -s to make all nouns plural in French.
102.correction: Many nouns do need an -s in the plural form but masculine nouns ending in -eau or -eu need -x adding in the plural form, and there are other exceptions.

99.belief: Add -s to all adjectives in the plural form.
99.statement: Add -s to all adjectives in the plural form.
99.correction: Most adjectives do need an 's' in the plural form, but there are exceptions. Masculine adjectives ending -eux don't change at all and those ending -al change to -aux in the plural form. The feminine plural versions of these adjectives are regular.

157.belief: All adjectives are postnominal in French; they come after the noun.
157.statement: All adjectives are postnominal in French; they come after the noun.
157.correction: Most adjectives in French come after the noun but there are a group of prenominal adjectives. We use BRAGS to remember that adjectives of Beauty, Rank, Age, Goodness and Size come before the noun like adjectives in English.

147.belief: Adjectives follow the same order and punctuation as in English.
147.statement: Adjectives follow the same order and punctuation as in English.
147.correction: If there is more than one adjective in a sentence, adjectives after the noun are separated by ‘et’. BRAGS adjectives go before the noun and do not need ‘et’. In some sentences, there are adjectives surrounding the noun.

10622.belief: Use one preposition for 'in' like in English.
10622.statement: Use one preposition for 'in' like in English.
10622.correction: There are a number of prepositions for 'in', depending on the number and gender of the noun. Use 'en' for feminine countries, à for cities, au with masculine nouns, à la with feminine nouns and aux with plural nouns and countries.

174.belief: Adverbs have the same word order in French as they do in English in two-verb sentences.
174.statement: Adverbs have the same word order in French as they do in English in two-verb sentences.
174.correction: Adverbs that tell us 'how' and 'how often' come before the infinitive e.g. 'Elle peut souvent visiter les musées'. 'Tu ne peux pas encore visiter Alger.'

9585.belief: The SSCs [om] and [on] always sound the same.
9585.statement: The SSCs [om] and [on] always sound the same.
9585.correction: When [om] or [on] appear at the end of a word or before a consonant, they have a nasal sound and are pronounced the same. However, before a vowel their sounds are oral, the 'm' and 'n' are pronounced more clearly, making these SSCs sound different.

2723.belief: There is an equivalent way to add -er onto adjectives to make comparisons like in English.
2723.statement: There is an equivalent way to add -er onto adjectives to make comparisons like in English.
2723.correction: We cannot change adjectives to make comparisons in French. To compare two people or things, we instead have to say that one is more or less 'something' than another. For example: 'Elle est plus grande que son frère.' She is taller than her brother.

5200.belief: There is only one word for 'better' in French: 'meilleur'.
5200.statement: There is only one word for 'better' in French: 'meilleur'.
5200.correction: The adjective 'meilleur(e)' means 'better' in French and describes a noun, e.g.'il a un meilleur ordinateur' ('he has a better computer'). To describe an action as 'better' we use the adverb 'mieux', e.g. 'il chante mieux' ('he sings better').

10579.belief: I only use adjectives with comparative structures like 'plus... que'.
10579.statement: I only use adjectives with comparative structures like 'plus... que'.
10579.correction: Adjectives help us to compare two nouns with comparative structures such as 'plus... que'. For example, 'Emily est plus petite que Lucy'. We can use adverbs in the same way to compare how people do things. For example, 'Emily va plus vite que Lucy'.

3120.belief: To form the present tense of 'prendre' in the 1st and 2nd persons plural, remove -re from the infinitive to get the stem.
3120.statement: To form the present tense of 'prendre' in the 1st and 2nd persons plural, remove -re from the infinitive to get the stem.
3120.correction: To get the stem for the plural forms of 'prendre' in the present tense, you also need to drop the 'd' before adding the correct endings.

42.belief: The 3rd persons singular and plural of 'prendre' sound the same, both end with silent letters.
42.statement: The 3rd persons singular and plural of 'prendre' sound the same, both end with silent letters.
42.correction: The pronunciation of 'prend' and 'prennent' is different. 'Prend' contains [en] like in 'enfant' whereas 'prennent' is an oral vowel.

5774.belief: Prepositions with the verbs 'depend' and 'reply' in English work the same way as prepositions with 'dépendre' and 'répondre' in French.
5774.statement: Prepositions with the verbs 'depend' and 'reply' in English work the same way as prepositions with 'dépendre' and 'répondre' in French.
5774.correction: 'Depend' is followed by 'on' in English and 'dépendre' by a form of 'de' in French. 'Répondre' is always followed by a form of 'à' in French whereas in English it can be translated as 'reply to' but also with 'answer', where there is no preposition.

2252.belief: To describe a language, where something or someone is from, use exactly the same word in French, as we do in English, e.g. 'I learn Spanish,' 'he is Spanish'.
2252.statement: To describe a language, where something or someone is from, use exactly the same word in French, as we do in English, e.g. 'I learn Spanish,' 'he is Spanish'.
2252.correction: When used as a noun for a language, the word needs a definite article. When used as an adjective to describe nationality of a person or thing, the word agrees with the noun it describes. When used for nationality, the word needs a capital letter.

3788.belief: 'Information' is used in French like it is in English.
3788.statement: 'Information' is used in French like it is in English.
3788.correction: 'Information' is a cognate but it is usually in the plural form in French ('des informations'). When used in the singular form, it means 'a piece of information'.

10839.belief: Verbs like 'ecrire' are formed the same way as verbs like 'lire'.
10839.statement: Verbs like 'ecrire' are formed the same way as verbs like 'lire'.
10839.correction: Although verbs like 'écrire' do have the same endings in the singular persons ('je', 'tu' and 'il'/'elle'), they are different in the plural form, so it is better to think of them as different types of -re verb.

11068.belief: If a word looks the same in French and English, it will always be a cognate.
11068.statement: If a word looks the same in French and English, it will always be a cognate.
11068.correction: There are lots of cognates, where English and French words are the same or similar. However, there are some words, known as 'false friends'. These are words whose meanings are not what they look like e.g. 'attendre' meaning 'to wait' not 'to attend'.

43.belief: The 3rd persons singular and plural with verbs like 'entendre' have different spellings but the same pronunciation.
43.statement: The 3rd persons singular and plural with verbs like 'entendre' have different spellings but the same pronunciation.
43.correction: The 'd' at the end of the 3rd person singular is a silent final consonant but the 'd' in the 3rd person plural is pronounced, whilst the -ent is silent.

10849.belief: The verbs 'traduire', 'conduire', 'interdire' and 'dire' follow exactly the same pattern as 'lire' in the present tense.
10849.statement: The verbs 'traduire', 'conduire', 'interdire' and 'dire' follow exactly the same pattern as 'lire' in the present tense.
10849.correction: The verbs 'traduire', 'conduire', 'interdire' and 'dire' follow exactly the same pattern as 'lire' in the present tense with one important exception. The 2nd person plural form of 'dire' is 'dites'.

10611.belief: If you use inversion or 'est-ce que' as a questioning device, you don't need to change your intonation.
10611.statement: If you use inversion or 'est-ce que' as a questioning device, you don't need to change your intonation.
10611.correction: Even if you are changing the word order to use inversion, or adding 'est-ce que', you still need to make your voice go up at the end of a sentence to show that you are asking a question.

4365.belief: To make an adjective plural in French we add an -s like in English.
4365.statement: To make an adjective plural in French we add an -s like in English.
4365.correction: In French there are various ways to make an adjective plural, including adding an -s, an -x or changing -al to -aux.

10718.belief: When using more than one adjective in French we need 'et' between them.
10718.statement: When using more than one adjective in French we need 'et' between them.
10718.correction: We only need 'et' between French adjectives if they come after the noun. For the B-R-A-G-S adjectives that come before the noun, no connective is needed.

4108.belief: The letter 'c' always makes the same sound in French.
4108.statement: The letter 'c' always makes the same sound in French.
4108.correction: The letter 'c' is naturally soft (sounds like 's') before 'e' or 'i'. It is hard (sounds like k) before 'a', 'o' or 'u'. The 'c' is sometimes softened before 'a', 'o' or 'u' with a cedilla: 'ç'.

3129.belief: When forming an inversion question in the perfect tense, the past participle comes after 'avoir'.
3129.statement: When forming an inversion question in the perfect tense, the past participle comes after 'avoir'.
3129.correction: When forming an inversion question in the perfect tense, only the verb avoir and the subject swap. The past participle remains at the end: as-tu commencé?

9443.belief: The sound-symbol correspondences [qu], [ch] and [th] are pronounced the same as in English.
9443.statement: The sound-symbol correspondences [qu], [ch] and [th] are pronounced the same as in English.
9443.correction: The SSCs [qu], [ch] and [th] are pronounced differently in French than in English.

5356.belief: All past participles follow the regular -er verb pattern: change the -er to -é: 'j'ai commencé' ('I started').
5356.statement: All past participles follow the regular -er verb pattern: change the -er to -é: 'j'ai commencé' ('I started').
5356.correction: Some past participles are irregular and do not follow the regular -er verb pattern: 'j'ai fait' ('I did').

4173.belief: Like in English, to talk about 'having' a meal, food or drink in French, use the verb 'avoir': j'ai le petit-déjeuner (I am having breakfast).
4173.statement: Like in English, to talk about 'having' a meal, food or drink in French, use the verb 'avoir': j'ai le petit-déjeuner (I am having breakfast).
4173.correction: To talk about 'having' a meal, food or drink in French, use the verb 'prendre', not 'avoir': je prends le petit-déjeuner.

5439.belief: The perfect tense in German is often only translated as 'have done'.
5439.statement: The perfect tense in German is often only translated as 'have done'.
5439.correction: Give clear examples of both translations 'have done' and 'did' with appropriate time adverbials. Emphasise the role of time adverbials in helping to decide on the correct English translation.

920.belief: There is no change in word order after time adverbials.
920.statement: There is no change in word order after time adverbials.
920.correction: Practise short examples with and without time adverbials, and use cards (or the pupils themselves) to move to demonstrate word order 2 with time adverbials at beginning of sentences.

1883.belief: Compound nouns are completely different words that cannot be understood or pronounced unless they have been met before.
1883.statement: Compound nouns are completely different words that cannot be understood or pronounced unless they have been met before.
1883.correction: Compound nouns are made up of two (or more) nouns, one or more of which pupils may already know. Knowledge of formation and read aloud can promote recognition as can activities where pupils produce compounds from known words.

6403.statement: Pupils often either forget 'haben' altogether in a sentence or question, or forget to change it when talking about different people.
6403.correction: Use cards or physical gestures to demonstrate the elements of the sentence to reinforce the core structure, then vary these to demonstrate changing 'haben' to match the subject of the sentence, and to demonstrate change in word order in questions.

10594.belief: We always use ‘du’ to mean ‘you’ in German.
10594.statement: We always use ‘du’ to mean ‘you’ in German.
10594.correction: 'Du' is informal 'you'. You should use 'Sie' (formal 'you') when speaking with adults that you address by surname. Use 'du' with friends, family, other people you know very well and other children.

4809.belief: Names of foreign cities and towns don't have English equivalents.
4809.statement: Names of foreign cities and towns don't have English equivalents.
4809.correction: Some cities around the world (e.g., München) have an English equivalent (e.g., Munich).

3246.belief: The German alphabet has the same number of letters (26) as the English alphabet.
3246.statement: The German alphabet has the same number of letters (26) as the English alphabet.
3246.correction: The German alphabet also includes the letters 'ä, ö, ü, ß' and so consists of 30 letters.

3245.belief: When German adjectives come before the noun, they don't change their spelling, just like in English, e.g., 'The dog is black'; 'The black dog is over there.'.
3245.statement: When German adjectives come before the noun, they don't change their spelling, just like in English, e.g., 'The dog is black'; 'The black dog is over there.'.
3245.correction: In German, when adjectives come after the verb 'sein' (to be) they don't change. However, adjectives in front of a noun add endings do; this is called adjective agreement. There are different endings depending on gender (m, f, nt) and on the article.

10854.belief: Verbs are always verbs and nouns are always nouns.
10854.statement: Verbs are always verbs and nouns are always nouns.
10854.correction: Sometimes words of one type can be used as another type. For example, 'ich mag das Schwimmen' (I like swimming) is the verb 'schwimmen' used as a noun. When used as nouns, verbs have a gender (neuter), the article 'das' and a capital letter.

11108.belief: Words will stick in my memory if I read them enough times.
11108.statement: Words will stick in my memory if I read them enough times.
11108.correction: It is the act of reaching for words that roots them deeper in memory, so testing oneself or working in pairs to try to recall words from memory is the most effective learning strategy for holding on to words in your long term memory.

8736.belief: The [r] sound in German is always the same, regardless of where it appears within the word.
8736.statement: The [r] sound in German is always the same, regardless of where it appears within the word.
8736.correction: German [r] can be pronounced in different ways. [r] is a gentle ‘rolling’ vibration pronounced from the back of the throat, if [r] is at a syllable start, after a consonant or between two vowels. [r] is a gentle ‘ah’ sound after a long vowel.

3306.belief: To give a reason in German, we use 'denn' or 'weil' and subject-verb word order, as in English.
3306.statement: To give a reason in German, we use 'denn' or 'weil' and subject-verb word order, as in English.
3306.correction: 'Denn' and 'weil' both mean 'because'. After 'denn' we use subject-verb word order (word order 1) but after 'weil' the verb goes to the end of the clause (word order 3).

10865.correction: ‘Weil’ in German sounds similar to ‘vile’ in English. However, ‘viel’ contains [v] which sounds like English ‘f’ and [ie] which is like English double ‘ee’.

5131.belief: There is just one German pronoun for singular informal 'you', as in English, e.g., 'you see me, I see you'.
5131.statement: There is just one German pronoun for singular informal 'you', as in English, e.g., 'you see me, I see you'.
5131.correction: German has two different pronouns in this scenario: 'du' is subject pronoun 'you', 'dich' is object pronoun 'you', e.g., 'du siehst mich, ich sehe dich'. This is similar to the 'I, me' difference in English, which German also shares: 'ich, mich'.

5361.belief: All past participles have the pattern 'ge-' + stem + '-t', e.g., 'gemacht'.
5361.statement: All past participles have the pattern 'ge-' + stem + '-t', e.g., 'gemacht'.
5361.correction: While most weak verbs form past participles like this, most strong verbs have the pattern ge- + stem + -en, e.g., 'gelesen', some with vowel changes, e.g., 'gesungen'. Verbs beginning with be-, er- or ver- don’t add ge-, e.g., 'erlebt', 'verbracht'.

3272.correction: ‘Die Uhr’ looks and sounds a bit like ‘hour’ but it means ‘clock’ and ‘um … Uhr’ means ‘at … o’clock’. 'Die Stunde' means ‘hour’.

10130.belief: To talk about the past using the perfect tense, we always use the present tense of ‘haben’ with a past participle.
10130.statement: To talk about the past using the perfect tense, we always use the present tense of ‘haben’ with a past participle.
10130.correction: Some verbs require the present tense of ‘sein’ with a past participle when forming the past perfect tense. These are mostly verbs of movement to a destination, e.g., ‘fahren’ to travel, ‘fliegen’ to fly.

10134.belief: When talking about travel, where and how you went can be given in any order, as is the case in English.
10134.statement: When talking about travel, where and how you went can be given in any order, as is the case in English.
10134.correction: When using adverbs to say where and how you went in the same sentence, manner (how) always comes before place (where).

5438.belief: The perfect tense in German is always formed with a part of 'haben' to express what someone has done.
5438.statement: The perfect tense in German is always formed with a part of 'haben' to express what someone has done.
5438.correction: Some verbs require a part of 'sein' to form the perfect tense, often with verbs of movement to a destination.

11105.belief: The words for 'the' and 'a' are always the same after prepositions.
11105.statement: The words for 'the' and 'a' are always the same after prepositions.
11105.correction: Prepositions take a specific case, e.g., 'durch' always takes the accusative. Some prepositions take different cases to create different meanings, e.g., 'in' and 'auf' can take the accusative, to show movement to, or the dative, to show location.

10185.belief: The terms 'weak verb' and 'strong verb' refer to whether the action is powerful or not.
10185.statement: The terms 'weak verb' and 'strong verb' refer to whether the action is powerful or not.
10185.correction: The term 'weak verb' is used to describe verbs that follow a regular pattern across all tenses. The term 'strong verb' describes verbs that have a stem change in either present or past tenses.

10842.belief: All verbs only need the -en ending changed to match the subject in the present tense.
10842.statement: All verbs only need the -en ending changed to match the subject in the present tense.
10842.correction: Some verbs need a change to the vowel in the stem in addition to the change to the -en ending, but only for 'du', 'er' and 'sie' (she).

3286.belief: 'Gern' is a verb meaning 'to like, liking' and can be used in front of the noun in sentence, e.g., 'ich gern Fußball'.
3286.statement: 'Gern' is a verb meaning 'to like, liking' and can be used in front of the noun in sentence, e.g., 'ich gern Fußball'.
3286.correction: 'Gern' is an adverb meaning 'gladly'. It is used to express liking doing an action and follows the verb that names the action, e.g., 'ich spiele gern Fußball'.

4947.belief: 'Nicht' goes before the verb like 'not' in English.
4947.statement: 'Nicht' goes before the verb like 'not' in English.
4947.correction: In German, 'nicht' usually goes before the element it negates — unless it's negating the whole sentence, in which case it tends to go at the end, e.g., 'Ich kaufe das Auto nicht' - 'I'm not buying the car'.

9202.belief: All separable verbs in German have their word-for-word English equivalent, e.g., 'stattfinden' - 'to take place', 'mitbringen' - to bring with, along'.
9202.statement: All separable verbs in German have their word-for-word English equivalent, e.g., 'stattfinden' - 'to take place', 'mitbringen' - to bring with, along'.
9202.correction: Many two-part separable verbs in German have single word English translations, e.g., 'einkaufen' - 'to shop', 'anfangen' - 'to start'. It is especially important with these verbs not to forget the separable prefix in German.

3259.belief: German has one general verb meaning 'to put, putting'.
3259.statement: German has one general verb meaning 'to put, putting'.
3259.correction: German has 3 placement verbs meaning 'to put'; 'stellen' - to make something stand (vertically), 'setzen' - to make something sit, and 'legen' - to make something lay down (horizontally). Equivalent position verbs are 'stehen', 'sitzen', 'liegen'.

3264.belief: The German pronoun for singular informal 'you' is always 'du'.
3264.statement: The German pronoun for singular informal 'you' is always 'du'.
3264.correction: German uses 'du' as subject pronoun, 'dich' as direct object pronoun, and 'dir' as indirect object pronoun. There are also two object pronouns for 'me'. E.g., 'Du fragst mich.' ('You ask me.'), 'Du antwortest mir.' ('You answer me'.).

10910.belief: If we want to say 'her' in German, the word is always 'ihr'.
10910.statement: If we want to say 'her' in German, the word is always 'ihr'.
10910.correction: After many verbs, the word for 'her' is 'sie'; same as the word for 'she', e.g., 'ich frage sie'. The word 'ihr' means 'her' after a dative verb, e.g., 'ich antworte ihr'. 'Ihr' is also the possessive adjective 'her', e.g., 'ihr Lieblingsgeschenk'.

5175.belief: There is one verb meaning 'to like' in German, and that is 'mögen'.
5175.statement: There is one verb meaning 'to like' in German, and that is 'mögen'.
5175.correction: 'Mögen' is 'to like', e.g., 'ich mag Mathe' ('I like maths'). However, 'gefallen' is another verb for expressing 'liking'. Its literal meaning is 'to please', so it's used with an indirect object, e.g., 'Mathe gefällt mir' - 'I like maths'.

5220.belief: After an opinion verb (e.g., 'denken') and the conjunction 'dass', we use normal subject-verb word order.
5220.statement: After an opinion verb (e.g., 'denken') and the conjunction 'dass', we use normal subject-verb word order.
5220.correction: To say 'I think that...' in German, we use the conjunction 'dass', which triggers word order 3 (WO3); e.g., 'Ich denke, dass Rapmusik toll ist.'.

10817.belief: If a verb is 'strong', its past participle always has a vowel change.
10817.statement: If a verb is 'strong', its past participle always has a vowel change.
10817.correction: In German, a strong verb has a stem change in one or more tenses. Some strong verbs have a stem change in the present tense but not in the perfect tense, e.g., 'sehen' - 'er, sie, es sieht' - 'hat gesehen'.

10815.belief: It is only the verb in a sentence that can tell us whether the action of the verb implies movement towards a destination or a static location.
10815.statement: It is only the verb in a sentence that can tell us whether the action of the verb implies movement towards a destination or a static location.
10815.correction: The case (form of the article 'the' or 'a') used after prepositions 'in' and 'auf' tells us whether movement or location are implied, e.g., when the article is in the accusative case ('in den', 'in die', 'ins') it means 'into' and indicates movement.

2353.belief: 'Was' and 'had' have different forms in German for 'ich' and 'er, sie'.
2353.statement: 'Was' and 'had' have different forms in German for 'ich' and 'er, sie'.
2353.correction: In German, 'war' means 'was', 'hatte' means 'had'. Both forms remain unchanged for 'ich' and 'er, sie', like in English.

163.belief: Adjectives work the same way in German as in English and do not change their spelling.
163.statement: Adjectives work the same way in German as in English and do not change their spelling.
163.correction: German adjectives change their ending when placed before the noun, depending on the case needed, and the gender of the noun they describe.

4177.belief: Like in English, a word for 'more' is needed in German when making comparisons like 'more difficult' or 'more interesting'.
4177.statement: Like in English, a word for 'more' is needed in German when making comparisons like 'more difficult' or 'more interesting'.
4177.correction: German adjectives form comparatives by adding -er; there is no need to include 'more', e.g., more interesting > 'interessanter'; more difficult >'schwieriger'. English does this with 1- and some 2-syllable adjectives, e.g., 'small' > 'smaller'.

3275.belief: The German verb for 'use' is needed when saying what used to happen.
3275.statement: The German verb for 'use' is needed when saying what used to happen.
3275.correction: 'Used to' in German is communicated by using the adverb 'früher' - 'in the past', 'in former times'. There is no need to include a German verb for 'use'.

2981.belief: Final [e] is a long vowel sound in German.
2981.statement: Final [e] is a long vowel sound in German.
2981.correction: Final [e] is a short [e] sound, as in 'Liebe'. Final [er] is a longer sound, as in 'lieber'.

9203.belief: Separable verbs work exactly the same as all other verbs in the present tense.
9203.statement: Separable verbs work exactly the same as all other verbs in the present tense.
9203.correction: Separable verbs use the same endings as all other present tense verbs, but in most sentences the separable verb prefix moves to the end of the sentence, e.g., 'anrufen' - 'ich rufe meinen Freund an'.

11071.belief: A word for 'do', 'does', 'is' or 'are' is needed when forming yes/no questions in German.
11071.statement: A word for 'do', 'does', 'is' or 'are' is needed when forming yes/no questions in German.
11071.correction: In German, yes/no questions can be formed simply by inverting the subject and the verb. There is no need for a word like 'do' or 'are' at the start, e.g. 'Läufst du schnell?' - 'Do you run fast?'.

3269.belief: German [st] and [sp] sound the same as in English, wherever they appear in the word.
3269.statement: German [st] and [sp] sound the same as in English, wherever they appear in the word.
3269.correction: At the start of words, German [sp-] and [st-] are pronounced 'schp-' and 'scht-'. If [sp] and [st] occur in the middle or end of a word, pronounce them as in English, except for compound nouns and separable verbs, which are also 'schp-' and 'scht-'.

11074.belief: Word order in German remains the same as English after ‘weil’ ('because').
11074.statement: Word order in German remains the same as English after ‘weil’ ('because').
11074.correction: When using ‘weil’ to give a reason, the verb moves to the end of the clause, e.g., ‘ich spiele gern Fußball, weil es Spaß macht'.

5203.belief: There is only one word in German for 'our' and 'their', just like in English.
5203.statement: There is only one word in German for 'our' and 'their', just like in English.
5203.correction: Possessive adjectives like 'unser' and 'ihr' change the spelling according to the gender of the noun and the case that is needed e.g. 'unser Hund', 'unsere Katze'; 'ihr Vater', 'ihre Mutter'.

5042.belief: Object pronouns like me, him, they are always the same in German, like English.
5042.statement: Object pronouns like me, him, they are always the same in German, like English.
5042.correction: German object pronouns can be direct or indirect; they change their spelling depending on the case needed, e.g. direct object pronoun 'dich' - you is accusative; indirect object pronoun 'dir' - you is dative. The case is often determined by the verb.

9175.belief: 'Seit' is always used with the continuous past, like in English, e.g. 'I have been learning German since June'.
9175.statement: 'Seit' is always used with the continuous past, like in English, e.g. 'I have been learning German since June'.
9175.correction: In German, 'seit' is used with the present tense to say 'for', e.g. 'Ich lerne seit vier Jahren Deutsch' - 'I have been learning German for 4 years', as well as 'since', e.g. 'Ich lerne seit Juni Deutsch' - 'I have been learning German since June'.

4515.belief: To mean 'for' with a period of time, use 'vor' in German.
4515.statement: To mean 'for' with a period of time, use 'vor' in German.
4515.correction: 'Vor' means 'ago', e.g. vor zwei Jahren - two years ago. To mean 'for' with a period of time in the present tense, use 'seit'; in the past, add 'lang' after the time phrase, but don't use a preposition for 'for'.

10582.belief: I can use 'an' and 'auf' interchangeably to mean 'on' or 'onto'.
10582.statement: I can use 'an' and 'auf' interchangeably to mean 'on' or 'onto'.
10582.correction: We use 'an' to mean 'on' or 'onto' when the position is vertical, e.g., 'on the wall' - 'an der Wand'. We use 'auf' to mean 'on' or 'onto' when the position is horizontal, e.g., 'on the table' - 'auf dem Tisch'.

1740.belief: Cognate recognition is the only strategy I need to understand texts in German.
1740.statement: Cognate recognition is the only strategy I need to understand texts in German.
