1740.correction: Cognates are helpful, but not always enough. You will understand much more if you know some common word and spelling patterns in German, and if you use your vocabulary and grammar knowledge creatively to work out the meanings of unfamiliar words.

595.belief: You can only begin an inversion sentence (word order two) with a time phrase, nothing else.
595.statement: You can only begin an inversion sentence (word order two) with a time phrase, nothing else.
595.correction: The emphasis is on whatever comes first in the sentence when using inversion (word order 2). It is acceptable to put the object of the sentence before the verb. For example, 'Den Kaffee trinken wir heute'.

10487.belief: If there are two verbs in a German sentence, the infinitive stays with the subject of the action.
10487.statement: If there are two verbs in a German sentence, the infinitive stays with the subject of the action.
10487.correction: If there are two verbs in a German sentence, the infinitive goes to the end of the sentence. This is different word order to English and is called the ‘two-verb rule’.

10614.belief: Always use 'müssen' in negative sentences to translate the idea of 'must not' in English.
10614.statement: Always use 'müssen' in negative sentences to translate the idea of 'must not' in English.
10614.correction: English often uses 'must not' in lieu of 'don't have to', 'not allowed to' and 'should not'. However, you should use the correct modal verb in German to express these ideas, e.g. 'du musst nicht', 'du darfst nicht', 'du sollst nicht'.

3939.correction: Both sounds in [kn] must be pronounced. This is different from English. Compare English 'knee' and German 'Knie'. Remember to pronounce the 'k' in German words containing [kn].

3252.correction: The German 'will' comes from 'wollen' and means 'want'. Do not confuse this with the future tense. 'Ich werde' means 'I will'.

106.belief: Always add 'zu' before the infinitive in two-verb structures.
106.statement: Always add 'zu' before the infinitive in two-verb structures.
106.correction: Some verbs, like 'werden' and modal verbs, do not require 'zu' before the infinitive in two-verb structures.

3281.belief: All German words that look or sound similar to words in English are cognates.
3281.statement: All German words that look or sound similar to words in English are cognates.
3281.correction: Similar looking and sounding words are only cognates if they share the same meaning in both languages. When the meaning is different, similar words are called false friends.

3280.belief: German word order is just like English - it's always subject-verb-object.
3280.statement: German word order is just like English - it's always subject-verb-object.
3280.correction: In English, word order is usually fixed: subject-verb-object, e.g., 'she eats an apple'. In German, the word order is more flexible because in main clauses the verb must be in second position. Any element can start a German sentence for emphasis.

5771.belief: After all prepositions, the case used depends on whether the verb describes 'location in' or 'movement to'.
5771.statement: After all prepositions, the case used depends on whether the verb describes 'location in' or 'movement to'.
5771.correction: Some prepositions always require dative endings regardless of the verb meaning; e.g., 'aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu'; other prepositions are only ever used with the accusative, e.g., 'durch, für'.

3274.belief: German [v] is always pronounced like English [f].
3274.statement: German [v] is always pronounced like English [f].
3274.correction: In many words, German [v] sounds like English [f]. However, in German words of foreign origin, [v] usually sounds the same as English [v], e.g., 'Universität', 'November', 'Aktivität'.

3309.belief: Giving the time as half past the hour works the same in German as it does in English, e.g., ‘halb neun’ is 'half past nine'.
3309.statement: Giving the time as half past the hour works the same in German as it does in English, e.g., ‘halb neun’ is 'half past nine'.
3309.correction: In German, half past is expressed as half of the next hour, so 'half past nine' is 'halb zehn', or 'half way to ten', the next hour.

3403.belief: To greet German speakers, use either ‘hallo’ or ‘guten Tag’.
3403.statement: To greet German speakers, use either ‘hallo’ or ‘guten Tag’.
3403.correction: Greetings in German-speaking countries vary depending on time of day, country/region and level of formality, e.g., ‘hallo’ in Germany but ‘servus’ in Austria and ‘hoi’ in Switzerland.

140.belief: Adjectives only change their spelling according to the gender of the noun they describe.
140.statement: Adjectives only change their spelling according to the gender of the noun they describe.
140.correction: Adjectives change their spelling to match both the gender of the noun and the case, e.g., 'das ist ein lustiger Hund', 'ich habe einen lustigen Hund'.

125.belief: When addressing questions to someone, I can just use 'du'.
125.statement: When addressing questions to someone, I can just use 'du'.
125.correction: Questions often need to be asked using 'Sie', in situations where respect should be shown, such as when asking a teacher or an unknown adult.

5665.belief: Poetry is always descriptive and doesn't tell stories.
5665.statement: Poetry is always descriptive and doesn't tell stories.
5665.correction: Ballads are poems that tell stories with a sequence of events. They include scene-setting, action, change moments and a conclusion. Ballads are also lyrical - they use poetic language, imagery, rhythm, rhyme - and dramatic - often with direct speech.

10979.belief: 'Wenn' can be used in question words to ask 'When?'.
10979.statement: 'Wenn' can be used in question words to ask 'When?'.
10979.correction: Use the question word 'Wann?' to ask 'When?' in German. Use 'wenn' to say 'when' in a present tense statement.

2744.belief: 'Es' is the only word used to translate 'it' in German.
2744.statement: 'Es' is the only word used to translate 'it' in German.
2744.correction: 'Es' is for neuter nouns or abstract ideas. Use the correct subject or object pronouns according to the grammatical gender of the noun they replace.

10639.belief: Use the same word order as English when using indirect object pronouns.
10639.statement: Use the same word order as English when using indirect object pronouns.
10639.correction: In German, the indirect object pronoun comes straight after the verb, not at the end of the sentence. For example, 'Musik ist mir wichtig.' - 'Music is important to me.'.

355.belief: -AR verbs have the same ending for the 'I' form of the present and preterite tense.
355.statement: -AR verbs have the same ending for the 'I' form of the present and preterite tense.
355.correction: In the present tense, the 1st person singular ends in '-o' and in the preterite, the 1st person singular ends in '-é'.

5784.belief: The present tense and the preterite tense of -ar verbs share the same endings for the 'I' form.
5784.statement: The present tense and the preterite tense of -ar verbs share the same endings for the 'I' form.
5784.correction: In Spanish, the 1st person of the present tense ends in -o and of the preterite ends in -é. These endings only apply to -AR verbs.

2355.belief: All the different persons of the -ar verbs in the preterite tense have the same endings, as in the English simple past, e.g. 'did', 'ate', 'went', 'learned'.
2355.statement: All the different persons of the -ar verbs in the preterite tense have the same endings, as in the English simple past, e.g. 'did', 'ate', 'went', 'learned'.
2355.correction: In Spanish, the endings for -ar verbs in the preterite tense differ depending on the grammatical person. The 'I' form ends in -é and the 'you' form ends in -aste.

10490.belief: Two vowels together are always read as one vowel.
10490.statement: Two vowels together are always read as one vowel.
10490.correction: In Spanish, when two strong vowels [a], [e] or [i] appear next to each other they are pronounced separately. This is why we call them 'strong' vowels.

2447.belief: It doesn't matter which Spanish translation of the verb 'to be' we use, as they both mean 'to be, being'.
2447.statement: It doesn't matter which Spanish translation of the verb 'to be' we use, as they both mean 'to be, being'.
2447.correction: The verb 'ser' is for permanent traits, and the verb 'estar' is for temporary states/moods and location. It sounds as odd to a Spanish person if we use the wrong verb 'to be' as it does when someone says 'I make sport' or 'I do a cake' in English.

10953.belief: When a weak vowel is next to a strong vowel, we pronounce them separately.
10953.statement: When a weak vowel is next to a strong vowel, we pronounce them separately.
10953.correction: When a weak vowel is next to a strong vowel, like for example [i] next to [a], [e] or [o], it merges with them to make a single syllable.

9097.belief: To say what 'we do' instead of what 'I do' in Spanish, you just change the pronoun from 'I' to 'we' and keep the verb the same.
9097.statement: To say what 'we do' instead of what 'I do' in Spanish, you just change the pronoun from 'I' to 'we' and keep the verb the same.
9097.correction: In Spanish it's the verb ending and not the pronoun that changes the subject of the verb, so you need to pay close attention to the verb form to know who is doing the action of the verb, e.g. 'I sell' - 'vendo', 'we sell' - 'vendemos'.

8700.correction: 'Qué' with an accent on the 'e' is the question word 'what'. 'Que' without an accent is a conjunction meaning 'that' - 'Creo que hay una solución'.

10005.belief: Subject pronouns, e.g. 'I', 'she', 'we', 'they', are used in the same way in Spanish and English.
10005.statement: Subject pronouns, e.g. 'I', 'she', 'we', 'they', are used in the same way in Spanish and English.
10005.correction: English always uses subject pronouns. Spanish often relies on verb endings alone to indicate the 'doer'. However, Spanish has subject pronouns, e.g. 'yo' (I), 'tú' (you), 'él' (he), 'ella' (she), which are used for emphasis and clarity, as needed.

5205.belief: There is just one word for ‘we’ and one word for ‘they’ in Spanish.
5205.statement: There is just one word for ‘we’ and one word for ‘they’ in Spanish.
5205.correction: Spanish has two words each for ‘we’ and ‘they’. The plural pronoun ‘we’ is ‘nosotros’ for boys/men or mixed gender groups, ‘nosotras’ for girls/women; ‘they’ also has two forms, 'ellos' and 'ellas'.

5782.belief: All present tense forms of the model verb 'poder' have the same vowel change in the stem, o-> ue.
5782.statement: All present tense forms of the model verb 'poder' have the same vowel change in the stem, o-> ue.
5782.correction: The 1st, 2nd, 3rd persons singular ('puedo', 'puedes', 'puede') and 3rd person plural ('pueden') forms all have a stem change from 'o' to 'ue' but 1st person plural 'we' form is 'podemos'; it keeps the same vowel as the infinitive 'poder'.

10489.belief: When there are two verbs together, e.g. 'I must go', we need to conjugate both.
10489.statement: When there are two verbs together, e.g. 'I must go', we need to conjugate both.
10489.correction: English confuses us here. We say 'I must go' rather than 'I must to go' as English uses an infinitive but without 'to'. In Spanish, after modal verbs 'deber', 'poder' and 'querer' the 2nd verb must always be an infinitive; 'I must go' is 'Debo ir'.

9481.belief: Spanish -er and -ir verbs share the same endings in the present tense.
9481.statement: Spanish -er and -ir verbs share the same endings in the present tense.
9481.correction: The verbs endings for Spanish -er and -ir verbs are the same for 'I', 'you (singular)', 'she', 'he', 'it' and 'they'. The 1st person plural ‘we’ ending for -er verbs is -emos, and for -ir verbs is -imos.

9296.belief: The simple present tense in Spanish is only for habitual actions, e.g. 'every week I do my homework'.
9296.statement: The simple present tense in Spanish is only for habitual actions, e.g. 'every week I do my homework'.
9296.correction: The simple present in Spanish is used for habitual actions and immediate plans. '¿Qué haces hoy?' means 'What are you doing today?' and 'hoy hago mis deberes' means 'today I am doing my homework'. English uses the present continuous here instead.

2725.belief: -er and -ir verbs have different endings in the preterite.
2725.statement: -er and -ir verbs have different endings in the preterite.
2725.correction: -er and -ir verbs share the same endings in the preterite. The 'I' form of both -er and -ir verbs is -í.

161.belief: All adjectives in Spanish go after the noun.
161.statement: All adjectives in Spanish go after the noun.
161.correction: Most adjectives in Spanish go after the noun, except prenominal adjectives, which go before the noun. Some prenominal adjectives are: 'último', 'primero', 'segundo', 'tercero', 'bueno', 'propio'.

11081.belief: The word 'pie' is pronounced like the English word 'pie'.
11081.statement: The word 'pie' is pronounced like the English word 'pie'.
11081.correction: In Spanish 'pie' is also a 1-syllable word but we hear each letter distinctly, and Spanish 'i' is pronounced 'i' as in the Spanish word 'idea'. To say it correctly, enunciate each letter but quickly so that the word sounds as one syllable, 'p-i-e'.

2686.belief: When in English there are two nouns together to describe a particular type of something, e.g. 'train ticket', in Spanish we translate them in the same order.
2686.statement: When in English there are two nouns together to describe a particular type of something, e.g. 'train ticket', in Spanish we translate them in the same order.
2686.correction: In Spanish, the word order changes and the preposition 'de' is used between the two nouns, e.g. 'train ticket' is 'billete de tren'.

5022.belief: All numbers from 13 to 19 begin with 'dieci-'.
5022.statement: All numbers from 13 to 19 begin with 'dieci-'.
5022.correction: Numbers 16 to 19 begin with 'dieci-' + number, e.g. 'dieciséis', 'diecisiete', but numbers 13 to 15 do not follow the same pattern, e.g. 'trece', 'catorce', 'quince'.

10818.belief: The verb 'tener' always means 'to have, having'.
10818.statement: The verb 'tener' always means 'to have, having'.
10818.correction: The verb 'tener' translates into English as 'to be' when used as part of idioms, e.g. 'tengo suerte' translates as 'I am lucky'.

11094.belief: All the words ending in '-ción' and '-ciones' must have an accent.
11094.statement: All the words ending in '-ción' and '-ciones' must have an accent.
11094.correction: If a word ends in 'n' or 's' and has final syllable stress, it must have an accent, e.g. 'la opción'. However, if a word ending in 'n' or 's' has penultimate syllable stress, it does not need an accent, e.g. 'las opciones'.

10802.belief: The verb 'dar' always translates as 'to give, giving'.
10802.statement: The verb 'dar' always translates as 'to give, giving'.
10802.correction: The verb 'dar' means 'to give, giving' but can also translate as 'to be' + adjective when describing how something makes people feel.

8932.belief: When revisiting vocabulary using the Leitner system, we need to revise all the words in the different boxes every day.
8932.statement: When revisiting vocabulary using the Leitner system, we need to revise all the words in the different boxes every day.
8932.correction: When learning vocabulary using the Leitner system, we use 4 boxes with words: words that need to be revised daily, words that need to be revised every 3 days, weekly and monthly.

39.belief: The 3rd person endings for -IR verbs include 'i', as -ER end in 'e' and 'en' and -AR verbs end in 'a' and 'an'.
39.statement: The 3rd person endings for -IR verbs include 'i', as -ER end in 'e' and 'en' and -AR verbs end in 'a' and 'an'.
39.correction: -IR verbs have the same present tense endings as -ER verbs.

10812.belief: The verb 'ir' is a regular verb so I can apply the regular conjugation rules for -ir verbs.
10812.statement: The verb 'ir' is a regular verb so I can apply the regular conjugation rules for -ir verbs.
10812.correction: The verb 'ir' is irregular, therefore, it does not follow the normal conjugation rules. To say 'I go' we say 'voy', 'you go' - 'vas' and 'she, he, it goes' - 'va'.

11079.belief: The word 'para' is always translated as 'for'.
11079.statement: The word 'para' is always translated as 'for'.
11079.correction: The word 'para' is translated as 'for' when it is followed by a noun, but it is translated as 'in order to' when followed by an infinitive.

9499.belief: In Spanish, the simple present can be used for routine as well as for ongoing events.
9499.statement: In Spanish, the simple present can be used for routine as well as for ongoing events.
9499.correction: The simple present is used to describe routine actions, and also immediate plans for today, but the present continuous is used to describe ongoing events.

3117.belief: To form the present continuous we just need to remove the -ar/-er/-ir from the infinitive and add -ando or -iendo.
3117.statement: To form the present continuous we just need to remove the -ar/-er/-ir from the infinitive and add -ando or -iendo.
3117.correction: To form the present continuous we need to use the correct form of the verb 'estar' and then the present participle which is formed by removing the -ar/-er/-ir from the infinitive and adding -ando or -iendo.

3429.correction: The 1st person of the present ends in -o, e.g. 'hablo', meaning 'I speak'. The 3rd person of the preterite ends in -ó, e.g. 'habló', meaning 'she, he, it spoke'.

173.belief: Adverbs of position are always followed by 'de'.
173.statement: Adverbs of position are always followed by 'de'.
173.correction: Adverbs of position are followed by 'de' when they refer to a place/person, by 'del' when they refer to masculine nouns, and by 'de la' when they refer to feminine nouns.

1982.correction: They both mean 'to know, knowing' but 'conocer' is used for knowing facts and information, while 'saber' is used to say that you are familiar or become familiar with a place, a person or a thing.

142.belief: Adjectives always come after the noun in Spanish.
142.statement: Adjectives always come after the noun in Spanish.
142.correction: In Spanish, adjectives generally come after the noun; however, certain prenominal adjectives come before the noun, e.g. 'último', 'mismo', 'propio', 'primero', 'segundo', 'tercero'.

60.belief: Accents don't affect how we pronounce Spanish words.
60.statement: Accents don't affect how we pronounce Spanish words.
60.correction: Accents are very important and can differentiate between past and present. When we pronounce words with accents, we must remember to stress that syllable. For example, the verb 'caminó' means 'he, she, it walked' while 'camino' means 'I walk'.

5799.belief: In the preterite tense, er and -ir verbs have different endings.
5799.statement: In the preterite tense, er and -ir verbs have different endings.
5799.correction: -er and -ir verbs share the same endings in the preterite: -í for 'I', -iste for 'you' and -ió for 'she, he, it'.

9493.belief: In Spanish the personal 'a' is required between verbs and all direct objects.
9493.statement: In Spanish the personal 'a' is required between verbs and all direct objects.
9493.correction: In Spanish you use the personal 'a' after the verb when the following direct object is a specific person or an animal we have a name for (a pet).

5761.belief: All prenominal adjectives ending in -o drop the -o before masculine nouns.
5761.statement: All prenominal adjectives ending in -o drop the -o before masculine nouns.
5761.correction: Not all prenominal adjectives ending in -o drop it before a masculine noun, although there are many common ones that do like 'bueno' and 'malo'. However 'segundo' and 'último' do not, and there are others that hold on to their -o too.

10615.belief: If you use 'me' in Spanish you need 'myself' in English.
10615.statement: If you use 'me' in Spanish you need 'myself' in English.
10615.correction: When the action of a verb is directed towards the self, Spanish always uses a reflexive pronoun. English does not always do this; for example, 'me levanto a las siete' - 'I get up at seven'.

4509.correction: 'Me' and 'te' are reflexive pronouns in Spanish and mean 'myself' and 'yourself' respectively. 'Mi' and 'tu' are the possessive adjectives 'my' and 'your' in Spanish.

9485.belief: In Spanish, like in English, the object always goes after the verb.
9485.statement: In Spanish, like in English, the object always goes after the verb.
9485.correction: In Spanish, unlike in English, the object can go before or after the verb. In object-first sentences, we add the object pronouns lo (masculine) or la (feminine) before the verb.

3984.correction: 'La' means 'the' in front of a noun but 'her' or 'it' when it comes before a verb.

3747.belief: The indirect object pronoun replaces the thing being given, not the person receiving it.
3747.statement: The indirect object pronoun replaces the thing being given, not the person receiving it.
3747.correction: The indirect object pronoun replaces the person who is receiving the action, not the thing being given. 'Le doy un regalo.' - 'I give a present to him, her.'

4505.belief: 'Me gusta' is always the correct way to say 'I like'.
4505.statement: 'Me gusta' is always the correct way to say 'I like'.
4505.correction: 'Me gusta' is 'I like' for a singular or uncountable noun, but plural nouns require 'me gustan'.

3420.belief: Gustar-type verbs do not agree in number with the subject.
3420.statement: Gustar-type verbs do not agree in number with the subject.
3420.correction: Gustar-type verbs agree with the subject in number: -a for singular nouns and -an for plural nouns.

5177.belief: There is only one verb for 'to be, being' in Spanish.
5177.statement: There is only one verb for 'to be, being' in Spanish.
5177.correction: There are two verbs for to be in Spanish: 'estar' for location and temporary states and 'ser' for general traits.

9514.belief: Spanish always uses subject pronouns with verbs, like English.
9514.statement: Spanish always uses subject pronouns with verbs, like English.
9514.correction: Spanish rarely uses subject pronouns; they are used for contrast or emphasis only. The ending of the verb in Spanish tells you who the subject is.

5198.belief: There is only one way to translate the Spanish present tense into English.
5198.statement: There is only one way to translate the Spanish present tense into English.
5198.correction: There are two ways of translating the Spanish present tense into English: the present simple (habit - 'I go') or the present continuous (ongoing action - 'I am going'). The context or time adverbs can help to tell us which one to choose in English.

10127.belief: To talk about completed events in the past with -ar verbs you always take off the -ar ending and add -é in the 1st person singular ('I').
10127.statement: To talk about completed events in the past with -ar verbs you always take off the -ar ending and add -é in the 1st person singular ('I').
10127.correction: For -ar verbs ending in -car, you remove the -car and add -qué in the 1st person singular, for example; 'sacar' - 'saqué' - 'I took out'.

9099.belief: To say 'my mum is a teacher', it's 'mi madre es una profesora.'.
9099.statement: To say 'my mum is a teacher', it's 'mi madre es una profesora.'
9099.correction: In Spanish, we do not need the indefinite article ('un', 'una') when referring to jobs, so we would just say 'mi madre es profesora.'

1844.belief: To compare two things in Spanish we can just change the adjective like in English, e.g. 'angry' becomes 'angrier.'.
1844.statement: To compare two things in Spanish we can just change the adjective like in English, e.g. 'angry' becomes 'angrier.'
1844.correction: To compare two nouns we use a comparative structure. To express 'more... than' we use 'más... que' and to say 'less... than' we use 'menos... que'. The adjective goes in the middle and still has to agree in gender and number with the first noun.

9090.belief: To say 'better than' in Spanish I can use 'más bueno que'. To say 'worse than' I can use 'menos malo que'.
9090.statement: To say 'better than' in Spanish I can use 'más bueno que'. To say 'worse than' I can use 'menos malo que'.
9090.correction: In English we don't say 'more good than' or 'more bad than'. We say 'better than' or 'worse than'. Spanish also has words for 'better' and worse'. To say 'better than' use 'mejor que' and to say 'worse than' use 'peor que'.

10391.belief: To translate 'Where do you keep these shoes?' I need the word for 'do' in Spanish.
10391.statement: To translate 'Where do you keep these shoes?' I need the word for 'do' in Spanish.
10391.correction: Spanish doesn't have a word for 'do' in questions. Only the main verb is used in the form that matches the subject of the question. So the translation would be '¿Dónde guardas estos zapatos?'.

2196.belief: When 'de' appears before 'el' it becomes 'de el'.
2196.statement: When 'de' appears before 'el' it becomes 'de el'.
2196.correction: When 'de' appears before a singular masculine noun with the definite article 'el' it merges with it to form 'del', e.g. 'la jugadora está fuera del estadio' - 'the player is outside the stadium'.

3965.belief: I know 'ir' in the present tense, so it will be easy to remember it in the preterite tense.
3965.statement: I know 'ir' in the present tense, so it will be easy to remember it in the preterite tense.
3965.correction: 'Ir' is an irregular verb in both the present and the preterite tense. This verb is very common and therefore needs to be learnt off by heart.

3131.belief: When forming a question the verb form changes in Spanish like it does in English (auxiliary 'did' + verb).
3131.statement: When forming a question the verb form changes in Spanish like it does in English (auxiliary 'did' + verb).
3131.correction: The verb stays the same in Spanish and only the intonation (spoken) or punctuation (written) marks the sentence as a question. There is no need to translate a form of 'do', 'did' etc.

9522.belief: All Spanish words with stress on the second-to-last syllable must have a written accent.
9522.statement: All Spanish words with stress on the second-to-last syllable must have a written accent.
9522.correction: If a word ends in a vowel, -n, or -s, it usually has that stress naturally and doesn’t need an accent. Accents are only used when the word sounds different from the normal rule.

353.belief: -ar, -er, and -ir verbs all share the same endings in the present tense for 'she, he, it' and 'they' forms.
353.statement: -ar, -er, and -ir verbs all share the same endings in the present tense for 'she, he, it' and 'they' forms.
353.correction: -er and -ir verbs share the same endings for 'she, he, it' and 'they' forms, but -ar verbs have a different ending.

3119.belief: To form the present continuous I use the present tense of 'estar' followed by an infinitive, as with other two-verb structures I know, i.e. modal verbs.
3119.statement: To form the present continuous I use the present tense of 'estar' followed by an infinitive, as with other two-verb structures I know, i.e. modal verbs.
3119.correction: To form the present continuous you use the present tense of 'estar' followed by the present participle. For -ar verbs this is formed by removing the -ar ending and adding -ando, e.g. 'estoy saltando' ('I am jumping').

9344.statement: Some singular forms of 'estar' and feminine demonstrative adjectives look and sound the same.
9344.correction: The feminine demonstrative adjectives 'esta' (this) and 'estas' (these) have no accent. The 2nd and 3rd person singular forms of 'estar' have an accent on the -a: 'estás' (you are) and 'está' (she, he is). They are pronounced with stress on the -a.

4179.belief: Just like modal verbs, 'estar' is followed by an infinitive to form the present continuous to express what is happening right now.
4179.statement: Just like modal verbs, 'estar' is followed by an infinitive to form the present continuous to express what is happening right now.
4179.correction: To form the present continuous, use a present tense form of 'estar' together with a present participle. To form this for -ar verbs, remove -ar from the infinitive and add -ando to the stem. For -er and -ir verbs, add -iendo to the verb stem.

3118.belief: To form the present continuous I just use 'está' + present participle.
3118.statement: To form the present continuous I just use 'está' + present participle.
3118.correction: To form the present continuous you first conjugate 'estar'; e.g. for 'they are' use 'están'. Then add the present participle; which is the verb stem + -ando for -ar verbs and -iendo for -er/-ir verbs, e.g. 'están hablando' - 'they are talking'.

10805.belief: The verb ending -o refers to 'she', 'he' or 'it' in the preterite tense.
10805.statement: The verb ending -o refers to 'she', 'he' or 'it' in the preterite tense.
10805.correction: The verb ending -o refers to 'I' in the present tense. The verb ending -ó (with accent) refers to 'she', 'he' or 'it' in the preterite tense.

3187.correction: 'Fui' means 'I went' and 'fue' means 'she, he, it went'. The two have similar spelling so are easily confused.

2257.belief: When describing future plans, 'ir' + a is followed by a conjugated verb.
2257.statement: When describing future plans, 'ir' + a is followed by a conjugated verb.
2257.correction: When describing future plans, 'ir' + a is followed by the infinitive form of a verb.

4023.belief: Languages don't change; they have a fixed number of words in them.
4023.statement: Languages don't change; they have a fixed number of words in them.
4023.correction: Languages are not fixed; they are changing all the time, adopting new words to reflect how people live and speak.

101.belief: Add -s to make all adjectives plural.
101.statement: Add -s to make all adjectives plural.
101.correction: Regular adjectives usually need -s adding in the plural form, however there are other patterns and differences between the masculine and the feminine form with adjectives ending in -x and -al.

98.belief: When you add a question word at the end of a question, there is no need to change your intonation.
98.statement: When you add a question word at the end of a question, there is no need to change your intonation.
98.correction: It is important to use your intonation by raising the pitch of your voice at the end of all questions in French.

5002.belief: 'On' and 'nous' both mean 'we' and can be used interchangeably.
5002.statement: 'On' and 'nous' both mean 'we' and can be used interchangeably.
5002.correction: 'On' and 'nous' both mean 'we' but 'on' is used more to talk about people generally, 'nous' is always used to talk about yourself and another person/people. The verb endings are different, 'on' uses il/elle verb endings and the 'nous' ending is -ons.

2646.belief: [en/an] and [on] sound the same in French.
2646.statement: [en/an] and [on] sound the same in French.
2646.correction: Although the sounds are simililar and both nasal vowels, [en/an] is a nasal 'a' and [on] is a nasal 'o'. The mouth should be wide for [en/an] and almost closed for [on].

175.belief: All adverbs that tell us how and how often something happens come straight after the verb and we add -ment to all adjectives to make them adverbs.
175.statement: All adverbs that tell us how and how often something happens come straight after the verb and we add -ment to all adjectives to make them adverbs.
175.correction: There are exceptions to the adverb placement and adverb formation rules. For example 'parfois' usually comes at the start of a sentence. 'Dur' is an adjective which often doesn't change even when it is used as an adverb with certain verbs.

5268.belief: [ou] and [u] are both the same 'u' sound.
5268.statement: [ou] and [u] are both the same 'u' sound.
5268.correction: Be careful not to mix up the similar but not identical sounds, people may not understand you or you could be saying a different word to the one you mean.

4686.belief: All modal verbs follow the same pattern in the 3rd person plural.
4686.statement: All modal verbs follow the same pattern in the 3rd person plural.
4686.correction: 'Devoir' and 'pouvoir' are formed the same way, 'vouloir' is the same with the addition of an 'l' instead of a 'v' and 'savoir' is different; it follows the same pattern as the 'nous'/'vous' forms.

3609.belief: 'Il faut' works like modal verbs, it changes for different subject pronouns.
3609.statement: 'Il faut' works like modal verbs, it changes for different subject pronouns.
3609.correction: 'Il faut' is only used in the 3rd person singular and it is impersonal, it is used to talk about what it is necessary for people in general to do or what they must do.

9441.belief: The sound-symbol correspondences [ai] and [é/er/ez] sound the same in French.
9441.statement: The sound-symbol correspondences [ai] and [é/er/ez] sound the same in French.
9441.correction: The letters 'ai/ay' are the same as the SSC [é/er/ez] in French but [ai] is pronounced as in 'vrai' with slightly more relaxed lips than 'ai/ay' in English.

1976.belief: 'Connaitre' and 'savoir' both mean 'know' so they can be used interchangeably.
1976.statement: 'Connaitre' and 'savoir' both mean 'know' so they can be used interchangeably.
1976.correction: 'Connaitre' and 'savoir' both mean 'know', but 'connaitre' is used for being familiar with people/places/things, whereas 'savoir' usually means 'to know how to' or used on its own/with 'que'.

1969.belief: I can conjugate 'mettre' and 'remettre' exactly like 'entendre'.
1969.statement: I can conjugate 'mettre' and 'remettre' exactly like 'entendre'.
1969.correction: 'Mettre' and 'remettre' do take the same verb endings as 'entendre'; however, they also drop a 't' in the singular present tense forms.

96.belief: Just add 'ne... jamais' around the verb to say 'never'; the rest of the sentence stays the same.
96.statement: Just add 'ne... jamais' around the verb to say 'never'; the rest of the sentence stays the same.
96.correction: Add 'ne... jamais' around the conjugated verb, but in addition, change any indefinite/partitive articles to de/d' after a negative.

11093.belief: Words ending in -c (like historic) also end in -c in French.
11093.statement: Words ending in -c (like historic) also end in -c in French.
11093.correction: Words ending in -c in English often end in -que in French: historique.

5163.belief: There is only one translation of a French infinitive into English.
5163.statement: There is only one translation of a French infinitive into English.
5163.correction: An infinitive can be translated into English using the -ing form or 'to...': conduire - to drive, driving.

4180.belief: Like nationality adjectives, nationality nouns use lowercase letters in French: il est anglais - c'est un anglais.
4180.statement: Like nationality adjectives, nationality nouns use lowercase letters in French: il est anglais - c'est un anglais.
4180.correction: Unlike nationality adjectives, nationality nouns use capital letters in French: il est anglais - c'est un Anglais.

4181.belief: Like non-person or object nouns, identity nouns exist in only one form and gender.
4181.statement: Like non-person or object nouns, identity nouns exist in only one form and gender.
4181.correction: Unlike non-person or object nouns, identity nouns can have both masculine and feminine forms: le chrétien - la chrétienne. This is the same as other French person nouns you may know, e.g. le directeur/la directrice.

5194.belief: There is one way of saying 'your' in French.
5194.statement: There is one way of saying 'your' in French.
5194.correction: 'Your' in French changes, depending on who you are talking to and what you are talking about. Use 'ton' (m), 'ta' (f) or 'tes' (pl) when talking to someone you know well. Use 'votre' (m/f) or 'vos' (mpl/fpl) when talking to someone formally.

4184.belief: Like the possessive adjectives 'mon' and 'ton', the possessive adjective 'leur' changes in the singular form based on the gender of the noun possessed.
4184.statement: Like the possessive adjectives 'mon' and 'ton', the possessive adjective 'leur' changes in the singular form based on the gender of the noun possessed.
4184.correction: Unlike the possessive adjectives 'mon' and 'ton', the possessive adjective 'leur' does not change in the singular form based on the gender of the noun possessed, it remains the same: leur chien, leur souris.

5127.belief: There is just one equivalent tense in English to the perfect tense in French.
5127.statement: There is just one equivalent tense in English to the perfect tense in French.
5127.correction: There are in fact two equivalent tenses in English to the perfect tense in French: the present perfect and the simple past. 'J'ai voyagé au Sénégal' can mean both 'I travelled to France' and 'I have travelled to France'.

3610.correction: 'Il faut' is from the impersonal verb 'falloir' - 'to be necessary'. 'Il' does not mean 'he'; we translate 'il faut' as 'it is necessary' or 'you must'. It works like a modal verb in that it is usually followed by a 2nd verb in the infinitive form.

3975.belief: Knowing the lower numbers is enough to be able to tell the time in French.
3975.statement: Knowing the lower numbers is enough to be able to tell the time in French.
3975.correction: As French uses 24-hour clock more than English and gives the minutes after the hour, you need to know numbers 1-59 well.

515.correction: Most of the time, we translate 'avoir' as 'to have/having' but there are expressions, where we would use the verb to be in English, where French uses 'avoir', usually expressing feelings/states e.g 'avoir froid', to be cold.

150.belief: All adjectives go after the noun in French.
150.statement: All adjectives go after the noun in French.
150.correction: While the majority of adjectives are placed after the noun, certain types of adjective go in front. Students should be aware of which adjectives go where in order to speak and write with greater accuracy.

10627.belief: Use the partitive article with all uncountable nouns, even negatives.
10627.statement: Use the partitive article with all uncountable nouns, even negatives.
10627.correction: After quantities and negatives use 'de/d' instead of the partitive article. E.g Il y a beaucoup de riz. Il n'y a pas de riz.

5357.belief: All past participles are formed in the same way.
5357.statement: All past participles are formed in the same way.
5357.correction: Regular -er verb past participles are formed by changing the -er at the end of the infinitive to é but there are other past participle patterns such as verbs like prendre changing to 'pris' and some irregular past participles.

171.belief: Adverbs always come in the same place in a sentence.
171.statement: Adverbs always come in the same place in a sentence.
171.correction: The type of adverb tells us where to place it. When and where adverbs usually come at the beginning or end of a sentence and how (often) adverbs usaully come straight after the first verb in a sentence.

4113.belief: The letter 'e' is always pronounced the same in French.
4113.statement: The letter 'e' is always pronounced the same in French.
4113.correction: The letter 'e' is often pronounced as the 'e' in 'je' is but can be pronounced like [è/ê]. Pronounce 'e' like [è/ê] before double consonants and the letters c/l if they are in the last syllable.

10654.belief: Always use the verb 'avoir' to help you form the perfect tense.
10654.statement: Always use the verb 'avoir' to help you form the perfect tense.
10654.correction: Remember - for movement verbs and 'rester' use 'être', instead of 'avoir', to help you form the perfect tense.

9053.belief: 'S' always sounds the same in French.
9053.statement: 'S' always sounds the same in French.
9053.correction: The 's' at the beginning of words and double 's' is a soft sound but 's' between two consonants is [s], pronounced as in 'maison'.

9048.belief: Every 's' at the end of a word is silent because of the silent final consonant rule.
9048.statement: Every 's' at the end of a word is silent because of the silent final consonant rule.
9048.correction: Usually 's' is silent at the end of a word but if the next word starts with a vowel, you usually hear liaison, whereby the final consonant is pronounced. When the final consonat is 's', it sounds like the hard 's' in 'maison'.

4584.belief: 'Mettre' is a verb like 'entendre' and it follows the same pattern.
4584.statement: 'Mettre' is a verb like 'entendre' and it follows the same pattern.
4584.correction: 'Mettre' has the same present tense endings as verbs like 'entendre' but the stem is different in the singular forms. Drop one of the 't's from the infinitive, leaving the remaining 't' as a silent final consonant.

8721.belief: 'Qui' is always used as a question word.
8721.statement: 'Qui' is always used as a question word.
8721.correction: 'Qui' is a question word meaning 'who' but is also used as a relative pronoun to introduce a relative clause, for example 'L'homme qui est grand est mon papa', meaning 'the man who is tall is my dad'.

10649.belief: Use subject pronouns after prepositions to link nouns/pronouns.
10649.statement: Use subject pronouns after prepositions to link nouns/pronouns.
10649.correction: Use the emphatic pronouns 'moi' and 'toi' instead of subject pronouns to link and emphasise nouns/pronouns.

4082.belief: Learning genders is not as important as learning the noun itself.
4082.statement: Learning genders is not as important as learning the noun itself.
4082.correction: Leaning the genders of words is essential because it affects other parts of the sentence such as which form of 'à/de' to use before a noun.

9120.belief: School years work the same in English and French.
9120.statement: School years work the same in English and French.
9120.correction: French uses 'la' before ordinal numbers for school years, the lower the number, the higher the school year e.g. 'sixième' is equivalent to Y7 and 'cinquième' is Y8. Use 'en' to say you're in a school year e.g. 'en sixième'.

95.belief: Add 'ième' to make all ordinal numbers.
95.statement: Add 'ième' to make all ordinal numbers.
95.correction: Add 'ième' to make the majority of ordinal numbers but 'first' (premier/première) is an exception and cardinal numbers ending -e, drop the final -e before adding 'ième'. There are a few other spelling exceptions like 'neuvième' and 'cinquième'.

3639.belief: The imperfect tense formation is different for ir/re verbs.
3639.statement: The imperfect tense formation is different for ir/re verbs.
3639.correction: The imperfect tense is formed exactly the same way as with -er verbs. Take the present tense nous form, remove -ons and add the imperfect endings.

3616.correction: 'Il y a' can mean 'there is' or 'there are' and can be used with singular or plural nouns.

196.belief: [ai] and [é] sound the same in French.
196.statement: [ai] and [é] sound the same in French.
196.correction: In some regional accents [ai] and [é] can sound similar. Officially there is a difference in pronunciation and meaning as the ending of the imperfect tense is supposed to be pronounced [ai], whereas a common ending of the past participle is [é].

10652.belief: You can use a time phrase to show whether you mean a completed action in the past or a regular past event/activity.
10652.statement: You can use a time phrase to show whether you mean a completed action in the past or a regular past event/activity.
10652.correction: In French, the verb alone already shows whether you mean a completed action in the past (use the formation rule for the perfect tense) or a regular past event/activity (use the formation rule for the imperfect tense). Time phrases can also be added.

5363.belief: Past participles with 'être' don't change, just like past participles with 'avoir'.
5363.statement: Past participles with 'être' don't change, just like past participles with 'avoir'.
5363.correction: Past participles with 'être' always agree in gender and number with the subject. Add 'e' to agree a feminine past participle and 's' to agree a plural past participle.

8762.belief: All -re and -ir verbs follow the same pattern.
8762.statement: All -re and -ir verbs follow the same pattern.
8762.correction: There are different groups of -ir and -re verbs that follow slightly different patterns. It's good to revisit these regularly in their own right and because they can help with other tenses.

3607.belief: 'Il' and 'elle' mean he and she and can only refer to people.
3607.statement: 'Il' and 'elle' mean he and she and can only refer to people.
3607.correction: Every noun has a gender in French. Therefore 'il' and 'elle' can mean 'it', and 'ils' and 'elles' mean 'they' (people and things).

10831.belief: All verbs can be followed by a direct object.
10831.statement: All verbs can be followed by a direct object.
10831.correction: Not all verbs can be followed by a direct object; J'habite dans une maison; 'une maison' is connected to the verb by the preposition 'dans'. The verb 'j'habite' (I live) stands alone and does not have a direct object; we cannot say: 'I live a house'.

4116.belief: The letter 'h' is pronounced like in English.
4116.statement: The letter 'h' is pronounced like in English.
4116.correction: The letter 'h' is in fact often silent in French: j'habite.

2396.belief: The direct object pronouns 'me' and 'you' are always 'me' and 'te' in French.
2396.statement: The direct object pronouns 'me' and 'you' are always 'me' and 'te' in French.
2396.correction: The direct object pronouns 'me' and 'te' change before a vowel in French, they become 'm' and 't'. This is an elision.

5023.belief: Numbers 70, 80 and 90 are one word numbers in French, just like 20 (vingt), 30 (trente), 40 (quarante) etc.
5023.statement: Numbers 70, 80 and 90 are one word numbers in French, just like 20 (vingt), 30 (trente), 40 (quarante) etc.
5023.correction: In French, the numbers 70 (soixante-dix), 80 (quatre-vingts), and 90 (quatre-vingt-dix) are not single-word numbers. Unlike 20 (vingt), 30 (trente), and 40 (quarante)—which are single words—70, 80, and 90 are constructed using compound expressions.

2395.belief: The direct object pronouns 'le' and 'la' change to 'l' ' if the noun starts with a vowel or a 'h': Je lis l'histoire.
2395.statement: The direct object pronouns 'le' and 'la' change to 'l' ' if the noun starts with a vowel or a 'h': Je lis l'histoire.
2395.correction: The direct object pronouns 'le' and 'la' change to 'l' ' if the verb starts with a vowel or a 'h', not the noun: J'achète le chapeau - je l'achète.

10485.belief: All two-verb sentences have à (to) before the infinitive.
10485.statement: All two-verb sentences have à (to) before the infinitive.
10485.correction: Modal verbs, verbs of like/dislike and 'aller' are followed directly by an infinitive to form two-verb structures but some verbs form two-verb structures with 'à' + infinitive; for example, 'aider', 'apprendre' and 'commencer'.

2197.belief: 'De' is always translated as 'to' in English.
2197.statement: 'De' is always translated as 'to' in English.
2197.correction: 'De' is often translated as 'to'. However, it can be translated as 'from' and is sometimes not translated at all.

3608.correction: 'Il est' can be used as an impersonal verb where 'il' means 'it' and is not referring to a specific thing but talking about 'it' in general. e.g. 'Il est difficile de croire' means 'It is difficult to believe'.

3612.correction: Impersonal verbs nearly always have the subject 'il'. This translates as 'it' instead of 'he', e.g. 'il fait beau' - 'it is nice weather'.

11110.belief: Words with [tion] are cognates, therefore pronounced the same in English and French.
11110.statement: Words with [tion] are cognates, therefore pronounced the same in English and French.
11110.correction: Although [tion] words are usually cognates, the sound is different and useful to revisit regularly.

3863.belief: All -ir verbs follow the same pattern in the present tense, like -er verbs.
3863.statement: All -ir verbs follow the same pattern in the present tense, like -er verbs.
3863.correction: -ir verbs can be grouped into verbs like 'choisir', verbs like 'partir', verbs like 'venir' and verbs like 'ouvrir'. By learning the stem formation and endings for these four verbs, students should be able to use wide range of -ir verbs.

4121.belief: The letters 'ain' and 'aim' are always pronounced the same way.
4121.statement: The letters 'ain' and 'aim' are always pronounced the same way.
4121.correction: Before a consonant or at the end of a word, [ain] and [aim] are nasal but before a vowel, they are non-nasal sounds.

10841.belief: Verbs like 'sortir' and 'choisir' follow the same patterns in the present and perfect tenses.
10841.statement: Verbs like 'sortir' and 'choisir' follow the same patterns in the present and perfect tenses.
10841.correction: Verbs like 'sortir' and 'choisir' follow the same patterns in the perfect tense - they need an auxiliary verb and a past participle ending in -i but follow different patterns in the present tense.

3130.belief: When forming inversion questions in the perfect tense, you just have to swap the subject and the verb.
3130.statement: When forming inversion questions in the perfect tense, you just have to swap the subject and the verb.
3130.correction: Swapping the position of the subject and the verb is an important step in forming inversion questions but remember to add a hyphen and -t- in the third person singular e.g. 'A-t-elle vendu sa maison?'

10828.belief: The verbs 'entendre' and 'venir' have the same auxiliary verb.
10828.statement: The verbs 'entendre' and 'venir' have the same auxiliary verb.
10828.correction: Although their past participles are formed in the same way (ending in u), ‘venir’ is always formed with the auxiliary verb 'être' and never with ‘avoir’.

4508.belief: 'Me' and 'te' are always the direct object pronouns 'me' and 'you'.
4508.statement: 'Me' and 'te' are always the direct object pronouns 'me' and 'you'.
4508.correction: 'Me' and 'te' are used as direct object pronouns but also the reflexive pronouns meaning 'myself' and yourself'.

8833.belief: Reflexive verbs can always be translated literally into English.
8833.statement: Reflexive verbs can always be translated literally into English.
8833.correction: There are sometimes more natural ways to translate reflexive verbs into English. For example, 'Je me prépare' is 'I prepare myself', but 'I get ready' sounds more natural.

10392.belief: Translate reflexive verbs literally into English with the reflexive pronoun.
10392.statement: Translate reflexive verbs literally into English with the reflexive pronoun.
10392.correction: Some verbs use reflexive pronouns in French, but we don’t always translate the reflexive pronoun in English e.g. 'Je me sens' meaning 'I feel'.

10331.belief: Time phrases like 'an and 'année' are interchangeable in French.
10331.statement: Time phrases like 'an and 'année' are interchangeable in French.
10331.correction: Although they have the same meaning, 'an', 'jour', 'soir' and 'matin' are used to indicate specific units of time whereas, 'année', 'journée', 'soirée' and matinée' are used for description or duration.

3110.belief: To form the imperfect tense with all verbs, take the 'nous' form of the present tense, remove -ons and add the appropriate endings.
3110.statement: To form the imperfect tense with all verbs, take the 'nous' form of the present tense, remove -ons and add the appropriate endings.
3110.correction: The verb 'être' is an exception to the rule. Use the stem -ét before adding the endings.

3644.belief: The imperfect tense is always translated as 'used to' in English.
3644.statement: The imperfect tense is always translated as 'used to' in English.
3644.correction: The imperfect tense is often translated as 'used to' in English but sometimes the simple past is used instead to convey repeated past actions.

8735.belief: [r] is the same as the English 'r' sound.
8735.statement: [r] is the same as the English 'r' sound.
8735.correction: [r] in French is a raspier sound, produced in the back of the throat, which you can practise.

3637.belief: The imperfect tense only describes what used to happen.
3637.statement: The imperfect tense only describes what used to happen.
3637.correction: The imperfect tense describes what was happening and what used to happen and can be used with the perfect tense and a conjunction like 'quand' or 'pendant que'.

3730.belief: Indefinite adjectives always agree in number and gender.
3730.statement: Indefinite adjectives always agree in number and gender.
3730.correction: 'Tout le' agrees in number and gender but 'même', 'autre' and 'quelque' agree in number only. 'Chaque' and 'plusieurs' do not change.

3271.belief: German has two ways to formulate present tense questions - just like in English; e.g., 'Do you do play guitar?'; 'Are you playing guitar?'.
3271.statement: German has two ways to formulate present tense questions - just like in English; e.g., 'Do you do play guitar?'; 'Are you playing guitar?'.
3271.correction: German just has one present tense; this means that the question 'Spielst du Gitarre?' means 'Do you play guitar?' and 'Are you playing guitar?'. The context and/or the temporal adverb (on Tuesdays, today) help us to use the correct translation.

3249.belief: German and English word order are the same.
3249.statement: German and English word order are the same.
3249.correction: English mostly uses subject-verb word order and time phrases appear most naturally at the end of phrases. German word order is much more variable. Any element (subject, object, time-manner-location adverb) can start a German sentence.

9094.belief: To say 'you' in German, we just use 'du'.
9094.statement: To say 'you' in German, we just use 'du'.
9094.correction: 'Du' is 'you' when talking to one person you address by first name. When talking to more than one person you know this well, use 'ihr'. The verb ending is -t.

3260.belief: 'You’ in German is just one word.
3260.statement: 'You’ in German is just one word.
3260.correction: German has four different words for 'you', depending on who you're talking to: 'du' – informal, singular; 'ihr' - informal, plural; 'Sie' - formal, singular; 'man' - people in general, one.

4851.belief: It is only necessary to use 'du' when saying 'you' in German.
4851.statement: It is only necessary to use 'du' when saying 'you' in German.
4851.correction: In German, there are four words for you: 'du' for friends or family; 'Sie' in formal situations e.g., talking to teachers or strangers; 'ihr' when speaking to several friends or family members; 'man' to talk about people in general.

3257.belief: German numbers 21 and above work the same as in English: ten followed by unit.
3257.statement: German numbers 21 and above work the same as in English: ten followed by unit.
3257.correction: In German, numbers 21 and above are structured unit-und-ten, e.g., 'einundzwanzig' - twenty-one. It translates literally as 'one and twenty'.

4949.belief: 'Nicht' is always used to make negative statements in German.
4949.statement: 'Nicht' is always used to make negative statements in German.
4949.correction: There are two ways of making negative statements: 'nicht' and 'kein'. It is not always obvious when 'kein' should be used to translate negative English statements, e.g., 'I don't have a car' is 'ich habe kein Auto'.

10832.belief: Verbs form their past participles by sandwiching the verb stem with 'ge-' and '-t' or '-en'.
10832.statement: Verbs form their past participles by sandwiching the verb stem with 'ge-' and '-t' or '-en'.
10832.correction: Not all verbs form past participles in the same way. For instance, verbs that start with inseparable prefixes or end '-ieren' do not add 'ge-'. Some groups of verbs have a vowel change in the stem, e.g., 'finden', 'gefunden'.

5193.belief: There is only one way of saying 'when' in German.
5193.statement: There is only one way of saying 'when' in German.
5193.correction: Use 'wenn' to mean 'when' for present or future events. The question word is 'wann'. The conjunction 'als' means 'when', for a one-off past event. It sends the verb to the end of the clause, like 'weil'.

1975.belief: All conjunctions send the verb to the end of the clause.
1975.statement: All conjunctions send the verb to the end of the clause.
1975.correction: Not all conjunctions send the verb to the end of the clause. For example, 'und' and 'denn' use word order one (standard word order). They are called co-ordinating conjunctions.

371.belief: There aren't any patterns in German nouns that help you identify their grammatical gender.
371.statement: There aren't any patterns in German nouns that help you identify their grammatical gender.
371.correction: There are some suffixes in German nouns that signal the noun is feminine, for example '-heit', '-ung', '-in'. There may be some exceptions!

2681.belief: As in English, there is only one word for 'every'.
2681.statement: As in English, there is only one word for 'every'.
2681.correction: In German, 'jed-' changes its spelling in the same way as 'der', 'die' and 'das', to match the gender and case of the noun that follows.

10494.belief: Two words are needed to express 'would like', as in English.
10494.statement: Two words are needed to express 'would like', as in English.
10494.correction: 'Möcht-' is a form of the verb 'mögen' and is used to mean 'would like'. 'Möcht-' can be used as part of a 2-verb structure to say what you would like to do. The second (infinitive) verb moves to the end of the sentence.

11084.belief: A word for 'to' is always required in two-verb sentences in German.
11084.statement: A word for 'to' is always required in two-verb sentences in German.
11084.correction: 'Zu' is needed after verbs like 'hoffen' but after modal verbs and 'werden', 'zu' is not needed, e.g., 'Ich werde als Arzt arbeiten'.

10486.belief: All two-verb structures with an infinitive use 'zu' before the infinitive.
10486.statement: All two-verb structures with an infinitive use 'zu' before the infinitive.
10486.correction: Some two-verb structures with an infinitive use 'zu' before the verb, but not all. It depends on the verb in the sentence; 'zu' is not needed following modal verbs or 'werden' meaning 'will', but is needed after the structure 'es ist' + adjective.

3782.correction: Many infinitives can be used as nouns. In German, infinitive nouns start with a capital letter, are always neuter, can be used with or without 'das' & are typically translated into English with the gerund -ing, e.g., '(das) Schwimmen' - 'swimmming'.

4870.belief: I only need to know the gender of the noun to choose the right spelling for the possessive adjective.
4870.statement: I only need to know the gender of the noun to choose the right spelling for the possessive adjective.
4870.correction: Possessive adjectives change spelling to match the gender of the noun, but they also change to match the required case. Verbs and prepositions affect the case that is needed for possessive adjectives.

3261.belief: All German past participles have the prefix ge-.
3261.statement: All German past participles have the prefix ge-.
3261.correction: German verbs starting with be-, ver- and er- do not have the prefix ge- added for the past participle, e.g., 'besucht' - 'visited' or 'verdient' - 'earnt'.

4586.belief: 'Mich' and 'dich' are only direct object pronouns meaning me and you.
4586.statement: 'Mich' and 'dich' are only direct object pronouns meaning me and you.
4586.correction: 'Mich' and 'dich' can also be reflexive pronouns and then mean myself and yourself. Reflexive pronouns are required when using a verb reflexively.

9111.belief: Saying times in 24-hour format in German works in exactly the same way as in English.
9111.statement: Saying times in 24-hour format in German works in exactly the same way as in English.
9111.correction: Saying the time in 24-hour format uses numbers like in English. The difference is that German needs 'Uhr' - 'o'clock' - between the hour and the minutes, e.g., 21:50 is 'einundzwanzig Uhr fünfzig'.

4516.belief: The meaning of all German phrases should be taken literally.
4516.statement: The meaning of all German phrases should be taken literally.
4516.correction: Just like English, German contains idioms, phrases that mean something other than their literal meaning, e.g., ‘da haben wir den Salat’ - 'we have the salad there', which should be understood as 'now we have a problem'.

9110.belief: When saying the time, 'half past' is expressed the same way in German as in English, i.e., half past the current hour.
9110.statement: When saying the time, 'half past' is expressed the same way in German as in English, i.e., half past the current hour.
9110.correction: In German, 'half past' is expressed as half of the next hour, e.g., 'halb neun' is half of nine o'clock, or half past eight.

11206.belief: 'Zu', meaning 'to', is always needed as part of two-verb infinitive structures, e.g., 'Ich hoffe, mehr in die Schule zu lernen.'.
11206.statement: 'Zu', meaning 'to', is always needed as part of two-verb infinitive structures, e.g., 'Ich hoffe, mehr in die Schule zu lernen.'.
11206.correction: 'Werden' and modal verbs do not need 'zu' before the second verb: 'Ich werde mehr in der Schule lernen'. Other verbs that do not require 'zu' include 'helfen', 'lassen' and 'mögen'.

10750.belief: When using two-verb constructions, the second verb is always in the infinitive and comes at the end of the clause.
10750.statement: When using two-verb constructions, the second verb is always in the infinitive and comes at the end of the clause.
10750.correction: When a two-verb construction follows a subordinating conjunction like ‘weil’, the short form of the verb moves to the end, after the infinitive (WO3), e.g., ‘Ich hoffe, dieses Jahr zu feiern, weil es Spaß machen wird.’.

11065.belief: The word for 'who' in German is 'wer'.
11065.statement: The word for 'who' in German is 'wer'.
11065.correction: We use 'wer' to ask or report a question: 'Wer ist das?', 'Ich weiß nicht, wer das ist.' But in sentences like 'that is someone, who...' we use a relative pronoun - 'der', 'die', 'das' - which matches the gender of noun it refers to.

3247.belief: German [d] is always pronounced as English [d].
3247.statement: German [d] is always pronounced as English [d].
3247.correction: German [d] at the beginning of a word or syllable sounds like English 'd'; [d] at the end of a syllable sounds like -t. For example, the sentence 'die Landschaft in Deutschland ist wunderschön' contains examples of both [d] sounds.

105.belief: You can add the suffix -los to any German noun to make an adjective.
105.statement: You can add the suffix -los to any German noun to make an adjective.
105.correction: You can't just add -los to any noun to form an adjective. It only works if the result makes real sense - usually where there’s a natural English -less equivalent (like 'hairless', 'hopeless', 'windowless').

9643.belief: Stress is always placed on the first syllable in German words.
9643.statement: Stress is always placed on the first syllable in German words.
9643.correction: Most German words place stress on the first syllable, but the 2nd syllable is stressed in words beginning with inseparable prefixes. Borrowed words stress the 2nd or final syllable.

9201.belief: Separable prefixes always move to the end of a clause.
9201.statement: Separable prefixes always move to the end of a clause.
9201.correction: Separable verbs have a prefix that goes to the end of the clause in word order one clauses (standard word order), but in word order three (verb to end) the prefix and the verb reunite. Separable prefixes are always joined to the past participle.

4685.belief: Modal verbs don't require a 2nd verb in the infinitive unless they are in the present tense.
4685.statement: Modal verbs don't require a 2nd verb in the infinitive unless they are in the present tense.
4685.correction: Modal verbs require a 2nd verb in the infinitive in other tenses, including the imperfect tense, e.g., 'ich konnte schwimmen'. They do not require a preceding 'zu' before the infinitive. Other verbs do.

10003.correction: The subject pronoun 'sie' means 'she' when used with a 3rd person singular verb ending or 'they' when used with a 3rd person plural verb ending. If written as 'Sie' and is used with a 3rd person plural verb ending, it can mean 'you (formal)'.

2651.belief: At the end of a word, [e] sounds the same as short [e].
2651.statement: At the end of a word, [e] sounds the same as short [e].
2651.correction: Final [e] sounds like 'uh', as in 'danke', 'Klasse'. Short [e] sounds more like 'eh' as in 'denken'.

4689.belief: Modal verbs require a 'zu' before the infinitive.
4689.statement: Modal verbs require a 'zu' before the infinitive.
4689.correction: Two-verb structures without a modal verb require 'zu' before the infinitive, e.g., 'Ich habe Lust, schwimmen zu gehen.'.

9440.belief: The sound-symbol correspondence [ie] is always pronounced as in 'Liebe'.
9440.statement: The sound-symbol correspondence [ie] is always pronounced as in 'Liebe'.
9440.correction: When [ie] is the final but unstressed syllable in a word, pronounce [i] and [e] as separate vowel sounds, e.g., 'Familie'.

3256.belief: The German number ‘Billion’ means billion in English.
3256.statement: The German number ‘Billion’ means billion in English.
3256.correction: The German word for 'billion' is ‘Milliarde’; ‘Billion’ in German means 'trillion' in English.

9114.belief: When saying your occupation, use an indefinite article, like in English.
9114.statement: When saying your occupation, use an indefinite article, like in English.
9114.correction: In German, when saying what your occupation is or what you would like to become, an indefinite article is not needed, e.g., 'Ich möchte in Zukunft Lehrer werden.' - 'In the future, I would like to become a teacher.'.

3220.belief: 'Gefallen' means ‘to like’ and works like a normal verb where I am the subject that does the action of ‘liking’.
3220.statement: 'Gefallen' means ‘to like’ and works like a normal verb where I am the subject that does the action of ‘liking’.
3220.correction: 'Gefallen' means ‘to please’, so works differently. You are not doing the ‘liking’, the thing you like is ‘pleasing’ you. E.g., 'das Kleid gefällt mir' - literally, 'the dress pleases me'. More naturally translated - 'I like the dress'.

1836.correction: The comparative form of 'gern' is 'lieber'. 'Besser' is the comparative form of 'gut'.

11063.correction: The past participle of 'fallen' ('to fall') is 'gefallen', as is the past participle of 'gefallen' ('to please'). The difference is that the auxiliary verb 'haben' is used with 'gefallen' (to please), but 'sein' is used with 'fallen' (to fall).

10533.belief: I have to understand every single word in a text in order to understand its general meaning.
10533.statement: I have to understand every single word in a text in order to understand its general meaning.
10533.correction: It is difficult to know all of the words in any given language! Use the words you do know and other contextual and linguistic clues to help you decipher the meaning of unfamiliar vocabulary.

23.belief: In 2-verb structures, the 2nd infinitive verb is always followed by 'zu'.
23.statement: In 2-verb structures, the 2nd infinitive verb is always followed by 'zu'.
23.correction: When followed by a 2nd verb in the infinitive, modal verbs and 'werden' never take 'zu'. Many other verbs do, for example 'versuchen, etwas zu tun' and 'helfen, etwas zu tun'.

321.belief: To answer the question 'why' you have to use 'weil' or 'denn', which mean 'because'.
321.statement: To answer the question 'why' you have to use 'weil' or 'denn', which mean 'because'.
321.correction: The structure 'um... zu' followed by an infinitive verb means 'in order to' and can be used to give a reason or say why something is done. This structure is the same for any tense.

10330.belief: The time-manner-place rule means that all sentences must have time before manner before place.
10330.statement: The time-manner-place rule means that all sentences must have time before manner before place.
10330.correction: German sentences can start with any adverb to emphasise that element. The TMP order is then retained for any other adverbs in that sentence. For example, 'Mit dem Zug (M) fahren wir morgen (T) nach Liechtenstein (P).'.

229.belief: Although some German words have more than one meaning, most of them have a main meaning and it's not important to know the other meanings.
229.statement: Although some German words have more than one meaning, most of them have a main meaning and it's not important to know the other meanings.
229.correction: Some very frequent words have several different meanings, all of them commonly used. It is important to know the meanings and to use context to select the right meaning. For example, 'vor' can mean 'in front of', 'before' and 'ago'.

10469.belief: When two object nouns are in a sentence, the word order is the same as English: direct object - indirect object.
10469.statement: When two object nouns are in a sentence, the word order is the same as English: direct object - indirect object.
10469.correction: When two object nouns are in a sentence, the indirect object (in dative) precedes the direct object (in accusative). This is different from English.

2393.belief: The direct object precedes the indirect object in a German sentence.
2393.statement: The direct object precedes the indirect object in a German sentence.
2393.correction: If there are two objects in a sentence and one is a pronoun, the pronoun will precede the noun, regardless of whether it is the direct or indirect object. However, if both objects are nouns, the indirect object is first.

2689.belief: English verbs use the same prepositions as in German.
2689.statement: English verbs use the same prepositions as in German.
2689.correction: German verbs often use different prepositions from those used with English verbs; for example 'ich hoffe auf' - 'I'm hoping for' (not 'hoping on').

5770.belief: The prepositions 'auf' and 'an' are always followed by the accusative case.
5770.statement: The prepositions 'auf' and 'an' are always followed by the accusative case.
5770.correction: 'Auf' and 'an' are followed by the accusative case when there is movement. They are followed by the dative case when a location is being described.

11102.belief: Words which look the same in English and German will have the same meaning.
11102.statement: Words which look the same in English and German will have the same meaning.
11102.correction: There are many false friends in German. These are words that look exactly the same but do not have the same meaning: for example, 'bald' means 'soon'.

10591.belief: We can use a da-compound to refer back to any object noun already mentioned.
10591.statement: We can use a da-compound to refer back to any object noun already mentioned.
10591.correction: We can only use a da-compound to replace inanimate (non-living) nouns. For animate objects (people and animals), we use direct or indirect object pronouns to replace the noun.

3122.belief: Form questions with prepositions in the same way as in English, by adding a preposition at the end, e.g., 'What does he find out about?'.
3122.statement: Form questions with prepositions in the same way as in English, by adding a preposition at the end, e.g., 'What does he find out about?'.
3122.correction: German doesn't leave prepositions hanging at the end of questions like in English. Form questions by placing the prefix 'wo-' or 'wor-' before the preposition at the start of the question.

5223.belief: All opinions phrases can be followed by 'dass' and word order 3 (subordination).
5223.statement: All opinions phrases can be followed by 'dass' and word order 3 (subordination).
5223.correction: Whilst many opinion verbs, including 'meinen', 'glauben' and 'denken' are usually followed by 'dass' and word order 3, this is not always the case. 'Meiner Meinung nach' must be followed by word order 2 (inversion).

3648.belief: The imperfect tense is used in written, but not usually in spoken German.
3648.statement: The imperfect tense is used in written, but not usually in spoken German.
3648.correction: The imperfect tense forms of 'sein', 'haben' and 'es gibt' are widely used in spoken German, along with imperfect modal verbs which, combined with a 2nd (infinitive) verb, are used to say what you and others wanted, were able or had to do.

10940.belief: The only way to communicate about past events in German is by using the 2-verb perfect tense, e.g., 'Ich bin nach Deutschland gefahren. Ich habe dort einen Strandurlaub gemacht.'.
10940.statement: The only way to communicate about past events in German is by using the 2-verb perfect tense, e.g., 'Ich bin nach Deutschland gefahren. Ich habe dort einen Strandurlaub gemacht.'.
10940.correction: We also use the single verb imperfect tense - 'war', 'hatte' and 'es gab', and imperfect modal forms - 'musste', 'konnte', 'wollte', with a 2nd (infinitive) verb, to talk about events in the past.

3277.belief: German verbs always stress the same syllable.
3277.statement: German verbs always stress the same syllable.
3277.correction: Generally German infinitive verbs stress the first syllable; however, words starting with inseparable prefixes be-, er-, ge-, ver-, ent- stress the 2nd syllable, which includes most past participles; -ieren verbs stress the 'ie' in present and past.

9524.belief: When we speak, the pitch of our voice rises and falls in the same way in German and English.
9524.statement: When we speak, the pitch of our voice rises and falls in the same way in German and English.
9524.correction: The rise and fall of our voice is similar in German and English sentences, but more marked in German and more noticeable with one-syllable words. Note the larger fall when saying 'gut' in German compared to 'good' in English.

4370.belief: Make the imperfect stem of strong verbs just by removing -en and changing the stem vowel.
4370.statement: Make the imperfect stem of strong verbs just by removing -en and changing the stem vowel.
4370.correction: Many strong verbs form their imperfect stem in this way: 'lesen' - 'las', 'geben', 'gab'. Other verbs have other small changes too: 'kommen' - 'kam', 'essen' - 'aß'. Others are more irregular: 'gehen' - 'ging', 'sein' - 'war', 'haben' - 'hatte'.

10856.belief: The only versions of Grimm brothers' fairy tales that exist are written in the imperfect tense.
10856.statement: The only versions of Grimm brothers' fairy tales that exist are written in the imperfect tense.
10856.correction: There are many versions of the Grimm brothers' fairy tales. Many are written in the imperfect tense but there are also simpler, modern adaptations written in the present or perfect tenses, especially in children's books.

10128.belief: To talk about the future in German you have to use the future tense with 'werden'.
10128.statement: To talk about the future in German you have to use the future tense with 'werden'.
10128.correction: In German, you can use the present tense and a future time phrase to talk about the future: 'ich spiele nächste Woche Tennis' - 'I'm playing/going to play tennis next week'. 'Planen' and 'vorhaben' in the present tense also express future intentions.

3640.belief: The imperfect tense in German is only used in writing.
3640.statement: The imperfect tense in German is only used in writing.
3640.correction: Whilst the imperfect is largely used in writing, modal verbs are also used in speaking, along with verbs like 'war', 'hatte' and 'gab'.

453.belief: When asking questions like 'Did you travel by plane?' in Spanish, I need to start by translating the word 'did'.
453.statement: When asking questions like 'Did you travel by plane?' in Spanish, I need to start by translating the word 'did'.
453.correction: To ask a 'did'-style question in Spanish, you can form an intonation question by simply raising your voice at the end of a past-tense sentence. It is not necessary to translate the word 'did'.

9102.belief: To say what I did in the past, remove the infinitive ending and add -é.
9102.statement: To say what I did in the past, remove the infinitive ending and add -é.
9102.correction: To say what I did in the past for a regular -ar verb, remove the infinitive ending and add -é. To say what I did in the past for a regular -er or -ir verb, remove the infinitive ending and add -í.

9100.belief: To say 'my' in Spanish we use 'mi'.
9100.statement: To say 'my' in Spanish we use 'mi'.
9100.correction: There are two ways of saying 'my' in Spanish. 'Mi' is for singular nouns (masculine or feminine), e.g. 'mi madre' (my mother) and 'mis' is for plural nouns, e.g. 'mis padres' (my parents).

4507.belief: 'Me' is a reflexive pronoun (myself) and a possessive adjective (my).
4507.statement: 'Me' is a reflexive pronoun (myself) and a possessive adjective (my).
4507.correction: 'Me' is a reflexive pronoun used to say that I do something to myself e.g. me despierto (I wake 'myself' up). 'Mi' is the possessive adjective 'my' used for masculine or feminine singular nouns e.g. 'mi madre', 'mi amigo'.

9999.belief: 'Su' is the only possessive adjective for 'his' and 'hers' in Spanish.
9999.statement: 'Su' is the only possessive adjective for 'his' and 'hers' in Spanish.
9999.correction: 'Su' is his', 'hers' or 'its' before a singular noun. 'Sus' is 'his' 'hers', or 'its' before a plural noun.

8832.belief: Reflexive verbs are just for routine activities.
8832.statement: Reflexive verbs are just for routine activities.
8832.correction: In Spanish there are many reflexive verbs and they are not just used to describe routine activities. This lesson includes the verb 'acordar' ('to agree') compared with the reflexive verb 'acordarse' ('to remember').

2394.belief: Direct object pronouns go after the verb, like in English.
2394.statement: Direct object pronouns go after the verb, like in English.
2394.correction: In Spanish, the direct object pronoun usually goes before the verb, e.g. 'pruebas el chocolate caliente' - 'lo pruebas.'

3421.belief: With gustar-type verbs, the verb agrees with the person who likes something.
3421.statement: With gustar-type verbs, the verb agrees with the person who likes something.
3421.correction: In gustar-type verbs, the verb agrees with the subject - the thing liked, literally, the thing that pleases - not the person, e.g. 'Me gusta la música.' Since 'música' is singular, the correct form is 'gusta'.

3746.belief: The indirect object pronoun 'le' changes to 'la' to match the gender of the person receiving the action.
3746.statement: The indirect object pronoun 'le' changes to 'la' to match the gender of the person receiving the action.
3746.correction: 'Le' means 'to him', 'to her' or 'to it' regardless of the person receiving the action, e.g. 'le doy un regalo a Lucía' or 'le doy un regalo a Daniel'.

3028.belief: The first noun in a sentence is always the subject.
3028.statement: The first noun in a sentence is always the subject.
3028.correction: If there is a personal 'a' before the first noun it is not the subject, it is the object (usually a person) receiving the action.
