1968.belief: To conjugate 2nd person plural -ar verbs, use the verb ending -ais.
1968.statement: To conjugate 2nd person plural -ar verbs, use the verb ending -ais.
1968.correction: To conjugate 2nd person plural -ar verbs, use the verb ending -áis. The accent on the 'a' is important as it tells us to stress the final syllable.

4175.belief: Like in English, I can use the same form of the verb to adress 'you' for one person and 'you' for several people.
4175.statement: Like in English, I can use the same form of the verb to adress 'you' for one person and 'you' for several people.
4175.correction: In Spanish, there are different verb endings to refer to 'you' (singular) and 'you' (plural). For -ar verbs these are -as and -áis.

2680.belief: As in English, there is one way of saying 'your' in Spanish.
2680.statement: As in English, there is one way of saying 'your' in Spanish.
2680.correction: Saying 'your' in Spanish depends on the number of people you are speaking to and the following noun. To mean ‘your’ for one person before a singular noun, use ‘tu’, and for more than one person, use 'vuestro' or 'vuestra'.

9512.belief: In Spanish, I can use the verb 'ser' to talk about 'being' in any context.
9512.statement: In Spanish, I can use the verb 'ser' to talk about 'being' in any context.
9512.correction: In Spanish, the verb 'ser' means 'to be, being' for general traits. To refer to a location, mood or state, use 'estar'.

4304.correction: 'Los' and 'las' mean 'the' in front of a plural noun but 'them' when they come before a verb.

11097.belief: All words ending in -n or -s need an accent.
11097.statement: All words ending in -n or -s need an accent.
11097.correction: Words ending in -n, -s or a vowel generally have penultimate syllable stress and no accent. Words ending in -n, -s or a vowel with final syllable stress have an accent on the final vowel. Note the difference: 'canción', 'canciones'.

9474.belief: All Spanish adverbs are made by simply adding -mente to any adjective form.
9474.statement: All Spanish adverbs are made by simply adding -mente to any adjective form.
9474.correction: When an adjective has masculine -o and feminine -a forms, you must use the -a form before adding -mente, e.g. 'rápido' - 'rápida' - 'rápidamente'.

5315.correction: The word 'para' doesn't always mean 'for'. It can also mean 'in order to' when followed by an infinitive verb.

9483.belief: The Spanish [h] is always silent, no matter which letter it appears next to.
9483.statement: The Spanish [h] is always silent, no matter which letter it appears next to.
9483.correction: The Spanish [h] is not pronounced, but [ch] is always pronounced like the [ch] in 'churros' and 'chocolate'.

10642.belief: We use 'ser' to describe the weather in Spanish.
10642.statement: We use 'ser' to describe the weather in Spanish.
10642.correction: In English we use the verb 'to be' for the weather (e.g. 'it is cold'), but in Spanish the verb 'hacer' is used. For example, to say 'it is sunny' you would say 'hace sol'.

3666.belief: It is impossible to tell whether the 1st person plural of -ar verbs ('we') is in the present tense or the preterite tense because the verb endings are the same.
3666.statement: It is impossible to tell whether the 1st person plural of -ar verbs ('we') is in the present tense or the preterite tense because the verb endings are the same.
3666.correction: The verb ending of the 1st person plural of -ar verbs is the same in the present and the preterite tense. Therefore we rely on time markers to indicate which time frame it is, e.g. 'ayer jugamos al tenis' - 'yesterday we played tennis'.

5484.belief: Peru has always been a Spanish-speaking country.
5484.statement: Peru has always been a Spanish-speaking country.
5484.correction: Spanish only arrived in Peru in 1532, when Francisco Pizarro reached the Inca Empire. The official language of the Inca Empire was Quechua, which is still spoken by more than 10 million people, mainly in Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador.

41.belief: The 3rd person singular preterite verb ending for -ar verbs is the same as the present tense 1st person singular verb ending: -o.
41.statement: The 3rd person singular preterite verb ending for -ar verbs is the same as the present tense 1st person singular verb ending: -o.
41.correction: The 3rd person singular preterite verb ending - ó has a very important accent which distinguishes it from the 1st person present tense. Compare 'hablo' - I talk, am talking and 'habló' - he, she, it talked. Without the accent it is a different tense!

2726.belief: -er and -ir verbs have the same verb ending in the 1st person plural, present tense.
2726.statement: -er and -ir verbs have the same verb ending in the 1st person plural, present tense.
2726.correction: -er and -ir verbs have different endings in the 1st person plural, present tense. For -er verbs, it is -emos and for -ir verbs, it is -imos.

3551.belief: 'Huir' works in exactly the same way as all regular -ir verbs, e.g. 'escribir'.
3551.statement: 'Huir' works in exactly the same way as all regular -ir verbs, e.g. 'escribir'.
3551.correction: The verb 'huir' has a spelling change (i → y) in the present tense in the 1st person singular, 2nd person singular, 3rd person singular, and 3rd person plural forms: huyo, huyes, huye, huyen. This makes the vowel pronunciation easier - huyo not huio.

5730.belief: Possessive adjectives in Spanish do not agree in number with the noun.
5730.statement: Possessive adjectives in Spanish do not agree in number with the noun.
5730.correction: Possessive adjectives in Spanish agree in number with the noun. For example, 'mi' becomes 'mis' when it refers to a plural noun.

4178.belief: Like 'mi' and 'tu', 'nuestro' does not agree with the noun in gender.
4178.statement: Like 'mi' and 'tu', 'nuestro' does not agree with the noun in gender.
4178.correction: Unlike 'mi' and 'tu', 'nuestro' agrees with the noun in gender. 'Nuestro' and 'nuestros' refer to masculine nouns, while 'nuestra' and 'nuestras' refer to feminine nouns.

5009.belief: 'Nuestro' does not agree with the noun in gender or number.
5009.statement: 'Nuestro' does not agree with the noun in gender or number.
5009.correction: 'Nuestro' agrees with the noun in both gender and number. 'Nuestro' and 'nuestros' refer to masculine nouns, while 'nuestra' and 'nuestras' refer to feminine nouns.

9494.correction: In Spanish, 'que' does not always translate as 'that'. For example, the phrase 'tengo que' translates as 'I have to'.

10820.belief: The verb 'tener' always translates as 'to have, having'.
10820.statement: The verb 'tener' always translates as 'to have, having'.
10820.correction: The verb 'tener' does not always translates as 'to have, having'. For example, in idiomatic expressions it can mean 'to be, being', e.g. 'tuve éxito' - 'I was successful'.

10412.correction: In Spanish, 'que' can mean different things depending on the context in which it's used. For example, it can mean 'who' or 'that' as a relative pronoun, or 'than' within a comparative structure.

2959.belief: The feminine plural demonstrative adjective for 'these' is the same as the 'tú' form of the verb 'estar'.
2959.statement: The feminine plural demonstrative adjective for 'these' is the same as the 'tú' form of the verb 'estar'.
2959.correction: Accents are really important in Spanish. The 'tú' form of 'estar' has an accent on the á: 'estás' (you are) whereas the demonstrative adjective for plural feminine nouns, 'estas' does not: 'estas flores' (these flowers).

3109.belief: To form the imperfect continuous instead of the present continuous both the form of 'estar' and the present participle need to change.
3109.statement: To form the imperfect continuous instead of the present continuous both the form of 'estar' and the present participle need to change.
3109.correction: To form the imperfect continuous, only the form of 'estar' needs to change, into the imperfect tense. The present participle stays the same, it is formed by removing the infinitive ending and adding -ando for -ar verbs and -iendo for all other verbs.

3636.belief: In the imperfect continuous I can tell who the subject of the verb is by looking at the form of 'estar' being used.
3636.statement: In the imperfect continuous I can tell who the subject of the verb is by looking at the form of 'estar' being used.
3636.correction: The 'I' and 'he, she, it' forms of the imperfect tense of 'estar' are the same: 'estaba'. Therefore you have to use the context to work out who the subject of the verb is when this form is being used.

10167.belief: When telling a story about a past event, I have to keep the full account in the same past tense.
10167.statement: When telling a story about a past event, I have to keep the full account in the same past tense.
10167.correction: Different past tenses describe different elements of a story. The imperfect continuous describes what was happening ('Estaba corriendo...') then the preterite tense describes an interruption to that activity ('... cuando llegó una vaca'.).

2443.belief: It doesn't matter if the action was completed or repeated - I can use any past tense verb.
2443.statement: It doesn't matter if the action was completed or repeated - I can use any past tense verb.
2443.correction: In Spanish, we choose between the preterite and imperfect based on how the action happened in the past. Use the preterite to communicate an action that happened once and the imperfect for actions that were repeated over a period of time.

10801.belief: The verb 'dar' means 'to give, giving' only.
10801.statement: The verb 'dar' means 'to give, giving' only.
10801.correction: 'Dar' usually translates as 'to give' but it is also used to describe how something makes people feel. e.g. da rabia - it makes me angry.

4498.belief: It does not matter whether I use the preterite or the imperfect as both refer to the past.
4498.statement: It does not matter whether I use the preterite or the imperfect as both refer to the past.
4498.correction: To talk about something completed in the past, we use the preterite tense. However, to talk about something that happened repeatedly in the past, with the meaning 'used to', we use the imperfect tense.

11095.belief: All words ending in -ia must have an accent.
11095.statement: All words ending in -ia must have an accent.
11095.correction: Words ending in a vowel usually stress the penultimate syllable. Words ending in -ía have stress on the final syllable, so they need an accent e.g., energía. Words ending in -ia stress the penultimate syllable, so no accent is needed e.g. ciencia.

9471.belief: In Spanish, all adjectives go after the noun.
9471.statement: In Spanish, all adjectives go after the noun.
9471.correction: Most Spanish adjectives go after the noun; they describe objective qualities (traits, origin, colours,...). However, some adjectives go before the noun; these prenominal adjectives often express subjective opinions or give emphasis.

3425.belief: 'Había' only means 'there used to be' or 'there was'.
3425.statement: 'Había' only means 'there used to be' or 'there was'.
3425.correction: 'Había' means 'there used to be', 'there was' or 'there were'.

10129.belief: When I talk about a past action I must always use the preterite.
10129.statement: When I talk about a past action I must always use the preterite.
10129.correction: The preterite is used for actions that are completed and finished in the past. The imperfect is used for ongoing, habitual, or background actions in the past - things that were happening or used to happen.

9480.belief: In Spanish the ending for 'you singular' and 'you plural' for -ar verbs is the same.
9480.statement: In Spanish the ending for 'you singular' and 'you plural' for -ar verbs is the same.
9480.correction: To refer to 'you' for one person with a present tense -ar verb, use the verb ending -as, e.g. 'buscas'; to refer to 'you' for two or more people with a present tense -ar verb, use the verb ending -áis, e.g. 'buscáis'.

5786.belief: A present tense verb can be used on its own to talk about the future.
5786.statement: A present tense verb can be used on its own to talk about the future.
5786.correction: When using the present tense to talk about the future, it is essential to include a temporal adverb (such as 'mañana', 'la próxima semana', 'el lunes', etc.) to make the future meaning clear.

5611.belief: The plural 'you' form is the same for both -er and -ir verbs.
5611.statement: The plural 'you' form is the same for both -er and -ir verbs.
5611.correction: To talk to more than one person ('you all') using -er verbs in the present tense, use the ending -éis, e.g. 'comprendéis' - 'you all understand'. For -ir verbs, use the ending -ís, e.g. 'escribís' - 'you all write'.

10803.belief: The verb ending for gustar-type verbs depends on who is affected, not on the subject.
10803.statement: The verb ending for gustar-type verbs depends on who is affected, not on the subject.
10803.correction: The verb ending depends on the subject, i.e. what causes the feeling of liking, interest, importance or concern, etc., e.g. 'le encanta el juego' - 'the game delights him, her', 'le encantan los juegos' - 'the games delight him, her'.

9513.belief: Spanish always uses English word order when using indirect objects (subject + verb + object).
9513.statement: Spanish always uses English word order when using indirect objects (subject + verb + object).
9513.correction: In Spanish, the indirect object can go before or after the verb. Both 'le doy un regalo a mi hermano' and 'a mi hermano le doy un regalo' are correct - the second just adds emphasis to who receives the gift.

9492.belief: Spanish has only one way to say 'you are,' like English.
9492.statement: Spanish has only one way to say 'you are,' like English.
9492.correction: In Spanish, the form of 'you are' changes depending on who you're talking to. To say ‘you are’ to one person, use ‘eres’. To say ‘you are’ to two or more people, use ‘sois’.

9477.belief: In Spanish, to compare things, we use 'más, menos' + adjective + 'de'.
9477.statement: In Spanish, to compare things, we use 'más, menos' + adjective + 'de'.
9477.correction: In Spanish, when we're comparing two things using an adjective, we use 'más, menos' + adjective + 'que', e.g. 'más caro que', 'menos sano que'.

4170.belief: Like in English, in Spanish there is only one word for 'that' and one for 'those'.
4170.statement: Like in English, in Spanish there is only one word for 'that' and one for 'those'.
4170.correction: In Spanish, to say ‘that’ for a singular masculine noun, use ‘ese’. To say ‘that’ for a singular feminine noun, use ‘esa’. To say ‘those’ for a plural masculine noun, use ‘esos’. To say ‘those’ for a plural feminine noun, use ‘esas’.

2752.belief: 'Esta' means both 'this' and 'she, he, it is'.
2752.statement: 'Esta' means both 'this' and 'she, he, it is'.
2752.correction: ‘Esta’ is a demonstrative adjective, it means ‘this’ and goes before a noun. ‘Está’ is a verb, means ‘she, he, it is’ and describes an state or location. As there is an accent, we must stress the last syllable.

9341.correction: When the [r] is at the beginning of a word, we do roll it. For example, 'respeto', 'religión'.

10665.belief: We have to use a word like 'did' in Spanish questions.
10665.statement: We have to use a word like 'did' in Spanish questions.
10665.correction: In Spanish, you don't need a word like do or did to ask questions. The verb ending itself shows the tense and subject, e.g. '¿Trabajaste en el campo?' - 'Did you work in the countryside?'.

3121.belief: To form the preterite tense I just take off the -er/-ir and add the correct ending (-ió - for she, he, it) to all the verbs.
3121.statement: To form the preterite tense I just take off the -er/-ir and add the correct ending (-ió - for she, he, it) to all the verbs.
3121.correction: Some verbs are irregular and don’t follow the pattern. e.g. hacer - hizo, tener - tuvo, ir - fue.

10837.belief: All verbs (including -er and -ir) use -an in the present and -aron in the preterite to mean 'they'.
10837.statement: All verbs (including -er and -ir) use -an in the present and -aron in the preterite to mean 'they'.
10837.correction: To conjugate -ar verbs for 'they', remove -ar and add -an for the present tense or -aron for the preterite tense. However, to conjugate -er/-ir verbs for 'they', remove -ar and add -en for the present tense or -ieron for the preterite tense.

2729.belief: -er verbs have the same ending in the 1st person plural of the present and preterite tenses.
2729.statement: -er verbs have the same ending in the 1st person plural of the present and preterite tenses.
2729.correction: Unlike -ir verbs, -er verbs do not have the same ending in these tenses. The verb ending -emos is used in the present tense and -imos is used in the preterite tense.

3606.belief: 'Il', 'elle', 'ils' and 'elles' only refer to people and not things. 'Il' therefore only means 'he' and 'elle' only means 'she'.
3606.statement: 'Il', 'elle', 'ils' and 'elles' only refer to people and not things. 'Il' therefore only means 'he' and 'elle' only means 'she'.
3606.correction: It is useful to keep in mind that 'il, elle' and 'ils, elles' can refer to things as well as people. In this case, 'il, elle' means 'it' rather than 'he, she'.

8763.belief: All -re verbs follow the same pattern in the present tense, just like regular -er verbs.
8763.statement: All -re verbs follow the same pattern in the present tense, just like regular -er verbs.
8763.correction: -re verbs can be divided into four groups, following the patterns of entendre, prendre, traduire and écrire. Encourage learners to be able to categorise -re verbs and to draw comparisons between the groups.

9052.belief: [s] is always a silent final consonant.
9052.statement: [s] is always a silent final consonant.
9052.correction: [s] is usually a silent final consonant, but is pronounced when between two vowels. It's helpful to look out for verbs that start with a vowel. With such verbs in the third person plural, the 's' on 'ils' and 'elles' is pronounced.

3151.belief: French adjectives always come after the noun they are describing.
3151.statement: French adjectives always come after the noun they are describing.
3151.correction: There are five categories of adjectives which come before the noun: beauty, rank, age, good/bad, size/quantity. Practise using these before the noun alongside other adjectives which come after the noun.

3864.belief: -ir verbs have the same verb endings in the present tense as -er verbs.
3864.statement: -ir verbs have the same verb endings in the present tense as -er verbs.
3864.correction: Only verbs like 'ouvrir' have the same endings in the present tense as -er verbs. There are also verbs like 'choisir', verbs like 'partir' and verbs like 'venir' which have different endings.

5870.belief: The pronouns ils and elles can only refer to people.
5870.statement: The pronouns ils and elles can only refer to people.
5870.correction: Ils and elles can refer to things as well as people. They are still translated as 'they'. We must use context and surrounding language to work out who or what they are referring to.

10397.correction: 'à' can be translated as 'to', 'at', 'in', 'on' or 'about', depending on the context. Particular care should be taken with verbs followed by 'à', e.g., 'réfléchir à' could be translated as 'to think about' or 'to reflect on'.

3132.belief: When forming yes/no questions, we need to translate the English 'do' or 'does' into French.
3132.statement: When forming yes/no questions, we need to translate the English 'do' or 'does' into French.
3132.correction: There is no equivalent to 'do' or 'does' in French. Use inversion, intonation or 'est-ce que' to form yes/no questions.

10813.belief: The verb jouer is always followed by the preposition à.
10813.statement: The verb jouer is always followed by the preposition à.
10813.correction: Use jouer à for sports but use jouer de for instruments.

4917.belief: All negative structures go around the short form of the verb only in two-verb structures.
4917.statement: All negative structures go around the short form of the verb only in two-verb structures.
4917.correction: Most negatives, such as 'ne...pas', 'ne...jamais' and 'ne...rien', go around the short form of the verb in two-verb structures. 'Ne...personne', however, goes around both verbs.

8831.belief: Reflexive verbs and pronouns are only used when a physical action is done to oneself.
8831.statement: Reflexive verbs and pronouns are only used when a physical action is done to oneself.
8831.correction: Reflexive verbs and pronouns indicate that the subject and object are the same person, but do not always represent a physical action. Sometimes there is no direct translation for the French reflexive pronoun in English.

10010.belief: The subject of a sentence precedes the verb and the object of a sentence always follows the verb.
10010.statement: The subject of a sentence precedes the verb and the object of a sentence always follows the verb.
10010.correction: When using direct object pronouns, the object precedes the verb.

10833.belief: All verbs in French end in -er, -ir or -re.
10833.statement: All verbs in French end in -er, -ir or -re.
10833.correction: Only infinitive verbs end in -er, -ir, or -re. When categorising words according to word class in Task A, draw attention to the different verb endings and discuss the possible subjects of each verb.

3167.belief: In French, 'to you' is translated literally from English e.g. I say to you 'je dis à toi'.
3167.statement: In French, 'to you' is translated literally from English e.g. I say to you 'je dis à toi'.
3167.correction: In French indirect object pronouns to me and to you are translated by single words: 'me' and 'te'. They go before the verb, not at the end of the sentence.

3148.belief: In France, the famous painting is called Mona Lisa, just like in English.
3148.statement: In France, the famous painting is called Mona Lisa, just like in English.
3148.correction: The French have their own name for the Mona Lisa, 'la Joconde', taken from the name of the lady in the painting - 'la Gioconda' in Italian.

3159.belief: French object pronouns go after the verb in place of the object, just as in English, e.g. 'the museum interests me'.
3159.statement: French object pronouns go after the verb in place of the object, just as in English, e.g. 'the museum interests me'.
3159.correction: French object pronouns go before the verb, e.g. 'le musée m'intéresse'. When speaking and writing French we have to take care to use the correct word, especially for object pronouns.

11100.belief: The words 'le', 'la' and 'l'' can only mean 'the' in French.
11100.statement: The words 'le', 'la' and 'l'' can only mean 'the' in French.
11100.correction: The meaning of 'le', 'la', and 'l'' depends on where they are in the sentence. When before a noun, they mean 'the', but when before a verb, they mean 'him', 'her' or 'it'.

10756.belief: When using the verb 'rappeler', you need to have a suitable word for 'about', e.g., 'I am reminding you about the party'.
10756.statement: When using the verb 'rappeler', you need to have a suitable word for 'about', e.g., 'I am reminding you about the party'.
10756.correction: When using the verb 'rappeler', there is no need to include a word for 'about'. 'Rappeler' contains this idea within the verb.

2359.belief: There are different words in French for the indirect object pronouns 'to him' and 'to her'.
2359.statement: There are different words in French for the indirect object pronouns 'to him' and 'to her'.
2359.correction: There is just one third person singular indirect object pronoun in French, 'lui', which means both 'to him' and 'to her'. It follows the same rule as other object pronouns - it precedes the verb.

3170.belief: All French verbs use 'avoir' as the auxiliary to form the perfect tense.
3170.statement: All French verbs use 'avoir' as the auxiliary to form the perfect tense.
3170.correction: Verbs expressing changes of state, location or condition often use 'être' to form the perfect tense.

10821.belief: Verbs never change their spelling to agree for gender or number.
10821.statement: Verbs never change their spelling to agree for gender or number.
10821.correction: Past participles with 'être' verbs do agree for gender and number. Embedding this knowledge requires practice, a component of which can be practice of sound-symbol correspondences [i], [u], [é], [SFC], and [SFE].

3869.belief: Only irregular verbs such as 'faire' and 'avoir' have unusual past participles.
3869.statement: Only irregular verbs such as 'faire' and 'avoir' have unusual past participles.
3869.correction: Verbs like 'ouvrir', 'traduire' and 'écrire' form their past participles differently to regular IR and RE verbs and should be seen as different types of verb when learning verb patterns.

9156.belief: The second element of the negative structure goes after the past participle when forming past tense phrases.
9156.statement: The second element of the negative structure goes after the past participle when forming past tense phrases.
9156.correction: The second element of the negative structure is always placed after the auxiliary verb and before the past participle. This requires practice as students are likely to misapply the negative structure learned with present tense.

4915.belief: The negative structure ne... personne is formed the same way as ne... pas and ne... jamais in the perfect tense.
4915.statement: The negative structure ne... personne is formed the same way as ne... pas and ne... jamais in the perfect tense.
4915.correction: Ne... personne is unusual in that the second component (personne) comes after the past participle in the perfect tense.

4916.belief: The negative structure 'ne... personne' is used in the same way as 'ne... pas' and 'ne... jamais' in the perfect tense.
4916.statement: The negative structure 'ne... personne' is used in the same way as 'ne... pas' and 'ne... jamais' in the perfect tense.
4916.correction: 'Personne' goes after the past participle instead of after the auxiliary verb. Careful study and practice is required to master this structure.

5201.belief: There is only one word for "it" in French.
5201.statement: There is only one word for "it" in French.
5201.correction: Nouns are either masculine or feminine. "It", when replacing a noun, also has a masculine and feminine form. Use 'le' for masculine nouns and 'la' for femnine nouns. 'Le' and 'la' shorten to 'l'' when the next word starts with a vowel sound.

9283.belief: Silent final consonants are always silent.
9283.statement: Silent final consonants are always silent.
9283.correction: The liaison rule means that Silent Final Consonants are pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel sound (including silent h).

4993.belief: The noun 'un être', meaning 'a being', changes to 'une être' when referring to a girl or woman. 'Un être humain' changes to 'une être humaine' in the feminine.
4993.statement: The noun 'un être', meaning 'a being', changes to 'une être' when referring to a girl or woman. 'Un être humain' changes to 'une être humaine' in the feminine.
4993.correction: The noun 'être' is masculine, even when referring to a girl or a woman. The phrase 'un être humain', 'a human being', refers to both genders.

5442.belief: The perfect tense can only be translated as what happened in French.
5442.statement: The perfect tense can only be translated as what happened in French.
5442.correction: The perfect tense refers to the past in two ways: what happened and what has happened. Context tells us the intended meaning. 'Hier, je suis allé en ville' - yesterday I went to town. 'Je suis déjà allé à Paris' - I have already been to Paris.

10693.belief: When using 'depuis' (for, since), sentences are framed in the past in French.
10693.statement: When using 'depuis' (for, since), sentences are framed in the past in French.
10693.correction: In French, when using 'depuis' to describe an action that started in the past but continues today, frame the sentence in the present tense.

11164.belief: When writing, talking about what someone does, has done using a text written in the first person for information, only the subject pronoun needs to be changed in each sentence.
11164.statement: When writing, talking about what someone does, has done using a text written in the first person for information, only the subject pronoun needs to be changed in each sentence.
11164.correction: When writing, talking in the third person using a text in the first person for information, change the subject pronoun, verb, object pronouns and possessive adjectives (words like 'my', 'your', 'his', 'her').

10008.belief: The subject of a sentence can only be a noun or pronoun.
10008.statement: The subject of a sentence can only be a noun or pronoun.
10008.correction: A verb can be used as the subject of a sentence. In French, it must be in its infinitive form. When translated to English, use the -ing form of the verb.

10753.belief: When using 'venir de' (to have just), the next word needs to be a past participle, like in English.
10753.statement: When using 'venir de' (to have just), the next word needs to be a past participle, like in English.
10753.correction: In French, 'venir de' is like every other French verb followed by 'de'. It is always followed by a second verb in the infinitive.

9289.belief: All similar looking French and English words have the same meaning.
9289.statement: All similar looking French and English words have the same meaning.
9289.correction: Often, French words have multiple meanings and it is important to choose the right one for the given context e.g. 'durable' means durable and sustainable.

10942.belief: The only way to form the singular of a feminine noun is to add -e. The only way to form the plural of a noun is to add -s.
10942.statement: The only way to form the singular of a feminine noun is to add -e. The only way to form the plural of a noun is to add -s.
10942.correction: There are 4 ways to form feminine nouns which need careful practice. Similarly, there is more than one way to form plural nouns depending upon the final letter of the singular noun.

5613.belief: Plural possessive adjectives agree with gender.
5613.statement: Plural possessive adjectives agree with gender.
5613.correction: Plural possessive adjectives only agree with number.

4065.belief: You can just learn set sentences by heart and produce them mechanically when requested.
4065.statement: You can just learn set sentences by heart and produce them mechanically when requested.
4065.correction: Both writing and speaking must be adapted to the question and have a level of personalisation and spontaneity.

145.belief: Adjectives ending in -al take -s to create the masculine plural form.
145.statement: Adjectives ending in -al take -s to create the masculine plural form.
145.correction: Adjectives ending in -al need a spelling change to create the masculine plural form. Remove the -l and add -ux for example 'familial' - 'familiaux' in the masculine plural form.

155.belief: Adjectives only have one possible translation.
155.statement: Adjectives only have one possible translation.
155.correction: In French, adjectives can be used as a noun. When preceded by a definite article, they are often translated as the (adjective) one e.g. le bleu is translated as the blue one, not blue or the blue.

10846.belief: The verbs 'refuser', 'demander', 'essayer', 'laisser' and 'éviter' are followed directly by an infinitive, e.g. 'éviter faire' ('to avoid doing'), 'refuser faire' ('to refuse to do').
10846.statement: The verbs 'refuser', 'demander', 'essayer', 'laisser' and 'éviter' are followed directly by an infinitive, e.g. 'éviter faire' ('to avoid doing'), 'refuser faire' ('to refuse to do').
10846.correction: These verbs are followed by 'de' plus an infinitive, e.g. 'éviter de faire' ('to avoid doing'), 'refuser de faire' ('to refuse to do').

8688.belief: [qu] is pronounced the same in French and in English.
8688.statement: [qu] is pronounced the same in French and in English.
8688.correction: [qu] is pronounced differently in French and in English. It is important to to recognise and pronounce sound-spelling links correctly to understand and be understood by other French speakers.

3153.belief: In French the idea of 'best' and 'worst' is translated as 'plus bon' or 'plus mauvais'.
3153.statement: In French the idea of 'best' and 'worst' is translated as 'plus bon' or 'plus mauvais'.
3153.correction: Just as in English, the French for 'best' and 'worst' are irregular adjectives and need to be learned carefully to avoid misunderstanding.

10052.belief: Superlative sentences have the same word order in English and French.
10052.statement: Superlative sentences have the same word order in English and French.
10052.correction: Take care when writing or translating superlative sentences as the French word order differs quite significantly from English, e.g., 'the most interesting lesson' > 'the lesson the most interesting'.

11103.belief: The words 'meilleur' and 'mieux' can be used interchangeably as they both translate the English word 'better'.
11103.statement: The words 'meilleur' and 'mieux' can be used interchangeably as they both translate the English word 'better'.
11103.correction: 'Meilleur' is an adjective and can only be used to describe nouns. 'Mieux' is an adverb and can only be used to describe verbs.

4599.belief: 'Mieux' and 'plus mal/moins bien' can be used interchangeably with 'le mieux' and 'le plus mal' or ''le moins bien'.
4599.statement: 'Mieux' and 'plus mal/moins bien' can be used interchangeably with 'le mieux' and 'le plus mal' or ''le moins bien'.
4599.correction: 'Le mieux' and 'le plus mal'/'le moins bien' are superlative adverbs to describe actions as '(the) best' or '(the) worst'. 'Mieux' and 'moins bien'/'plus mal' describe actions as 'better' or 'less well'/'worse' and are comparative adverbs.

9724.statement: Students should develop their answers in role play tasks.
9724.correction: In role play tasks, students should concentrate on clearly communicating the stated information in a complete phrase and with conjugated verbs. There is no advantage to developing their answer further than is required.

2326.belief: 'Devoir' (must) and 'pouvoir' (can) do not require the second verb to be in the infinitive form because an infinitive is not required in English.
2326.statement: 'Devoir' (must) and 'pouvoir' (can) do not require the second verb to be in the infinitive form because an infinitive is not required in English.
2326.correction: 'Devoir' means to have (to) and 'pouvoir' means to be able. Therefore, when followed by a second verb, this verb must always be in the infinitive form.

9107.belief: When saying what you would like to do, a French word for 'would' is needed before the verb 'aimer' to like.
9107.statement: When saying what you would like to do, a French word for 'would' is needed before the verb 'aimer' to like.
9107.correction: In French, to say what you would like to do, use the conditional stem of the verb vouloir together with the appropriate ending - -ais for 'je' and 'tu', -ait for 'il' and 'elle'.

10822.belief: Verbs with 'de' e.g. 'persuader de', 'conseiller de' do not need to be followed by a second verb in its infinitive form.
10822.statement: Verbs with 'de' e.g. 'persuader de', 'conseiller de' do not need to be followed by a second verb in its infinitive form.
10822.correction: All French verbs with 'de' are always followed by a second verb in its infinitive form. There may be a preposition or an object pronoun between the two verbs but a second verb in its infinitive form will always follow.

11096.belief: All words ending in -ment are adverbs.
11096.statement: All words ending in -ment are adverbs.
11096.correction: Whilst many words ending in -ment are adverbs where the feminine form of the adjective has been taken and -ment added to create the adverb, not all words ending in -ment are adverbs. Some nouns end in -ment e.g. 'le règlement' rule, regulation.

4120.belief: The letter x in the words 'sixième' and 'dixième' is pronounced the same as in English.
4120.statement: The letter x in the words 'sixième' and 'dixième' is pronounced the same as in English.
4120.correction: The letter x is pronounced as z due to liaison in these words and should be carefully practised to develop an authentic pronunciation.

2092.belief: To create antonyms in French, always add the prefix in- to the start of an adjective or adverb e.g. 'utile' becomes 'inutile'.
2092.statement: To create antonyms in French, always add the prefix in- to the start of an adjective or adverb e.g. 'utile' becomes 'inutile'.
2092.correction: Some antonyms are formed by adding the prefix im-. This is when the original word begins with p, b or m: possible become impossible; buvable (drinkable) becomes imbuvable (undrinkable); 'mature' becomes 'immature'.

8689.belief: [qu] is pronounced the same way in French as in English.
8689.statement: [qu] is pronounced the same way in French as in English.
8689.correction: In French, [qu] is always a hard sound and must be carefully practised in order to ensure clear communication with French speakers.

944.belief: 'Chaque' and 'plusieurs' change form and can be written as 'chaques' and 'plusieur'.
944.statement: 'Chaque' and 'plusieurs' change form and can be written as 'chaques' and 'plusieur'.
944.correction: The indefinite adjectives 'chaque' and 'plusieurs' are invariable and only have the one form. As they are highly useful, encourage students to use them frequently in their work.

908.belief: [ch] is pronounced the same in French as it is in English.
908.statement: [ch] is pronounced the same in French as it is in English.
908.correction: [ch] is a softer sound in French and students will need directed practice in order to pronounce it correctly. It is more like the sound 'sh' in English.

8701.belief: Que can be used in a subject relative clause e.g. le prof que s'appelle M. Jones est sympa.
8701.statement: Que can be used in a subject relative clause e.g. le prof que s'appelle M. Jones est sympa.
8701.correction: When the relative clause introduces a verb to describe a subject, 'qui' must be used and not 'que'. E.g. le prof qui s'appelle M. Jones est sympa.

8861.belief: The relative pronouns 'qui' and 'que' can be used interchangeably to translate 'that', 'which' or 'who/whom'.
8861.statement: The relative pronouns 'qui' and 'que' can be used interchangeably to translate 'that', 'which' or 'who/whom'.
8861.correction: Use 'qui' to introduce a subject-relative clause. Use 'que' to introduce an object-relative clause.

9070.belief: The same imperative form of a verb is used for both 'tu' and 'vous'.
9070.statement: The same imperative form of a verb is used for both 'tu' and 'vous'.
9070.correction: There are separate imperative forms for 'tu' and 'vous' which must be used in exactly the same way as in conversation i.e. formal or information situations and singular and plural subjects.

10004.belief: The subject pronoun is used with the verb to make an imperative.
10004.statement: The subject pronoun is used with the verb to make an imperative.
10004.correction: Imperative instructions do not include the subject pronoun e.g. Écoute! Écoutez!

10898.belief: The 'vous' form of address is only used for plural situations.
10898.statement: The 'vous' form of address is only used for plural situations.
10898.correction: In formal situations, it is essential to address somebody as 'vous' in order to be polite and to show respect. Careful consideration of the context of a conversation is very important.

4117.belief: The letter 'o' is consistently pronounced in French words.
4117.statement: The letter 'o' is consistently pronounced in French words.
4117.correction: An 'o' sound can be open or closed. 'O' is open when it is followed by a consonant (votre). 'O' is closed when it is written with a circumflex (ô), it is the last sound in a syllable (trop) or is followed by a 'z' sound (rose).

10826.belief: All verbs ending 'aitre' form the perfect tense in the same way.
10826.statement: All verbs ending 'aitre' form the perfect tense in the same way.
10826.correction: Whilst this group of verbs behaves very similarly, the verb 'naitre' is irregular in the perfect tense. Students should be aware that it uses 'être' to form the perfect tense and its past participle is 'né'.

10475.belief: There are two present tenses in French.
10475.statement: There are two present tenses in French.
10475.correction: There is only one present tense in French which translates both the simple present (I do) and the present continous (I am doing).

10001.correction: There are a number of impersonal verbs such as 'il faut', 'il neige' and 'il pleut'. Verbs such as 'il fait' and 'il est' can also be used in an impersonal sense. In these cases, the English meaning is 'it' or impersonal 'you', 'we' as appropriate.

3171.belief: French word order is the same as English to express something being missing.
3171.statement: French word order is the same as English to express something being missing.
3171.correction: Take care to model 'il manque' with students. 'Il manque' is followed by a noun and the English translation is inverted. 'Il manque une personne' means 'a person is missing'. 'Il manque' is also used with plural nouns and translates as 'are missing'.

3602.belief: Idioms are the same in different languages.
3602.statement: Idioms are the same in different languages.
3602.correction: Idioms can be specific to a language, culture or group of people. They are often impossible to translate directly. Their use adds variety and authenticity to students' work but it is necessary to discuss the idiom carefully when it is taught.

2652.belief: The ending -aient is pronounced differently to -ais and -ait.
2652.statement: The ending -aient is pronounced differently to -ais and -ait.
2652.correction: Although the third person plural ending of the imperfect tense contains a lot of letters, it is pronounced the same way as -ais and -ait. Students will need a lot of practice saying the -aient ending out loud to become confident with this verb form.

3643.belief: The imperfect tense is only translated by 'was doing' in English e.g. I was listening to the radio.
3643.statement: The imperfect tense is only translated by 'was doing' in English e.g. I was listening to the radio.
3643.correction: The imperfect tense has more than one translation in English according to its use in French. Students need to be aware of the different meanings that might be conveyed when they encounter the imperfect tense e.g. I listened, I used to listen.

3642.belief: The imperfect tense only has one translation e.g. 'used to'.
3642.statement: The imperfect tense only has one translation e.g. 'used to'.
3642.correction: Students must be aware that the imperfect tense can be translated differently according to context and intended meaning e.g. 'used to', 'was doing' or 'did'.

10422.belief: 'Être' is used to translate the phrase 'there used to be'.
10422.statement: 'Être' is used to translate the phrase 'there used to be'.
10422.correction: Although in English, 'there used to be' has the idea of 'being', this is not the case in French. The phrase 'il y a' means there is but the verb is 'a' which comes from 'avoir'. It's the same with 'there used to be' - 'il y avait'.

9540.belief: When speaking or writing about what you did regularly in the past, use the perfect tense to state the action of the sentence.
9540.statement: When speaking or writing about what you did regularly in the past, use the perfect tense to state the action of the sentence.
9540.correction: When speaking or writing about what you did regularly in the past, use the imperfect tense to state the action. This is because you are talking about something that didn't have a clear start and end point. Perfect tense is not appropriate.

4849.belief: Only the near future and future tenses can be used to refer fo the future.
4849.statement: Only the near future and future tenses can be used to refer fo the future.
4849.correction: It is possible to refer to the future using the conditional mood: phrases like 'je voudrais' and 'il voudrait' which are followed by an infinitive. This creates the idea of what someone would like to do, clearly referring to possible future events.

4112.belief: The letter combinations [en] and [an] are pronounced differently in French.
4112.statement: The letter combinations [en] and [an] are pronounced differently in French.
4112.correction: The letter combinations [en] and [an] make the same sound in French, as can be heard in the word 'enfant'.

2631.belief: 'Elle' only means 'she' and 'elles' only means 'they', when naming a group of girls or women.
2631.statement: 'Elle' only means 'she' and 'elles' only means 'they', when naming a group of girls or women.
2631.correction: When used as emphatic pronouns, 'elle' means 'her' and 'elles' means 'them'.

5004.correction: 'Nous' means 'we' when used as a subject pronoun. 'Nous' means 'us' when used as an emphatic pronoun.

9198.belief: Sentences such as 'when I was little, I would do the shopping with my mother' can be translated by using both the imperfect tense and the conditional mood.
9198.statement: Sentences such as 'when I was little, I would do the shopping with my mother' can be translated by using both the imperfect tense and the conditional mood.
9198.correction: In French, when writing or translating sentences about what used to happen, all verbs should be in the imperfect tense. 'Used to' and 'would' (meaning habitually) are translated by the imperfect.

2682.belief: The English phrase 'I am going' is translated as 'je suis' + 'aller'.
2682.statement: The English phrase 'I am going' is translated as 'je suis' + 'aller'.
2682.correction: 'I am going' can only be translated as 'je vais' in French. This is particularly important for students to understand when using the future structure 'aller' + infinitive.

9106.belief: When saying what you will do in French, a separate word is needed for 'will'.
9106.statement: When saying what you will do in French, a separate word is needed for 'will'.
9106.correction: The simple future in French is a simple tense because it is made of one word. The idea of 'will' is created through the correct verb stem and ending. Most -er verbs use the infinitive as stem for the simple future.

2730.belief: All -er verbs use the infinitive as the stem for the simple future tense.
2730.statement: All -er verbs use the infinitive as the stem for the simple future tense.
2730.correction: Some -er verbs require a small change to the stem before adding the correct simple future ending, for example 'acheter', 'compléter' and 'protéger'. For each verb, the first -e changes to -è.

3166.belief: In French, the stress is placed on the first syllable of a word, like in English.
3166.statement: In French, the stress is placed on the first syllable of a word, like in English.
3166.correction: In French, the stress is ususally placed on the final syllable of a word, although stress is not as strong in French as it is in English.

75.belief: In the acronym PALM used to help structure a response to a picture, M for Mood only includes how people are feeling.
75.statement: In the acronym PALM used to help structure a response to a picture, M for Mood only includes how people are feeling.
75.correction: In PALM, Mood can be both people's emotions and the surrounding conditions, such as weather, time of day.

9087.belief: To say 'I am doing' in French, use the present tense of 'être' as part of the verb phrase.
9087.statement: To say 'I am doing' in French, use the present tense of 'être' as part of the verb phrase.
9087.correction: There is only one present tense in French. It translates both simple present and present continuous in English. To say 'I am doing' use the French for 'I do' ('je fais').

10132.belief: When talking about being hungry, thirsty, right, wrong or afraid, use 'être' as the verb.
10132.statement: When talking about being hungry, thirsty, right, wrong or afraid, use 'être' as the verb.
10132.correction: In French, ideas like being hungry and thirsty are expressed using 'avoir' plus a noun. In French, 'j'ai faim' is correct. It translates literally as 'I have hunger'. Ideas like being thirsty and afraid are expressed the same way.

9294.belief: The simple future stem of 'aller' is its infinitive, like most -er verbs.
9294.statement: The simple future stem of 'aller' is its infinitive, like most -er verbs.
9294.correction: 'Aller' is an irregular verb and its stem in the simple future is ir-. The normal simple future endings are added to this stem.

3157.correction: In common usage, the Internet is translated as 'internet' in French. It does not require a capital letter as it counts as a common noun. It is one of very few common nouns that doesn't require a determiner in common usage.

9109.correction: 'Plus' can mean 'plus' or 'more'. Then, the 's' should be pronounced. However, 'plus' can also mean 'no longer' as part of the negative phrase 'ne... plus'. When used in this way, the 's' is silent.

937.belief: When changing a positive to a negative statement, words like 'un', 'une', 'du', 'de la' and 'des' stay the same, e.g. 'je mange du gateau' - 'je ne mange pas du gâteau'.
937.statement: When changing a positive to a negative statement, words like 'un', 'une', 'du', 'de la' and 'des' stay the same, e.g. 'je mange du gateau' - 'je ne mange pas du gâteau'.
937.correction: When making a sentence negative, 'un', 'une', 'du', 'de la' and 'des' change to 'de', e.g. 'je mange du gâteau' - 'je ne mange pas de gâteau'.

3733.belief: Indefinite and partitive articles are used after negative structures.
3733.statement: Indefinite and partitive articles are used after negative structures.
3733.correction: After a negative structure has been used, indefinite and partitive articles replaced by 'de', e.g. 'je n'ai pas de pain'.

3734.belief: The indefinite and partitive articles are used with the structure 'ne... ni... ni', e.g. 'Tu n'as ni des pommes ni du fromage'.
3734.statement: The indefinite and partitive articles are used with the structure 'ne... ni... ni', e.g. 'Tu n'as ni des pommes ni du fromage'.
3734.correction: When using 'ne... ni... ni', the nouns do not require an indefinite or partitive article, e.g. 'Tu n'as ni pommes ni fromage'.

4284.belief: Longer written tasks do not require careful planning and structuring.
4284.statement: Longer written tasks do not require careful planning and structuring.
4284.correction: It is essential to carefully plan and structure longer written tasks to avoid students writing off the topic and their work becoming unwieldy. The use of the acronym BORDER helps students to plan and review a relevant response.

1744.belief: Cognates are pronounced the same way in English and French.
1744.statement: Cognates are pronounced the same way in English and French.
1744.correction: Cognates often sound very different in French. Students must carefully practise the French pronunciation of these words.

8773.belief: Reading or listening texts are only useful for developing general comprehension skills.
8773.statement: Reading or listening texts are only useful for developing general comprehension skills.
8773.correction: Careful use of reading and listening texts to enrich topic-specific vocabulary is beneficial for students.

4161.belief: Like English, German uses adjectives to describe nationality.
4161.statement: Like English, German uses adjectives to describe nationality.
4161.correction: German uses nouns to describe nationality.

3251.belief: German forms the present continuous tense by using sein with a verb e.g. "ich bin spielen" to say "I am playing".
3251.statement: German forms the present continuous tense by using sein with a verb e.g. "ich bin spielen" to say "I am playing".
3251.correction: German only has one present tense and does not use sein with a verb.

5000.belief: Nouns in German only change for the plural, like in English.
5000.statement: Nouns in German only change for the plural, like in English.
5000.correction: Adjectival nouns, weak masculine nouns and dative plural nouns all change their spelling.

3266.belief: German says double digits the same way as English.
3266.statement: German says double digits the same way as English.
3266.correction: In German, we say units first and then tens.

3279.belief: The German [w] is pronounced like the English 'w'; the German [v] is pronounced like the English 'v'.
3279.statement: The German [w] is pronounced like the English 'w'; the German [v] is pronounced like the English 'v'.
3279.correction: The German [w] is pronounced like the English 'v'; the German [v] is pronounced like the English 'f'.

5180.belief: There is only one way to form the plural in German.
5180.statement: There is only one way to form the plural in German.
5180.correction: German has several rules for forming plurals. The best way to correctly form plurals is to learn the rules, use an example for each rule as a guide, and frequently practise them. As in English, some nouns are used without plurals.

4948.belief: 'Nicht' means 'not' when negating in all German sentences.
4948.statement: 'Nicht' means 'not' when negating in all German sentences.
4948.correction: 'Nicht' negates in many sentences, but 'kein' replaces the indefinite article 'a/an' to negate nouns. For example, 'I have no car', and 'I haven't got a car' are both 'Ich habe kein Auto' in German.

3255.belief: All German nouns form their plural by adding 's'.
3255.statement: All German nouns form their plural by adding 's'.
3255.correction: Plural rules in German are complex and need to be learnt. Pronunciation is also important, as umlauts [ä], [ö] and [ü] can change meaning; for example, Vater, Väter. Accurate pronounciation can help with vocabulary, reading aloud and transcription.

853.belief: [ß] is a capital B and sounds like [b].
853.statement: [ß] is a capital B and sounds like [b].
853.correction: [ß] sounds the same as [ss]. [ß] is used after long vowels, [ss] after short vowels. In words with 's' as the final sound, the spelling [-s] or [ß] needs to be learnt; for example, 'Glas' or 'Spaß'.

3267.belief: In German sentences, the word order changes every time you use a conjunction.
3267.statement: In German sentences, the word order changes every time you use a conjunction.
3267.correction: Word order does not change after common co-ordinating conjunctions. 'Und', 'aber', 'oder', 'denn' just join two standard sentences together. 'Subordinating' conjuctions send the verb to the end of the sentence. Practise with 'weil', 'wenn', 'dass'.

10811.belief: Verb infinitives only ever mean 'to do' something.
10811.statement: Verb infinitives only ever mean 'to do' something.
10811.correction: Verb infinitives can be 'nouned' or nominalised by capitalising the first letter. These words are 'neuter' and can be used with or without 'das'. They do not need an ending (like the '-ing' in English) and are useful for extending vocabulary.

5186.belief: There is only one way to say 'there is' in German.
5186.statement: There is only one way to say 'there is' in German.
5186.correction: In German, we use 'es gibt' to talk about something more generally, and 'da ist' and 'da sind' to point out what there is in a specific place at a specific moment in time.

4162.belief: Like English, German uses 'it' and 'they' as subject pronouns to replace nouns.
4162.statement: Like English, German uses 'it' and 'they' as subject pronouns to replace nouns.
4162.correction: In German, subject pronouns 'er', 'sie', 'es', 'sie' mean 'it' and 'they' and match the grammatical gender and number of the noun.

962.correction: Using a checklist can ensure pupils use a range of language and know what to look for when checking for accuracy.

5355.belief: All past participles follow either the strong or weak verb rules.
5355.statement: All past participles follow either the strong or weak verb rules.
5355.correction: Some past participles are irregular and need to be learned as vocabulary items. Practise them with the infinitive so that the students learns the sound as well as the spelling.

3646.belief: The imperfect tense is never used in spoken German.
3646.statement: The imperfect tense is never used in spoken German.
3646.correction: The most common irregular verbs 'haben' and 'sein' are very common in speaking, along with 'es gab'. Other verbs in the imperfect mainly appear in written texts.

3278.belief: The German vowel sounds [a], [o] and [u] are the same as in English.
3278.statement: The German vowel sounds [a], [o] and [u] are the same as in English.
3278.correction: German vowel sounds can be either long or short. Pronouncing them correctly ensure more authentic pronunciation, more accurate transcription and better understanding. Keep the simple rules in mind and practise reading aloud regularly.

5360.belief: Past participles of -ieren verbs start with 'ge-' like most other past participles.
5360.statement: Past participles of -ieren verbs start with 'ge-' like most other past participles.
5360.correction: Unlike most other past participles, most German -'ieren' verbs act like some other weak German verbs, meaning that they do not have 'ge' at the beginning of their participles (for example, verbs beginning with 'be', 'er', and 'ver').

454.belief: Asking yes/no questions in the past is much more complicated than the present tense, as the rules are different. You need to translate 'did'.
454.statement: Asking yes/no questions in the past is much more complicated than the present tense, as the rules are different. You need to translate 'did'.
454.correction: The English 'did' isn't needed. Swap subject and verb for a yes/no question. 'Er sprach' (imperfect) becomes 'Sprach er?'. In the perfect tense, the past participle stays at the end of the sentence: 'Er hat gesprochen' - 'Hat er gesprochen?'.

11168.belief: In a written dictation in German, the only thing that matters is the correct sound-symbol correspondences (SSCs).
11168.statement: In a written dictation in German, the only thing that matters is the correct sound-symbol correspondences (SSCs).
11168.correction: SSCs are important, but the text needs to make sense grammatically. Check for correct spelling of known words, verb forms and tenses, and singular or plural nouns. Encourage students to check the details and to read back the texts in their head.

5726.correction: Possessive adjectives take the same endings as 'ein'.

3250.belief: German forms comparatives in the same way as English.
3250.statement: German forms comparatives in the same way as English.
3250.correction: Use 'als' to compare things that are different and 'so... wie' to compare things that are the same.

5725.belief: Possessive adjectives don't change their endings, like in English.
5725.statement: Possessive adjectives don't change their endings, like in English.
5725.correction: German possessive adjectives change their endings based on case and gender.

93.belief: Add -er to form all comparative adverbs.
93.statement: Add -er to form all comparative adverbs.

10667.belief: I should use word order two after phrases of opinion.
10667.statement: I should use word order two after phrases of opinion.
10667.correction: Use word order two after 'meiner Meinung nach' and word order three after 'ich denke, dass' and 'ich glaube, dass'.

323.belief: When answering conversation questions, it’s good to keep answers as short as possible, as in a role-play task.
323.statement: When answering conversation questions, it’s good to keep answers as short as possible, as in a role-play task.
323.correction: To give strong answers in conversation, it’s important to answer in full sentences and give details in our answers, including opinions and reasons, where appropriate.

10006.belief: Subject pronouns 'er' and 'sie' and object pronouns 'ihn' and 'sie' can only refer to people.
10006.statement: Subject pronouns 'er' and 'sie' and object pronouns 'ihn' and 'sie' can only refer to people.
10006.correction: Subject pronouns 'er' and 'sie' can mean 'he' and 'she' or they can refer to masculine and feminine nouns, meaning 'it'. The same is true for the object pronouns 'ihn' and 'sie', which can mean 'him' and 'her' but also 'it'.

2688.belief: English verbs followed by prepositions can be directly translated into German.
2688.statement: English verbs followed by prepositions can be directly translated into German.
2688.correction: Whilst many of the same verbs are followed by prepositions in both languages, different prepositions are often used, so these must be learnt.

2154.belief: Da-compounds can be used to refer back to any noun already mentioned.
2154.statement: Da-compounds can be used to refer back to any noun already mentioned.
2154.correction: Da-compounds can only be used with inanimate nouns. For people and animals, use object pronouns.

2155.correction: 'Damit' has a double identity! It can be used as a conjunction meaning 'so that' as well as a da-compound meaning 'with it' or 'with them'.

10830.belief: Verbs are only followed by the dative case if we translate the verb with 'to' or 'for' in English.
10830.statement: Verbs are only followed by the dative case if we translate the verb with 'to' or 'for' in English.
10830.correction: There are several impersonal verbs in German which require the dative case, e.g., 'gelingen' (to succeed).

10836.belief: All verbs in German are followed by the accusative case, apart from 'sein' which takes the nominative case.
10836.statement: All verbs in German are followed by the accusative case, apart from 'sein' which takes the nominative case.
10836.correction: A number of verbs are followed by the dative case. These must be learnt and carefully identified when translating into German.

5777.belief: The present continuous in German is different to the simple present.
5777.statement: The present continuous in German is different to the simple present.
5777.correction: The present continuous in German is the same as the simple present, so 'sie essen' means 'they eat' and 'they are eating'.

10847.belief: Verbs have the same meaning whether they are used reflexively or non-reflexively.
10847.statement: Verbs have the same meaning whether they are used reflexively or non-reflexively.
10847.correction: Some verbs have the same or similar meanings when used reflexively and non-reflexively, e.g. nennen, to call, sich nennen, to call oneself. However, some verbs completely change their meaning e.g. anziehen, to attract, sich anziehen, to get dressed.

10575.belief: We always use accusative reflexive pronouns ('mich', 'dich', etc.) with reflexive verbs.
10575.statement: We always use accusative reflexive pronouns ('mich', 'dich', etc.) with reflexive verbs.
10575.correction: If there is already an accusative object in the sentence, we use dative reflexive pronouns ('mir', 'dir', etc.) instead, e.g., 'Ich wasche mir die Hände'.

8719.belief: Questions words all have fixed spellings.
8719.statement: Questions words all have fixed spellings.
8719.correction: 'Wer', meaning 'who', changes spelling according to its case. This also used to be the case in English, but the 'whom' form is often not used nowadays.

3273.belief: In German, you always use 'müssen' to say what you have to do.
3273.statement: In German, you always use 'müssen' to say what you have to do.
3273.correction: The verb 'sollen' is another way of expressing an obligation, something you have to do. It has several uses, including strong commands (e.g. 'you should ring the doctor straightaway'), which are similar to the 'have to, must' meaning of 'müssen'.

3941.belief: 'Können' and 'dürfen' both translate as 'can' in English.
3941.statement: 'Können' and 'dürfen' both translate as 'can' in English.
3941.correction: 'Können' and 'dürfen' are often used incorrectly in both German and English. 'Dürfen' refers to permission - 'may I/am I allowed to?'. 'Können' refers to the ability to do something - 'can I/am I able to?', whether or not permission is given.

9200.belief: All sentences with 'wenn' use word order 3 and send the verb to the end.
9200.statement: All sentences with 'wenn' use word order 3 and send the verb to the end.
9200.correction: Distinguish between a clause and a sentence. 'Wenn' clauses need a second clause to complete a sentence. A clause starting with 'wenn' sends the verb to the end. If the 'wenn' clause is first, the second clause (after the comma) uses inversion.

3574.belief: 'Ich will' in German means 'I will' in English.
3574.statement: 'Ich will' in German means 'I will' in English.
3574.correction: 'Ich will' (from the verb 'wollen') means 'I want to', but is a common false friend. The future tense in German needs 'werden' with a 2nd verb in the infinitive.

10659.belief: Use 'würd-' whenever you want to say 'would'.
10659.statement: Use 'würd-' whenever you want to say 'would'.
10659.correction: 'Würd-' works for very many cases and is easy to remember because it sounds like the English 'would'. But 'haben' and 'sein' are important exceptions, especially in spoken German. 'Hätte' means 'I would have' and 'wäre' means 'I would be'.

9401.belief: 'Solange' and 'sobald' have to be used with 'als' to translate the 'as' in 'as long/soon as'.
9401.statement: 'Solange' and 'sobald' have to be used with 'als' to translate the 'as' in 'as long/soon as'.
9401.correction: The single word 'solange' is the translation for three English words - 'as long as' - and the same for 'sobald' - 'as soon as'.

10663.belief: Use 'wer' in German whenever you want to say 'who'.
10663.statement: Use 'wer' in German whenever you want to say 'who'.
10663.correction: There are 3 different forms of 'who' in German, which should be used correctly to match the case required in each sentence. There are different forms in English (who, whom), but we don't often use 'whom'. The rules in German are stricter.

11203.belief: 'z' is pronounced the same way in both English and German.
11203.statement: 'z' is pronounced the same way in both English and German.
11203.correction: German [z] sounds like the English 'ts'. German [s-] is pronounced like the English 'z'. Use example words to remind you of the difference, e.g., 'Zug' (train) and 'Suche' (search).

132.belief: When an adjective follows 'ein', always add 'en'.
132.statement: When an adjective follows 'ein', always add 'en'.
132.correction: Adjective endings reflect the case and gender of the word they refer to. Dative case adjectives end in -en. In nominative and accusative, use -e for feminine and -es for neuter. Masculine -er and -en match (d)er (nominative) and (d)en (accusative).

9095.belief: To say 'it' in German, always use 'es'.
9095.statement: To say 'it' in German, always use 'es'.
9095.correction: As a pronoun, 'es' only replaces a neuter noun. 'Das Buch? Ich lese es gern.' ('A book? I like reading it.'). Use 'ihn' or 'sie' for masculine and feminine nouns. 'Der neue Film? Ich finde ihn (it) toll.'. 'Berlin? Ich besuche sie (it) gern.'.

223.belief: Alll German words of foreign origin form their plural by adding 's'.
223.statement: Alll German words of foreign origin form their plural by adding 's'.
223.correction: Inanimate nouns add 's': 'Interviews', 'Songs'. Person nouns ending in -er (e.g., 'Reporter') do not change in the masculine plural. Weak masculine nouns (e.g., 'Journalist') add -en in the plural. Feminine plurals add -nen (e.g., 'Journalistinnen').

4684.belief: Modal verbs must add ge- in the imperfect tense.
4684.statement: Modal verbs must add ge- in the imperfect tense.
4684.correction: Modal verbs are normally used in the imperfect to describe past events. The imperfect is a different tense from the perfect and is formed differently.

10845.belief: Verbs that are reflexive in English must be reflexive in German and vice versa.
10845.statement: Verbs that are reflexive in English must be reflexive in German and vice versa.
10845.correction: Different verbs are reflexive in different languages. For example, 'sich erinnern' is not reflexive in English.

3641.belief: The imperfect tense of the modal verb 'mögen' is formed like other modal verbs.
3641.statement: The imperfect tense of the modal verb 'mögen' is formed like other modal verbs.
3641.correction: The stem of 'mögen' in the imperfect tense is 'moch-'. It is normally followed by a noun rather than a second verb in the infinitive.

10640.belief: I should use the same word order in German as in English.
10640.statement: I should use the same word order in German as in English.
10640.correction: German word order is different from English word order. In word order 2, the subject and verb are inverted.

50.belief: 'Aber' and 'sondern' mean the same thing and can be used interchangeably.
50.statement: 'Aber' and 'sondern' mean the same thing and can be used interchangeably.
50.correction: Use 'aber' to contradict a preceding statement that does not contain a negative. Use 'sondern' to mean 'but' or 'rather' following a negative statement.

322.belief: I can answer a role-play question with one or two words.
322.statement: I can answer a role-play question with one or two words.
322.correction: Role-play questions need to be answered in full sentences with at least one verb.

676.correction: 'Bis' has several meanings and uses. As a preposition it can mean 'until', 'up to' or 'by'. As a conjunction it usually means 'until'.

5359.belief: All past participles in German start with 'ge-'.
5359.statement: All past participles in German start with 'ge-'.
5359.correction: Verbs beginning with 'be-', 'ent-' or 'er-' do not require 'ge-' at the beginning. Past participles of separable verbs have the prefix first then the past participle of the main verb. They are written as one word, e.g., 'eingeladen', 'ausgegangen'.

10844.belief: All verbs with prefixes are separable.
10844.statement: All verbs with prefixes are separable.
10844.correction: Some prefixes are separable in some verbs but inseparable in others. For example, 'wieder' in 'wiedersehen' is separable, but not in 'wiederholen'. The stress always falls on the separable prefix.

8690.belief: [qu] sounds the same in English and German.
8690.statement: [qu] sounds the same in English and German.
8690.correction: In German, the SSC [qu] is pronounced 'k' then 'w' (which in German is like the English 'v' sound). Avoid confusion with English - for example, 'Qualität' vs 'quality'. In German, 'kw' appears only in complound words, e.g., 'Trinkwasser'.

149.belief: Adjectives in German don't have endings.
149.statement: Adjectives in German don't have endings.
149.correction: Adjectives have endings when they precede a noun. Compare 'der Hund ist groß' with 'der große Hund ist schwarz'. Adjective endings agree in case, gender and number with nouns. There are useful tables that can be learned to support correct usage.

2219.belief: Definite and indefiniete articles are used the same way in German as in English.
2219.statement: Definite and indefiniete articles are used the same way in German as in English.
2219.correction: Differences occur with some country names, some abstract nouns and professions: e.g., 'die Schweiz' (Switzerland), 'die Freiheit' (freedom). It's 'Er ist Arzt' (He is a doctor), but an article is needed before the adjective - 'Er ist ein guter Arzt'.

4415.belief: Many English superlatives use 'most', so you need to use 'meist' in German.
4415.statement: Many English superlatives use 'most', so you need to use 'meist' in German.
4415.correction: German superlatives use 'am -sten'. 'Most interesting' ist 'am interessantesten', and 'most difficult' is 'am schwierigsten'. No additional German word is required for 'most'.

5610.belief: Plural adjectival nouns always end in '-en'.
5610.statement: Plural adjectival nouns always end in '-en'.
5610.correction: All plural adjectival nouns preceded by 'die' and all in the dative end in '-en', but for plural adjectival nouns without articles, use '-e' in the nominative and accusative.

10329.belief: Time, manner, place adverbs must always be used in the order TMP.
10329.statement: Time, manner, place adverbs must always be used in the order TMP.
10329.correction: When using WO1, the order TMP applies. However, each of the elements can be used at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis. In that case, use WO2 and put the remaining elements in the order time before manner before place.

5772.belief: All prepositions are followed by either the accusative or the dative.
5772.statement: All prepositions are followed by either the accusative or the dative.
5772.correction: The prepositions ‘hinter’, ‘neben’, ‘unter’, ‘über’, ‘vor’, ‘zwischen’ and ‘in’ are used with the accusative case when there is movement but the dative case when there is no movement.

5499.belief: The phrase 'zu Hause' means 'to home' because 'zu' means 'to'.
5499.statement: The phrase 'zu Hause' means 'to home' because 'zu' means 'to'.
5499.correction: 'Zu Hause' means 'at home' and 'nach Hause' is used for 'going (to) home'.

10661.belief: We use 'wann' to say what we did, do or will do 'when'.
10661.statement: We use 'wann' to say what we did, do or will do 'when'.
10661.correction: 'Wann' is a question word and means 'when' in questions and indirect questions. Use 'als' for 'when' when referring to specific past events or points in time and 'wenn' for repeated actions or conditions in the present or future.

10892.belief: Vor' and 'bevor' and 'nach' and 'nachdem' are interchangeable because they mean 'before' and 'after'.
10892.statement: Vor' and 'bevor' and 'nach' and 'nachdem' are interchangeable because they mean 'before' and 'after'.
10892.correction: 'Vor' and 'nach' are prepositions and are followed by a noun, 'bevor' and 'nachdem' are conjunctions which link clauses and trigger word order 3.

10526.belief: 'Um' always means 'at' and is used with clock times.
10526.statement: 'Um' always means 'at' and is used with clock times.
10526.correction: Whilst 'um' is used commonly with clock times to mean 'at', it can also mean 'around' when referring to places, e.g., 'around the corner', or 'about, approximately' with numbers, e.g., 'about 10km'. It also follows some verbs, e.g., 'es geht um'.

9168.belief: If we see a reflexive pronoun, e.g., 'uns' or 'sich', this always means that the subject (doer) and object (receiver) of the verb are the same.
9168.statement: If we see a reflexive pronoun, e.g., 'uns' or 'sich', this always means that the subject (doer) and object (receiver) of the verb are the same.
9168.correction: Some plural reflexive verbs are reciprocal, meaning the action of the verb is done 'to each other' rather than 'to oneself'. The word 'gegenseitig' can be used to emphasise reciprocal use. Otherwise, use context to work out which meaning is intended.

3108.belief: To form the imperative, simply remove the subject pronoun and say the present tense verb form on its own.
3108.statement: To form the imperative, simply remove the subject pronoun and say the present tense verb form on its own.
3108.correction: To use the 'ihr' form of the imperative, simply remove the pronoun 'ihr' and say the verb form, e.g., 'Kommt!'. To use the 'du' form of the imperative, remove the pronoun 'du' but also remove the '-st' verb ending, e.g., 'Komm!'.

2172.belief: 'Darum' is a da-compound and its meaning is always directly related to the preposition 'um'.
2172.statement: 'Darum' is a da-compound and its meaning is always directly related to the preposition 'um'.
2172.correction: 'Darum' can be used as a da-compund, meaning 'around it' or 'about it' but it is also a conjunction meaning 'therefore' or 'that's why'.

10816.belief: For verb stems ending in ‘-el’, remove the 'e' from the stem in all present tense forms.
10816.statement: For verb stems ending in ‘-el’, remove the 'e' from the stem in all present tense forms.
10816.correction: For verb stems ending in ‘-el’, remove the 'e' from the stem in the first person singular of the present tense only.

9651.belief: Strong verbs never keep their stem changes in the 'du' form of the imperative.
9651.statement: Strong verbs never keep their stem changes in the 'du' form of the imperative.
9651.correction: Strong verbs keep stem vowel changes, e.g. 'e' to 'i', 'e' to 'ie', but omit the umlaut ('ä') in the imperative.

10179.belief: Only the tense of the verb can tell us whether a sentence is referring to present, past or future events.
10179.statement: Only the tense of the verb can tell us whether a sentence is referring to present, past or future events.
10179.correction: Adverbs of time are also very important in helping us to identify time frames, particularly when the present tense is used for future meaning.

10012.belief: The subject and verb in a 'zu' clause must match the subject and tense of the linked clause.
10012.statement: The subject and verb in a 'zu' clause must match the subject and tense of the linked clause.
10012.correction: We always use the infinitive and never a subject and finite verb in constructions with 'zu'. This applies to all tenses.

4995.belief: Nouns created from verbs are always formed from the infinitive and are always neuter.
4995.statement: Nouns created from verbs are always formed from the infinitive and are always neuter.
4995.correction: Nouns can be formed from the infintive and those nouns are always neuter. However, other nouns can be formed from the verb stem rather than the infinitive. Nouns ending in the suffix '-ung' are always feminine.

2312.belief: When developing a conversation about future plans, it is important to consistently use the future time frame in answers.
2312.statement: When developing a conversation about future plans, it is important to consistently use the future time frame in answers.
2312.correction: Whilst it is important to be able to refer to the future confidently, it is also helpful to add in different time frames to give more detail and to develop your sentences.

3745.belief: Indirect object nouns are always preceded by the words 'to' or 'for' in English, and this tells us we need to use the dative case for the indirect object in German.
3745.statement: Indirect object nouns are always preceded by the words 'to' or 'for' in English, and this tells us we need to use the dative case for the indirect object in German.
3745.correction: Whilst the inclusion of 'to' or 'for' in English can be a helpful indicator that the dative case is needed in German, not all verbs require this in English, and many can use the same word order as German.

9196.belief: When a sentence contains both a direct object and an indirect object, the indirect object always comes first.
9196.statement: When a sentence contains both a direct object and an indirect object, the indirect object always comes first.
9196.correction: When a sentence contains both a direct object noun and an indirect object noun, the indirect object always comes first. When a pronoun is used to replace either noun, the pronoun comes first.

137.belief: Adjectives and adverbs which are identical in German can be translated identically into English.
137.statement: Adjectives and adverbs which are identical in German can be translated identically into English.
