137.correction: English adjectives and adverbs differ, often with the adverb ending in '-ly', so care must be taken when translating German adjectives used as adverbs.

128.belief: Adjectival nouns behave like adjectives in every way.
128.statement: Adjectival nouns behave like adjectives in every way.
128.correction: Adjectival nouns, like adjectives, change endings according to gender, case and the article used with them. However, like nouns, they have a grammatical gender and a capital letter. Abstract adjectival nouns are neuter.

10660.belief: Use 'würde' whenever you want to say 'would'.
10660.statement: Use 'würde' whenever you want to say 'would'.
10660.correction: 'Würde' works in most cases, but for the conditional with 'haben' and 'sein', we usually use 'hätte' ('I would have') and 'wäre' ('I would be').

10867.correction: Use 'viel' and 'wenig' with uncountable nouns (i.e., you cannot put a number in front of it) and use 'viele' and 'wenige' with countable nouns (i.e., you can put a number in front of it).

5783.belief: The present tense in German can only be used to refer to the present.
5783.statement: The present tense in German can only be used to refer to the present.
5783.correction: The present tense can also be used with appropriate adverbs of time to refer to the near future, e.g., 'Am Samstag spiele ich Tennis.'.

10814.belief: The verb 'mögen' takes regular verb endings.
10814.statement: The verb 'mögen' takes regular verb endings.
10814.correction: The verb 'mögen' is irregular in the singular present tense forms, and the first and third person singular are identical: 'ich mag', 'er mag'.

3265.belief: German question words, like English, do not change their spelling.
3265.statement: German question words, like English, do not change their spelling.
3265.correction: Whilst most question words, such as 'wo', 'was' and 'warum' have a fixed spelling, 'welch-' changes according the gender and case of the noun that follows.

3970.belief: If you know the usual meanings of prepositions, choosing which preposition to use with each verb is straightforward, as we translate the preposition directly from English.
3970.statement: If you know the usual meanings of prepositions, choosing which preposition to use with each verb is straightforward, as we translate the preposition directly from English.
3970.correction: Verb and preposition combinations need to be learnt. The prepositions often lose their usual meaning when combined with verbs, and we often use different prepositions after verbs in English and in German.

8709.belief: Question words can replace definite articles as relative pronouns in relative clauses.
8709.statement: Question words can replace definite articles as relative pronouns in relative clauses.
8709.correction: Question words, such as 'wo', can be used as pronouns in relative clauses, but they should not be used to translate 'who' or 'which' when adding information about the noun in the main clause.

5831.belief: When producing written work in German, I should stick to short simple sentences.
5831.statement: When producing written work in German, I should stick to short simple sentences.
5831.correction: When producing written work in German, you should try to develop and extend your sentences to demonstrate grammatical complexity.

10603.belief: Always use the imperfect tense to translate the English simple past, e.g., 'I chatted online.'.
10603.statement: Always use the imperfect tense to translate the English simple past, e.g., 'I chatted online.'
10603.correction: The perfect tense is far more common in German, used for past events in speaking and informal writing. The imperfect is used mainly to narrate past events in more formal writing. However, 'hatte', 'war' and 'es gab' are used in speaking too.

3780.belief: Infinitives and nominalised infinitives look exactly the same.
3780.statement: Infinitives and nominalised infinitives look exactly the same.
3780.correction: Infinitives can be turned into nouns by capitalising the first letter, so although they sound the same, they look different. They are always neuter. Use surrounding words, such as 'beim' and 'am' to identify nominalised infinitives when listening.

10588.belief: Always use the comparative form of an adjective as the starting point for forming the superlative.
10588.statement: Always use the comparative form of an adjective as the starting point for forming the superlative.
10588.correction: Superlatives can change in the same way as comparatives, such as adding an umlaut, (alt, älter, der/die/das älteste). Where the comparative removes ‘e’, use the original adjective to form the superlative (teuer, teurer, der/die/das teuerste).

3202.belief: In the future tense and other 2-verb structures, the 2nd (infinitive) verb always comes at the end of the sentence.
3202.statement: In the future tense and other 2-verb structures, the 2nd (infinitive) verb always comes at the end of the sentence.
3202.correction: The 2nd (infinitive) verb always comes at the end of the sentence in WO1 and 2. In WO3, where the main verb goes to the end of the sentence, the 2nd (infinitive) verb is in 2nd-last place - 'Ich weiß, dass du nächste Woche nach Berlin fahren wirst.'.

9112.belief: Saying or writing years in German is the same as in English, e.g., 1066 is 'zehn sechsundsechzig'.
9112.statement: Saying or writing years in German is the same as in English, e.g., 1066 is 'zehn sechsundsechzig'.
9112.correction: Block the numbers in pairs as in English, but in German you must use 'hundert' or 'tausend'. 1066 is 'zehnhundertsechsundsechszig'. 2025 is 'zweitausendfünfundzwanzig'.

1743.belief: Cognates are pronounced the same as the English words.
1743.statement: Cognates are pronounced the same as the English words.
1743.correction: Cognates may share similar spelling and meanings, but it is important to remember German pronunciation rules.

5723.belief: A possessive adjective must match whoever possesses the noun in gender, number and case.
5723.statement: A possessive adjective must match whoever possesses the noun in gender, number and case.
5723.correction: A possessive adjective matches the gender, number and case of the noun it describes, not the person possessing it, e.g., 'his school' - 'seine Schule'. The possessor is male but the noun they possess is feminine.

10672.correction: 'To' is expressed in different ways in German. 'In' and 'nach' also mean 'to'. 'Zu' can also mean 'shut', 'closed' or 'off'.

10850.belief: All verbs use the auxiliary verb 'haben' to form the perfect tense.
10850.statement: All verbs use the auxiliary verb 'haben' to form the perfect tense.
10850.correction: A small number of verbs use the auxiliary verb 'sein' to form the perfect tense. These verbs usually refer to movement or a change of physical state.

8714.belief: Questions are formed in the same way in both German and English.
8714.statement: Questions are formed in the same way in both German and English.
8714.correction: English uses 'do you...?' or 'are you...?' when forming questions. German inverts the position of the subject and verb in a statement to form a closed question. Add a question word at the start to change it into an open question.

2243.correction: Not all conjunctions trigger word order 3. 'Denn' means 'because' and is followed by word order 1. 'Weil' also means 'because', but triggers word order 3.

2742.correction: Use 'es gibt' to translate 'there is, there are' when making a general statement that something exists. Use 'da ist' when referring to a particular thing in a particular place at a particular time; for instance, in a photograph: 'Da ist die Kirche.'.

11034.correction: Use 'wissen' with facts (e.g., 'Ich weiß nicht!') and 'kennen' with people or things you are familiar with ('Ich kenne deinen Freund.').

3638.belief: The imperfect tense is only ever written.
3638.statement: The imperfect tense is only ever written.
3638.correction: Whilst the imperfect tense is mainly used to narrate past events in written German, some forms are regularly used in spoken German, such as 'es gab', 'war' and 'hatte'.

144.belief: Adjectives don’t have capital letters in German, so to say ‘the green ones’ in German, no capital letter is needed.
144.statement: Adjectives don’t have capital letters in German, so to say ‘the green ones’ in German, no capital letter is needed.
144.correction: Whilst adjectives don't have capital letters, adjectival nouns always have capital letters; ‘die Grünen’ - 'the green ones'.

2454.belief: If I don't have a dictionary in an exam, I won't be able to work out the meaning of unfamiliar words.
2454.statement: If I don't have a dictionary in an exam, I won't be able to work out the meaning of unfamiliar words.
2454.correction: If you cannot use a dictionary, look at the surrounding words. Is the word part of a compound noun? Is it a cognate? Using the words and grammar you know, generate a working translation and try to fill the gap. Consider the topic of the text, too.

10007.belief: Subject pronouns are always used with a verb to indicate the subject.
10007.statement: Subject pronouns are always used with a verb to indicate the subject.
10007.correction: Subject pronouns are not always used with a verb. Verb endings alone often tell us the subject.

220.belief: 'Alguno' can be used before a singular or uncountable masculine noun.
220.statement: 'Alguno' can be used before a singular or uncountable masculine noun.
220.correction: 'Alguno' cannot be used before a singular or uncountable masculine noun. 'Algún' must be used instead.

160.belief: Adjectives in Spanish only ever appear after the noun.
160.statement: Adjectives in Spanish only ever appear after the noun.
160.correction: Most adjectives in Spanish appear after the noun. However, some are used before it. These are called prenominal adjectives.

2656.belief: The ending -ió is always used with -er and -ir verbs to refer to she, he or it in the preterite tense.
2656.statement: The ending -ió is always used with -er and -ir verbs to refer to she, he or it in the preterite tense.
2656.correction: For -er and -ir verbs whose stem ends in a vowel, add -yó to refer to 'he', 'she' or 'it in the preterite tense.

103.belief: Add an -s to any Spanish noun to make it plural.
103.statement: Add an -s to any Spanish noun to make it plural.
103.correction: Add an -s to Spanish nouns ending in a vowel to make them plural. Add -es to Spanish nouns ending in a consonant to make them plural.

11075.belief: Word order in questions is the same in Spanish and English.
11075.statement: Word order in questions is the same in Spanish and English.
11075.correction: Prepositions appear at the start of Spanish questions. They usually appear at the end of English questions.

2612.belief: 'El' and 'lo' are interchangeable, as 'la' (article) and 'la' (DOP) and 'las' (article) and 'las' (DOP) look exactly the same.
2612.statement: 'El' and 'lo' are interchangeable, as 'la' (article) and 'la' (DOP) and 'las' (article) and 'las' (DOP) look exactly the same.
2612.correction: Remember that direct object pronouns (lo, la, los and las) come before a verb. 'El' is the masculine singular form of the definite article 'the'.

4687.belief: Modal verbs are followed by a conjugated verb which changes its ending to match the person who is speaking.
4687.statement: Modal verbs are followed by a conjugated verb which changes its ending to match the person who is speaking.
4687.correction: Modal verbs are followed by the infinitive.

154.belief: All adjectives go after the noun in Spanish.
154.statement: All adjectives go after the noun in Spanish.
154.correction: There are some adjectives that can also go before the noun and these are called prenominal adjectives.

9498.belief: Spanish sentences always start with the subject.
9498.statement: Spanish sentences always start with the subject.
9498.correction: Spanish sentences can start with the subject or with the indirect object. This is important when using indirect object pronouns as they can come before the verb (e.g. 'me interesan las matemáticas').

9519.belief: Spanish word order is identical to English so I can translate sentences with indirect object pronouns literally from one language to another.
9519.statement: Spanish word order is identical to English so I can translate sentences with indirect object pronouns literally from one language to another.
9519.correction: Spanish word order is different to English. Indirect object pronouns come before the conjugated verb. With 2-verb structures, they can go before the first verb or after the infinitive, attached to it.

10135.belief: When talking about the weather, I can translate directly from English (e.g. 'it's cold').
10135.statement: When talking about the weather, I can translate directly from English (e.g. 'it's cold').
10135.correction: It's important to remember that Spanish uses the verb 'hacer' when talking about the weather. For example, 'it's cold' translates as 'hace frío'.

180.belief: The affirmative imperative is the same as 2nd person singular form of the verb.
180.statement: The affirmative imperative is the same as 2nd person singular form of the verb.
180.correction: When talking to somebody familiar to you, using 'tú', the affirmative imperative is the same as the 3rd person singular form of the verb.

4506.belief: 'Me' means 'to me' and 'my', and 'te' means 'to you' and 'your'.
4506.statement: 'Me' means 'to me' and 'my', and 'te' means 'to you' and 'your'.
4506.correction: 'Me' and 'te' look very similar to the possessive adjectives 'mi' and 'tu', but their meanings are different.

10401.belief: 'She, he is doing' translates as 'es haciendo' in Spanish.
10401.statement: 'She, he is doing' translates as 'es haciendo' in Spanish.
10401.correction: 'She, he is doing' is 'está haciendo'. To form the present continuous, use 'estar' and a verb in the present participle (-ando, -iendo).

5779.belief: All present participles follow regular rules and there are no spelling exceptions.
5779.statement: All present participles follow regular rules and there are no spelling exceptions.
5779.correction: Verbs whose stems end in a vowel ('leer', 'construir') have a i->y spelling change when in the past participle ending.

9348.belief: You are (singular) and you are (plural) are translated the same in Spanish - 'estás'.
9348.statement: You are (singular) and you are (plural) are translated the same in Spanish - 'estás'.
9348.correction: To say ‘you are’ (singular), we say 'estás'; To say ‘you are’ (plural), we say 'estáis'.

232.belief: 'I am reading' and 'I read' both translate as 'leo'.
232.statement: 'I am reading' and 'I read' both translate as 'leo'.
232.correction: 'I am reading' is the present continuous and therefore it translates as 'estoy leyendo'. 'I read' is the present simple and it translates as 'leo'. We need to use context and time markers to know when to use each.

8828.belief: Reflexive pronouns appear after a conjugated verb.
8828.statement: Reflexive pronouns appear after a conjugated verb.
8828.correction: The reflexive pronoun 'se' appears before a conjugated verb in any tense.

2989.belief: The final ‘-s’ in ‘sus’ refers to more than one person.
2989.statement: The final ‘-s’ in ‘sus’ refers to more than one person.
2989.correction: The final ‘s’ refers to a plural noun.

5210.belief: There is only one word for 'your' in Spanish.
5210.statement: There is only one word for 'your' in Spanish.
5210.correction: 'Tu' means 'your' when addressing one person. 'Vuestro' means 'your' when addressing more than one person.

10840.belief: Verbs like 'poner', 'venir' and 'hacer' follow the rules of regular -er/-ir verbs in the present tense.
10840.statement: Verbs like 'poner', 'venir' and 'hacer' follow the rules of regular -er/-ir verbs in the present tense.
10840.correction: Verbs like 'poner', 'venir' and 'hacer' are irregular and add -g- in the 1st person singular present (e.g. 'pongo', 'vengo', 'hago', and 'decir' - 'digo').

1746.belief: Cognates are words that look and sound like English.
1746.statement: Cognates are words that look and sound like English.
1746.correction: Cognates may look very similar to English but sound quite different so attention must be paid to pronunciation.

3431.belief: 'Hacer' only translates as 'to do, make; doing, making'.
3431.statement: 'Hacer' only translates as 'to do, make; doing, making'.
3431.correction: 'Hacer' can be used to talk about the weather and therefore we can't always translate phrases with 'hacer' literally. 'Hace sol' translates as 'it's sunny' and 'hizo calor' translates as 'it was hot'.

9502.belief: In Spanish, subject pronouns are never necessary as verb endings indicate who is doing the action.
9502.statement: In Spanish, subject pronouns are never necessary as verb endings indicate who is doing the action.
9502.correction: We can use subject pronouns 'tú' (you, sing) and 'vosotros/as' (you all) to give emphasis or to present a contrast.

10459.belief: 'Tu' is both the subject pronoun 'you' and the possessive adjective 'your'.
10459.statement: 'Tu' is both the subject pronoun 'you' and the possessive adjective 'your'.
10459.correction: 'Tu' without an accent is a possessive adjective: you; 'tú' with an accent is a subject pronoun: you.

9347.belief: All the singular persons of -ar, -er, and -ir verbs in the preterite have an accent.
9347.statement: All the singular persons of -ar, -er, and -ir verbs in the preterite have an accent.
9347.correction: Only the 'I' and 'she, he, it' forms have an accent. For -ar verbs, the endings are -é and -ó; for -er and -ir verbs the endings are -í and -ió.

4264.belief: As long as I get the gist of the meaning of a Spanish question, I can answer successfully.
4264.statement: As long as I get the gist of the meaning of a Spanish question, I can answer successfully.
4264.correction: In conversation it is important to listen carefully to the tense of questions before answering. Otherwise your answers might not be relevant. For example, 'What did you do after school yesterday?' 'I usually do my homework.'

1971.belief: Any conjugated form of 'ir' ('voy', 'vas', 'va') can refer to routines or future events. For example, 'voy al parque' means 'I'm going to the park' or 'I'm going to go to the park'.
1971.statement: Any conjugated form of 'ir' ('voy', 'vas', 'va') can refer to routines or future events. For example, 'voy al parque' means 'I'm going to the park' or 'I'm going to go to the park'.
1971.correction: We can use 'ir' to talk about routines and to talk about the future, but when referring to future intentions, 'ir' needs to be followed by 'a' + infinitive.

170.belief: Adverbs 'antes de' and 'después de' and the preposition 'sin' are always followed by a gerund (-ing) in Spanish, the same as in English.
170.statement: Adverbs 'antes de' and 'después de' and the preposition 'sin' are always followed by a gerund (-ing) in Spanish, the same as in English.
170.correction: Adverbs 'antes de' and 'después de' and the preposition 'sin' are always followed by an infinitive in Spanish, unlinke English that uses a gerund (-ing).

2471.belief: I don't need to have a strategy when tackling a translation.
2471.statement: I don't need to have a strategy when tackling a translation.
2471.correction: It is important to read Spanish sentences carefully before translating them into English. Identifying the tense in each sentence, for example, can really help to improve accuracy.

10409.belief: The only translation of 'fuimos' is 'we went'.
10409.statement: The only translation of 'fuimos' is 'we went'.
10409.correction: 'fuimos' can mean 'we went' or 'we were' depending on the context. The verbs 'ser' and 'ir' are identical in the preterite tense.

4854.belief: It is always necessary to use subject pronouns before Spanish verbs.
4854.statement: It is always necessary to use subject pronouns before Spanish verbs.
4854.correction: It is not usually necessary to use subject pronouns before Spanish verbs as the verb ending shows the subject. However, they can be used to emphasise a change of subject.

9489.belief: In Spanish, all masculine nouns end in -o and all feminine nouns end in -a.
9489.statement: In Spanish, all masculine nouns end in -o and all feminine nouns end in -a.
9489.correction: This is often the case, but it is not a blanket rule. For example, words ending in -ista, -ente and -ante can be masculine or feminine depending on the context.

9488.belief: In Spanish, all masculine adjectives end in -o.
9488.statement: In Spanish, all masculine adjectives end in -o.
9488.correction: Many masculine adjectives end in -o, but this is not always the case. For example, many masculine adjectives of nationality end in -és e.g. 'inglés' and 'francés'.

3791.correction: 'inglés' can be an adjective, as in 'la comida inglesa' (English food), or a noun, as in 'el inglés' (the English person (m)). The process of making a noun in this way from an adjective or verb is called nominalisation.

5113.belief: Once you've learnt a word once, it will stay in your memory forever.
5113.statement: Once you've learnt a word once, it will stay in your memory forever.
5113.correction: If you learn a word once and don't revisit it, it is unlikely to stay in your long-term memory. It is important to revisit prior learning regularly to retain knowledge in the long-term memory.

2674.belief: As in English, double negatives structures in Spanish are not considered acceptable in formal language.
2674.statement: As in English, double negatives structures in Spanish are not considered acceptable in formal language.
2674.correction: Double negative structures are commonly used in Spanish and are considered acceptable in formal language.

4474.belief: The masculine singular form of 'ninguna' is 'ninguno'.
4474.statement: The masculine singular form of 'ninguna' is 'ninguno'.
4474.correction: When used as an adjective, the masculine singular form of 'ninguna' is 'ningún'. The word 'ninguno' does, however, exist as a pronoun.

9482.belief: In Spanish, [g] is always pronounced as in 'gol'.
9482.statement: In Spanish, [g] is always pronounced as in 'gol'.
9482.correction: The pronunciation of [g] varies depending on the vowels that follow. [g] followed by [a], [o] or [u] is hard, whereas [g] followed by [i] or [e] is soft.

10219.belief: Their is only one way to say 'your' in Spanish.
10219.statement: Their is only one way to say 'your' in Spanish.
10219.correction: There are six ways to say 'your' in Spanish depending on the gender and number of the following noun, and whether the owner is singular or plural: tu, tus, vuestro, vuestra, vuestros and vuestras

9505.belief: The only Spanish translation of 'in' is 'en'.
9505.statement: The only Spanish translation of 'in' is 'en'.
9505.correction: There are several Spanish words for 'in' depending on the context. For example, the phrase 'por la tarde' means 'in the afternoon'.

639.belief: It is best to stick to short, one-word answers when responding to role-play prompts.
639.statement: It is best to stick to short, one-word answers when responding to role-play prompts.
639.correction: It is advisable to include at least one verb in each answer given as part of a role-play.

10411.belief: The only translation of 'iba' is 'I used to go'.
10411.statement: The only translation of 'iba' is 'I used to go'.
10411.correction: 'iba' can means 'I used to go' or 'she, he, it used to go'. As 'iba' has several meanings, it’s important to consider to context of the sentence to work out who it refers to.

62.belief: Accents are present in several forms of 'ir' and -ar verbs in the imperfect tense.
62.statement: Accents are present in several forms of 'ir' and -ar verbs in the imperfect tense.
62.correction: Accents are only present in the 1st person singular (we) form of 'ir' ('íbamos') and -ar verbs (-ábamos) in the imperfect tense.

2266.belief: When describing photos in speech and writing, a one-word answer will suffice.
2266.statement: When describing photos in speech and writing, a one-word answer will suffice.
2266.correction: When describing photos in Spanish, it is important to use full sentences and convey a range of information.

2051.belief: The correct Spanish translation of 'I am hungry' is 'estoy hambre'.
2051.statement: The correct Spanish translation of 'I am hungry' is 'estoy hambre'.
2051.correction: The correct translation of 'I am hungry' is 'tengo hambre'. Sometimes Spanish uses ‘tengo’ + noun where the English would be ‘I am’ + adjective. Other examples of this structure are ‘tengo frío’ (I am cold) and ‘tengo miedo’ (I am scared).

326.belief: When answering reading comprehension questions, you should translate as much of the text as possible in the hope of including the correct answer.
326.statement: When answering reading comprehension questions, you should translate as much of the text as possible in the hope of including the correct answer.
326.correction: You should make sure that your answers to reading comprehension questions are specific by locating relevant vocabulary in the text before responding.

3647.belief: The imperfect tense is only used to talk about something that used to happen repeatedly.
3647.statement: The imperfect tense is only used to talk about something that used to happen repeatedly.
3647.correction: The imperfect is used to talk about something that used to happen repeatedly, but it has other uses in different contexts. For example, it can be used to set the scene in a narrative account or story, and to describe general situations in the past.

2731.belief: 'Era' only means 'she, he, it was' or 'she, he, it used to be'.
2731.statement: 'Era' only means 'she, he, it was' or 'she, he, it used to be'.
2731.correction: 'Era' also means 'I was' or 'I used to be'. Look for the pronouns 'yo', 'él' and 'ella' to understand the meaning of 'era' in context.

2746.belief: 'Eso' and 'esto' can appear before a noun.
2746.statement: 'Eso' and 'esto' can appear before a noun.
2746.correction: 'Eso' and 'esto' cannot appear before a noun because they are pronouns. Instead it is necessary to use 'este' and 'esta' (to mean 'this') and 'ese' and 'esa' (to mean 'that').

8860.belief: The relative pronouns 'que', 'donde' and 'cuando' have a written accent.
8860.statement: The relative pronouns 'que', 'donde' and 'cuando' have a written accent.
8860.correction: The relative pronouns 'que' (who/that), 'donde' (where) and 'cuando' (when) do not have a written accent. However, the question words 'qué' (what), 'dónde' (where) and 'cuándo' (when) do have a written accent.

9467.belief: All Spanish adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun.
9467.statement: All Spanish adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun.
9467.correction: Most adjectives in Spanish agree in gender and number with the noun. However, adjectives ending in -e only agree with the noun in number.

10043.belief: The suffix -ito is added to the end of any noun to give the meaning 'small'.
10043.statement: The suffix -ito is added to the end of any noun to give the meaning 'small'.
10043.correction: The final letter is removed from nouns ending in ‘a’ or ‘o’ before adding -ito or -ita.

2130.belief: 'Cuál' and 'cuáles' may appear directly before a noun.
2130.statement: 'Cuál' and 'cuáles' may appear directly before a noun.
2130.correction: 'Cuál' and 'cuáles' may not appear directly before a noun. As they are pronouns, they either stand alone or appear before a verb.

9506.belief: The Spanish translation of 'I've broken my arm' is 'me he roto mi brazo'. You use the possessive adjective for body parts.
9506.statement: The Spanish translation of 'I've broken my arm' is 'me he roto mi brazo'. You use the possessive adjective for body parts.
9506.correction: When referring to body parts, Spanish speakers replace possessive adjectives with definite articles, e.g. 'me he roto el brazo'.

10407.belief: The only translation of 'the best' in Spanish is 'el mejor'.
10407.statement: The only translation of 'the best' in Spanish is 'el mejor'.
10407.correction: The superlative 'el mejor' must agree with the noun it describes in number and gender. Its other forms are 'la mejor', 'los mejores' and 'las mejores'.

8991.belief: Role-play and conversation answers should be kept brief.
8991.statement: Role-play and conversation answers should be kept brief.
8991.correction: Role-play answers should be kept relatively brief, whereas conversations present the opportunity to develop answers.

4690.belief: Modal verbs such as 'me gustaría' and 'quisiera' can be followed by simple present verbs.
4690.statement: Modal verbs such as 'me gustaría' and 'quisiera' can be followed by simple present verbs.
4690.correction: Modal verbs such as 'me gustaría' and 'quisiera' cannot be followed by simple present verbs. To say what you would like to do, use a modal verb followed by an infinitive.

134.belief: The adjective used in a comparative or superlative structure does not need to agree with any noun.
134.statement: The adjective used in a comparative or superlative structure does not need to agree with any noun.
134.correction: The adjective used in a comparative or superlative structure must agree with the preceding noun.

9497.belief: In Spanish, you can always repeat language used in the question to form your answer.
9497.statement: In Spanish, you can always repeat language used in the question to form your answer.
9497.correction: If 2nd person language is used in a Spanish question, this must be converted into 1st person language for the answer.

3111.belief: To form the inflectional future tense, take off the infinitive ending before adding -é, -ás, -á.
3111.statement: To form the inflectional future tense, take off the infinitive ending before adding -é, -ás, -á.
3111.correction: To form the inflectional future tense, add the endings -é, -ás, -á, to the infinitive.

9511.belief: The Spanish translation of 'I will have' is 'teneré'.
9511.statement: The Spanish translation of 'I will have' is 'teneré'.
9511.correction: The verb 'tener' is irregular in the inflectional future. The Spanish translation of 'I will have' is 'tendré'.

11062.belief: Any word that ends in -é is in the preterite tense.
11062.statement: Any word that ends in -é is in the preterite tense.
11062.correction: Some words that end in -é are in the inflectional future. In this case, the -é ending is added to the infinitive - 'trabajaré' (I will work) - rather than the stem, as in the preterite - 'trabajé' (I worked).

10399.belief: 'More than' is always translated as 'más que'.
10399.statement: 'More than' is always translated as 'más que'.
10399.correction: 'More than' can be translated as 'más que' or 'más de'. 'Más de' is followed by numbers.

3785.belief: In the inflectional future with all verbs, the endings are added to the infinitive and they are the same for -ar, -er and -ir verbs.
3785.statement: In the inflectional future with all verbs, the endings are added to the infinitive and they are the same for -ar, -er and -ir verbs.
3785.correction: A small number of verbs are irregular in the inflectional future and have irregular future stems.

325.belief: When answering questions, I can use the verb in the question to start my answer.
325.statement: When answering questions, I can use the verb in the question to start my answer.
325.correction: You can start your answer using the question verb but it's important to not copy the question word-for-word. If questions use 2nd person verbs, you need to change them to 1st person, changing 'you' verbs into 'I' or 'we' forms.

2348.belief: There is no difference between 'ningún' and 'ninguno'.
2348.statement: There is no difference between 'ningún' and 'ninguno'.
2348.correction: 'Ningún' and 'ninguno' look very similar but they are used differently in Spanish. 'Ninguno' is a pronoun and it replaces a masculine singular noun. 'Ningún' is an indefinite adjective and it comes before a masculine singular noun.

10393.belief: I can translate sentences with 'desde hace' word for word.
10393.statement: I can translate sentences with 'desde hace' word for word.
10393.correction: In Spanish, 'desde hace' appears together with a verbs in the present tense to say how long you've been doing something. We use a different tense in English. 'Vivo aquí desde hace años' - 'I have been living here for years'.

2897.belief: The only factor in understanding listening tasks is vocabulary. If I know enough words, I don’t need any strategies to comprehend what I hear.
2897.statement: The only factor in understanding listening tasks is vocabulary. If I know enough words, I don’t need any strategies to comprehend what I hear.
2897.correction: A strong knowledge of high frequency vocabulary is key to unlocking effective listening comprehension. However, strategies such as prediction, synonym recognition and identifying distractors can also improve listening skills.

9508.belief: The Spanish translation of 'I have' + past participle, e.g. 'I have listened', is 'tengo' + past participle, e.g. 'tengo escuchado'.
9508.statement: The Spanish translation of 'I have' + past participle, e.g. 'I have listened', is 'tengo' + past participle, e.g. 'tengo escuchado'.
9508.correction: The Spanish translation of 'I have listened' is 'he escuchado'. In Spanish, the auxiliary verb used in the formation of the perfect tense is 'haber', not 'tener'.

2685.belief: The English translation of 'he visitado' is 'I visited'.
2685.statement: The English translation of 'he visitado' is 'I visited'.
2685.correction: The perfect tense is used to express what has happened. The English translation of 'he visitado' is 'I have visited'.

5588.correction: 'I played' in Spanish is 'jugué'. An extra 'u' is added after the 'g' to preserve the hard [g] sound.

10949.belief: The only way of saying 'I played' in Spanish is 'jugué'.
10949.statement: The only way of saying 'I played' in Spanish is 'jugué'.
10949.correction: 'I played' could be translated as 'jugué' or 'jugaba'. The preterite verb 'jugué' implies a single, completed action in the past, whereas the imperfect verb 'jugaba' implies a habitual action in the past.

3113.belief: To form the past participle of any verb in Spanish, remove the infinitive ending and add -ado.
3113.statement: To form the past participle of any verb in Spanish, remove the infinitive ending and add -ado.
3113.correction: To form the past participle of regular -ar verbs, remove the -ar and add -ado. However, to form the past participle of regular -er and -ir verbs, remove the -er/-ir and add -ido.

9487.correction: In Spanish 'mañana' has two meanings. It can mean 'morning' or 'tomorrow'.

4511.belief: To mean 'you' in an impersonal, general sense use 'tú'.
4511.statement: To mean 'you' in an impersonal, general sense use 'tú'.
4511.correction: 'Tú' means 'you' when directed at a specific person. To mean 'you' in an impersonal, general sense use 'se' e.g. 'se puede' (you can).

9605.belief: Stem-changing verbs like 'encontrar' and 'pensar' have a stem change in all conjugations of the simple present.
9605.statement: Stem-changing verbs like 'encontrar' and 'pensar' have a stem change in all conjugations of the simple present.
9605.correction: Stem-changing verbs 'encontrar' and 'pensar' have a stem change in persons 1, 2, 3 and 6 of the simple present. The stem reverts back to the original for persons 4 and 5.

9510.belief: The Spanish translation of 'it is sunny' is 'es sol'.
9510.statement: The Spanish translation of 'it is sunny' is 'es sol'.
9510.correction: When describing weather conditions, the verb 'hace' translates as 'it is'. The Spanish translation of 'it is sunny' is 'hace sol'.

9496.belief: Spanish questions have the same punctuation as in English.
9496.statement: Spanish questions have the same punctuation as in English.
9496.correction: Spanish questions begin with an upside down question mark (¿).

3304.belief: 'To give' is always a natural translation of 'dar'.
3304.statement: 'To give' is always a natural translation of 'dar'.
3304.correction: When 'dar' appears with a noun of feeling or emotion, it is more natural to use 'to be' + adjective in English.

5358.belief: Past participles do not have gender and number marking.
5358.statement: Past participles do not have gender and number marking.
5358.correction: In passive sentences with 'ser' + past participle, the past participle must agree in number with the noun it acts on.

10945.belief: The only way to mean 'you (sg)' in Spanish is 'tú'.
10945.statement: The only way to mean 'you (sg)' in Spanish is 'tú'.
10945.correction: There are two ways to mean 'you (sg)' in Spanish. Use 'tú' to mean 'you' in an informal context, and 'usted' to mean 'you' in a formal context.

9503.belief: In Spanish, 'tú' and 'tu' mean the same thing.
9503.statement: In Spanish, 'tú' and 'tu' mean the same thing.
9503.correction: In Spanish, 'tú' and 'tu' do not mean the same thing. 'Tú' is a subject pronoun meaning 'you' (informal), whereas 'tu' is a possessive adjective meaning 'your' (informal).

5464.belief: When performing a role-play, one-word answers are enough.
5464.statement: When performing a role-play, one-word answers are enough.
5464.correction: When preparing and performing role-plays, it is important to answer using short phrases or sentences, avoiding one-word answers.

10165.belief: To tell somebody who is familiar to you to do something, use the 2nd person singular form of the verb.
10165.statement: To tell somebody who is familiar to you to do something, use the 2nd person singular form of the verb.
10165.correction: To tell somebody who is familiar to you to do something, use the affirmative imperative. For -ar verbs this ends in -a, and for -er/-ir verbs this ends in -e.

10413.belief: The only translation of 've' in Spanish is 'she, he, it sees'.
10413.statement: The only translation of 've' in Spanish is 'she, he, it sees'.
10413.correction: In Spanish, the verb 've' usually means 'she, he, it sees', but it is also the affirmative imperative form of 'ir', meaning 'go'.

3033.belief: The first thing I hear correctly and understand is usually the answer to a listening comprehension question.
3033.statement: The first thing I hear correctly and understand is usually the answer to a listening comprehension question.
3033.correction: It is important to listen to the whole text before answering a listening comprehension question, as information may not be presented in an obvious order.

1866.belief: When completing a photo description in Spanish, I should stick to short, simple sentences.
1866.statement: When completing a photo description in Spanish, I should stick to short, simple sentences.
1866.correction: When describing photos in Spanish, it is important to plan extended sentences to talk for a prolonged period of time.

5354.belief: A past participle is used after 'acabar de'.
5354.statement: A past participle is used after 'acabar de'.
5354.correction: An infinitive is used after 'acabar de'.

11087.belief: There is always a word for 'do' or 'did' in Spanish.
11087.statement: There is always a word for 'do' or 'did' in Spanish.
11087.correction: There is no word for 'do' or 'did' in Spanish questions.

5732.belief: It is possible to describe a photo without needing to use verbs.
5732.statement: It is possible to describe a photo without needing to use verbs.
5732.correction: It is necessary to use full sentences to successfully describe a photo. Sentences always include a verb.

8829.belief: Reflexive pronouns always come before the conjugated verb.
8829.statement: Reflexive pronouns always come before the conjugated verb.
8829.correction: Reflexive pronouns can go in two plaes: before the conjugated verb or or after the infinitive, attached to it, with 2-verb modal structures.

2753.belief: 'Estaba' only means 'I was' in the imperfect.
2753.statement: 'Estaba' only means 'I was' in the imperfect.
2753.correction: 'Estaba' means 'I was' but also 'she, he, it was' in the imperfect.

8776.belief: Reading and re-reading a text is always an effective way to read for understanding and get the right answers to comprehension questions.
8776.statement: Reading and re-reading a text is always an effective way to read for understanding and get the right answers to comprehension questions.
8776.correction: Simply reading and re-reading a text isn't always the most effective way to read for understanding. Using active reading strategies such as reading the title and reading and annotating the questions can boost comprehension and accuracy in responses.

1972.belief: When conjugating verbs in Spanish, you always need to start by taking off the infinitive ending.
1972.statement: When conjugating verbs in Spanish, you always need to start by taking off the infinitive ending.
1972.correction: Some verb tenses, such as the inflectional future, are formed by adding the relevant ending to the infinitive. As such, the infinitive ending is not taken off.

3784.belief: The inflectional future communicates what is 'going to' happen.
3784.statement: The inflectional future communicates what is 'going to' happen.
3784.correction: The inflectional future communicates what 'will' happen. 'Voy a + infinitive' communicates what is 'going to' happen.

5832.belief: When producing written work in Spanish, I should stick to short simple sentences.
5832.statement: When producing written work in Spanish, I should stick to short simple sentences.
5832.correction: When producing written work in Spanish, you should try to develop and extend your sentences to demonstrate grammatical complexity.

9501.belief: In Spanish, the SSC [qui] is pronounced as in 'queen'.
9501.statement: In Spanish, the SSC [qui] is pronounced as in 'queen'.
9501.correction: In Spanish, the SSC [qui] is pronounced as in 'equipo'.

9509.belief: The Spanish translation of 'I played football on Monday' is 'jugué al fútbol en lunes'.
9509.statement: The Spanish translation of 'I played football on Monday' is 'jugué al fútbol en lunes'.
9509.correction: Rather then the preposition 'en', Spanish uses the definite article before days of the week. As such, the Spanish translation of 'I played football on Monday' is 'jugué al fútbol el lunes'.

8919.belief: When responding to conversation questions, it will suffice to give one-word answers.
8919.statement: When responding to conversation questions, it will suffice to give one-word answers.
8919.correction: Conversation answers should be consistently developed with 2-3 clauses. One-word answers are not enough.

3124.belief: To form any verb in the conditional, add a conditional ending to the infinitive.
3124.statement: To form any verb in the conditional, add a conditional ending to the infinitive.
3124.correction: Not all verbs are regular in the conditional and some don't follow this pattern. Some verbs have irregular stems in the conditional, e.g. 'tener' ('tendr-') and 'poder' ('podr-').

9473.belief: In Spanish, all adjectives must be placed after the noun.
9473.statement: In Spanish, all adjectives must be placed after the noun.
9473.correction: The position of adjectives in Spanish can be flexible. When adjectives follow nouns, this communicates a literal, objective description. If an adjective is placed before a noun, this can communicate a figurative, subjective description.

4118.belief: The letter 'r' is always pronounced the same in Spanish.
4118.statement: The letter 'r' is always pronounced the same in Spanish.
4118.correction: In Spanish, 'r' is pronounced differently depending on its position within a word. 'r' in the middle or at the end of a word is pronounced as in 'pero', whereas 'r' at the beginning of a word and 'rr' are pronounced as in 'perro'.

5199.belief: One-word answers are sufficient in the role play.
5199.statement: One-word answers are sufficient in the role play.
5199.correction: It's important to say a few words or a short phrase/sentence in response to each prompt/bullet rather than one-word answers.

3660.belief: It is important to use a range of verb tenses and complex language in role-play answers.
3660.statement: It is important to use a range of verb tenses and complex language in role-play answers.
3660.correction: Role-play answers must consist of short words or phrases. Overcomplicating answers runs the risk of introducing ambiguity through grammatical error.

5768.belief: The preposition 'à' is used to mean 'to' or 'in' for both cities and countries.
5768.statement: The preposition 'à' is used to mean 'to' or 'in' for both cities and countries.
5768.correction: Prepositions can be tricky to master. Students must practise them carefully and thoroughly. Use 'à' before a city or town. Use 'en' before a feminine country or region. Use 'au' before a masculine country or region and 'aux' before a plural country.

10835.belief: All verbs in French can be used before an infinitive without a preposition.
10835.statement: All verbs in French can be used before an infinitive without a preposition.
10835.correction: Certain verbs require 'à' or 'de' before a an infinitive. Learning which verbs this applies to is helpful. Teachers might like to point out the more frequently occurring verbs of this type to help students develop their confidence in using them.

3588.belief: The ideas 'to', 'in', 'of' always have the same translation in French.
3588.statement: The ideas 'to', 'in', 'of' always have the same translation in French.
3588.correction: Prepositions are tricky to master in another language. Students should be given plenty of practice of 'à', 'en' and 'de' to see how their use varies according to context.

3155.belief: French indirect object pronouns are all the same as direct object pronouns.
3155.statement: French indirect object pronouns are all the same as direct object pronouns.
3155.correction: While some object pronouns are the same when used both indirectly and directly (e.g. me, te), there are some differences that students need to learn. It is a good idea to provide plenty of practice in this area to help students gain confidence.

9205.belief: There are separate indirect object pronouns in French to replace masculine and feminine nouns.
9205.statement: There are separate indirect object pronouns in French to replace masculine and feminine nouns.
9205.correction: French indirect object pronouns make no distinction for gender (unlike direct object pronouns). 'Lui' means both '(to) him' and '(to) her'. 'Leur' means '(to) them' and can refer to both masculine and feminine nouns.

10907.belief: I want to avoid using object pronouns because my writing will be longer and therefore better if I just repeat all the nouns.
10907.statement: I want to avoid using object pronouns because my writing will be longer and therefore better if I just repeat all the nouns.
10907.correction: Although object pronouns use fewer words, it is much better style to use them to avoid repeating nouns. Appropriate use of object pronouns is also positively rewarded in exams as an example of complexity.

1745.belief: Cognates are pronounced the same way in French as they are in English.
1745.statement: Cognates are pronounced the same way in French as they are in English.
1745.correction: Cognates are often pronounced very differently in French. Students should not overlook the importance of practising pronunciation of cognates in order to better respond to listening stimuli as well as to develop a more authentic pronunciation.

5873.belief: The pronouns 'y' and 'en' go after the verb, as 'there' and 'of it/them' do in English.
5873.statement: The pronouns 'y' and 'en' go after the verb, as 'there' and 'of it/them' do in English.
5873.correction: 'Y' and 'en' go before the verb in a present tense sentence e.g. 'elle y va' and 'elle en boit'.

5441.belief: In the perfect tense, the pronouns y and en go before the past participle.
5441.statement: In the perfect tense, the pronouns y and en go before the past participle.
5441.correction: Both y and en go before the auxiliary verb in the perfect tense e.g. il y est allé, il en a mangé.

2444.belief: It doesn't matter if you address a stranger in France as 'tu' or as 'vous'.
2444.statement: It doesn't matter if you address a stranger in France as 'tu' or as 'vous'.
2444.correction: Using the correct register of address is very important for students. Practising role-plays in both formal and informal settings allows students to understand when to use the appropriate form of 'you'.

3635.belief: The imperative can only be used in the 'tu' and 'vous' forms in French, to instruct others to do something.
3635.statement: The imperative can only be used in the 'tu' and 'vous' forms in French, to instruct others to do something.
3635.correction: The imperative can be used in the 'nous' form in French. In this case, the imperative is suggesting what we should do, and is translated as 'let's' in English.

10002.belief: A subject pronoun or noun is always required when using a verb in French.
10002.statement: A subject pronoun or noun is always required when using a verb in French.
10002.correction: When using the imperative, neither subject pronoun nor noun is required. Match the spelling of the verb to the person or people who are being instructed.

4391.belief: When making suggestions, 'let's' needs to be said in French as a separate idea.
4391.statement: When making suggestions, 'let's' needs to be said in French as a separate idea.
4391.correction: In French, use the imperative in the 'nous' form to create the phrase 'let's + verb', e.g. 'allons...' means 'let's go...'.

10476.belief: There are two present tenses in French, simple present and present continuous, like English.
10476.statement: There are two present tenses in French, simple present and present continuous, like English.
10476.correction: There is only one present tense in French, which is used to communicate both English present tenses. For example, 'je joue au foot' can be translated as both I play football and I am playing football.

10599.belief: I use the French present participle -ant to translate -ing in English.
10599.statement: I use the French present participle -ant to translate -ing in English.
10599.correction: The present participle -ant is not the only way to translate -ing in English. Sometimes the French infinitive is needed, where English uses the -ing form as a noun, e.g., 'visiter le Maroc aide à mieux connaître sa culture'.

5780.belief: Present participles are always preceeded by 'en'.
5780.statement: Present participles are always preceeded by 'en'.
5780.correction: The present participles 'ayant', 'étant' and 'faisant de' can be used without the preposition 'en' e.g. 'Ayant une grand-mère musulmane, je sais beaucoup sur l'Islam' - having a muslim grandmother, I know a lot about Islam.

4366.belief: To make a comparative adjective in French, add the suffix -er to an adjective.
4366.statement: To make a comparative adjective in French, add the suffix -er to an adjective.
4366.correction: Most comparatives are formed using 'plus... que' (more... than), 'moins... que' (less... than), and 'aussi... que' (as... as). The adjective to compare goes in the middle and agrees with gender and number of the noun being compared.

4367.belief: To make comparatives and superlatives in French, add suffixes -er and -est to adjectives.
4367.statement: To make comparatives and superlatives in French, add suffixes -er and -est to adjectives.
4367.correction: Suffixes -er and -est do not exist in French. To form comparatives, use the forms 'more', 'less... than' - 'plus... que' and 'moins... que'. To form superlatives, use the forms 'the most', 'the least' - 'le, la, les plus' and 'le, la, les moins'.

10051.belief: The superlative in French always goes before the noun it describes, like in English.
10051.statement: The superlative in French always goes before the noun it describes, like in English.
10051.correction: Superlatives may go before or after the noun they describe. The rule that applies is BRAGS - if an adjective goes before the noun according to the BRAGS rule, its superlative form will also go before the noun.

4997.statement: Some nouns ending in -ion or -ation are masculine.
4997.correction: Every noun ending in -ion and -ation is feminine. There are no exceptions.

188.belief: All agent nouns are formed by adding either -eur or -ateur to the stem of the verb.
188.statement: All agent nouns are formed by adding either -eur or -ateur to the stem of the verb.
188.correction: Most agent nouns follow this rule but there are exceptions, for example 'éduquer' - 'to educate', becomes 'éducateur' - 'educator'. A stem change is needed here.

189.belief: All agent nouns in French end in -eur, e.g. 'joueur'.
189.statement: All agent nouns in French end in -eur, e.g. 'joueur'.
189.correction: Many French agent nouns have the '-ateur' ending, for example 'consommateur', which means 'consumer'. This is because these agent nouns are linked to the original Latin forms that French has maintained today.

5003.correction: 'Nous' means 'we' when used as a subject pronoun, but it means 'us' when used as a direct object pronoun and '(to) us' when used as an indirect object pronoun.

5202.belief: There is only one word in French to translate 'mine', 'yours', 'his', 'hers'.
5202.statement: There is only one word in French to translate 'mine', 'yours', 'his', 'hers'.
5202.correction: In French, possessive pronouns match the gender and number of the noun they replace in a sentence. They are formed of the definite article and the pronoun, for example: 'les chocolats, ce sont les miens,' meaning 'the chocolates, they are mine'.

2397.belief: Direct object pronouns can be used with verbs followed by 'à' like 'demander' and 'donner'.
2397.statement: Direct object pronouns can be used with verbs followed by 'à' like 'demander' and 'donner'.
2397.correction: Indirect object pronouns should be used with these verbs because you ask 'of' and give 'to' someone in French. In English, the 'to' is often dropped with these kinds of verbs, e.g. 'je lui donne un cadeau' - 'I give (to) him, her a present'.

2423.belief: There are distinct words required in French to translate 'will' and 'would'.
2423.statement: There are distinct words required in French to translate 'will' and 'would'.
2423.correction: The 1-verb future tense describes 'will + verb'. The conditional describes 'would + verb'. Students should be aware that both verb forms are 'simple' forms as all the meaning is contained within a single word.

3163.belief: In French, there is a separate word for 'would'.
3163.statement: In French, there is a separate word for 'would'.
3163.correction: The conditional verb form expresses the idea of 'would + verb' in its spelling. Students should be encouraged to used the conditional form of verbs instead of being over reliant on 'vouloir' in the conditional.

3872.belief: It isn't important to answer both bullet points in the longer writing task equally.
3872.statement: It isn't important to answer both bullet points in the longer writing task equally.
3872.correction: Students should plan carefully to address both bullet points in an equal manner, giving detailed answers and using a rich selection of language. Using the BORDER acronym helps students to fully answer the task.

9207.belief: A separate word for 'will' and 'would' needs to be translated into French when using future or conditional verbs.
9207.statement: A separate word for 'will' and 'would' needs to be translated into French when using future or conditional verbs.
9207.correction: The 1-verb future and conditional verb forms express 'will' and 'would' in their spellings. No separate word is required.

10630.belief: Use the present tense after 'si' and before the conditional to say what you would do.
10630.statement: Use the present tense after 'si' and before the conditional to say what you would do.
10630.correction: French uses the combination of 'si' + imperfect + conditional to express what would happen if a certain condition occurred e.g. If I won the lottery, I would move to France.

1921.belief: The conditional can always be used on its own without a prior conditional being described.
1921.statement: The conditional can always be used on its own without a prior conditional being described.
1921.correction: Apart from the verbs 'aimer' and 'vouloir', always use the conditional form of verb with a 'si' + imperfect sentence. It is not logical to say in French 'I would buy a villa' without an accompanying condition e.g. if I had lots of money.

9206.belief: There is a separate word for 'will' in French when talking about the future.
9206.statement: There is a separate word for 'will' in French when talking about the future.
9206.correction: The spelling of a verb in the 1-verb future form contains the idea of 'will' + verb e.g. il visitera = he will visit.

3164.belief: In French, there is a separate word for 'would' that is used with an infinitive to express what someone 'would' do.
3164.statement: In French, there is a separate word for 'would' that is used with an infinitive to express what someone 'would' do.
3164.correction: The conditional form of verbs expresses 'would' + verb e.g. je visiterais - I would visit. There is no word for 'would' in French.

5785.belief: Only the present tense is required when performing the photo description task.
5785.statement: Only the present tense is required when performing the photo description task.
5785.correction: The present tense will mostly be used to describe a photo; however, other tenses are required for the follow-up questions based on the topic of the photo. Students should be able to use future and conditional verbs to discuss future plans.

10834.belief: Verbs in French that relate to personal actions are only composed the same as in English.
10834.statement: Verbs in French that relate to personal actions are only composed the same as in English.
10834.correction: Many verbs relating to daily routine are reflexive in French and require a reflexive pronoun to be used, e.g., 'je me lève'. This reflexive pronoun is not always used in English.

10852.belief: All verbs using reflexive pronouns are reflexive.
10852.statement: All verbs using reflexive pronouns are reflexive.
10852.correction: Reciprocal verbs use the reflexive pronouns 'se', 'nous' and 'vous'. They are used to express actions that two or more people perform with, or for, each other, e.g. 'nous nous écrivons souvent' - 'we often write to each other'.

8830.belief: Reflexive pronouns are only used to talk about actions done to oneself.
8830.statement: Reflexive pronouns are only used to talk about actions done to oneself.
8830.correction: Reflexive pronouns are also used with verbs to indicate a reciprocal (shared) action between two or more subjects. Verbs can only be reciprocal with plural subjects, i.e. 'nous', 'vous' and 'ils/elles'.

8720.correction: When used in an interrogative sense, 'qui?' means 'who?'. As a relative pronoun, 'qui' introduces more information about the subject in the main clause and can be translated as 'who', 'which' or 'that'.

3645.belief: The imperfect tense is only used to describe how things were or used to be in the past.
3645.statement: The imperfect tense is only used to describe how things were or used to be in the past.
3645.correction: The imperfect tense is also used to say what was happening when another thing occurred where it is used in combination with the perfect tense e.g. il regardait la télé quand son portable a sonné.

327.belief: Answers to conversation questions should only be given in the same tense as the question.
327.statement: Answers to conversation questions should only be given in the same tense as the question.
327.correction: Students should develop answers to conversation questions in order to give additional information and detail. Using different tenses allows students to give a more detailed and complex answer.

3169.belief: There is a French verb 'to can'.
3169.statement: There is a French verb 'to can'.
3169.correction: The English idea of 'can' is translated in French by the verb 'pouvoir' meaning 'to be able to'.

2567.belief: It is easy to predict the past participles of irregular verbs.
2567.statement: It is easy to predict the past participles of irregular verbs.
2567.correction: The past participles of irregular verbs must be learnt carefully. There are, however, similarities that are worth noting e.g. many irregular past participles end -u e.g. pu, voulu, cru, su.

10657.belief: You must only use verbs in the same tense as the task question in your answer.
10657.statement: You must only use verbs in the same tense as the task question in your answer.
10657.correction: Students should practise combining different tenses of verbs when giving their answers (ensuring they give a relevant response to the task) in order to demonstrate a wider knowledge of language and to give a richer response.

3168.belief: French uses the present participle after the preposition 'sans'.
3168.statement: French uses the present participle after the preposition 'sans'.
3168.correction: 'Sans' is followed by an infinitive in French where in English the present participle would be used, e.g. 'without knowing', 'without looking'.

351.belief: The 'après avoir' + past participle structure applies to all verbs.
351.statement: The 'après avoir' + past participle structure applies to all verbs.
351.correction: Verbs which take 'être' in the perfect tense use the structure 'après être' + past participle. The past participle must agree with the subject of the sentence, e.g. 'après être arrivée, elle a fait ses devoirs'.

9073.belief: There are always the same number of words used when translating between languages.
9073.statement: There are always the same number of words used when translating between languages.
9073.correction: As languages are complex, many ideas are expressed differently in different languages. When translating, more or fewer words might be needed to convey the information e.g. avant de passer un examan - before sitting an exam.

8848.belief: All regular verbs have a past participle ending in 'é', 'u' or 'i'.
8848.statement: All regular verbs have a past participle ending in 'é', 'u' or 'i'.
8848.correction: There are other groups of regular verbs with different endings to the main -er, -re, -ir groups. These verbs are very commonly used and students should practise them regularly.

5353.belief: Past participle agreement only occurs in the perfect tense.
5353.statement: Past participle agreement only occurs in the perfect tense.
5353.correction: In the passive voice, all past participles are combined with a form of 'être'. As such, past participle agreement rules apply to all verbs, e.g. 'la scène est critiquée par le journaliste'.

191.belief: There is no agreement needed with 'avoir' verb past participles in the passive voice.
191.statement: There is no agreement needed with 'avoir' verb past participles in the passive voice.
191.correction: Because the passive voice uses 'être', all past participles used must agree in number and gender with the noun subject, including 'avoir' verbs. E.g. La fille est choisie par le réalisateur.

2870.belief: The expression 'j'ai mal' only means 'I have a pain'.
2870.statement: The expression 'j'ai mal' only means 'I have a pain'.
2870.correction: The French expression 'avoir mal' covers a number of symptoms which might be variously translated into English as an ache, a pain and sore or hurting body parts. Students should think about what sounds most natural when translating into English.

4867.belief: You need to include 'pas' when using a negative subject pronoun.
4867.statement: You need to include 'pas' when using a negative subject pronoun.
4867.correction: The whole negative meaning is contained in the negative subject pronoun (rien or personne) with 'ne' before the following verb. An additional negative element is not necessary e.g. Personne ne mange sainement - nobody eats healthily.

5615.belief: 'Plusieurs' and 'chaque' have singular and plural forms.
5615.statement: 'Plusieurs' and 'chaque' have singular and plural forms.
5615.correction: 'Plusieurs' is always written with an 's' and introduces a plural noun e.g. plusieurs problèmes. 'Chaque' is always written in the singular and introduces a singular noun e.g. chaque problème.

10619.belief: Use 'ne... pas' to mean 'no, not one, not any'.
10619.statement: Use 'ne... pas' to mean 'no, not one, not any'.
10619.correction: The structure 'ne... pas' is used to negative a verb. To say that there was 'no, not one, not any' of a noun, use the structure 'ne... aucun/aucune', e.g. 'il n'y a aucun fruit ici'.

2872.belief: An extended 150-word writing task should be planned as one complete task.
2872.statement: An extended 150-word writing task should be planned as one complete task.
2872.correction: It is helpful to break down an extended writing task into two paragraphs and then to further break down those paragraphs. This allows students to manage the length of the task by treating it as four smaller connected tasks.

5775.belief: The present continous in English has a direct translation in French.
5775.statement: The present continous in English has a direct translation in French.
5775.correction: Students need to take care to translate both the simple present and the present continous with the present tense in French e.g. I listen and I am listening are translated exactly the same way: j'écoute.

10312.belief: There are only three types of regular verbs and they form their past participles in the same way.
10312.statement: There are only three types of regular verbs and they form their past participles in the same way.
10312.correction: There are distinct groups of 'ir' and 're' verbs which form their past participles differently from the regular pattern (-i, -u). Students will find it beneficial to learn these verbs together as a group.

65.belief: It is acceptable to only give short answers in the conversation element of the speaking exam.
65.statement: It is acceptable to only give short answers in the conversation element of the speaking exam.
65.correction: Students should focus on giving answers in conversation that include at least three verb clauses. They should also regularly practise developing their answers with different verb tenses, subjects, opinions and reasons.

3688.belief: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
3688.statement: I should include as much detail as possible in role-play answers.
3688.correction: When performing a role-play, answers should contain one verb and be concise. Do not add unnecessary detail.

4473.belief: All masculine nouns are made feminine by adding 'e' and plural by adding 's'.
4473.statement: All masculine nouns are made feminine by adding 'e' and plural by adding 's'.
4473.correction: A masculine noun can be made feminine by changing the article, adding 'e', changing 'eur' to 'ice' or 'n' to 'nne'. Nouns can be made plural by adding 's' or 'aux'. Nouns ending in 's' or 'x' don't have a plural form.

318.belief: I can only answer conversation questions in the same tense as the question.
318.statement: I can only answer conversation questions in the same tense as the question.
318.correction: After responding appropriately to the initial question, it is a good idea to use different tenses in your answer to develop your response and to give interesting detail.

10636.belief: Use the same articles for nouns after negative structures.
10636.statement: Use the same articles for nouns after negative structures.
10636.correction: After a negative structure (e.g. 'je n'ai pas'), indefinite and partitive articles change to 'de', e.g. 'je n'ai pas d'information' - 'I don't have any information'.

3877.belief: There isn't much I can do to prepare for the French reading exam.
3877.statement: There isn't much I can do to prepare for the French reading exam.
3877.correction: Regularly revising vocabulary is an excellent method of preparation for the reading exam as well as being mindful of strategies such as spotting distractors and using synonyms to find the correct answer.

851.belief: I can't use the imperfect and perfect tenses together.
851.statement: I can't use the imperfect and perfect tenses together.
851.correction: The two past tenses work together well to give a full description of past events. Use the perfect tense for completed actions and the imperfect to describe what things were like.

10851.belief: All verbs use their infinitive to form the stem in the future tense.
10851.statement: All verbs use their infinitive to form the stem in the future tense.
10851.correction: There are key irregular verb stems to learn for the future tense. Confident use of these verbs will add greatly to overall accuracy and help students to express themselves confidently in the future tense.

3876.belief: There isn't much I can do to prepare for the French listening exam.
3876.statement: There isn't much I can do to prepare for the French listening exam.
3876.correction: Students with a firm knowledge of French SSCs and strong vocabulary recall will find the listening exam less daunting. It is important to listen actively and use strategies for success such as awareness of distractors and synonyms.

3779.belief: Infinitive verbs are only used when they follow a conjugated verb.
3779.statement: Infinitive verbs are only used when they follow a conjugated verb.
3779.correction: When an infinitive is used at the start of a clause, it becomes a noun, e.g. 'Étudier est un bon moyen de trouver un meilleur emploi.'. ('Studying is a good way to find a better job.')

3172.belief: In French there is a word for 'do/does' in yes/no questions.
3172.statement: In French there is a word for 'do/does' in yes/no questions.
3172.correction: The English verb 'do/does' isn't translated directly into French when asking a yes/no question. Instead, use intonation, inversion or 'est-ce que' to ask yes/no questions, e.g. 'Aimes-tu les réseaux sociaux?' - 'Do you like social media?'.

10335.belief: The more times I read the text, the better I’ll understand it.
10335.statement: The more times I read the text, the better I’ll understand it.
10335.correction: Simply re-reading without purpose doesn’t necessarily lead to better comprehension. Strategies such as reading through the text and questions, using each question to find the relevant part of the text, avoiding distractors, etc., are more effective.

2401.belief: There is a direct translation in French of the English verbs 'must' and 'can'.
2401.statement: There is a direct translation in French of the English verbs 'must' and 'can'.
2401.correction: The idea of 'must' is conveyed by the verb 'devoir' (to have to do something). 'Can' is expressed with 'pouvoir' (to be able to do something).

10939.belief: The only way an adjective is made feminine is by adding the letter 'e' to a masculine adjective.
10939.statement: The only way an adjective is made feminine is by adding the letter 'e' to a masculine adjective.
10939.correction: Although many feminine adjectives are formed by adding 'e' to a masculine adjective, there are other feminine endings and rules governing these, e.g. -se, -elle, -enne, -ve, -ère.

5763.belief: I can only prepare for the listening exam by learning vocabulary and grammar.
5763.statement: I can only prepare for the listening exam by learning vocabulary and grammar.
5763.correction: While a strong grasp of grammar and excellent recall of vocabulary is essential, there are also strategies to help students achieve success in the listening exam. Prediction of words and phrases is one method to actively engage with listening.

644.belief: It is better to give long answers in the role-play task than short responses.
644.statement: It is better to give long answers in the role-play task than short responses.
644.correction: The role-play task is a short exercise requiring relevant answers to each bullet point that contain a verb. Longer answers are not appropriate to this task.

10609.belief: Always use the infinitive to translate the '-ing' verb form into French.
10609.statement: Always use the infinitive to translate the '-ing' verb form into French.
10609.correction: The infinitive used as a noun in French translates the idea of 'doing' something, e.g. 'fumer est mauvais' ('smoking is bad'). The present participle translates the present continuous in English, e.g. 'étant célèbre' ('being famous').

2309.belief: I should develop my answers as much as possible for all parts of the speaking exam.
2309.statement: I should develop my answers as much as possible for all parts of the speaking exam.
2309.correction: It is not necessary to develop your answers extensively for all parts of the speaking exam. Remember to keep your answers short and succinct in the role-play section.

9596.belief: I should start transcribing as soon as the dictation begins.
9596.statement: I should start transcribing as soon as the dictation begins.
9596.correction: It is useful to listen to the full sentence once before transcribing to get an idea of its meaning. This will help you write the sentence down and check it during the second and third times that the audio is played.

2265.belief: When describing the photo in the writing exam, I should develop my sentences with justified opinions and a range of verb tenses.
2265.statement: When describing the photo in the writing exam, I should develop my sentences with justified opinions and a range of verb tenses.
2265.correction: You should keep photo description sentences short and simple in the writing exam.

328.belief: Answers in listening comprehension questions are usually obvious.
328.statement: Answers in listening comprehension questions are usually obvious.
328.correction: Listening comprehension passages do not always make answers obvious, often containing synonyms and distractors to test your attention to detail.

1639.belief: I can choose which bullet points I answer for the essay questions in the writing paper.
1639.statement: I can choose which bullet points I answer for the essay questions in the writing paper.
1639.correction: You must answer all bullet points for the essay questions in the writing paper.

9067.belief: The same amount of words are used when translating between French and English.
9067.statement: The same amount of words are used when translating between French and English.
9067.correction: Due to the nature of the languages, there may be differences in how some words or ideas are translated e.g. I need is 'j'ai besoin de' in French. More or fewer words might be necessary to complete an accurate translation.

10838.belief: Verbs with inseparable prefixes do not change when forming their past participle.
10838.statement: Verbs with inseparable prefixes do not change when forming their past participle.
10838.correction: Verbs with inseparable prefixes do not add 'ge-' when forming their past participle, but many do have vowel changes, e.g., 'vermeiden' becomes 'vermieden', 'empfehlen' becomes 'empfohlen'.

597.correction: 'Bei' can mean 'at (the)' or 'with (the)' when followed by a noun, but it can also be used to mean 'whilst' or 'in the process of' before a nominalised infinitive.

4084.belief: You always leave out the subject pronoun when using the imperative.
4084.statement: You always leave out the subject pronoun when using the imperative.
4084.correction: The 'du' and 'ihr' forms of the imperative omit the subject pronoun, but the 'Sie' form retains it.

324.belief: When answering a question about yourself, just change the verb form in the question to a 1st person verb.
324.statement: When answering a question about yourself, just change the verb form in the question to a 1st person verb.
324.correction: It is important to change the verb form, but it might also be necessary to change other language, such as subject pronouns, possessive adjectives and reflexive pronouns in order to change the 2nd person question into a 1st person answer.

9650.belief: Strong verbs follow a different pattern to weak verbs in every person of the verb.
9650.statement: Strong verbs follow a different pattern to weak verbs in every person of the verb.
9650.correction: Strong verbs only change their stem vowel in the 'du' and 'er, sie, es' forms of the verb. Otherwise they follow the regular pattern of weak verbs.

89.belief: When adapting a question to a different form of 'you', just change the pronoun, e.g., from 'du' to 'Sie'.
89.statement: When adapting a question to a different form of 'you', just change the pronoun, e.g., from 'du' to 'Sie'.
89.correction: When adapting a question from 'du' to a different form of you ('ihr' or 'Sie'), it's important to also change the verb form. With strong verbs, this can also involve a stem vowel change e.g., 'isst du?' becomes 'essen Sie?'.

11066.correction: As an adjective, 'laut' means 'loud', and as an adverb it means 'loudly'. However, when used as a preposition followed by the dative case, it means 'according to'.

3844.belief: Intonation doesn't make much difference when reading aloud.
3844.statement: Intonation doesn't make much difference when reading aloud.
3844.correction: Using correct intonation can also help you correctly pronounce German sounds and help you communicate clearly, such as pausing briefly when you see commas or full stops, or the rising pitch of your voice when asking questions.

5154.belief: There is one set of adjective endings in German.
5154.statement: There is one set of adjective endings in German.
5154.correction: Adjective endings agree in case, gender and number with nouns, and there are different sets of adjective endings, depending on what word comes before the adjective. There are useful tables that can be learned to support correct usage.

5443.belief: The perfect tense is used only in speaking and the simple past only in writing.
5443.statement: The perfect tense is used only in speaking and the simple past only in writing.
5443.correction: The perfect tense can be used in informal writing and to describe a past event which has relevance to the present. The simple past is normally for writing, but 'war', 'hatte', 'gab' and modal verbs ('musste', 'wollte') are commonly used in speech.

10848.belief: All verbs with a second infinitive need 'zu'.
10848.statement: All verbs with a second infinitive need 'zu'.
10848.correction: Although some verbs do need 'zu' when used with a second verb in the infinitive (e.g., 'versuchen', 'planen', 'vergessen', 'hoffen'), modal verbs never use 'zu'.

8708.belief: The question word 'wer' is used whenever we want to say 'who'.
8708.statement: The question word 'wer' is used whenever we want to say 'who'.
8708.correction: 'Wer' means 'who' in the nominative case only. It changes to 'wen' in accusative and 'wem' in the dative case. In English, 'wen' and 'wem' also mean 'whom', although this word is used less frequently.

4136.correction: It is easy to confuse the words 'Liebe', 'liebe' and 'lieber', particularly in spoken German. Pay careful attention to pronunciation and listen out for [er]. 'Liebe' is a noun (love), 'liebe' is a verb (love) and 'lieber' is an adverb (more gladly).

10616.belief: Use 'mehr' with adjectives and adverbs to make comparisons.
10616.statement: Use 'mehr' with adjectives and adverbs to make comparisons.
10616.correction: Use the comparative form of adjectives and adverbs to make comparisons, e.g., 'interessanter als', not 'mehr interessant als'.
