129.belief: Adjectival nouns do not require a capital letter because they come from adjectives.
129.statement: Adjectival nouns do not require a capital letter because they come from adjectives.
129.correction: Adjectival nouns require a capital letter, just like all nouns in German.

10829.belief: Only verbs expressing a change of state take 'sein' in the perfect tense.
10829.statement: Only verbs expressing a change of state take 'sein' in the perfect tense.
10829.correction: Verbs referring to motion, which don't require a direct object (e.g., 'gehen'), take 'sein' in the perfect tense. Most verbs meaning 'happen' (e.g., 'geschehen', 'passieren') and the verbs 'bleiben' and 'sein' also use 'sein'.

4998.belief: All nouns ending '-n' must be in the dative case.
4998.statement: All nouns ending '-n' must be in the dative case.
4998.correction: The definite article 'den' shows the dative plural form as well as the '-n' added to the end of the dative plural. However, a number of nouns form their plural by adding '-(e)n' and are not in the dative case.

10662.belief: Use 'welche' to translate 'which' in a relative clause.
10662.statement: Use 'welche' to translate 'which' in a relative clause.
10662.correction: Do not use a question word to translate 'which' when adding information about the noun in the main clause. ‘Was’ can be used as a relative pronoun meaning ‘that' or 'which’ when referring to a whole clause, not a specific noun.

10987.belief: Whenever two-verb structures are used, the second verb - the infinitive or the past participle - always goes to the end of the clause or sentence.
10987.statement: Whenever two-verb structures are used, the second verb - the infinitive or the past participle - always goes to the end of the clause or sentence.
10987.correction: The second verb goes to the end with normal word order and WO1 conjunctions like 'und', 'aber', 'oder' and 'sondern'. But with WO3 conjunctions, the main or finite verb is sent to the end of the clause.

10032.belief: You can only succeed in listening comprehension if you know all the vocabulary.
10032.statement: You can only succeed in listening comprehension if you know all the vocabulary.
10032.correction: Whilst vocabulary knowledge is the most important element for success, other strategies can help, for example, close pre-reading of the questions, predicting vocabulary, avoiding distractors and checking answers carefully.

10658.belief: Always use 'würd-' and a 2nd (infinitive) verb at the end of the sentence to mean 'would'.
10658.statement: Always use 'würd-' and a 2nd (infinitive) verb at the end of the sentence to mean 'would'.
10658.correction: This works for many verbs, but 'haben' and 'sein' have their own forms - 'hätte' ('would have') and 'wäre' ('would be'). No second infinitive is required.

5773.belief: All prepositions are followed by only one case - for example, the accusative or the dative.
5773.statement: All prepositions are followed by only one case - for example, the accusative or the dative.
5773.correction: The prepositions 'an, 'auf', 'in', ‘über’, 'unter', ‘vor’, 'hinter', 'neben' and ‘zwischen’ are used with the accusative case when there is movement, but the dative case when there is no movement.

8716.belief: All questions in German invert the subject and verb. Apart from that the word order is the same as English.
8716.statement: All questions in German invert the subject and verb. Apart from that the word order is the same as English.
8716.correction: Subject and verb are inverted, but word order differs from English for a verb with a preposition - 'What are you talking about?'. In German, a preposition never ends a question. Use 'wo(r)' + preposition to start the question - 'Worüber redest du?'.

3940.correction: Whilst we often use 'can' to translate both verbs in English, they are different in meaning. 'Dürfen' refers to permission - 'may I/am I allowed to?'. 'Können' refers to the ability to do something - 'can I/am I able to?'.

3270.belief: The German subject pronoun 'man' must always be translated using the English subject pronoun 'one'.
3270.statement: The German subject pronoun 'man' must always be translated using the English subject pronoun 'one'.
3270.correction: 'Man' has a range of possible translations, including 'people' and 'you'. It can also be used to say what 'is done' or 'was done' by people in general.

1973.belief: The conjunction 'obwohl' has the same effect on word order whether it starts the sentence or a second clause in a sentence.
1973.statement: The conjunction 'obwohl' has the same effect on word order whether it starts the sentence or a second clause in a sentence.
1973.correction: The conjunction 'obwohl' always triggers word order 3 in a clause. However, if the sentence starts with the 'obwohl' clause, we then use the verb-comma-verb rule, meaning the second clause starts with the verb.

11152.belief: When writing in German, accuracy is the most important thing, so it's best to keep sentences short and clear.
11152.statement: When writing in German, accuracy is the most important thing, so it's best to keep sentences short and clear.
11152.correction: When producing written work in German, try to develop and extend your sentences to demonstrate grammatical complexity. This must, of course, be balanced with accuracy, which enables you to communicate your ideas clearly.

2153.belief: Da-compounds can always be translated literally, with the preposition retaining its usual meaning.
2153.statement: Da-compounds can always be translated literally, with the preposition retaining its usual meaning.
2153.correction: German verb and preposition combinations need to be learnt. We often use different prepositions after verbs in English and in German. Some da-compounds have also taken on slightly different meanings when used as adverbs or in idiomatic phrases.

4901.belief: We need to use the present continuous in German when describing photos.
4901.statement: We need to use the present continuous in German when describing photos.
4901.correction: There is only one present tense in German. The present continuous in German is the same as the simple present, so 'sie essen' means 'they eat' and 'they are eating'. When translating English present continuous sentences, use the simple present.

8869.belief: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions.
8869.statement: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions.
8869.correction: Whilst strategies such as prediction and avoiding distractors are very helpful, the single most important factor in successfuly answering listening questions is having a secure knowledge of vocabulary.

3262.belief: All German past participles start with 'ge-'.
3262.statement: All German past participles start with 'ge-'.
3262.correction: Verbs starting with inseparable prefixes like 'be-', 'er-', 'ent-' and 'ver-' do not need 'ge'. Neither do verbs ending in '-ieren', e.g., 'interessiert'. Separable prefixes appear before 'ge-' in the perfect tense, e.g., 'aufgemacht', 'eingeführt'.

8871.belief: I can rely on strategies like recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all reading comprehension questions.
8871.statement: I can rely on strategies like recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all reading comprehension questions.
8871.correction: Whilst strategies such as recognising synonyms and avoiding distractors are very helpful, they are only possible with a really secure and broad knowledge of the vocabulary list. Consolidating vocabulary is therefore the most important preparation.

10664.belief: Always use 'werden' and a 2nd verb in the infinitive to express future ideas.
10664.statement: Always use 'werden' and a 2nd verb in the infinitive to express future ideas.
10664.correction: In German future ideas can be expressed by the present tense with a future time phrase. They can also be expressed by 'werden' plus a 2nd verb, or by 'möcht-' to say what you would like to do in the future.

4185.belief: Like in a role-play, I should keep answers short and concise in a conversation.
4185.statement: Like in a role-play, I should keep answers short and concise in a conversation.
4185.correction: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.

4186.belief: Like in a role-play, I should keep my answers short and concise in a conversation.
4186.statement: Like in a role-play, I should keep my answers short and concise in a conversation.
4186.correction: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.

4187.belief: Like in a role-play, pupils should keep their answers short and concise in a conversation.
4187.statement: Like in a role-play, pupils should keep their answers short and concise in a conversation.
4187.correction: Conversation answers should be developed and extended with at least three verb clauses.

1974.belief: All conjunctions cause the verb to be sent to the end of the clause.
1974.statement: All conjunctions cause the verb to be sent to the end of the clause.
1974.correction: Subordinating conjunctions, such as 'weil', 'dass', 'ob' and 'obwohl' send the verb to the end of the clause. Coordinating conjunctions, such as 'und', 'aber', 'denn' and 'oder' are followed by word order 1 (standard subject-verb-object word order).

3778.belief: The infinitive or past participle always comes at the end of the clause when using two-verb structures.
3778.statement: The infinitive or past participle always comes at the end of the clause when using two-verb structures.
3778.correction: In standard word order (word order 1), the infinitive or past participle always comes at the end of the clause. However, after certain conjunctions (word order 3), the conjugated verb is sent to the end of the clause.

10941.belief: The only way to extend my sentences to add complexity is to add a subordinate clause with 'weil'.
10941.statement: The only way to extend my sentences to add complexity is to add a subordinate clause with 'weil'.
10941.correction: There are many ways to add complexity, including using subordinate clauses with a wide range of conjunctions, as well as adding relative clauses or infinitive constructions.

10402.belief: When translating into English from German, I only need to understand the gist of the sentences.
10402.statement: When translating into English from German, I only need to understand the gist of the sentences.
10402.correction: When translating, it's important to ensure that you have accounted for the meaning of every German word, even though you might not translate word-for-word into English.

4183.belief: Like in a picture description and conversation, I should develop my role-play answers as much as possible.
4183.statement: Like in a picture description and conversation, I should develop my role-play answers as much as possible.
4183.correction: When performing a role-play, answers should be a short phrase or sentence. Pupils should not add too much unnecessary detail.

3658.belief: It is important to say as much as possible when carrying out any speaking task.
3658.statement: It is important to say as much as possible when carrying out any speaking task.
3658.correction: When completing a role-play exam task, it is important to use at least one verb for each prompt. However, this is not the time to show off extended and developed sentences; it's more important to get the message across accurately and succinctly.

3263.belief: All German past participlies start with 'ge-'.
3263.statement: All German past participlies start with 'ge-'
3263.correction: Verbs starting with inseparable prefixes like 'be-', 'er-', 'ent-' and 'ver-' do not need 'ge'. Neither do verbs ending in '-ieren', e.g., 'interessiert'. Separable prefixes appear before 'ge-' in the perfect tense, e.g., 'aufgemacht', 'eingeführt'.

10410.belief: The only translation of 'hablamos' is 'we speak'.
10410.statement: The only translation of 'hablamos' is 'we speak'.
10410.correction: The ending -amos also corresponds to the 1st person plural form of the preterite for -ar verbs. Therefore, 'hablamos' can also mean 'we spoke'. The context of the verb should clarify which is the correct translation.

10823.belief: Verbs must always have different subjects and objects.
10823.statement: Verbs must always have different subjects and objects.
10823.correction: Verbs do not always have different subjects and objects. For example, reflexive verbs have the same subject and object.

9521.belief: Spanish words ending in a consonant other than -n or -s always show final syllable stress.
9521.statement: Spanish words ending in a consonant other than -n or -s always show final syllable stress.
9521.correction: Spanish words ending in a consonant other than -n or -s show final syllable stress unless otherwise indicated by an accent.

5781.belief: As in the present tense, -er and -ir verbs have different endings in the preterite tense.
5781.statement: As in the present tense, -er and -ir verbs have different endings in the preterite tense.
5781.correction: Verbs ending in -er and -ir have the same endings in the preterite tense.

9507.belief: The Spanish translation of 'the money is hers' (for exampl) is 'el dinero es suya' because the owner is feminine.
9507.statement: The Spanish translation of 'the money is hers' (for exampl) is 'el dinero es suya' because the owner is feminine.
9507.correction: The Spanish translation of 'the money is hers' is 'el dinero es suyo' because the object is masculine. Possessive adjectives agree with the object, not the owner.

4518.correction: 'Por' can mean several things in Spanish. For example, in addition to 'for', it can also mean 'by' and 'in' in certain contexts.

3748.belief: Indirect object pronouns are the same as emphatic pronouns.
3748.statement: Indirect object pronouns are the same as emphatic pronouns.
3748.correction: Indirect object pronouns refer to a person or thing indirectly affected by the verb and go before 'interesar'-type verbs, while emphatic pronouns are used for emphasis after prepositions.

10178.belief: 'Tener' + noun always translates in English as 'to have' + noun.
10178.statement: 'Tener' + noun always translates in English as 'to have' + noun.
10178.correction: The idiomatic expression 'tener' + noun is translated in English as 'to be' + adjective.

8699.correction: [que] is pronounced as in the word 'porque', and [cue] as in the word 'cuerpo'.

5330.belief: All participles in Spanish end in -ado or -ido.
5330.statement: All participles in Spanish end in -ado or -ido.
5330.correction: Regular verbs do follow this pattern, but irregular ones do not. Some irregular verbs are: 'decir' - 'dicho', 'morir' - 'muerto', 'romper' - 'roto', 'volver' - 'vuelto', 'descubrir' - 'descubierto', 'cubrir' - 'cubierto'.

2254.belief: To describe the past we can use both the preterite and the imperfect interchangeably.
2254.statement: To describe the past we can use both the preterite and the imperfect interchangeably.
2254.correction: We use the imperfect to set the scene, to give background information and to describe onling states. And we use the preterite to express completed actions that move the plot forward.

1863.belief: For completed events and actions in the past I can use either the preterite or the imperfect.
1863.statement: For completed events and actions in the past I can use either the preterite or the imperfect.
1863.correction: The imperfect is used to set the scene, give background information and for repeated actions in the past and the preterite to say what happened, talk about completed events and actions in the past.

2255.belief: I can describe a photo using single words.
2255.statement: I can describe a photo using single words.
2255.correction: When describing photos in Spanish, it is important to use full sentences with verbs. To make the description even more interesting and complex add justifications and contrasts.

2745.belief: 'Ese' and 'esa' are the only words for 'that' before a noun in Spanish.
2745.statement: 'Ese' and 'esa' are the only words for 'that' before a noun in Spanish.
2745.correction: 'Aquel' and 'aquella' also mean 'that' and refer to something far away in space or time.

10810.belief: The verb 'hacer' follows the same rule as 'poner' for forming the 1st person singular of the present tense.
10810.statement: The verb 'hacer' follows the same rule as 'poner' for forming the 1st person singular of the present tense.
10810.correction: The letter 'g' replaces the 'c' in hacer in the first person singular of the present tense.

10042.belief: It is sufficient to give one-word answers in a role-play.
10042.statement: It is sufficient to give one-word answers in a role-play.
10042.correction: In a role-play pupils need to answer each question with a short phrase or sentence.

2675.belief: As in English, indirect object pronouns follow the verb in Spanish.
2675.statement: As in English, indirect object pronouns follow the verb in Spanish.
2675.correction: In 1-verb constructions, indirect object pronouns precede the verb in Spanish. This word order is different to English.

18.belief: The 1st person singular form of 'influir' is 'influo'.
18.statement: The 1st person singular form of 'influir' is 'influo'.
18.correction: The verb 'influir' does not follow the normal pattern of -ir verbs. Verbs ending in -uir gain a 'y' in persons 1,2,3 and 6 to aid pronunciation. As such, the 1st person singular forms of 'influir' is 'influyo'.

2032.belief: Conversation answers should be kept as short and simple as possible.
2032.statement: Conversation answers should be kept as short and simple as possible.
2032.correction: It is important to develop conversation answers to showcase a range of vocabulary and grammar. This can be achieved by using adverbs to add more detail and by incorporating a range of grammatical persons.

3305.belief: To give an order or command to 'tú' (you, informal), you should use the 2nd person singular form of the verb.
3305.statement: To give an order or command to 'tú' (you, informal), you should use the 2nd person singular form of the verb.
3305.correction: When talking to somebody familiar to you ('tú') with the affirmative imperative of an -ar verb, use the ending -a, and for an -er or -ir verb, use the ending -e. Irregular imperative verbs include: 'sé', 've', 'ten', 'ven', 'haz', 'di', 'pon', 'sal'.

3114.belief: To form the plural imperative of a reflexive verb, add the pronoun -os to a plural imperative verb.
3114.statement: To form the plural imperative of a reflexive verb, add the pronoun -os to a plural imperative verb.
3114.correction: To form the plural imperative of a reflexive verb, drop the final -d and add the pronoun -os to a plural imperative verb.

4465.belief: I should mark down the first thing I hear as the correct answer when answering listening questions.
4465.statement: I should mark down the first thing I hear as the correct answer when answering listening questions.
4465.correction: It is important not to rush, and to listen to the whole text before answering a listening question.

2613.belief: 'El que' and 'el cual' are completely interchangeable.
2613.statement: 'El que' and 'el cual' are completely interchangeable.
2613.correction: 'El cual' tends to appear in more formal contexts than 'el que'.

4233.belief: 'Lo que' can refer to a specific noun or a person.
4233.statement: 'Lo que' can refer to a specific noun or a person.
4233.correction: 'Lo que' means 'what' or 'the thing that'. It refers to a general idea, rather than a specific noun or person.

2133.belief: 'Cuando' is always followed by the subjunctive.
2133.statement: 'Cuando' is always followed by the subjunctive.
2133.correction: 'Cuando' + subjunctive is used for future actions, while 'cuando' + present is used for everyday present actions.

2134.belief: After ‘cuando’ I always need the subjunctive forms 'tenga', 'tengas', 'tenga' to mean ‘I have', 'you have', 'she, he, it has’.
2134.statement: After ‘cuando’ I always need the subjunctive forms 'tenga', 'tengas', 'tenga' to mean ‘I have', 'you have', 'she, he, it has’.
2134.correction: After ‘cuando’ we use the subjunctive forms only when the action is not yet real, or is uncertain. When the action happens regularly, we use the indicative forms ‘tengo’, 'tienes', 'tiene’.

3978.belief: Knowing and using one listening strategy is enough.
3978.statement: Knowing and using one listening strategy is enough.
3978.correction: All three sets of strategies work together, and you should be flexible in applying them as needed throughout the listening process.

2739.belief: 'Es' + adjective + 'que' is always followed by the subjunctive.
2739.statement: 'Es' + adjective + 'que' is always followed by the subjunctive.
2739.correction: The subjunctive is used after 'es' + adjective + 'que' when the action is uncertain, desired or not a fact. When the verb before 'que' expresses certainty, the action after 'que' is more a statement of fact and does not require the subjunctive.

8723.belief: 'Quiero', espero', 'deseo', 'prefiero' are always followed by infinitives.
8723.statement: 'Quiero', espero', 'deseo', 'prefiero' are always followed by infinitives.
8723.correction: Use 'quiero' + infinitive when you want to do something yourself. Use 'quiero' + 'que' + subjunctive when you want someone else to do something. Both forms often talk about the future, but the change of subject triggers the use of subjunctive.

10014.belief: The subjunctive is a matter of the speaker's attitude so when I am the speaker I can always choose whether to use the subjunctive or not.
10014.statement: The subjunctive is a matter of the speaker's attitude so when I am the speaker I can always choose whether to use the subjunctive or not.
10014.correction: Certain situations and structures always require the subjunctive: 'cuando' + subjunctive + future tense for events that have not yet happened; 'es' + adjective + que for subjective points of view; verbs of wishing that someone else does something.

1775.belief: Command/request verbs are always followed by an infinitive, as in English, e.g. 'I want you to go', 'I'm asking you to leave'.
1775.statement: Command/request verbs are always followed by an infinitive, as in English, e.g. 'I want you to go', 'I'm asking you to leave'.
1775.correction: When the sentence refers to only one person, these verbs are followed by an infinitive, but if the sentence mentions two people, the command/request verbs are followed by a subjunctive.

9346.belief: The singular imperative form for 2nd person 'tú' is the same as the present tense ending: -as or -es.
9346.statement: The singular imperative form for 2nd person 'tú' is the same as the present tense ending: -as or -es.
9346.correction: The singular imperative form for 2nd person 'tú' is the same as the 3rd person present tense - the ending is -a for -ar verbs, and -e for -er and -ir verbs.

2201.belief: If I decide to use BORDER I will apply it once for the whole writing.
2201.statement: If I decide to use BORDER I will apply it once for the whole writing.
2201.correction: If you choose to use BORDER, apply it to each paragraph separately. This will help you respond clearly and completely to each bullet point.

10394.belief: I can translate verbs like 'basta' and 'hace falta' word-for-word.
10394.statement: I can translate verbs like 'basta' and 'hace falta' word-for-word.
10394.correction: Verbs like 'basta' and 'hace falta' can’t always be translated word-for-word - they don’t work the same way as English verbs. You need to choose the most idiomatic or natural-sounding translation based on the context.

9491.belief: Spanish is the official language only in Spain.
9491.statement: Spanish is the official language only in Spain.
9491.correction: Spanish is the official language in 21 countries across 3 different continents.

889.belief: [ce], [ci] and [z] always sound like the 'th' in 'think' in Spain, the Canary Islands and Latin America.
889.statement: [ce], [ci] and [z] always sound like the 'th' in 'think' in Spain, the Canary Islands and Latin America.
889.correction: [ce], [ci] and [z] sound like the 'th' in 'think' in most of Spain, and 's' in Latin America and the Canary Islands.

5362.belief: All past participles in Spanish end in -ado (-ar verbs) or -ido (-er/-ir verbs).
5362.statement: All past participles in Spanish end in -ado (-ar verbs) or -ido (-er/-ir verbs).
5362.correction: Although most Spanish past participles do follow these regular patterns, some verbs have irregular past participles which just need to be learnt, e.g. 'escrito' ('written'), 'visto' ('seen'), 'hecho' ('done'), 'dicho' ('said').

10625.belief: We always use 'para que' + subjunctive to express intentions in Spanish.
10625.statement: We always use 'para que' + subjunctive to express intentions in Spanish.
10625.correction: We only use 'para que' + subjunctive to express intentions when the subject of the 2nd verb in the sentence is different from the first. Where the subject is the same in the whole sentence, express intentions with 'para' + infinitive.

10406.belief: Translating word-for-word is an effective strategy when tackling translation tasks.
10406.statement: Translating word-for-word is an effective strategy when tackling translation tasks.
10406.correction: Effective translation requires more than direct word-for-word substitution. Applying knowledge of grammar and using proofing strategies, such as the VAN check (Verbs, Adjectives, Nouns), can significantly improve accuracy.

10408.belief: The only translation of 'fue' is 'she, he, it was'.
10408.statement: The only translation of 'fue' is 'she, he, it was'.
10408.correction: 'Fue' can mean 'she, he, it was' or 'she, he, it went' depending on the context. The verbs 'ser' and 'ir' are identical in the preterite tense.

10385.belief: I can translate 'the best thing was' word-for-word in Spanish.
10385.statement: I can translate 'the best thing was' word-for-word in Spanish.
10385.correction: In Spanish, we use the structure 'lo' + adjective, so we do not include the word 'thing', e.g. 'lo mejor fue el final' translates into English as 'the best thing was the ending'.

10585.belief: I can only use BORDER for short pieces of writing.
10585.statement: I can only use BORDER for short pieces of writing.
10585.correction: BORDER is also a very useful strategy for extended pieces of writing. Simply apply it to each paragraph separately. This will help you respond clearly and completely to each bullet point.

10825.belief: Verbs of emotion like 'gustar', 'encantar', 'dar', 'molestar', etc. are always followed by the infinitive.
10825.statement: Verbs of emotion like 'gustar', 'encantar', 'dar', 'molestar', etc. are always followed by the infinitive.
10825.correction: Use a verb of emotion + infinitive to react to your own actions. Use a verb of emotion + 'que' + subjunctive to react to someone else’s. Both forms often talk about emotions, but the change of subject triggers the use of subjunctive.

2313.belief: When developing a conversation about future travel plans, it is important to consistently use the future time frame in answers.
2313.statement: When developing a conversation about future travel plans, it is important to consistently use the future time frame in answers.
2313.correction: Whilst it is important to be able to refer to the future confidently, it is also helpful to add in different time frames to give more detail as well as opinions.

4273.belief: As long as I say something about the topic, it doesn't matter what tense I use.
4273.statement: As long as I say something about the topic, it doesn't matter what tense I use.
4273.correction: You must respond to the bullet point using the correct tense (e.g. past, present, future) to fully address it. Other tenses can add depth, but they don't replace the need to respond directly in the specified tense.

4904.belief: I always need to use subject pronouns in Spanish to show who is doing an action.
4904.statement: I always need to use subject pronouns in Spanish to show who is doing an action.
4904.correction: It is not usually necessary to use subject pronouns in Spanish to show who is doing an action. The subject of an action is usually shown by the verb ending.

8870.belief: I can rely on strategies like prediction to successfully complete listening comprehension questions.
8870.statement: I can rely on strategies like prediction to successfully complete listening comprehension questions.
8870.correction: Strategies like prediction can be useful, but the most important way to successfully answer listening comprehension questions is by having a broad vocabulary.

4688.belief: Modal verbs like 'quiero' can be followed with a 1st person singular verb like 'compro'.
4688.statement: Modal verbs like 'quiero' can be followed with a 1st person singular verb like 'compro'.
4688.correction: Modal verbs like 'quiero' must be followed with an infinitive verb like 'comprar'. For example, 'I want to buy' in Spanish is 'quiero comprar'.

9642.belief: The stress in 'me gustaría' falls on the second syllable 'ta'.
9642.statement: The stress in 'me gustaría' falls on the second syllable 'ta'.
9642.correction: The stress in 'me gustaría' falls on the 'í'. We can tell this because it has an accent.

10414.belief: The only translation of 'I visited' in Spanish is 'visité'.
10414.statement: The only translation of 'I visited' in Spanish is 'visité'.
10414.correction: In Spanish, 'visité' means 'I visited' for a single, completed action in the past. You could also, however, use 'visitaba' to mean 'I visited' for an action that happened repeatedly over a period of time.

4751.belief: There is not much I can do to prepare for Spanish reading exams.
4751.statement: There is not much I can do to prepare for Spanish reading exams.
4751.correction: You can prepare for Spanish reading exams by revising vocabulary to make sure you can understand as many words as possible.

5778.correction: As the stem of 'leer' ends in a vowel, it has a spelling change in the present participle, forming 'leyendo'. This is the same with other verbs with a stem ending in a vowel e.g. 'constuyendo' from the verb 'construir'.

9476.belief: In Spanish, the auxiliary verb 'he' sounds like the English 'he'.
9476.statement: In Spanish, the auxiliary verb 'he' sounds like the English 'he'.
9476.correction: In Spanish, the auxiliary verb 'he' sounds different to the English 'he'. It has a silent 'h' and 'e' is pronounced as in 'elefante'.

9472.belief: All Spanish adjectives have masculine and feminine forms.
9472.statement: All Spanish adjectives have masculine and feminine forms.
9472.correction: Many Spanish adjectives have masculine and feminine forms, but some are invariable. Adjectives ending in -e (e.g. 'grave') and in consonants like -l, -r and -n (e.g. 'dificil', 'mejor', 'marrón') are invariable.

3945.belief: I should keep my answers short in a conversation and avoid extending my sentences.
3945.statement: I should keep my answers short in a conversation and avoid extending my sentences.
3945.correction: In a conversation, you should extend and develop your sentences to include at least three verb clauses.

10400.correction: When 'have' means 'to possess something' e.g. 'I have a car', use 'tengo' - 'tengo un coche'. When 'have' is part of the perfect tense, to say you have done something, use the verb 'haber' e.g. 'I have played' - 'he jugado'.

10946.belief: The only way to mean 'you (singular)' in Spanish is 'tú'.
10946.statement: The only way to mean 'you (singular)' in Spanish is 'tú'.
10946.correction: There are two ways to mean 'you (singular)' in Spanish. Use 'tú' to mean 'you' in an informal context, and 'usted' to mean 'you' in a formal context.

3944.belief: I should keep my answers to the follow-up questions after the photo description short without extra detail.
3944.statement: I should keep my answers to the follow-up questions after the photo description short without extra detail.
3944.correction: You need to try and develop your answers to the follow-up questions with at least 3 verb clauses.

4750.belief: There is not much I can do to prepare for the listening exam.
4750.statement: There is not much I can do to prepare for the listening exam.
4750.correction: You can prepare for the listening exam by revising vocabulary and being ready to listen out for synoynms and distractors.

9088.belief: To say 'when I am older I will work in a hospital', say 'cuando soy mayor trabajaré en un hospital'.
9088.statement: To say 'when I am older I will work in a hospital', say 'cuando soy mayor trabajaré en un hospital'.
9088.correction: To say 'when I am older I will work in a hospital', say 'cuando sea mayor trabajaré en un hospital'. After 'cuando', use the subjunctive to talk about an event that hasn't yet happened.

8868.belief: I can rely on strategies like listening out for synonyms and distractors to do well in my listening exam.
8868.statement: I can rely on strategies like listening out for synonyms and distractors to do well in my listening exam.
8868.correction: Strategies like listening out for synonyms and distractors are useful for listening exams, but the most important thing is to have a broad vocabulary.

10404.belief: When translating from Spanish to English, I should translate each word in the order it appears in the Spanish sentence.
10404.statement: When translating from Spanish to English, I should translate each word in the order it appears in the Spanish sentence.
10404.correction: When translating from Spanish to English, make sure your translations sound natural in English. This may mean you need to change the word order from the original Spanish sentence.

10389.belief: I should translate each English word individually when translating into Spanish.
10389.statement: I should translate each English word individually when translating into Spanish.
10389.correction: It is important to read the whole sentence first and translate chunks of language rather than each individual word.

3303.belief: I should give long, developed answers to role-play prompts.
3303.statement: I should give long, developed answers to role-play prompts.
3303.correction: It is not necessary to give long, developed answers to role-play prompts. It is best to respond using a short phrase or sentence.

10618.belief: I can use my knowledge of sound-symbol correspondences (SSCs) to successfully complete a read-aloud task.
10618.statement: I can use my knowledge of sound-symbol correspondences (SSCs) to successfully complete a read-aloud task.
10618.correction: Simply re-reading without purpose doesn't necessarily lead to better comprehension. Strategies such as reading through the text and questions, using each question to find the relevant part of the text, avoiding distractors, etc., are more effective.
